name: Abhayagiri fraternity (Abhayagiri-vāsins)

tradition.text: founded when King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya built the Abhayagiri monastery (1st c. BCE, per the Mahāvaṃsa); absorbed in the 12th-c. unification

scholarly.text: 1st c. BCE – 12th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Mahāvihāra chronicles) to have accepted the Vetulya texts and to have had contacts with Mahāyāna teachers.
The Vimuttimagga is associated with this fraternity by some scholars (a scholarly hypothesis, not a tradition's claim).
summary: The rival Sri Lankan fraternity to the Mahāvihāra, known mainly through Mahāvihāra chronicles and foreign reports; its own literature is largely lost, which is why the Mahāvihāra commentaries became the Theravāda norm.
notes: Known largely through the reports of its rivals (Mahāvaṃsa, Cūḷavaṃsa) — treat characterizations as reported by opponents. Created by U37.

name: Adhyātma movement (Adhyātma-mata)
alt_names: Banārasī-mata / Vāṇārasīya-mata (name used by its Śvetāmbara critics)

scholarly.text: from c. 1620s (Banārsīdās's circle in Agra) into the 18th c. (Jaipur, Ṭoḍarmal)

transmissions_received.what: Kundakunda's Samayasāra read through Amṛtacandra's Ātmakhyāti and its kalaśa verses, with Pāṇḍe Rājamalla's vernacular commentary; later the Gommaṭasāra's guṇasthāna teaching
transmissions_received.evidence: Banārsīdās's own account in the Ardhakathānaka and the preface of the Samayasāra Nāṭaka (recalled)

transmissions_given.what: the anti-bhaṭṭāraka, study-centred ethos and the Hindi Adhyātma literature (tradition's account; the scholarly account also links the two)
the niścaya-centred reading of the Samayasāra and the vernacular Adhyātma literature (Samayasāra Nāṭaka, Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka), revived in the 20th c. (recent)

distinctive_positions: The soul's own pure nature, known by the ultimate standpoint (niścaya-naya) and by direct self-experience (anubhava), is the heart of the Jina's teaching; ritual and outer conduct belong to the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra).
Lay study circles (śailī) read the Samayasāra and its commentaries in Hindi/Braj rather than relying on monks or bhaṭṭārakas.

Critique of ritual formalism, of the authority of the Digambara bhaṭṭārakas and (by its Śvetāmbara-born members) of Śvetāmbara monastic claims; its critics say it rejected image worship with flowers and similar rites.

After an early one-sided emphasis on niścaya (described by Banārsīdās himself as a fall into disregard of conduct), the mature position holds both standpoints together, with the fourteen guṇasthānas as the map of progress (Samayasāra Nāṭaka's closing chapter).
summary: A seventeenth-century lay mystical movement of north-Indian Jains centred on Banārsīdās of Agra (1587–c. 1643). Its members, many of them Śvetāmbara-born merchants, studied the Digambara Kundakunda's Samayasāra with Amṛtacandra's commentary in vernacular circles and taught the priority of the soul's own knowing nature over ritual. The tradition's account links it to the Digambara Terāpantha reform and to Ṭoḍarmal of Jaipur; the scholarly account sees the same line of descent but dates the Terāpantha's formal emergence to the later 17th–18th c. The broader Śvetāmbara 'adhyātma' writing of Ānandaghana, Yaśovijaya and Devacandra is a parallel current, not part of this circle (Yaśovijaya criticised it).
notes: Owned by U35. Membership of Dyānatrāy, Bhūdhardās and Daulatrām in the movement is by affinity of their Hindi Adhyātma writing (moderate/low confidence); Ṭoḍarmal is normally counted in the Digambara Terāpantha.

name: Advaita Vedānta

tradition.text: Guru-paramparā from Nārāyaṇa through Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, Parāśara, Vyāsa and Śuka to Gauḍapāda, Govinda and Śaṅkara; Śaṅkara commonly dated 788–820 CE, and 509–477 BCE in the Kāñcī and Dvārakā maṭha reckonings

scholarly.text: Gauḍapāda c. 6th c. CE; Śaṅkara c. 700–750 CE (Hacker, Nakamura; others to c. 800); continuous commentarial tradition to the present

transmissions_received.what: the mahāvākyas and the Upaniṣadic teaching of the self
transmissions_received.evidence: all Advaita works are exegeses of the Upaniṣads

transmissions_received.what: hermeneutics (six marks of purport), theory of verbal knowledge, and the six means of knowledge in empirical matters
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāntasāra's six liṅgas; Vedāntaparibhāṣā's pramāṇa chapters

transmissions_received.what: the eight limbs as auxiliaries of nirvikalpa samādhi; vocabulary of samādhi
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāntasāra; Aparokṣānubhūti's reinterpreted limbs; BSBh 2.1.3 accepts Yoga's practices while rejecting its dualism

transmissions_received.what: dialectical and (later) Navya-Nyāya technique
transmissions_received.evidence: Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya, Tattvapradīpikā, Advaitasiddhi

transmissions_received.what: vocabulary and dialectic of non-origination in Gauḍapāda's fourth prakaraṇa (scholarly hypothesis; the tradition denies dependence, cf. GK 4.99)
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis; see coverage C (owned by U49)

transmissions_given.what: the Daśanāmī sannyāsa order and the four āmnāya maṭhas founded, in the tradition's account, by Śaṅkara
Advaita doctrine and Daśanāmī (Purī) sannyāsa lineage (recent)
Advaita doctrine and Daśanāmī (Sarasvatī) sannyāsa (recent)
the Advaita prakaraṇa texts Ramaṇa rendered into Tamil (Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka, Ātmabodha) (recent)

distinctive_positions: Brahman alone is real (satya); the world is not ultimately real (mithyā); the individual self is not other than Brahman (Brahmajñānāvalīmālā 20; VC 20).
Bondage is superimposition (adhyāsa) of the not-self on the self and vice versa, which is called ignorance (avidyā) (BSBh introduction).
The world is an apparent transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, not a real transformation (pariṇāma).
Three levels of reality: ultimate (pāramārthika), empirical (vyāvahārika), illusory (prātibhāsika).
Liberation is not produced; it is the self's own nature revealed by knowledge alone; action cannot remove ignorance (Ātmabodha 3).
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is possible; the body continues until the karma that began it (prārabdha) is exhausted (BS 4.1.15, 4.1.19).
The qualified seeker (with the four qualifications) hears (śravaṇa), reflects (manana) and contemplates (nididhyāsana) the Upaniṣadic teaching.
Saguṇa Brahman (Īśvara) is real at the empirical level and the proper object of worship; nirguṇa Brahman is the ultimate.
Scripture teaches by provisional superimposition and subsequent retraction (adhyāropa-apavāda).
Post-Śaṅkara Advaita divides into the Vārttika (Sureśvara), Bhāmatī (Vācaspati) and Vivaraṇa (Prakāśātman) lines over the locus of ignorance and how the one appears as many.
summary: The Vedānta school of strict non-dualism: Brahman, pure consciousness without a second, is the self of all; the world of plurality is an appearance of Brahman through māyā/avidyā, real for empirical purposes but sublated by knowledge. Rooted in Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkya Kārikā and systematized by Śaṅkara's commentaries on the prasthāna-traya, it developed through Maṇḍana, Sureśvara, Padmapāda, Vācaspati and Prakāśātman into the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa lines, a dialectical literature (Śrīharṣa, Citsukha, Madhusūdana), popular manuals (Pañcadaśī, Vedāntasāra, Vedāntaparibhāṣā) and a living monastic order (Daśanāmī).

name: Aghora (Aghor panth; Aghorī and Aughaṛ ascetics)
regions: Varanasi (Kīnārām Sthal / Krīm Kuṇḍ at Śivālā; Parāo)

tradition.text: Kīnārām, born Vikrama 1658 (1601 CE) at Rāmgaṛh near Varanasi, lived to 1771 CE; Dattātreya is the ādiguru

scholarly.text: the Kīnārāmī lineage is attested from the 18th c.; any continuity with the medieval Kāpālikas is a scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Dattātreya as ādiguru; Girnar as the place of Kīnārām's vision
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition's account (Kīnārām hagiography).

transmissions_received.what: Kīnārām's first (Vaiṣṇava) initiation under Śivarām and the Rāma-devotional language of his works (Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl)
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition's account; titles of Kīnārām's works.

transmissions_received.what: cremation-ground practice, skull bowl, transgression of purity rules
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis; not the tradition's own account.

transmissions_given.what: the Aghora lineage re-shaped toward social service (1961 onward)

distinctive_positions: Non-discrimination (abheda): nothing is to be shunned as impure; the aghora (the 'not-terrible') Śiva is present in what is feared and loathed.
Freedom from the eight fetters — disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste (the Kaula list, Kulārṇava 13.90) — is the mark of the free one.
The cremation ground (śmaśāna) is the place of practice; the skull bowl (khappar) is carried.
The guru is Śiva; the lineage descends from Dattātreya through Kālūrām and Kīnārām.
The ultimate is named also as Rām / nirguṇa (Kīnārām's works); the state sought is sahaja and unmanī.
Recent teachers (Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām) direct Aghora toward service of the sick and outcaste and rejection of caste distinctions.
summary: Aghora is the lineage of Śaiva ascetics centred on Bābā Kīnārām's seat at Krīm Kuṇḍ in Varanasi, who trace their teaching to Dattātreya through Bābā Kālūrām. Its ascetics practise in the cremation ground and cultivate non-discrimination (abheda), overcoming disgust, fear and the other fetters. Kīnārām's Hindi works (Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī) join this with devotion to Rām as the attributeless; in the twentieth century Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh and turned the lineage toward service. Practice details are secret and only summarised here.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the tradition's own rejection of Vedic ritual authority (see dsp:natha-varna-and-ritual (Aghora shares the Nāth position)) nor its overlap with the Buddhist Mahāsiddhas (C; brw:natha-mahasiddha). Tradition's dates for Kīnārām are recorded as the tradition gives them; they are not independently confirmed.

name: Aitihāsikas (the legend-school of Vedic interpretation)
distinctive_positions: Vedic figures are persons of old narratives: Vṛtra is an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ (Nirukta 2.16); the Aśvins are two pious kings (Nirukta 12.1); Yama and Yamī are the twins born to Saraṇyū (Nirukta 12.10).
summary: Interpreters named in Yāska's Nirukta who read the hymns through old stories (itihāsa); known only from Yāska's reports.
notes: Known only through the Nirukta, which reports their views alongside the Nairuktas' own.

checks.note: All three reports were found in the Nirukta. At 2.16: 'tvāṣṭro 'sura ity aitihāsikāḥ'. At 12.1: 'rājānau puṇyakṛtāv ity aitihāsikāḥ'. At 12.10: 'yamaṃ ca yamī ca ity aitihāsikāḥ … tvāṣṭrī saraṇyūr vivasvata ādityād yamau mithunau janayāṃcakāra'. The school is known only through Yāska, as the entry says.

name: Ājīvika
alt_names: Terāsiya / Trairāśika (identification by Jain commentators, disputed)
regions: later South India (Tamil and Karnataka country)

tradition.text: Gosāla, in the Jain account, claims to be the 24th and last tīrthaṅkara of this descending age; Buddhist texts name Nanda Vaccha and Kisa Saṅkicca as earlier leaders.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra) to the last South Indian references in inscriptions of c. 13th–14th c. CE; cave donations by Aśoka and Daśaratha in the 3rd c. BCE.

transmissions_received.what: the eightfold Mahānimitta (prognostication) that the six disācaras drew from the Pūrvas, taught to Gosāla
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhagavatī Sūtra 15 (Jain account — reported by an opponent)

transmissions_received.what: the doctrine of seven unmade bodies reported of Pakudha Kaccāyana appears merged with Ājīvika niyati in Ja 545 and MN 76
transmissions_received.evidence: textual parallel

distinctive_positions: (As reported) Niyati: all beings are without control, power or energy; they are 'transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature' (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā) and experience pleasure and pain in six classes (DN 2).

(As reported) Purification through saṃsāra (saṃsāra-suddhi): fool and wise alike, after transmigrating through 8,400,000 great aeons, make an end of suffering, like a ball of string that unwinds to its end; no vow or austerity ripens unripe karma (DN 2).
(As reported) Six classes of birth (abhijāti) from black to supremely white, the supreme white being the three Ājīvika leaders (AN 6.57).
(As reported) There is no exertion, action, strength, energy or human effort; all things are fixed (Uvāsagadasāo 7).
(Jain account) Reanimation (pauṭṭa-parihāra): a soul may enter successive bodies; Gosāla claimed to be the seventh such re-entry.
(Jain account) Mastery of the eightfold Mahānimitta and of the fiery power (tejoleśyā).
(Tamil account) Five principles — life (uyir) and four kinds of indestructible atoms — and six births ending in release in the supreme white birth (Maṇimēkalai 27).
Naked austerities (acelaka) and severe fasting rules (MN 36; Sthānāṅga 4).
summary: The Ājīvikas were a naked ascetic order of Gosāla Maṅkhaliputta and his predecessors. No Ājīvika text survives; the doctrine is known only through hostile Buddhist, Jain and Tamil sources, which report a doctrine of total determinism (niyati) in which every being reaches the end of suffering after a fixed round of rebirths. The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra (book 15) tells Gosāla's life, quarrel with Mahāvīra and death; the Aśokan and Daśaratha cave inscriptions record royal donations; the Tamil Maṇimēkalai and Nīlakēci attest a later South Indian community that has since disappeared.
notes: Everything doctrinal is reported_by_opponent. Scholarly metadata: Aśoka's Barābar caves (12th and 19th regnal years) and Daśaratha's Nāgārjunī caves were dedicated to the Ājīvikas; Pillar Edict 7 names them among the orders supervised by the dhamma-mahāmātras; Tamil inscriptions record a tax on Ājīvikas (ācīvakak-kācu) into the Cōḻa period (exact latest date not recalled — gap).

name: Ajñāna (the sceptics)

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (Sañjaya, contemporary of the Buddha); the Jain catalogue of 67 ajñānika views is given in the canonical commentaries (Niryukti, Śīlāṅka, 9th c.).

transmissions_given.what: Sāriputta, Moggallāna and 250 of Sañjaya's wanderers (Vinaya Mv 1.23–24)

distinctive_positions: (As reported) On whether there is another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds, or the Tathāgata after death, in each of the four forms, Sañjaya refuses every alternative: 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so' (DN 2).
(As reported) Four grounds of such evasion: fear of false speech, fear of grasping, fear of cross-examination, and dullness (DN 1).
(Jain report) Ignorance is better (ajñānam eva śreyaḥ): 'who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it?'; 67 varieties (Śīlāṅka).
summary: The Ajñānikas refused to affirm or deny any proposition about what lies beyond experience. The Pali texts call them 'eel-wrigglers' (amarāvikkhepika) and give Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta's formula as the type; the Jain canon counts ajñāna as one of the four 'assemblies' (samavasaraṇa) of rival doctrines, with 67 sub-kinds. No text of the school survives; all is reported by opponents.

name: Alaṅkāraśāstra and Nāṭyaśāstra (poetics, dramaturgy and the theory of rasa)

tradition.text: drama (nāṭya) was made by Brahmā as a fifth Veda at the gods' request and taught to Bharata (NŚ 1.11–17)

scholarly.text: Nāṭyaśāstra compiled c. 200 BCE–400 CE; Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin c. 7th c.; Ānandavardhana c. 850; Abhinavagupta c. 975–1025; Jagannātha 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Nāṭyaveda drawn from the four Vedas: recitation from the Ṛg, song from the Sāman, gesture from the Yajus, rasas from the Atharva (NŚ 1.17)
transmissions_received.evidence: tea:natyasastra:1.17

transmissions_received.what: the term and model of dhvani, and pratibhā
transmissions_received.evidence: Dhvanyāloka 1.13 vṛtti credits the grammarians (reference from memory)

transmissions_received.what: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's 'bhāvanā' (bhāvakatva) modelled on Mīmāṃsā's word-power of bringing-about
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly reading of the reports in the Abhinavabhāratī

transmissions_received.what: Śaṅkuka's theory of rasa as inference
transmissions_received.evidence: Abhinavabhāratī on NŚ 6

transmissions_received.what: Abhinavagupta's reading of rasa as relish of consciousness itself (camatkāra, viśrānti)
transmissions_received.evidence: Abhinavabhāratī; Locana

transmissions_given.what: the rasa apparatus (sthāyibhāva, vibhāva, anubhāva, vyabhicārin, sāttvika) turned into bhakti-rasa by Rūpa Gosvāmī
rasa as the aim of music and the assignment of notes and rāgas to rasas (ŚR; Nāṭyaśāstra 29)
Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Bhaktirasāyana treating devotion as a rasa

distinctive_positions: Drama is a fifth Veda made for all classes, since the Vedas may not be heard by śūdras (NŚ 1.12); it imitates the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.107) and gives rest to the afflicted (NŚ 1.114).
Rasa arises from the union of determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva) and transient states (vyabhicāribhāva) (the rasa-sūtra, NŚ 6).
There are eight rasas in drama (NŚ 6.15); many later authorities add śānta as the ninth, with dispassion, calm or knowledge of reality as its stable emotion.
Rasa is relished (āsvādyate) as food flavoured by many ingredients is tasted by the discerning (NŚ 6.31–33).
Suggestion (dhvani) is the soul of poetry (Dhvanyāloka 1.1), and rasa is known only by suggestion.
Aesthetic relish is 'the twin brother of tasting Brahman' (brahmāsvāda-sahodara, SD 3.2), free of contact with other objects — akin to, but not identical with, realization.
For Abhinavagupta, rasa is the relish of one's own consciousness freed from personal limitation through generalization (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa); it is blocked by seven obstacles (vighna).
Poetry yields fame, wealth, knowledge of conduct, removal of evil, immediate supreme bliss and counsel like that of a beloved (KP 1.2).
summary: The science of drama and poetry from Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra to Jagannātha. Its central doctrine is rasa: the relish of an emotion, universalized through the art-work, in the heart of the sensitive spectator (sahṛdaya). The debate on how rasa arises (Lollaṭa, Śaṅkuka, Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka, Abhinavagupta), Ānandavardhana's theory of suggestion, and the recognition of śānta ('peace') as a rasa akin to liberation made poetics a theory of aesthetic experience that later fed devotional theology (bhakti-rasa).

name: Alīkākāravāda (False-Aspect Yogācāra)
distinctive_positions: The images appearing in cognition are false (alīka), superimposed by beginningless imprints; only the luminous, image-free cognition is real.
In meditation and at buddhahood cognition is without any image.
summary: A late Indian Yogācāra position (and Tibetan doxographic class) holding that the appearing aspects of cognition are unreal and only pure self-luminous awareness is real; defended above all by Ratnākaraśānti.
notes: As with lin:satyakaravada, the classification is largely Tibetan doxographic; Ratnākaraśānti presents his view as the meaning of Madhyamaka too, and later Tibetan authors (Jonang) read the Maitreya texts in a related way.

name: The Āḻvārs (Tamil Vaiṣṇava saint-poets) and their hymn tradition
regions: Vaṭa nāṭu (Tiruvēṅkaṭam and the northern sites sung)

tradition.text: The hagiographies place the first three Āḻvārs at the close of the Dvāpara age and the rest in the first centuries of the Kali age (i.e. several thousand years BCE on the Kali-yuga reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 6th–9th c. CE (the first Āḻvārs c. 6th–7th c.; Tirumaṅkai c. 8th c. under the Pallava Nandivarman II; Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ c. 9th c.; Nammāḻvār c. 9th c.)

transmissions_received.what: the Kṛṣṇa and Rāma stories and the Lord's avatāras, sung in Tamil
transmissions_received.evidence: allusions throughout the Prabandham (Kṛṣṇa's childhood, the Bhārata war, Rāma's exile)

transmissions_received.what: Viṣṇu's cosmic deeds and avatāra narratives (Trivikrama, Varāha, Narasiṃha, the churning, the Lord on the serpent in the milk ocean)
transmissions_received.evidence: allusions throughout the Prabandham; the direction relative to the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is disputed (brw:alvar-to-puranic-dravida-devotees)

transmissions_given.what: the four thousand hymns as the Tamil Veda (ubhaya-vedānta); the theology of surrender at the Lord's feet with Śrī as mediator; temple-centred devotion at the divya-deśas; recitation in temple and home
the Prabandham and its Maṇipravāḷa commentaries as primary scripture; Madhurakavi's devotion to the teacher as the model of ācārya-niṣṭhā
the Prabandham as Tamil Veda, read together with the Sanskrit Vedānta (Deśika's Dramiḍopaniṣat-tātparya-ratnāvalī, Munivāhanabhoga)

distinctive_positions: The Lord is Tirumāl/Nārāyaṇa with Śrī (Tiru), supreme beyond all (paratva) and yet easy of access to those who love him (saulabhya: 'eḷiyavaṉ', TVM 1.3.1).
The Lord is fully present in the temple image (arcā) at the sites the Āḻvārs sang (the 108 divya-deśas); devotion is temple-centred and pilgrim.
Knowledge-and-love (matinalam) is itself the Lord's gift, not the soul's achievement ('he graciously gave me knowledge-and-love free of delusion', TVM 1.1.1).
Surrender at the Lord's feet, with Śrī as the one who never leaves his chest, is the refuge of those who have nothing (TVM 6.10.10; Kulaśekhara's Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 5.1).
The soul's nature is servitude (aṭimai) to the Lord at all times (TVM 3.3.1); the Lord's devotees, of whatever birth, are one's masters (TVM 3.7.9; Tirumālai; Amalaṉātipirāṉ 1).
Love is sung in the voices of Tamil akam poetry: the poet becomes the girl in love (Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī, Parakāla-nāyakī), the mother, the friend; the Lord is sought as lover, child, master and friend.
The divine name, above all 'Nārāyaṇa', is the refuge found after long searching (Tirumaṅkai, Periya Tirumoḻi 1.1).
The Tamil hymns are Veda: Nammāḻvār's four works answer to the four Vedas and Tirumaṅkai's six to the six aṅgas (the tradition's account).

Caste and learning do not measure a devotee: the tradition's twelve include a king, brāhmaṇas, a Vellāḷa (Nammāḻvār), a bard of a community held low (Tiruppāṇ), a Kaḷḷar chieftain (Tirumaṅkai) and a woman (Āṇṭāḷ).
summary: The Āḻvārs — twelve in the tradition's standard list — are the Tamil saint-poets of Viṣṇu whose some four thousand verses, gathered by Nāthamuni as the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, became the Tamil Veda of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. Their hymns celebrate Tirumāl with Śrī in his temple images, teach surrender, service and the saving name, and voice love for God through the conventions of Tamil love poetry. Placed here also, as Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional literature of the same milieu, are the precursor Paripāṭal hymns to Tirumāl and Kampaṉ's Rāmāyaṇa (neither is an Āḻvār work).
notes: Status 'absorbed': the Āḻvārs were not an order; their hymns live on inside Śrīvaiṣṇava temple and home worship (lin:visistadvaita, lin:vadakalai, lin:tenkalai). Some lists count ten Āḻvārs, omitting Āṇṭāḷ (held to be Bhūdevī herself) and Madhurakavi (who sang only of Nammāḻvār).

name: Añcala Gaccha (Vidhipakṣa)

scholarly.text: 12th c. CE (c. 1156 CE is often given; low confidence)

distinctive_positions: uses the hem (añcala) of the garment instead of the mouth-cloth when laymen perform rites (hence the name, per the usual explanation)
'Vidhipakṣa' — the party of the correct rite; strongest in Kacch
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha founded in the 12th c. by Āryarakṣitasūri as a ritual reform, concentrated in Kacch and among Kacchī Jains.

name: Andhakas (as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary)
alt_names: the Andhra schools: Pubbaseliya, Aparaseliya, Rājagiriya, Siddhatthika (Pali commentary)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold, among others, that an arahant can be defiled by emissions induced by deities, can have ignorance and doubt, and can be instructed by others.
Reported to hold that the four truths are penetrated gradually.
The Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes many of the refuted views to the Andhakas (low confidence on specific attributions).
summary: A group of Mahāsāṅghika-derived schools of the Andhra region to which the Kathāvatthu commentary attributes many of the views refuted in the Kathāvatthu.
notes: Known here only through the Theravāda commentary (reported by an opponent). Created by U37 to name the opponents of Kathāvatthu debates; U38 owns lin:mahasanghika.
alt_summary: The Pali commentarial name for the Mahāsāṃghika-derived schools of Andhra.

name: Aparaśaila
alt_names: Xishan zhu bu 西山住部
distinctive_positions: Shares the Pubbaseliya positions in the Kathāvatthu commentary (Kv 2.1–2.4).
summary: An Andhra branch of the Mahāsāṃghika, named with the Pūrvaśailas.

name: Ārādhya Śaiva (Andhra)

scholarly.text: from the 12th c. (Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya)

distinctive_positions: Wear the liṅga and worship Śiva exclusively while retaining the sacred thread and Vedic rites.
Look to Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya, contemporary of Basava, as their founding teacher.
summary: A Telugu-speaking Vīraśaiva group, traditionally brāhmaṇa, tracing itself to Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya; it combines liṅga-wearing and exclusive Śiva devotion with retention of Vedic rites and the sacred thread.
notes: Low confidence on current practice details; recorded as a side in dsp:virasaiva-veda-agama-authority.

name: Arthaśāstra (the science of statecraft and wealth)
distinctive_positions: Artha is foremost among the three aims, since dharma and kāma are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).

The four sciences are investigation (ānvīkṣikī — Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics (vārttā) and governance (daṇḍanīti); investigation is 'the lamp of all sciences' (Arthaśāstra 1.2.1–12).
summary: The śāstra of the second aim of life (artha): kingship, administration, law, diplomacy and wealth, represented by Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, which cites earlier schools (Mānavas, Bārhaspatyas, Auśanasas and others). Recorded here for its teaching on the aims of life and the order of the sciences.
notes: New lineage id (not in the registry) created by U02 for the puruṣārtha scope; the orchestrator may reassign.

checks.note: Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7 was found: 'artha eva pradhāna iti kauṭilyaḥ | arthamūlau hi dharmakāmāv iti'. Arthaśāstra 1.2.1–12 was found, with the four vidyās (1.2.1, 1.2.8) and ānvīkṣikī as Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Lokāyata (1.2.10). 'pradīpaḥ sarvavidyānām' closes the section; in the GRETIL file it is joined into 1.2.11, which is Kangle's 1.2.11–12. The earlier schools (Mānavas, Bārhaspatyas, Auśanasas) are cited at 1.2.2–7. The id is a new, non-registry lineage created by the unit, so its placement is for the orchestrator.

name: Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja

tradition.text: founded by Nāgārjuna and his disciples Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi and Candrakīrti — identified with the Madhyamaka masters

scholarly.text: the tantric authors c. 9th–10th c., distinct from the Madhyamaka authors of the 2nd–7th c.

transmissions_given.what: the Ārya Guhyasamāja exegesis (Tsongkhapa's Rim lnga gsal sgron)
Marpa's Guhyasamāja from Nāropa

distinctive_positions: The completion stage is five (or six) stages: speech isolation (vajra recitation), mind isolation, self-consecration (illusory body), clear light (abhisambodhi) and union (yuganaddha) (Pañcakrama).
The four empties (śūnya, atiśūnya, mahāśūnya, sarvaśūnya) arise as winds dissolve; the fourth is clear light (Pañcakrama 2.4–5).
The illusory body arisen from wind-and-mind is the conventional truth, clear light the ultimate; their union is buddhahood (Pañcakrama 3.13, 5.11).
The root tantra is coded and must be read through the explanatory tantras (Vajramālā, Sandhivyākaraṇa, Caturdevīparipṛcchā) and the six alternatives (Pradīpoddyotana).
summary: The exegetical school of the Guhyasamāja tantra associated with the tantric Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi and Candrakīrti, which systematized the completion stage in five stages leading through the four empties to clear light, illusory body and union; its Akṣobhya-centred 32-deity maṇḍala was taken into Tibet (Marpa, Gö Khukpa Lhetse) and made central by Tsongkhapa.

name: Ārya Samāj

scholarly.text: founded 1875 CE

distinctive_positions: Only the four Saṃhitās are revealed (the Brāhmaṇas, Purāṇas and later texts are human works to be accepted only where they agree with them).
The Vedas teach one formless God; Agni, Indra and the other names denote that one God.
The Vedas contain no history of persons or places; their knowledge (and the sacred thread and Vedic study) is open to all, women and men of every birth.
Image worship and birth-based caste are rejected; the daily fire offering (havana/agnihotra) and Vedic study are kept.
summary: A Vedic-revival movement founded by Dayānanda Sarasvatī that reads the Saṃhitās as the sole revelation of one God; recorded here only for its reading of the Saṃhitās (recent, post-1800).
notes: Not in the registry; created by U01 because its founder's commentary is a major reading of the Saṃhitās. Positions recalled from memory (moderate). Flag for inclusion/exclusion (section H logic).

checks.note: Confirmed: founded by Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Bombay, 10 April 1875; strongest in Panjab/North India and the diaspora. (Inclusion outside the registry is a policy question for the orchestrator, not a factual one.)

name: Atimārga

tradition.text: from Śiva's descent as Lakulin, the last of his 28 yoga-teacher incarnations (Liṅga P. 1.24; Kūrma P. 1.51)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (Lakulīśa) to c. 14th c. CE (last Kālāmukha and Pāśupata records); the name 'Atimārga' is used by Śaiva tantras from c. 6th–7th c.

transmissions_given.what: technical vocabulary (pati, paśu, pāśa), the five brahma-mantras, ash observances; the Mantramārga scriptures describe and rank the Atimārga below themselves
Kālāmukha temples and monasteries in Karnataka (disputed; see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva)

distinctive_positions: The Śaiva scriptures divide Śaiva revelation into the Atimārga and the Mantramārga; the Niśvāsamukha counts the Atimārga as the fourth of five 'streams' (laukika, vaidika, ādhyātmika, atimārga, mantra).
The Atimārga observances are for initiated ascetics and aim at liberation (duḥkhānta, the end of suffering); in the Pāśupata case initiation is restricted to brahmin men.
Its observances are defined as beyond the āśramas (atyāśrama: the Pāśupata) or beyond the world (lokātīta: the skull observance of the Lākulas and Kāpālikas).

The Svacchanda Tantra says the Atimārga lies 'beyond the states of the intellect' and that its skull-observers and Pāśupatas are not re-created, but it places their goals at levels below Śiva (Aiśvara pada, Dhruva).
The Lord (Paśupati, Rudra) is the independent cause; souls are eternal paśus; liberation is attained by the Lord's grace.
summary: The Atimārga ('path beyond') is the name the Śaiva scriptures give to the older of Śaivism's two great divisions, beside the Mantramārga ('path of mantras'). It comprises the Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas, who trace themselves to Lakulīśa and the Pāśupata Sūtra, the Lākulas (known in Karnataka as Kālāmukhas), and - in some sources and some modern accounts - the Kāpālikas or Somasiddhāntins. Its observances are ascetic and aim at liberation. Apart from the Pāśupata Sūtra with Kauṇḍinya's commentary and the Gaṇakārikā with its Ratnaṭīkā, it is known mainly from inscriptions, from the Mantramārga scriptures that describe it, and from opponents' reports.
notes: The division Atimārga/Mantramārga is the scriptures' own (Niśvāsa corpus; Svacchanda 11.182-190). Grouping the Kāpālikas as a third Atimārga division follows some scholarly reconstructions (Sanderson); other sources link the Kāpālika cult to the Mantramārga's Bhairava tantras. The Kūrma Purāṇa (2.37.146) lists 'Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula' together, with Vāma and Bhairava, as non-Vedic Śaiva teachings.

name: The school of Ātreya (Ātreya-sampradāya, the physicians' line)
distinctive_positions: Primacy of internal medicine (kāyacikitsā).
Ātreya taught six disciples, each of whom composed a tantra; Agniveśa's was first (Ca Sū 1.30-33).
Surgical procedures are left to the Dhānvantarīyas (Ca Ci 5.44).
summary: The lineage of Punarvasu Ātreya and his six disciples (Agniveśa, Bhela, Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara, Hārīta, Kṣārapāṇi) whose tantras were approved by the assembly of sages (Ca Sū 1.30-40); Agniveśa's, redacted by Caraka and completed by Dṛḍhabala, survives as the Caraka Saṃhitā.
notes: 'Ātreya-sampradāya' is the later name for this line; the classical texts speak of Ātreya's disciples. Its separateness is now scholastic: all later Āyurveda draws on both schools.

name: Āyurveda
regions: Gandhāra and the north-west (tradition: Takṣaśilā; Pañcanada for Dṛḍhabala)
Tibet, Central Asia and Sri Lanka (transmissions)

tradition.text: beginningless (śāśvata, Ca Sū 30.27); revealed by Brahmā and brought to earth by Bharadvāja (Ca Sū 1) or by Dhanvantari as Divodāsa of Kāśī (Su Sū 1)

scholarly.text: classical compendia c. 2nd c. BCE – 7th c. CE; commentaries 9th–16th c.; living

transmissions_received.what: Atharvavedic healing and the self-description of Āyurveda as an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6; Ca Sū 30.21)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: the principles and the three guṇas in the account of the person (Ca Śā 1.16-17, 1.63-66; Su Śā 1.3-9)
transmissions_received.evidence: textual-parallel

transmissions_received.what: the six categories (sāmānya, viśeṣa, guṇa, dravya, karma, samavāya) as the foundations (Ca Sū 1.28-29, 1.44-52)
transmissions_received.evidence: textual-parallel

transmissions_given.what: the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (translated into Tibetan, Tengyur) and its three-doṣa medicine, in the tradition's own later account received into the Four Tantras
shared three-humour doctrine and Sanskrit medical vocabulary (direction disputed)
doṣa vocabulary used for the purposes of the cleansing acts and breath retentions (HYP 2.21)
the frame of rasāyana and the pharmacological categories (rasa, guṇa, vīrya, vipāka) into which mercurial medicine was absorbed

distinctive_positions: Āyus (life) is the union of body, senses, mind and self; Āyurveda is the knowledge of what is wholesome and unwholesome, happy and unhappy life and its measure (Ca Sū 1.41-42).
Its purpose is twofold: protecting the health of the healthy and allaying the disorder of the sick (Ca Sū 30.26; Su Sū 1.14).
Health is the equilibrium (sāmya) of the dhātus, disease their disequilibrium (Ca Sū 9.4; AHS Sū 1.20).
The body has three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha); the mind has two (rajas and tamas) (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21).
Three causes of all disease: wrong contact of senses and objects, failure of discernment (prajñāparādha), and time/transformation (pariṇāma) (Ca Sū 11.43).
Three kinds of therapy: resting on the divine (daiva-vyapāśraya), on reasoned application (yukti-vyapāśraya), and conquest of the mind (sattvāvajaya) (Ca Sū 11.54).
Four means of valid knowledge: authoritative testimony, perception, inference and yukti (Ca Sū 11.17).
Rebirth is established by all four means (Ca Sū 11.6-33); liberation (mokṣa) is the complete cessation of all feeling, attained through yoga and the recollection of truth (Ca Śā 1.137-155).
Āyurveda is beginningless and eternal; only its understanding and teaching have a beginning (Ca Sū 30.27).
It is a science of life, not itself a path of liberation: health is the root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa (Ca Sū 1.15).
Like cures unlike: increase by the similar (sāmānya), decrease by the dissimilar (viśeṣa) (Ca Sū 1.44).
summary: The science of life (āyus), taught in the tradition's account by Brahmā and brought to earth through Indra — to Bharadvāja and Ātreya Punarvasu (the physicians' school) and to Dhanvantari as King Divodāsa of Kāśī (the surgeons' school). Its classical compendia (Caraka, Suśruta, Vāgbhaṭa) teach the three doṣas, seven dhātus and malas, the digestive fires, ojas and the channels; constitution; diet, daily and seasonal routine and good conduct; the eight branches; rejuvenation; and, in Caraka, a doctrine of the self, rebirth, yoga and liberation. It regards itself as eternal and as a limb of the Atharvaveda, and was practised across Vedic, Buddhist and Jain communities.
notes: family 'shared': the texts describe Āyurveda as an upaveda/upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6; Ca Sū 30.21), but its authors and users include Buddhists (the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya's opening and its ten sinful acts; Ravigupta; the Bower manuscript) and Jains (Ugrāditya). Decision logged in REPORT.

name: Bahuśrutīya
distinctive_positions: The Buddha's teachings on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self and nirvāṇa are supramundane, the rest mundane (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra is associated with this school in some Chinese accounts (disputed).
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch distinguishing the Buddha's supramundane from his mundane teachings.

name: The White Lotus school of Mao Ziyuan (Bailian zong)

scholarly.text: 12th c. (Mao Ziyuan d. 1166) to Yuan; later 'White Lotus' sects of the Ming–Qing are distinct and partly millenarian

distinctive_positions: Lay societies keeping the five precepts, confirmed by five recitations of Amitābha's name; repentance halls; Tiantai-style 'four lands and three contemplations'.
summary: Lay Pure Land repentance societies founded by the monk Mao Ziyuan (Cizhao zongzhu, d. 1166) on the model of Huiyuan's Lotus society; repeatedly banned, defended by Pudu's Lushan lianzong baojian (1305). The later 'White Lotus teachings' of Ming–Qing sectarian religion took the name but are outside this entry.
notes: Scope limited to the Song–Yuan Buddhist societies as described in T1973.

name: Balarāmī sampradāya

scholarly.text: early 19th c.; Balarām Hāḍi c. 1785–1850

distinctive_positions: Founded by a man of the Hāḍi (sweeper) caste, held by his followers to be the supreme God (Hāḍirām).
Rejection of brahmanical ritual, caste and the Vedic gods; worship of the human.
summary: A small Bengali sect founded by Balarām Hāḍi of Meherpur, of 'untouchable' birth, which rejected caste and brahmanical religion and venerated its founder as God.
notes: Known mainly from 20th-c. ethnographic reports (Sudhir Chakrabarti and others); low confidence.

name: Baotang school

scholarly.text: later 8th c.

distinctive_positions: No-thought alone; rejection of ritual, recitation and conventional observances (Lidai fabao ji; Zongmi's criticism).
Claim that Bodhidharma's robe passed from Huineng via Empress Wu to Zhishen and on to Wuzhu (Lidai fabao ji).
summary: The radical Sichuan community of Wuzhu (714–774), which rejected all formal practice in favour of no-thought and claimed the patriarchal robe; its record is the Dunhuang Lidai fabao ji.

name: Bāul

scholarly.text: the word bāula (a madman of God) appears in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 19, Advaita's riddle); Bāuls as a distinct community are documented from the 18th–19th c.; Lalon Fakir d. 1890

transmissions_received.what: the sahaja doctrine, the body as the place of the divine couple, rasa and rati, the practice of the couple, secret language
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; see brw:vaisnava-sahajiya-to-baul

transmissions_received.what: body-yoga vocabulary: reversal (ulṭā), the tenth door, the lotuses and currents
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; see brw:natha-to-baul

transmissions_received.what: the Vraja līlā, Caitanya and Nityānanda as figures of the songs, nāma-kīrtana
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit mention in the songs (e.g. Lalon's 'tin pāgale holo melā nadey ese')

distinctive_positions: The Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ), the Unknown Bird (achin pākhi), the Uncatchable Man (adhar mānuṣ) dwells in this body; he is to be sought within, not in temple, mosque or scripture.
Body-theology (deha-tattva): 'what is in the vessel (the body) is in the universe' (je āche bhāṇḍe tā āche brahmāṇḍe).
What is present and verifiable in the body (bartamān) is trusted over inference, hearsay and scripture (anumān).
Caste and religious labels are rejected: 'everyone asks what caste Lalon is; I have never seen the form of caste'.
The guru (murśid) is the living human through whom the Man is found; worship of the human (mānuṣ bhajan).
The song (gān) is teaching, practice and code: sung with the ektārā and dotārā at ākhṛās and melās.
A secret practice of the couple and of the bodily substances, reversing the downward flow (ulṭā / ujān sādhanā) — recorded here only in summary (restricted).
summary: The Bāuls are wandering and householder singer-practitioners of Bengal, both Hindu (Vaiṣṇava-Sahajiyā-derived) and Muslim (Fakir), who seek the Man of the Heart within the human body under a living guru, reject caste, scripture and sectarian worship, and teach through songs; Lalon Fakir (d. 1890) is their most celebrated master.
notes: Family 'shared' because the tradition draws on Vaiṣṇava, Nāth and (on a scholarly hypothesis) Buddhist Sahajiyā streams and includes Muslim Fakirs; the Sufi side is recorded as context only. Most Bāul teaching is oral and much of it is deliberately secret; many teachers are post-1800 and flagged recent.

name: Bengali and Assamese Śākta tantra

tradition.text: Kāmarūpa is the seat where Satī's yoni fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42); Śiva himself revealed the tantras taught there

scholarly.text: Kālikā Purāṇa c. 10th–11th c.; Yoginī and Kāmākhyā Tantras c. 16th–17th c.; Kṛṣṇānanda c. late 16th–17th c.; the Śākta padāvalī 18th–19th c.

transmissions_received.what: Dakṣiṇakālī and the Mahāvidyās
transmissions_received.evidence: Tantrasāra quotes the Kālī Tantra and Muṇḍamālā

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual (pañcatattva, bhāvas)
transmissions_received.evidence: Kaulāvalīnirṇaya, Kulārṇava cited in the digests

transmissions_received.what: the Satī myth and the pīṭhas; Kāmākhyā
transmissions_received.evidence: Kālikā Purāṇa, Devī Bhāgavata

transmissions_given.what: Ramakrishna's Kālī devotion and his tantric sādhana under the Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī (recent)
shared songs and body-centred esoteric vocabulary (contested)

distinctive_positions: Kāmākhyā in Kāmarūpa is the seat where Satī's yoni fell; the Goddess there is the great vidyā in the form of the yoni and is all four aims of life (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4, 1.9).
The pīṭhas are the places where the parts of Satī's body fell and Śiva stays as a liṅga beside each (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.36-50).
Satī shows Śiva her ten Mahāvidyā forms, stationed in the ten directions, before going to Dakṣa's sacrifice (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa madhya 6.125-134).
Blood offering is taught (Kālikā Purāṇa ch. 67, 'rudhirādhyāya', summary only) together with substitutes (pumpkin, sugarcane, liquor as 'equal to' a victim) and prohibitions for brāhmaṇas.
The Dakṣiṇakālī form (four-armed, garland of heads, standing on Śiva) is set out in Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra, quoting the Kālī Tantra.
The Mahāvidyā mantras are 'siddha' vidyās needing no preliminary checks — which Kṛṣṇānanda reads as praise, not a rule (Tantrasāra, siddhādiśodhana).
Devotional Śāktism: the poet-saints sing to Kālī/Śyāmā as Mother, and to Umā in the homecoming (āgamanī) and farewell (vijayā) songs.
summary: The Śākta tantric culture of Kāmarūpa (Assam) and Bengal: the Kālikā Purāṇa on Kāmākhyā, the pīṭhas and the offerings; the Yoginī and Kāmākhyā Tantras; the Satī–Mahāvidyā myth of the Bṛhaddharma and Mahābhāgavata Purāṇas; the great digests of the 16th–19th centuries (Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra, Brahmānanda's Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī and Tārārahasya, Pūrṇānanda's Śrītattvacintāmaṇi and Śyāmārahasya, Sarvānanda's Sarvollāsa, the Prāṇatoṣiṇī); the Tārā cult of Tārāpīṭh; and the Śākta devotional songs of Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta.

name: Bhadrayānīya
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya; no separate doctrines recorded beyond the school's list membership.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in the lists of the eighteen schools.

name: Early Bhāgavata devotion (the Nārāyaṇīya / Sātvata–Ekāntika dharma)
regions: Mathurā and the Śūrasena country; Vidiśā (Besnagar); Rajasthan (Ghosuṇḍī); western Deccan (Nānāghāṭ) — on the scholarly (inscriptional) evidence
Badarī (Nara–Nārāyaṇa's hermitage) and Śvetadvīpa in the tradition's account

tradition.text: the Sātvata dharma was given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and handed down (MBh 12.336)

scholarly.text: worship of Vāsudeva attested from c. 4th–2nd c. BCE (Pāṇini 4.3.98 'vāsudevaka'; Heliodorus's Garuḍa pillar at Besnagar, late 2nd c. BCE, whose donor calls himself a bhāgavata; the Ghosuṇḍī and Nānāghāṭ inscriptions naming Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, c. 1st c. BCE); the Nārāyaṇīya's theology c. 1st c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories in which the fourfold form is stated
transmissions_received.evidence: 12.326.100 calls the teaching 'made by Sāṃkhya-yoga, called Pañcarātra'

transmissions_received.what: sacrificial worship reoriented to Nārāyaṇa; the Vedas as part of the teaching
transmissions_received.evidence: Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323–324); 12.336.76 joins Sāṃkhya-yoga, the Vedāraṇyaka and Pañcarātra

transmissions_given.what: the fourfold form (caturvyūha) and the Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva
lists of the Lord's manifestations (prādurbhāva/avatāra) and Kṛṣṇa devotion (Harivaṃśa, Bhāgavata and Viṣṇu Purāṇas)
devotion to Nārāyaṇa/Kṛṣṇa as the one refuge
the Gītā, Nārāyaṇīya and Viṣṇu Sahasranāma as authorities for Nārāyaṇa's supremacy and surrender

distinctive_positions: Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva is the one supreme Lord, the knower of the field whose self is without guṇas (12.326.38).
The fourfold form (caturvyūha): from Vāsudeva comes Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), from him Pradyumna (the mind), from him Aniruddha (the ego), from whom Brahmā arises (12.326.68–69; 12.327.26).
The liberated ascend through the sun into Aniruddha, Pradyumna and Saṃkarṣaṇa and finally Vāsudeva; the one-pointed devotees (ekāntins) enter Vāsudeva directly (12.332.13–18; 12.336.3).
The Lord appears again and again (prādurbhāva) as Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi and at Mathurā, and earlier as Haṃsa and Hayaśiras (12.326.71–94); cf. BhG 4.7–8.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti), worship according to rule without desire, is the highest dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga (12.336.4, 12.336.69).
Worship by sacrifice without slaughter (Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice; the dispute over 'aja' as goat or grain, 12.323–324).
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas and Pāśupata are distinct systems, yet Nārāyaṇa is the culmination seen in all (12.337.59–67).
Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).
The teaching Kṛṣṇa gave Arjuna before the battle is this dharma (12.336.8); taking refuge in the Lord alone frees from all sins (BhG 18.66), even for women, vaiśyas and śūdras (BhG 9.32).
summary: The early devotional religion of Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) as found in the Nārāyaṇīya of the Mahābhārata, the Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of devotion and surrender, the Harivaṃśa and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma: exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to one Lord in a fourfold form, worship without animal sacrifice, and the Lord's repeated appearances to protect dharma. It flows into the Pāñcarātra, the Purāṇic Vaiṣṇavism and the later Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas.

queries: Heliodorus pillar bhagavata three immortal steps
Ghosundi Nanaghat Samkarshana Vasudeva 1st century BCE
checks.note: Least-sure inscriptional metadata confirmed: Heliodorus pillar c. 113 BCE (donor a bhāgavata; the three immortal precepts dama, cāga and apramāda, paralleled at MBh 11.7.19 and 5.43.14, both located). Ghosuṇḍī and Nānāghāṭ (1st c. BCE) name Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva. Pāṇini 4.3.98 (vāsudevaka) located locally. The Sātvata/ekāntin dharma of the Nārāyaṇīya is located at 12.336.

notes: Owned by U05. Scholarly (labeled) observation: the three 'immortal steps' of Heliodorus's inscription — self-restraint, renunciation, heedfulness (dama, cāga, apramāda) — match the triad 'damas tyāgo 'pramādaś ca' at MBh 11.7.19 and 5.43.14.

name: Bhakti-śāstra: the sūtra tradition of devotional theory (Nārada, Śāṇḍilya)
alt_names: Bhakti-mīmāṃsā (name sometimes given to the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra)

tradition.text: Nārada and Śāṇḍilya are ancient sages of the Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra tradition; the sūtras are attributed to them

scholarly.text: Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra and Nārada Bhakti Sūtra usually placed c. 10th–13th c. CE or later (both post-date the Bhāgavata Purāṇa on most scholarly views); Vopadeva's Muktāphala 13th c.; Viṣṇupurī's Bhaktiratnāvalī c. 14th–15th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata's teaching of devotion (the gopīs as the model of love; the nine forms; devotion free of the guṇas)
transmissions_received.evidence: NBS 21 names the gopīs of Vraja; NBS 82's eleven attachments overlap the Bhāgavata's forms of devotion

transmissions_received.what: the Gītā's teaching on devotion, cited as scripture
transmissions_received.evidence: the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra argues from the Gītā's words (e.g. that the devotee is 'higher' than ritualist, knower and yogin)

transmissions_received.what: the sūtra form and the opening 'athāto ... jijñāsā'; Bādarāyaṇa cited by name
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚBS 1 imitates Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1; ŚBS names Bādarāyaṇa and Kāśyapa

transmissions_given.what: the definition of bhakti as love and as its own fruit (background to the Gauḍīya prema theory)

distinctive_positions: Bhakti is supreme love (parama-prema) for the Lord, of the nature of nectar/immortality (NBS 2–3); it is supreme attachment (parānurakti) to Īśvara (ŚBS 2).
Bhakti is not a means but the fruit itself (phala-rūpa), higher than action, knowledge and yoga (NBS 25–26, 30).
Bhakti is not knowledge: even one who hates the Lord may know him (ŚBS); knowledge of a king or of food does not please the king or appease hunger (NBS 31–32).
Love must include knowledge of the Lord's greatness (māhātmya-jñāna) and seek his happiness, not one's own — the gopīs' love is the model, the paramour's love is not (NBS 21–24).
Bhakti is attained chiefly by the grace of great souls or by a drop of the Lord's grace; the company of the great is itself won by his grace (NBS 38–40).

Among devotees there is no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family, wealth or occupation, 'because they are His' (NBS 72–73); the lowest births are eligible (ŚBS, on the tradition of eligibility).
Secondary devotion (gauṇī) is graded by the guṇas or by the motive of the devotee; primary devotion is one, though it appears as eleven attachments (NBS 56, 82).
The devotee should not engage in disputation (NBS 74–75) but reflect on the bhakti-śāstras and keep the virtues (NBS 76–78).
summary: Not an institutional order but the textual tradition of the Bhakti Sūtras: the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (84 sūtras) and the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra (100 sūtras, with Svapneśvara's commentary), which define devotion, rank it above works, knowledge and yoga, name its means and signs, and cite a line of 'bhakti teachers' (bhaktyācāryas: Kumāra, Vyāsa, Śuka, Śāṇḍilya, Garga, Uddhava, Bali, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa and others, NBS 83). Later Sanskrit systematizations of Bhāgavata devotion (Vopadeva's Muktāphala with Hemādri's commentary; Viṣṇupurī's Bhaktiratnāvalī) are grouped here.
notes: Created by U25 as a sub-lineage because the texts themselves name a 'bhakti-śāstra' (NBS 76) and a line of 'bhaktyācāryas' (NBS 83). Parent set to lin:bhagavata-early on the tradition's account (Nārada and Śāṇḍilya as Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra sages — cf. the Pāñcarātra claim that Śāṇḍilya, not finding the highest good in the four Vedas, received this śāstra, quoted in Śaṅkara's BSBh 2.2.45); this is not a claim of historical continuity. Keeps convergence counts from treating the sūtras as an independent root.

name: Bhāmatī school (Bhāmatī-prasthāna)

scholarly.text: From Vācaspati Miśra (9th or 10th c.) through Amalānanda (13th c.) and Appayya Dīkṣita (16th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Maṇḍana Miśra's Brahmasiddhi, which Vācaspati followed on several points
transmissions_received.evidence: Vācaspati also commented on the Brahmasiddhi (Tattvasamīkṣā, lost)

distinctive_positions: Ignorance resides in the individual selves (jīvāśrita) and has Brahman as its object; the mutual dependence of jīva and avidyā is beginningless like seed and sprout.
Avidyās are many, one for each jīva; hence many jīvas (aneka-jīva).
Limitation theory (avaccheda-vāda): the jīva is Brahman as delimited by the inner organ, as space is delimited by a pot.
The Upaniṣadic sentence yields mediate (parokṣa) knowledge; the mind purified by sustained contemplation is the instrument of direct realization.
Contemplation (nididhyāsana, prasaṅkhyāna) is the principal means; hearing and reflection are auxiliaries.
Vedic works produce the desire to know (vividiṣā), not knowledge itself.
summary: The line of post-Śaṅkara Advaita founded on Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī, drawing on Maṇḍana Miśra, continued by Amalānanda's Kalpataru and Appayya Dīkṣita's Parimala. It places ignorance in the individual selves, explains the jīva by limitation, admits many jīvas, and holds that the mind, perfected by contemplation, turns the verbal knowledge of the mahāvākya into direct realization.

name: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā
regions: North and South India; strong later centres at Vārāṇasī (Khaṇḍadeva's circle), Mithilā, the Tamil country and Kerala (Mānameyodaya)

scholarly.text: from Kumārila (c. 6th–7th c. CE) to the present; the dominant school of Mīmāṃsā

transmissions_given.what: six means of knowledge (including postulation and non-apprehension), used by Advaita for empirical matters (e.g. Vedāntaparibhāṣā)

distinctive_positions: Six means of knowledge: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation (arthāpatti) and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi / abhāva-pramāṇa).
Sentence meaning by 'connection of the expressed' (abhihitānvaya): words first convey their own meanings, which then combine into the sentence meaning (Śabara on MS 1.1.25; ŚV vākya 342–343).
Error as apprehension of a thing as other than it is (viparītakhyāti): the related items are real, only their relation is unreal (Śāstradīpikā).
Cognition is not itself perceived; it is inferred from the 'knownness' (jñātatā / prākaṭya) it produces in the object.
The injunctive suffix expresses a verbal efficient force (śābdī bhāvanā) that prompts the person's own effort (ārthī bhāvanā) with its three expectancies: what, by what, how.
Obligatory and occasional rites destroy past sin and avert the demerit of omission (Tantravārttika).

Liberation: the one seeking release avoids desire-prompted and prohibited acts, performs obligatory and occasional rites, knows the self, and when past karma is exhausted by experience no new body arises (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 102–111).
Pārthasārathi: liberation is the absolute dissolution of the threefold bond (body, senses, objects) and is without bliss; some Bhāṭṭas held that the liberated self enjoys its innate bliss.
Words are the eternal letters; the grammarians' sphoṭa is superfluous (ŚV sphoṭavāda).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati and a total dissolution of the world (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116).
summary: The school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, built on his Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā and developed by Maṇḍana Miśra, Umbeka, Sucarita, Pārthasārathi Miśra and, later, Khaṇḍadeva, Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara. It defends six means of knowledge, the abhihitānvaya theory of sentence meaning, the bhāvanā theory of injunction, and a realist ontology; its epistemology was adopted by Advaita Vedānta for worldly matters.
notes: 'Tautātita-mata' (the doctrine of Tutāta, an epithet of Kumārila) is attested in the title of Bhavadeva's Tautātitamatatilaka; low confidence on the epithet's general currency. Maṇḍana Miśra is placed here by tradition (as Kumārila's pupil) though several of his positions differ (e.g. iṣṭasādhanatā as the meaning of injunction; defence of sphoṭa).

name: Bhedābheda Vedānta (Bhāskara's school and the early difference-and-non-difference Vedāntins)

scholarly.text: pre-Śaṅkara (Bhartṛprapañca) to 16th c. (Vijñānabhikṣu); Bhāskara c. 8th–9th c. CE

transmissions_given.what: the pariṇāma (real transformation) reading of the Brahma Sūtras and the jīva-as-part (aṃśa) doctrine, which Rāmānuja received through his first teacher Yādavaprakāśa and then criticised
the general bhedābheda frame (difference and non-difference of Brahman, souls and world)

distinctive_positions: Brahman is both different and non-different from the individual souls and the world: one as cause, many as effect.
The world is a real transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman or of its power (śakti), not an appearance (vivarta).
Bhāskara: the difference of the soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural (aupādhika-bhedābheda).
Yādavaprakāśa: both difference and non-difference are natural (svābhāvika-bhedābheda); Brahman itself becomes Īśvara, souls and matter.
Liberation requires knowledge combined with lifelong ritual and social duty (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) — Bhartṛprapañca, Bhāskara.
Bhāskara denies liberation while living (jīvanmukti): release comes when the body, a real adjunct, falls away.
Bhāskara attacks Śaṅkara's doctrine of māyā as a teaching of the Mahāyāna Buddhists.
Vijñānabhikṣu (16th c.) restates the position as avibhāga (non-separation) of souls and prakṛti from Brahman, harmonising Vedānta with Sāṃkhya-Yoga.
summary: The oldest continuous current of Brahma Sūtra interpretation: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world, which are its real transformations. Known for Bhartṛprapañca only through fragments reported by his Advaita critics; its classic statement is Bhāskara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya; Yādavaprakāśa (Rāmānuja's first teacher) gave a 'natural' version; Vijñānabhikṣu revived the frame in the 16th c. No living order continues the school; its ideas passed into the Vaiṣṇava Vedāntas.

name: Bhūta stream (tantras for spirits)
distinctive_positions: Tantras for the control and exorcism of spirits (bhūta, graha), issued from the western face (Sadyojāta) (Kāmika pūrva 1.26; the Śrīkaṇṭhīya as quoted by Jayaratha: 'in the west, the Bhūta tantras').
summary: The Śaiva scriptural stream concerned with spirit-possession and exorcism; known mostly from lists and fragments.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08; the Kāmika's printed text names twenty Bhūta tantras 'beginning with Kaula' (reading uncertain). family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Bīsapantha (Digambara)
distinctive_positions: worship of Jina images with fresh flowers, fruits and lamps and seated worship
acceptance of the bhaṭṭārakas as religious authorities
worship of guardian and attendant deities (Padmāvatī, Kṣetrapāla)
summary: The 'older' mode of Digambara temple practice, loyal to the bhaṭṭāraka institution and to the attendant deities, as distinguished from the reforming Terāpantha.

name: Bön (Yungdrung Bön)
regions: Western Tibet (Zhang Zhung, Mount Kailash region)
exile communities (Dolanji, India; Triten Norbutse, Kathmandu)

tradition.text: taught by Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche in Ölmo Lungring (Tagzig) many millennia before Śākyamuni (a traditional Bön reckoning places his birth in 16,017 BCE); transmitted through Zhang Zhung to Tibet

scholarly.text: an organized Yungdrung Bön with its own canon is attested from the 11th c., when Shenchen Luga (996-1035) and others recovered treasure texts; earlier Tibetan and Zhang Zhung ritual traditions lie behind it

transmissions_given.what: shared Dzogchen and treasure frameworks; direction disputed (see dsp:bon-and-buddhism)

distinctive_positions: Bön is the teaching of Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche, a fully enlightened teacher from Ölmo Lungring in Tagzig, independent of and prior to Śākyamuni's Buddhism.
The teaching is ordered as nine ways (theg pa rim dgu), four causal ways and five fruitional ways, and in another scheme as four portals and a fifth, the treasury (sgo bzhi mdzod lnga).
Its Dzogchen (the A-khrid, the Dzogchen Yangtse Longchen and the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü) teaches the base of all (kun gzhi) inseparable from awareness (rig pa).
The swastika (g.yung drung) is the emblem of the indestructible and eternal; circumambulation is counter-clockwise.
Tibetan Buddhist historians' portrait of Bön as a pre-Buddhist or derivative religion is rejected by the Bön tradition.
notes: OPTIONAL per coverage map B6: 'Bön shares Dzogchen but lies outside the Buddhist family'. family set to 'shared' because Bön is neither Vedic nor an Indian śramaṇa tradition, yet shares Dzogchen, tantra and monasticism with the Buddhist family (decision by U45, logged in REPORT.md).
summary: The Bön religion of Tibet in its Yungdrung ('eternal', swastika) form: the teaching attributed to Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche, transmitted from Tagzig through Zhang Zhung, persecuted under the Tibetan kings, preserved in treasures recovered from the 10th-11th c., and organized monastically from Menri (1405). It has its own canon, nine ways, deities, monastic discipline and Great Perfection teachings closely parallel to the Nyingma, while insisting on its separate origin.

name: New Bön (Bön Sar)

scholarly.text: from c. the 14th c.; strengthened in the 18th-19th c.

distinctive_positions: Integrates figures and treasures shared with the Nyingma (Padmasambhava as a form of Drenpa Namkha's lineage) into Bön; regarded with reserve by Yungdrung Bön monastics (low confidence).
notes: Optional (Bön). Reconstructed from general knowledge; names of founders and texts omitted rather than guessed (see REPORT.md gaps).
summary: A current within Bön, attested from the late medieval period, that integrates treasures and figures shared with the Nyingma; distinguished from the 'Eternal' Yungdrung Bön.

name: Borān kammaṭṭhāna (old meditation; the yogāvacara tradition)

tradition.text: presented in its manuals as the Buddha's own method handed down by yogāvacaras; brought to Kandy with the Siamese ordination mission of 1753 (the tradition's account)

scholarly.text: attested in manuscripts from at least the 17th–18th c.; probably older; marginalized by the 19th–20th c. reforms

transmissions_given.what: the placing of meditative objects at bodily locations and syllable recitation (scholarly hypothesis of continuity)

distinctive_positions: Meditation proceeds by installing meditative qualities (the five kinds of rapture, the tranquillities, etc.) at specific points of the body in a fixed order, using Pali syllables and recitations.
Symbolic correspondences between the stages of meditation, embryology, the letters of the Pali alphabet and the Abhidhamma lists.
Teaching was given by a teacher to a qualified pupil after preliminary rites (offerings, requesting the meditation subject).
summary: The pre-reform meditation system of mainland Southeast Asian and Sri Lankan Theravāda, known from manuals such as the Yogāvacara's Manual, which uses bodily placement, syllables and ritual; largely displaced by the 19th–20th-century reforms and now studied and partly revived.
notes: Low confidence throughout: the tradition is known through a few published manuscripts and recent scholarship; its practices are recorded here in summary only. 'Tantric Theravāda' is a contested scholars' label, not the tradition's own.

name: Brahma saṃhati (Dāmodarīyā)
distinctive_positions: Traces itself to the brahmins Dāmodaradeva and Harideva; brahmin sattrādhikārs.
More accommodating of image worship and of brahmanical rites than the other saṃhatis.
Bhaṭṭadeva's prose renderings of the Bhāgavata and Gītā belong to it.
summary: The saṃhati of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras descended from Dāmodaradeva and Harideva, with brahmin leadership and greater accommodation of brahmanical practice; it includes several of the great Majuli sattras patronised by the Ahom kings (identification of individual sattras to verify).

scholarly.text: formed after Mādhavadeva's death (1596), 17th c.

name: Caitika
alt_names: Zhiduo shan bu 制多山部
distinctive_positions: Founded by a (second) Mahādeva who revived the five points at the end of the second century (Vasumitra); associated with caitya worship.
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch in all lists; in Vasumitra's account founded by a Mahādeva at a caitya hill; connected with the Andhra Śaila schools.

name: Caityavāsī (temple-dwelling monks)

scholarly.text: prominent c. 5th–11th c. CE in western India; opposed by Haribhadra and defeated in debate by Jineśvarasūri (1024)

distinctive_positions: monks resided permanently in temples, administered their property and handled money — criticized by reformers as contrary to the Āgamas
summary: The temple-dwelling Śvetāmbara monks of early medieval western India, against whom Haribhadra's Sambodhaprakaraṇa and the Kharatara reform (vasativāsa) were directed; their clothed resident successors are sometimes seen in the later yatis and śrīpūjyas.

name: Cakrasaṃvara (Saṃvara, Heruka) tradition in India
regions: the 24 pīṭhas of the Heruka maṇḍala

tradition.text: Heruka subdued Maheśvara (Bhairava) and his retinue at the twenty-four sites; the tantra is an abridgement of a larger tantra of 100,000 verses

scholarly.text: Laghuśaṃvara c. late 8th–9th c.; explanatory tantras 9th–10th c.

transmissions_given.what: the three Indian lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) and the Vajrayoginī cycles
the three Indian lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) and the Vajrayoginī cycles
the three Indian lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) and the Vajrayoginī cycles
Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī as the principal esoteric deities

distinctive_positions: Heruka (Cakrasaṃvara) in union with Vajravārāhī is the embodiment of great bliss and emptiness.
The maṇḍala's twenty-four sacred sites (pīṭha etc.) are located in the outer land and, inwardly, in the yogin's body as channels (the body maṇḍala).
Three Indian lineages of practice: Lūipa's (with Vajravārāhī's cycle), Ghaṇṭāpa's (the five-deity body maṇḍala) and Kāṇha's (Kṛṣṇācārya's).
The Vajrayoginī (Vajravārāhī) sādhanas of Nāropa, Indrabhūti and Maitrīpa belong to this cycle.
summary: The Yoginī-tantra tradition centred on Heruka Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī, based on the Laghuśaṃvara and its explanatory tantras, with the twenty-four sacred sites (shared with Śaiva pīṭha lists) mapped onto the body, and three Indian practice lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) that passed to Tibet and the Newars.

name: Caodong house

tradition.text: founded by Dongshan Liangjie (807–869) and Caoshan Benji (840–901)

scholarly.text: 9th c.; nearly extinct in the 10th c.; revived in the Northern Song by Touzi Yiqing; living

transmissions_given.what: Rujing's line to Dōgen (and Dongming Huiri's line to Tōmyō Enichi)

distinctive_positions: The five ranks of the real and the apparent (zheng-pian wuwei) and the five ranks of merit.
Mutual interfusion and non-interfusion (huihu 回互) of principle and phenomena (Cantongqi).
Silent illumination (mozhao) as the Song Caodong practice (Hongzhi).
'Precious Mirror Samādhi' (Baojing sanmei): the reflection and the one reflected.
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, named from Dongshan Liangjie and Caoshan Benji in the line of Qingyuan and Shitou, known for the five ranks and later for Hongzhi's silent illumination; source of Japanese Sōtō.

name: Cārvāka / Lokāyata

tradition.text: Taught by Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods, to delude the asuras (Maitrī Up. 7.9; Viṣṇu Purāṇa); handed to his disciple Cārvāka (Prabodhacandrodaya).

scholarly.text: Materialist views are reported in the early Pali and Jain canons (c. 5th–3rd c. BCE); 'Lokāyata' is named with Sāṃkhya and Yoga in the Arthaśāstra; sūtra fragments and named commentators are quoted from c. 7th c. CE (Purandara, Kamalaśīla) to c. 12th c.; no surviving lineage.

transmissions_received.what: the natthika/uccheda view (no gift, no fruit of deeds, no other world, the person made of four elements)
transmissions_received.evidence: doctrinal parallel between DN 2 (Ajita) and the later Bṛhaspati fragments; no lineage link in the texts

distinctive_positions: (As reported) The principles (tattva) are the four elements — earth, water, fire, air; their aggregate is called body, senses and objects (Bṛhaspati Sūtra fragments).

(As reported) Consciousness arises from the elements when they are transformed into a body, like the intoxicating power from fermenting ingredients (madaśaktivat); the person is the body qualified by consciousness.
(As reported) Because there is no one who goes to another world, there is no other world (paralokino 'bhāvāt paralokābhāvaḥ).

(As reported) Perception is the only means of knowledge; inference is not valid because invariable concomitance cannot be established — or, according to Purandara, inference is valid only within worldly experience.
(As reported) Pleasure is the aim of life; heaven is pleasure, hell is pain, the only lord is the king known to the world, liberation is the death of the body.
(As reported) The Vedic sacrifices and the funeral offerings are a livelihood devised by those lacking intelligence and manliness.
Jayarāśi's Tattvopaplavasiṃha, the only surviving work, argues that no means of knowledge can be established at all, so that even the four elements 'do not stand when examined'.
summary: Cārvāka or Lokāyata is the Indian school of materialism. Its root text, the Bṛhaspati Sūtra, and all its commentaries are lost; its positions are known from quotations and summaries by opponents — Buddhist (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla, Candrakīrti), Jain (Haribhadra, Guṇaratna), Nyāya (Jayanta), Vedānta (Śaṅkara, Sadānanda, the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha) — and from one surviving sceptical work, Jayarāśi's Tattvopaplavasiṃha. Jayanta distinguishes 'rogue' (dhūrta) from 'well-educated' (suśikṣita) Cārvākas.
notes: The Mahābhārata's Cārvāka (12.39) is a rākṣasa in mendicant's disguise who teaches no doctrine; the link between that figure and the school's name is not made by the epic. Bṛhaspati is recorded under the registry id tch:brhaspati (the tradition identifies the teacher with the preceptor of the gods); split if the merge prefers to keep the Lokāyata author apart.

name: Chan (Chinese Meditation school)
alt_names: Foxin zong 佛心宗 (school of the buddha-mind)
regions: China (Song-shan, Huangmei, Caoxi, Jiangxi, Hunan, Zhejiang, Fujian, Sichuan)

tradition.text: from Bodhidharma's arrival in China (traditionally 520 or 527 CE); transmitted from Śākyamuni through 28 Indian patriarchs

scholarly.text: a self-conscious lineage from the late 7th c. (East Mountain, Northern school); classical Tang Chan 8th–10th c.; dominant public Buddhism of the Song (960–1279); living

transmissions_received.what: Laṅkāvatāra, Prajñāpāramitā (Diamond Sūtra), Vimalakīrti, Nirvāṇa-sūtra buddha-nature teaching, Awakening of Faith
transmissions_received.evidence: Bodhidharma's gift of the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra to Huike (Xu gaoseng zhuan, T2060 juan 16); Huineng's awakening on the Diamond Sūtra (Platform Sūtra)

transmissions_given.what: Chan lineages and practice (Nine Mountain schools, from the 9th c.)
Linji (Huanglong, Yangqi), Caodong and Ming Linji (Ōbaku) transmissions to Japan
Chan lineages in Vietnam (Thiền), culminating in the Trúc Lâm school (U55)

distinctive_positions: A 'separate transmission outside the teachings, not dependent on words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind: see the nature and become a buddha' (the tradition's four-line self-description, assembled by the Song).
The mind (xin 心) or self-nature (zixing 自性) is originally pure and complete; delusion and awakening differ, the nature does not (Platform Sūtra).
Transmission from mind to mind (yi xin chuan xin 以心傳心) through a line of patriarchs, authenticated by a living teacher.
Samādhi and prajñā are one in substance (lamp and light); no-thought is the tenet, no-form the substance, non-abiding the root (Platform Sūtra).
Sudden awakening (dunwu 頓悟) is upheld against 'gradual' views; the relation of awakening to cultivation is debated within Chan itself.
Encounter dialogue, shouts and blows, and later public cases (gong'an) and the critical phrase (huatou) as means of awakening.
Monastic life organised by the 'pure rules' (qinggui) with communal work (puqing) as practice.
summary: The Chinese school of the 'meditation' (chan 禪, from dhyāna) lineage, which traces itself through 28 Indian patriarchs to Bodhidharma and six Chinese patriarchs ending with Huineng, divides into the Northern and Southern schools and later the Five Houses, and teaches seeing one's own nature as buddha through direct pointing, sitting meditation, encounter dialogue and kōan practice.

name: Caraṇdāsī sampradāya
alt_names: Śuka-sampradāya (because Caraṇdās's guru is said to be Śukadeva)

tradition.text: Caraṇdās received initiation from Śukadeva (the Bhāgavata's Śuka) in person

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Caraṇdās 1703–1782

distinctive_positions: A synthesis of Sant nirguṇa devotion with Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa devotion and aṣṭāṅga yoga.
The guru is exalted above Hari (Sahajobāī).
Notable women teachers: Sahajobāī and Dayābāī.
summary: The Delhi sampradāya of Caraṇdās (1703–1782), which joined nirguṇa Sant teaching with Kṛṣṇa devotion and yoga, and is remembered for its women poet-saints Sahajobāī and Dayābāī.

name: Chengshi school (Satyasiddhi school)
regions: Japan (one of the six Nara schools, attached to Sanron)

scholarly.text: 5th–7th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra (affiliation with the Sautrāntika or the Bahuśrutīya is debated)

distinctive_positions: The Satyasiddhiśāstra teaches the emptiness of persons and of dharmas and was studied in China as a bridge to Mahāyāna until Jizang classed it as 'Hīnayāna'.
summary: The Chinese exegetical tradition centred on Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra (translated by Kumārajīva, 411–412).

name: Chokling Tersar (the New Treasures of Chokgyur Lingpa)

scholarly.text: mid-19th c.

distinctive_positions: Treasures revealed by Chokgyur Lingpa, often jointly with Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and codified by Jamgön Kongtrul, notably the Tukdrub Barche Künsel guru sādhana.
summary: The recent treasure lineage of Chokgyur Dechen Lingpa (1829-1870), closely tied to the Rimé masters.

name: Dādū Panth

tradition.text: Dādū Dayāl, 1544–1603; his fifty-two disciples founded fifty-two seats (thāmbā)

scholarly.text: late 16th c. onward; the Vāṇī compiled by the early 17th c.; the anthologies (Pañcvāṇī, Sarvāṅgī) from the 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: Kabīr's songs, which the Dādūpanthī anthologies preserve alongside Dādū's
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit: the Pañcvāṇī collects Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and Hardās with Dādū

distinctive_positions: Remembrance of the nirguṇa Rām, the one God of Hindu and Turk, without idols or temples.
Impartiality (nipakh) and the middle way (madh): neither Hindu nor Turk, neither indulgence nor harsh austerity.
The guru met 'in the unseen' (gaib) and devotion to the guru; the Vāṇī itself is honoured in the panth's seats.
Five divisions in the later panth: Khālsā (the Naraina seat), Virakt (wandering renunciants), Uttarādhī, Khākī and the armed Nāgā.
Anthologies arranged by aṅg (topic), which preserved much of the Rajasthani Kabīr.
summary: The panth founded by Dādū Dayāl (1544–1603) in Rajasthan, with its chief seat at Naraina. It preserved Dādū's Vāṇī and, in its anthologies, the western recension of Kabīr and other Sants; its scholars (Rajjab, Sundardās) gave the Sant teaching systematic and learned form.
notes: Division names and the 'fifty-two disciples' are from the panth's tradition as commonly reported; moderate confidence.

name: Dārṣṭāntika

scholarly.text: c. 1st c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (named in the Mahāvibhāṣā)

distinctive_positions: Mental karma is volition together with covetousness, malice and wrong view themselves (AKBh 4, Pradhan p. 237: 'abhidhyādaya eva manaskarmeti dārṣṭāntikāḥ').
Rejection of several Vaibhāṣika real entities (reported in the Mahāvibhāṣā).
Teaching by illustrative stories and examples (dṛṣṭānta), as in Kumāralāta's Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā.
summary: The Dārṣṭāntikas are a dissenting current within the Sarvāstivāda named and refuted in the Mahāvibhāṣā; they are generally regarded as forerunners of (or identical with) the later Sautrāntikas.

name: Daruma school (Japan)

scholarly.text: late 12th c.; proscribed 1194 together with Eisai's movement; its members joined Dōgen's community in the 1240s

transmissions_received.what: Nōnin sent disciples to China (1189) who obtained a certificate from Zhuoan Deguang, an heir of Dahui
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition records; scholarly accounts

distinctive_positions: Awakening without a teacher (mushi dokugo); criticised by Eisai for rejecting precepts and practice (Kōzen gokoku ron).
summary: The first independent Zen movement in Japan, founded by Dainichi Nōnin, whose certificate came by proxy from Dahui's disciple Zhuoan Deguang; its monks later became leading disciples of Dōgen.

name: Dāyabhāga school of Dharmaśāstra (Bengal)
distinctive_positions: Ownership of the father's property passes to the heirs only on the father's death or fall (uparamasvatva), not by birth.
Heirship follows capacity to benefit the deceased by ancestral offerings (piṇḍa).
summary: The Bengal tradition following Jīmūtavāhana's Dāyabhāga (c. 12th c.), which argues against the Mitākṣarā on inheritance and the basis of kinship.

queries: Dayabhaga Mitakshara inheritance by birth death
checks.note: The Dāyabhāga (eBhāratī, with commentary) argues that ownership arises only on the father's death or fall: 'uparama eva svatvam', 'pitṛmaraṇakālīnam'. It also makes heirship follow benefit through piṇḍa offerings. Wikipedia's Dāyabhāga article agrees on both points. The c. 12th c. date matches the tch:jimutavahana check.

name: Dhammakāya meditation tradition (Vijjā Dhammakāya; Wat Paknam)
regions: Bangkok (Wat Paknam Bhasicharoen; Wat Phra Dhammakaya, Pathum Thani)

tradition.text: Luang Pu Sodh Candasaro rediscovered the Dhammakāya knowledge in 1917 (the tradition's account: the method had been lost some 500 years after the Buddha)

scholarly.text: 1910s onward; Wat Phra Dhammakaya founded 1970

transmissions_received.what: bodily centres and syllable recitation
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis of continuity with borān kammaṭṭhāna

distinctive_positions: The mind is brought to rest at the centre of the body (the seventh base, two finger-breadths above the navel) while visualizing a bright crystal sphere and reciting 'sammā arahaṃ'.
Successive refined inner bodies appear, culminating in the Dhammakāya, the Buddha-body within.
Nibbāna is described as a true self (attā) — a teaching contested by other Thai Theravāda scholars.
summary: The Thai meditation tradition founded by Luang Pu Sodh Candasaro (1884–1959) of Wat Paknam, teaching concentration at the body's centre leading to the inner Dhammakāya; continued by Wat Paknam and by the Wat Phra Dhammakaya movement.

name: Dhammayuttika Nikāya (Dhammayut order)

tradition.text: founded by the monk-prince Vajirañāṇa (later King Mongkut) in the 1830s

scholarly.text: founded c. 1833; royal recognition later

transmissions_given.what: strict Vinaya discipline; the early forest masters were Dhammayut
