distinctive_positions: Reform of monastic discipline according to the Pali Vinaya (as read by the reformers), with a renewed Mon ordination lineage.
Emphasis on Pali textual study and suspicion of practices not found in the canon (a factor in the decline of borān kammaṭṭhāna).
summary: The reformist Thai monastic order founded by Vajirañāṇa (King Mongkut) in the 1830s; the order of the early Thai Forest masters.

name: The school of Dhanvantari (Dhānvantara-sampradāya, the surgeons' line)
distinctive_positions: Surgery (śalya) is the first and foremost of the eight limbs, being quick in effect and using instruments, knives, caustics and cautery (Su Sū 1.17-18).
The person treated is the union of the five elements with the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).
Knowledge must be both textual and practical; the surgeon learns by practice on models (Su Sū 9).
summary: The lineage of Dhanvantari, born as King Divodāsa of Kāśī, who taught Suśruta and his fellow students with surgery as the root (Su Sū 1.3-21). Caraka names its specialists 'the Dhānvantarīyas' (Ca Ci 5.44, 5.63).

name: Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth (Chhattisgarhī śākhā)

tradition.text: Kabīr promised Dharamdās a line of forty-two generations (vaṃś) of ācāryas

scholarly.text: the line's texts and seats are dated by scholars to the 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: A hereditary line of householder ācāryas beginning with Dharamdās's son Cūṛāmaṇi (Muktāmaṇi) Nām.
The Anurāg Sāgar's cosmogony of Kāl Nirañjan and the Sat Puruṣ, and the caukā ritual with the pān-parvānā (betel-leaf 'passport') for souls.
Kabīr as the Sat Puruṣ incarnate.
summary: The largest branch of the Kabīr Panth, centred in Chhattisgarh among many lower-caste and tribal followers, led by a hereditary line of ācāryas from Dharamdās.

name: Dharmaguptaka
regions: China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan (through its Vinaya)

tradition.text: Split from the Mahīśāsaka, claiming Maudgalyāyana as its teacher (Vasumitra); from the Mahiṃsāsaka (Dīpavaṃsa)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE – ; living through its Vinaya

transmissions_received.what: descent in Vasumitra's and the Pali lists
transmissions_received.evidence: Samayabhedoparacanacakra; Dīpavaṃsa 5

transmissions_given.what: the Four-Part Vinaya (Sifen lü) as the standard monastic code of East Asian Buddhism; the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī ordination lineages of China, Korea, Vietnam and Taiwan
the Four-Part Vinaya ordination brought to Japan by Jianzhen (Ganjin)

distinctive_positions: Though the Buddha is included in the Saṅgha, a gift to the Buddha yields greater fruit than a gift to the Saṅgha; offerings to stūpas bring great fruit (Vasumitra).
The liberation of the Buddha and of the disciples is one, though their paths differ (Vasumitra).
Outsiders (non-Buddhists) cannot obtain the five superknowledges (Vasumitra; low confidence).
The Four-Part Vinaya: 250 rules for bhikṣus and 348 for bhikṣuṇīs.
A canon in which the Dīrghāgama (T1) is affiliated with this school; a Bodhisattva Piṭaka and a Dhāraṇī Piṭaka are reported in its canon (low confidence).
summary: The Dharmaguptaka, a Sthavira-derived school of the north-west, is known above all for its Four-Part Vinaya (Sifen lü), translated into Chinese in 410–412, which became the monastic code of East Asian Buddhism and carries the only continuous bhikṣuṇī ordination lineage. The Chinese Dīrghāgama and the earliest Gāndhārī manuscripts (British Library) are associated with it.

name: Dharmaśāstra (the science of dharma; Dharmasūtra and Smṛti)
regions: Āryāvarta and Madhyadeśa (the land defined in MDh 2.17–24 and VDh 1.8–9)

tradition.text: Manu Svāyambhuva received dharma from Svayambhū at the beginning of creation and taught it to the seers through Bhṛgu (MDh 1.58–60); each world-age has its own authoritative code (Parāśarasmṛti 1.24: Manu in Kṛta, Gautama in Tretā, Śaṅkha-Likhita in Dvāpara, Parāśara in Kali).

scholarly.text: Dharmasūtras c. 3rd–1st c. BCE; metrical smṛtis c. 2nd c. BCE – 1st millennium CE; commentaries and digests c. 8th–18th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Dharmasūtras as the dharma-portion of the Kalpasūtras
transmissions_received.evidence: Āpastamba and Baudhāyana Kalpasūtras contain their Dharmasūtras

transmissions_received.what: the Brāhmaṇa doctrines of the debts (TS 6.3.10.5; ŚB 1.7.2.1), the five great sacrifices (ŚB 11.5.6.1) and upanayana (ŚB 11.5.4)
transmissions_received.evidence: direct parallels

transmissions_received.what: rules of interpretation (nyāya) applied to conflicting smṛti texts in the commentaries and digests
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit use of Mīmāṃsā maxims by Medhātithi, Vijñāneśvara, Jīmūtavāhana

transmissions_received.what: the teaching of the self and its knowledge placed at the summit of dharma (MDh 12.85; YS 1.8; ĀpDh 1.8.22–23)
transmissions_received.evidence: doctrinal parallels

transmissions_given.what: saṃskāra, śrāddha and prāyaścitta rules re-used and expanded in the Purāṇas
rules for the renouncer (MDh 6; VDh 10; YS 3) taken up by the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads and the ascetic orders

distinctive_positions: The sources of dharma are the whole Veda, the recollection (smṛti) and conduct of those who know it, the practice of good people (sadācāra) and what satisfies oneself (MDh 2.6, 2.12; YS 1.7 adds desire born of right intention); where the Veda is silent, the agreement of those who know dharma is authoritative (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2).

Dharma is specified by class (varṇa) and life-stage (āśrama); alongside these stands a dharma common to all four classes — non-injury, truth, not stealing, purity and restraint of the senses (MDh 10.63; YS 1.122).
A person is born owing three debts — to the seers, the gods and the ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5; four in ŚB 1.7.2.1) — and must discharge them before setting the mind on liberation (MDh 6.35–37).

The householder supports the other orders as air supports living beings (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90); whether the celibate orders are a free choice, a sequence, or not Vedic at all is disputed within the tradition (GDh 3.1, 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27; VDh 7.3; MDh 6).
Life is consecrated by rites (saṃskāra) from conception to cremation, and sins are removed by expiation, confession, remorse, austerity and recitation (MDh 2.26–28; 11.227–229).
The highest dharma is seeing the self by yoga (YS 1.8); knowledge of the self is the highest of all practices, by which immortality is won (MDh 12.85).
Acts of mind, speech and body bear fruit in rebirth, and the three guṇas govern the resulting destinies (MDh 12.3–51).
Dharma differs from age to age (MDh 1.81–86; Parāśarasmṛti 1.24); later authorities list practices forbidden in the Kali age (kalivarjya).

The customs of regions, castes and families are authoritative where they do not conflict with the Veda (GDh 11.20; ĀśGS 1.7.1); whether regional customs that the śiṣṭas disapprove of are valid is debated (BDh 1.1.2.1–8).
summary: The literature and learned tradition that set out dharma — ritual, moral, social and legal duty — for the twice-born and for all: the Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha; the metrical smṛtis of Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Viṣṇu, Parāśara, Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana; and the commentaries and digests (nibandha) built on them. Its core teachings are the four classes and four life-stages, the four aims of life, the three debts, the five great daily sacrifices, the rites of passage from conception to cremation, the ancestral offerings, purity and impurity, expiation, kingship and law, and — at its summit — self-knowledge and liberation.

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: The tradition account was found at MDh 1.58–60: Svayambhū taught the śāstra to Manu, Manu taught Marīci and the other sages, and 'this Bhṛgu will recite it to you'. ParSm 1.24 was also found (Manu in Kṛta, Gautama in Tretā, Śaṅkha-Likhita in Dvāpara, Parāśara in Kali). The distinctive positions rest on MDh 2.6, 2.12, 10.63, YS 1.7, 1.122, TS 6.3.10.5, ŚB 1.7.2.1, and ĀpDh 1.1.1.2 ('dharmajñasamayaḥ pramāṇam'). All of these were text-located. The scholarly span matches the dates in the checked source entries.

name: Dharmottarīya
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya (Vasumitra; Dīpavaṃsa); its own doctrines are not separately recorded.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in all the major lists; no separate texts survive.

name: Digambara

tradition.text: the Digambaras regard themselves as continuing the original naked practice of Mahāvīra; their account traces the division to Bhadrabāhu's migration south during a twelve-year famine (Maurya period)

scholarly.text: a distinct Digambara identity is attested from roughly the early centuries CE; the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kundakunda's works are dated by scholars between the 2nd and 8th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Complete nudity is required of the fully renounced monk; one who wears clothes cannot attain liberation
Liberation is not possible in a female body; a woman must first be reborn as a man (nuns, āryikās, keep a white robe and are ranked with the most advanced laity)
The omniscient does not take food (no kavalāhāra); hunger and thirst are among the eighteen faults absent in the Jina
The original Aṅgas and Pūrvas were gradually lost; only portions survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa; the Śvetāmbara Āgamas are not accepted
Scripture is arranged in four anuyogas (narrative, cosmological-karmic, conduct, substance)
In Mahāvīra's life: no embryo transfer, sixteen dreams of the mother, and no marriage; Mallinātha was a man
summary: The 'sky-clad' branch of the Jain tradition, whose monks go naked and eat once a day from their hands. It holds that the Aṅgas were lost and bases itself on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa and the works of Kundakunda, Umāsvāti and later ācāryas; it denies liberation in a female body and eating by the omniscient. It includes the Bīsapantha and Terāpantha modes of worship and the aniconic Tāraṇapantha.

name: Dilun school (Chinese 'Daśabhūmika treatise' school)

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE; absorbed into Huayan by the 7th c.

transmissions_given.what: the study of the Daśabhūmika and the nature of the ālaya

distinctive_positions: Founded on Vasubandhu's commentary on the Daśabhūmika translated by Bodhiruci and Ratnamati (508–511).
Split (as usually reported) into a northern branch holding the ālaya to be defiled and a southern branch (Huiguang) identifying the pure aspect of the ālaya with true suchness / buddha-nature.
summary: An early Chinese Yogācāra-derived exegetical tradition centred on Vasubandhu's Daśabhūmika commentary, later absorbed into Huayan.

name: Drāviḍa Saṅgha

tradition.text: founded by Vajranandi, a pupil of Pūjyapāda, at Madhurā (Madurai) according to the Darśanasāra

scholarly.text: c. 5th–13th c. CE in Tamil country and Karnataka

distinctive_positions: charged by the Darśanasāra with allowing monks to eat seeds and to engage in trade and agriculture for temples (low confidence)
summary: A southern Digambara lineage associated with Vajranandi and the Tamil country, criticized in the Darśanasāra; later inscriptions treat it as a respected Digambara saṅgha.

name: Dudjom Tersar (the New Treasures of Dudjom)

scholarly.text: late 19th - 20th c.

distinctive_positions: Treasures of Dudjom Lingpa and of his reincarnation Dudjom Jigdral Yeshe Dorje, including Dzogchen instructions on 'buddhahood without meditation'.
summary: The recent treasure lineage of Dudjom Lingpa (1835-1904) and Dudjom Rinpoche Jigdral Yeshe Dorje (1904-1987), widely practised in exile communities.

name: Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda; the Mādhva sampradāya)
alt_names: Brahma-sampradāya (its place in the later scheme of four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas)

tradition.text: the tradition traces the teaching to Nārāyaṇa (as Haṃsa) through Brahmā and a line of teachers; Vyāsa (an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa) fixed it in the Brahmasūtras; in the Kali age Madhva, the third avatāra of Vāyu, re-proclaimed it

scholarly.text: founded by Madhva in the 13th c. CE; living

transmissions_received.what: the Brahmasūtras as the root text, commented on by Madhva
transmissions_received.evidence: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, Anuvyākhyāna, Nyāyavivaraṇa, Aṇubhāṣya

transmissions_received.what: ten principal Upaniṣads, read as teaching difference and Viṣṇu's supremacy
transmissions_received.evidence: Madhva's ten Upaniṣad bhāṣyas

transmissions_received.what: the Pañcarātra accepted as valid scripture (sadāgama); mantra and worship lore
transmissions_received.evidence: Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1 (list of sadāgamas); Tantrasārasaṅgraha

transmissions_received.what: the Mahābhārata and the Gītā as scripture of the highest rank
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya; Gītābhāṣya; Gītātātparya-nirṇaya

transmissions_received.what: Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas insofar as they agree with the sadāgamas
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhāgavata-tātparya-nirṇaya; Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1

transmissions_received.what: authorless Veda, intrinsic validity, the marks of purport (upakrama etc.) — adapted
transmissions_received.evidence: Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1; Rāghavendra's Bhāṭṭasaṅgraha

transmissions_received.what: debate theory and logical vocabulary — adopted in part and criticized
transmissions_received.evidence: Kathālakṣaṇa; Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Vyāsatīrtha's Tarkatāṇḍava

transmissions_given.what: Dvaita doctrine (Hari's supremacy, gradation of souls) sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas, several of them disciples of Mādhva ascetics (Śrīpādarāja, Vyāsatīrtha, Vādirāja)
the Gauḍīya tradition claims descent from Madhva's line through Mādhavendra Purī; the claim is disputed (see brw:dvaita-gaudiya-parampara)

distinctive_positions: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa, Hari) alone is independent (svatantra); Lakṣmī, all souls, matter, time and the Veda are dependent (paratantra) on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1; Tattvaviveka 1).
Five real and eternal differences (pañca-bheda) — God–soul, God–matter, soul–soul, soul–matter, matter–matter — hold in every state, including liberation (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 1.68–71).
The world is real (satya); the Advaita doctrines of māyā, the world's falsity (mithyātva) and the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) are refuted (the ten prakaraṇas; Nyāyāmṛta).

Souls are innately graded (tāratamya) and fall into three classes — fit for liberation (mukti-yogya), ever-transmigrating (nitya-saṃsārin), fit for blinding darkness (tamo-yogya); a soul's fitness is beginningless and unalterable (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 4–7; MBTN 1.86–95).
Liberation is the soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss, graded even among the liberated (ānanda-tāratamya), in eternal difference from and dependence on Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu is full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of every defect; 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities; his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are not different from him (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 3).
Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge there is no abundant grace (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.1).
Bhakti is firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness (MBTN 1.85); it continues in liberation as eternal bliss (MBTN 1.104).

Three means of valid knowledge — perception, inference, authoritative word; perception is sevenfold, the witness (sākṣin) plus six senses; what the sākṣin establishes is never sublated (Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Anuvyākhyāna).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa) is the highest of souls; grace descends through the higher beings; Madhva is Vāyu's third avatāra after Hanumān and Bhīma (MBTN 32.162–166).
God is the efficient cause of the world, not its material cause; prakṛti is the material cause.

All words, letters and scriptures in their primary sense designate Viṣṇu; the Veda is authorless; valid scripture (sadāgama) is the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas that agree with them (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God — dependent on and similar to its original (bimba), and eternally distinct from it.
Chāndogya 6.8.7 is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), taught nine times with examples to show difference (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
summary: The Vedānta school founded by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called by its adherents Tattvavāda, 'the doctrine of reality'. It teaches that Viṣṇu alone is the independent reality, that souls and matter are real, dependent and eternally distinct from him and from one another (the five differences), that souls are innately graded, and that liberation — the soul's enjoyment of its own bliss in Viṣṇu's presence — comes only by his grace, won through knowledge and devotion. Its classical literature runs from Madhva's thirty-seven works through Jayatīrtha's commentaries and Vyāsatīrtha's polemics to Rāghavendra; it is carried by ascetic maṭhas (the eight of Uḍupi with their biennial rotation of Kṛṣṇa worship, and the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) and was sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas.
notes: The tradition's teacher line before Madhva (the 'Haṃsa paramparā': Haṃsa-Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the Sanaka group, Durvāsas, then a line of ascetics ending in Acyutaprekṣa) is recalled here only in outline; the intermediate names are not listed because they were not verified in this pass. A traditional verse likens the doctrine to a tree: seed sown by Vyāsa in the soil of śruti, sprouted by Madhva, branched by Jayatīrtha, leaved by Vyāsarāja, flowered by Vijayīndra and fruited by Rāghavendra (quoted as a preface verse in a modern edition in the raw_etexts corpus; author not identified). Further maṭhas (Śrīpādarāja maṭha at Mulbagal, Subrahmaṇya, Bhīmanakaṭṭe, Bhaṇḍārakeri; the Gauḍa Sārasvata Mādhva maṭhas of Kāśī and Gokarṇa-Partagāḷī) are mentioned without separate entries — details not verified.

name: Dvaitādvaita (Nimbārka Sampradāya)

tradition.text: founded by Haṃsa (Viṣṇu) and transmitted through the four Kumāras and Nārada to Nimbārka in a former age

scholarly.text: Nimbārka variously dated 7th–13th c.; many place him c. 12th–13th c.

transmissions_given.what: Keśava Kāśmīrin's Kramadīpikā (Kṛṣṇa-mantra liturgy) used in Gauḍīya ritual codes (low confidence)
the Haridāsī tradition of Svāmī Haridās is sometimes affiliated to the Nimbārka line (contested)

distinctive_positions: Natural (svābhāvika) difference-and-non-difference: souls and world are both different and non-different from Brahman by their very nature, like sun and rays or snake and coils (BS 3.2.27).
Three realities: cit (souls), acit (non-conscious: prākṛta, aprākṛta, kāla) and Īśvara.
Brahman is Kṛṣṇa, free of all faults and a mass of auspicious qualities, worshipped together with Rādhā on his left (Daśaślokī 4–5): yugala-upāsanā.
The soul is atomic, a knower, a part (aṃśa) of the Lord and wholly dependent on him; infinite in number.
Five things to be known (arthapañcaka): the worshipped, the worshipper, the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, the obstacles.
Five means (upāya): karma, vidyā, upāsanā (dhyāna), prapatti (surrender) and gurūpasatti (surrender to the teacher).
Liberation is attainment of the Lord's nature and service after death, with difference preserved; grace arises for the humble (Daśaślokī 9).
summary: The Vaiṣṇava Vedānta of Nimbārka: Brahman as Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā, and souls and matter as his naturally different-yet-non-different powers. Its root texts are Nimbārka's brief Brahma Sūtra commentary (Vedāntapārijātasaurabha) and the ten-verse Daśaślokī, expanded by Śrīnivāsa's Vedāntakaustubha and Keśava Kāśmīrin's Kaustubhaprabhā; Śrī Bhaṭṭa and Harivyāsadeva gave it Braj-language devotional poetry. It counts itself one of the four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas (the Sanakādi/Kumāra line) and lives today with seats at Salemabad and in Braj.

name: Dzogchen (the Great Perfection, Atiyoga)

tradition.text: taught by Samantabhadra beyond time; first taught among humans by Garab Dorje in Oḍḍiyāna, then by Mañjuśrīmitra, Śrī Siṃha and Jñānasūtra; brought to Tibet by Vairocana, Vimalamitra and Padmasambhava in the 8th c.

scholarly.text: Great Perfection literature attested from the late 8th-10th c. (Dunhuang fragments incl. the Cuckoo of Awareness); the Seventeen Tantras and Nyingthig surface in the 11th-12th c.

transmissions_given.what: Nyingthig instruction adopted by Kagyu masters (e.g. the Third Karmapa Rangjung Dorje)

distinctive_positions: The ground (gzhi) is primordial purity (ka dag) and spontaneous presence (lhun grub); its three aspects are essence (ngo bo: empty), nature (rang bzhin: luminous) and compassion (thugs rje: all-pervading).
Awareness (rig pa) is distinguished from ordinary mind (sems): the path is recognizing awareness, not fabricating a meditative state.
Three series: mind (sems sde), space (klong sde) and instruction (man ngag sde); the Heart-essence (snying thig) belongs to the innermost secret cycle of the instruction series.
Cutting through (khregs chod) to primordial purity; direct crossing (thod rgal) of spontaneous presence through four visions; the fruit can include the rainbow body ('ja' lus).
Thoughts self-liberate (rang grol) in awareness; effort and contrivance are called a sickness (Kunjed Gyalpo).
Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have one ground and two paths: recognition (Samantabhadra) and non-recognition (beings).
summary: The Great Perfection: the Nyingma (and Bön) teaching that the mind's nature, awareness (rig pa), is already perfect buddhahood — empty in essence, luminous in nature, all-pervading in responsiveness — and that liberation comes from recognizing it through a master's introduction and resting in it, rather than by constructing it. Transmitted through Garab Dorje, Mañjuśrīmitra, Śrī Siṃha, Jñānasūtra, Vimalamitra, Padmasambhava and Vairocana; organized in three series and systematized by Longchenpa.

name: Early Buddhism (the Dhamma-Vinaya of the Nikāyas)
alt_names: the teaching of the Nikāyas and Āgamas

tradition.text: The Buddha's teaching career of 45 years ending with the parinibbāna in 544/543 BCE (Theravāda Buddhist-era reckoning)

scholarly.text: the Buddha's lifetime and the first generations of disciples, c. 5th–4th c. BCE (parinibbāna variously dated c. 486 or c. 400 BCE); the Nikāya/Āgama literature took shape orally c. 5th–3rd c. BCE

transmissions_received.what: the wandering ascetic life (pabbajjā), the vocabulary of kamma, rebirth and liberation, meditative attainments learned from Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta (MN 26, MN 36), and the practice of the rains retreat
transmissions_received.evidence: MN 26 and MN 36 narrate the bodhisatta's training under the two teachers of the formless attainments; the Buddha is called samaṇa Gotama

transmissions_received.what: vocabulary re-defined in a new sense: brāhmaṇa (the true brahmin is the one who is pure in conduct), tevijjā (the three knowledges), brahmavihāra, the sacrifice re-interpreted as giving and virtue (DN 5), and deities such as Brahmā and Sakka accepted as beings within saṃsāra
transmissions_received.evidence: DN 5, DN 13, MN 93, MN 98 / Snp 3.9, Dhp 26 (Brāhmaṇavagga)

transmissions_given.what: the Dhamma-Vinaya as preserved in Pali
the Āgamas and Vinaya transmitted in Sanskrit; the Abhidharma built on the mātikās
the sūtras and a Vinaya after the first schism
the four truths, dependent origination, the thirty-seven wings, the jhānas, retained and re-read as the 'śrāvaka' path
shared meditative and kleśa vocabulary (see the borrowings of U10)

distinctive_positions: A middle way that avoids both devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification (SN 56.11).
Four noble truths: suffering, its origin in craving, its cessation, and the noble eightfold path leading to it (SN 56.11).
The five aggregates are impermanent, suffering and not-self: 'this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self' (SN 22.59).
Dependent origination: 'when this exists, that comes to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases' (SN 12.21, MN 38); whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma (MN 28).
Kamma is intention (cetanā) (AN 6.63); beings are owners and heirs of their deeds (MN 135).
Nibbāna — the destruction of greed, hatred and delusion (SN 38.1), the deathless, the unconditioned — is to be realized in this very life.
The gradual training of virtue, concentration and wisdom (MN 27, DN 2; AN 3.88) culminating in the knowledge of the destruction of the effluents.

Certain questions (whether the world is eternal or finite, whether the soul is the same as the body, whether the Tathāgata exists after death) are set aside as not conducive to liberation (MN 63, MN 72).
Rejection of the authority of the Veda and of purity by birth: one becomes a brahmin by deeds, not birth (Snp 3.9, MN 93, DN 27).
After the Teacher's death the Dhamma and Vinaya he taught are to be the teacher; the disciple is to be an island and refuge to himself, with the Dhamma as island (DN 16).
A fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen (DN 16); women can realize the fruits of the path from stream-entry to arahantship (Cullavagga 10.1).
summary: The teaching and community of the Buddha Gotama and his first generations of disciples as preserved in the Pali Nikāyas and Vinaya (with parallels in the Chinese Āgamas and the other early schools' Vinayas): the four noble truths, not-self, dependent origination, kamma and rebirth, and a gradual path of virtue, meditative concentration and wisdom leading to nibbāna in this life. As a label this is an umbrella for what all the early schools share; the tradition itself speaks of 'the Dhamma and Vinaya' (dhammavinaya) taught by the Buddha.
notes: 'Early Buddhism' is used here as the umbrella for the shared Nikāya/Āgama teaching; the living carrier in Pali is lin:theravada, the other early schools belong to U38. Status 'absorbed': it survives through its descendant schools. No parent is set so that it counts as its own root in convergence counts; its śramaṇa milieu is recorded under transmissions_received.

name: East Mountain teaching
regions: Huangmei (Hubei), Mount Shuangfeng and East Mountain

scholarly.text: c. 624–674 (Daoxin and Hongren's communities)

distinctive_positions: Guarding the one (shouyi 守一) and 'one-practice samādhi' (Daoxin).
Guarding the original true mind (shou benzhen xin 守本真心) (Hongren).
Large settled communities combining meditation and labour.
summary: The communities of the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs Daoxin and Hongren at Huangmei, from which both the Northern school and Huineng's line claimed descent.

name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma

tradition.text: Śaṅkaradeva 1449–1568

scholarly.text: late 15th – 16th c.; sattra network from the 16th–17th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as supreme scripture
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation throughout

transmissions_received.what: a non-dual reading of the Bhāgavata through Śrīdhara Svāmin's commentary
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis; tradition cites Śrīdhara (verify)

distinctive_positions: Single refuge (eka-śaraṇa) in Kṛṣṇa alone: no other deity is worshipped, and Vedic ritual and animal sacrifice are rejected.
The name (nāma) is the chief means; of the nine forms of devotion, hearing (śravaṇa) and singing (kīrtana) are foremost.
The four real things (cāri vastu): the name, God (deva), the guru and the community of devotees (bhakta).
Devotion is that of the servant (dāsya); Rādhā is not worshipped and the erotic mood is not cultivated.
The true devotee does not desire even liberation.
In the nāmghar and sattra a sacred book — the Bhāgavata (or the Kīrtana-ghoṣā) — sits on the guru-āsana in place of an image.
Initiation (śaraṇ) is open to all castes, tribes and to Muslims; the sattras house celibate (kevaliyā) and married devotees.
Drama (bhāonā), song (bargīt) and dance are forms of worship.
summary: The Ekaśaraṇa ('single refuge') Dharma of Assam, founded by Śaṅkaradeva (1449–1568 by tradition) and continued by Mādhavadeva, teaches exclusive servant-devotion to Kṛṣṇa through his name, the guru and the congregation, without images, other gods or Vedic rites. Its scriptures — the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, the Nām-ghoṣā, the bargīts and one-act plays — are sung and performed in village nāmghars and in the sattras (monasteries), which after Mādhavadeva divided into four saṃhatis.

name: Ekavyavahārika
distinctive_positions: All dharmas are mere names (reported etymology: 'one utterance'); in Vasumitra its doctrines are said to agree with the Mahāsāṃghika (low confidence).
summary: An early branch of the Mahāsāṃghika in all lists.

name: Epic teaching (the Mahābhārata's Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Mokṣadharma milieu)
regions: northern India — the epics' settings: Kurukṣetra, Hāstinapura, Indraprastha, Mithilā (Videha), Naimiṣa forest, Badarī, Ayodhyā

tradition.text: the Kurukṣetra war and Vyāsa's composition at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali yugas (Kali traditionally from 3102 BCE); the Rāmāyaṇa in the earlier Tretā yuga

scholarly.text: the epic teaching layers c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the imperishable self and Brahman, the hierarchy of senses, mind and intellect, the paths after death, and whole verses
the sacrificial frame (yajña) and the wheel of sacrifice, reinterpreted inwardly
transmissions_received.evidence: BhG 3.9–16; 4.24–33; Anugītā 14.20–24 (the inner sacrifice of the senses)

transmissions_received.what: the enumeration of principles and the discrimination of puruṣa from prakṛti, in Kapila's line
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account: Pañcaśikha, 'Āsuri's first disciple', teaches Janadeva Janaka (MBh 12.211.6–18); Kapila named as proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60)

transmissions_given.what: the Bhagavad Gītā as the smṛti-prasthāna commented on by every Vedānta school
pre-classical Sāṃkhya enumerations (24/25/26 principles) — on the scholarly account, precursors of Īśvarakṛṣṇa's system
epic yoga vocabulary: dhāraṇā, the five faults of yoga, yoga-power (yogabala), the first dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra
cosmology of the ages and dissolution, lists of the Lord's manifestations, dharma teaching
the Gītā through Jñāneśvar's Jñāneśvarī
Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and the Anuśāsana's teaching on gifts, fasts and funerary offerings

distinctive_positions: Action is unavoidable for the embodied; what binds is attachment to the fruit, not action itself (BhG 3.5, 2.47, 18.11).
Several disciplines — knowledge (sāṃkhya), disciplined action (yoga), meditation and devotion — lead to one goal; 'one who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, sees' (BhG 3.3, 5.4–5, 13.24–25).
The self in the body is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.12–30).
Prakṛti with its three guṇas is the agent of all action; the puruṣa experiences and witnesses (BhG 3.27, 13.19–22).
The principles are counted as 24 with the puruṣa as 25th, and the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya dialogues add a 26th, the awakened (MBh 12.294–296, 12.306).
Sāṃkhya and Yoga differ in method — Yoga relies on direct perception and argues that without a Lord no one is freed; Sāṃkhya relies on the teaching of the śāstra — yet both are true (MBh 12.289.3–7).
Dharma is subtle: conduct, not birth alone, is said to make a brāhmaṇa (3.177.16, 12.181.10), while the duties of the varṇas are also upheld (BhG 18.41–48; 12.60).
Non-cruelty (ānṛśaṃsya) and non-violence (ahiṃsā) are called the highest dharma (3.297.55; 1.11.12; 13.116), alongside the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war (BhG 2.31–33).
Liberation (brahmanirvāṇa, entering the Lord) can be won in this life by one whose mind rests in equality (BhG 5.19, 5.26, 2.72).

Time (kāla), nature (svabhāva), fate (daiva) and human effort are debated as causes; the Gītā counts daiva as one of five causes of action (18.14) and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not succeed without effort (13.6.7).
Dharma, artha and kāma are one whole (trivarga) grounded in dharma; 'from dharma come artha and kāma — why is it not practised?' (18.5.49).
summary: The teaching layer of the two Sanskrit epics, above all the Mahābhārata: the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhīṣma's instruction in the Śāntiparvan (Rājadharma, Āpaddharma, Mokṣadharma) and Anuśāsanaparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, Mārkaṇḍeya's discourses, and the dharma teaching of the Rāmāyaṇa. It is not a school with a single doctrine but a milieu in which Upaniṣadic, early Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Vedic ritual, devotional (Bhāgavata) and ascetic ideas are set side by side in dialogues, and which later schools (Vedānta, classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the Purāṇas, bhakti traditions) all claim as authority.

checks.note: The texts, dialogues, teachers and transmission statements it lists are confirmed in the local critical text. As the entry itself says, "epic teaching" is a descriptive grouping (a milieu), not a recognized school or order, so its "founder" (Vyāsa) and "status" are the unit's construction and cannot be confirmed as such. Dating accounts kept as entered.

notes: Owned by U05. 'Lineage' here names a teaching milieu (a body of texts and dialogues), not an initiatory succession; the tradition itself names chains of transmission within it (BhG 4.1–3; 12.211; 12.336 for the Sātvata dharma).

name: Fayan house

tradition.text: founded by Fayan Wenyi (885–958)

scholarly.text: 10th c.; faded in the Song (11th c.)

transmissions_given.what: Goryeo monks trained under Yongming Yanshou (tradition says 36)

distinctive_positions: Use of Huayan categories (the six characteristics) within Chan (Rentian yanmu).
'Not knowing is most intimate' (Luohan Guichen to Fayan).
Harmony of Chan with the scriptural teachings and with Pure Land practice (Yongming Yanshou).
summary: The last of the Five Houses to form, from Fayan Wenyi (885–958) in the line of Xuansha and Luohan Guichen; it drew on Huayan doctrine, produced Yongming Yanshou's synthesis of Chan and the teachings, and faded by the 11th century.

name: Fuke school

tradition.text: traced to Puhua, Linji's eccentric companion, and brought to Japan by Shinchi Kakushin (13th c.)

scholarly.text: organised as a Rinzai-affiliated order of mendicant shakuhachi players (komusō) in the Edo period; abolished 1871; revived by lay players

distinctive_positions: Blowing the bamboo flute (suizen 吹禪) as meditation.
summary: A Japanese order of mendicant flute-playing monks (komusō) that traced itself to the Tang eccentric Puhua; its origin legend is regarded by scholars as late.

name: Garībdāsī panth

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Garībdās 1717–1778

distinctive_positions: Kabīr is the supreme God, who met Garībdās in person as a child.
Garībdās's Bāṇī (his 'Granth Sāhib') is the scripture.
summary: The panth of Garībdās of Chhuḍānī (1717–1778), a Jat householder saint who held Kabīr to be the supreme God and left a large collection of Sant verse.

name: Gāruḍa stream (tantras of Garuḍa)
distinctive_positions: Mantras of Garuḍa and associated goddesses (e.g. Tvaritā) used against snake-poison and other poisons.
Issued from the eastern (Tatpuruṣa) face of Sadāśiva (Kāmika pūrva 1.21, 1.24; Śrīkaṇṭhīya as quoted by Jayaratha).
summary: The Śaiva scriptural stream dealing with the neutralisation of poison by Garuḍa mantras; its lore survives partly in later compilations and in regional poison-healing traditions.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08; low certainty on which surviving texts belong here. The Pāñcarātra Kāśyapa Saṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava analogue (listed for cross-reference only). family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism (Caitanya Sampradāya; Acintya Bhedābheda)

tradition.text: Caitanya appeared at Navadvīpa on Phālguna Pūrṇimā, Śaka 1407 (1486 CE), as Kṛṣṇa himself in the mood of Rādhā

scholarly.text: founded early 16th c. CE; theology systematised by the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs c. 1530–1600

transmissions_received.what: a guru-paramparā through Mādhavendra Purī and Īśvara Purī traced to Madhva
transmissions_received.evidence: Kavikarṇapūra's Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā; Baladeva's Prameyaratnāvalī (tradition's account; contested by scholars)

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as the 'spotless Purāṇa' and supreme pramāṇa
transmissions_received.evidence: Tattvasandarbha

transmissions_received.what: the rasa framework of Bharata's school, recast as bhakti-rasa
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu; Ujjvalanīlamaṇi

transmissions_received.what: deity-worship and initiation ritual
transmissions_received.evidence: Haribhaktivilāsa

transmissions_given.what: Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa theology and the rasa vocabulary, reinterpreted (Sahajiyā use is rejected by the Gosvāmī orthodoxy)
Vaiṣṇava vocabulary of love and the name

distinctive_positions: Inconceivable difference-and-non-difference (acintya-bhedābheda) between the Lord and his powers (śakti), souls and world.
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself (svayaṃ bhagavān, BhP 1.3.28); the one non-dual reality is called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11), Bhagavān being fullest.
Three powers: internal (svarūpa/cit: sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), marginal (taṭasthā: the souls) and external (māyā).
Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa's hlādinī-śakti and the peak of love (mahābhāva); Caitanya is Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one form.
Pure devotion (uttamā bhakti) is the means and prema is the supreme goal (the 'fifth aim' beyond mokṣa).
Devotion is a rasa: five primary (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, mādhurya) and seven secondary rasas.
Practice (sādhana-bhakti) is rule-based (vaidhī) or spontaneous, following the Vraja residents (rāgānugā); stages from faith to love (BRS 1.4.15–16).

Congregational chanting of the name (nāma-saṅkīrtana), above all the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra, is the dharma of the Kali age; the name is non-different from Kṛṣṇa; ten offences against the name are to be avoided.
Rūpa and Viśvanātha hold paramour love (parakīyā) of the gopīs to be the highest; Jīva holds it to be svakīyā in truth — a recorded internal debate.
Caste and birth do not bar one from being a teacher of Kṛṣṇa (CC 2.8.128).
summary: The devotional tradition that grew from Caitanya (1486–1533) of Navadvīpa and Purī, his associates Nityānanda and Advaita, and the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana, who gave it a theology (Jīva's Ṣaṭ Sandarbha: acintya-bhedābheda), an aesthetics of devotion (Rūpa's Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi), a ritual code (Haribhaktivilāsa) and a hagiography (Caitanya Caritāmṛta, Caitanya Bhāgavata). Its practice centres on chanting the divine name, deity service, hearing the Bhāgavata, residence in Vraja and meditative participation in Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's eternal play.

name: Guiyang house

tradition.text: founded by Guishan Lingyou (771–853) and Yangshan Huiji (807–883)

scholarly.text: 9th c.; the first of the Five Houses to die out (by the late 10th c.)

distinctive_positions: Circle-figures (yuanxiang 圓相) as a teaching device, said to come from Nanyang Huizhong through Danyuan (Rentian yanmu).
Sudden awakening to principle with gradual removal of habit energies (Guishan).
summary: The earliest of the Five Houses, from Guishan Lingyou and his heir Yangshan Huiji in the line of Baizhang; known for the harmony of master and disciple and for circle-figures, it disappeared as a distinct line by the Song.

name: Nine Mountain Seon schools

scholarly.text: 9th–10th c.

distinctive_positions: Mostly Hongzhou-line transmissions from Mazu's heirs (Xitang Zhizang, Magu Baoche, Nanquan); one (Sumisan) from the Caodong line.
summary: The nine Seon monastic lineages founded in late Silla and early Goryeo by monks returning from Tang China, the roots of all later Korean Seon.

name: Haimavata
distinctive_positions: Vasumitra identifies the Haimavatas with the original Sthaviras, who withdrew to the Himalaya when the Sarvāstivāda became dominant.
The bodhisattva is an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) (Vasumitra; low confidence).
summary: A Sthavira branch that Vasumitra identifies with the original Elders displaced to the Himalaya by the Sarvāstivāda; listed among the later schools in the Pali chronicles.

name: Haridāsī sampradāya (Sakhī sampradāya)
regions: Vṛndāvana (Nidhivan; Bāṅke Bihārī temple; Ṭaṭṭī Sthān)

tradition.text: Bāṅke Bihārī manifested at Nidhivan in response to Svāmī Haridās's singing (16th c.)

scholarly.text: 16th c.

transmissions_given.what: Svāmī Haridās as the revered teacher of dhrupad singers (Tānsen) in north Indian music tradition

distinctive_positions: Worship in the grove (nikuñja-upāsanā): the natural, eternal pair (sahaja jorī) Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā play for ever in the inner grove, beyond birth, avatāra and separation.
The devotee witnesses and serves as a sakhī; Svāmī Haridās is held to be the sakhī Lalitā.
Singing (dhrupad, samāj-gāyan) is itself worship.
Two branches: householder gosvāmīs serving Bāṅke Bihārī, and strict renunciants (virakta) of the Ṭaṭṭī Sthān.
Its relation to the Nimbārka sampradāya is disputed (see dsp:haridasi-nimbarka-affiliation).
summary: The Haridāsī or Sakhī sampradāya of Vṛndāvana, founded by the singer-saint Svāmī Haridās (16th c.), whose songs brought forth the image of Bāṅke Bihārī. It contemplates the ever-united divine pair in the inner grove as their sakhī and treats music as worship.

name: Haṭha Yoga (the haṭha and rājayoga textual tradition)

tradition.text: taught by Ādinātha (Śiva) and handed down by Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the Mahāsiddhas (HYP 1.1–9)

scholarly.text: earliest text c. 11th c. CE (Amṛtasiddhi); classical compilation c. 1450 (Haṭhapradīpikā); large compilations 17th–18th c.; living in ascetic orders

transmissions_received.what: the doctrine of bindu, the moon and sun in the body, and the three practices mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha (Amṛtasiddhi)
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly: Mallinson & Szántó's edition of the Amṛtasiddhi shows a Buddhist tantric setting; the tradition itself names Ādinātha

transmissions_received.what: kuṇḍalinī, the cakras and the upward-moving śakti; transgressive vocabulary reinterpreted (HYP 3.47–49)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; scholarly reconstruction

transmissions_received.what: the lineage of Matsyendra and Gorakṣa, the Siddha ideal of the immortal body
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition account (HYP 1.4–9)

transmissions_received.what: the eight limbs (Dattātreyayogaśāstra, Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā, Yoga Yājñavalkya) and 'rājayoga' as the goal
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit: DYŚ 25–26 names Yājñavalkya's eight-limbed yoga; Jyotsnā on HYP 1.1 glosses rājayoga as asamprajñāta yoga

transmissions_received.what: the non-dual doctrine framing samādhi (HYP 4; Śiva Saṃhitā 1; Gheraṇḍa 7)
transmissions_received.evidence: HYP 4.58 quotes the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha; SS 1.67 uses adhyāropa-apavāda

transmissions_given.what: haṭha verses and doctrine in the southern recensions of the Yoga Upaniṣads
the practice manuals used by Nāth yogīs
haṭha practice among Daśanāmī ascetics
haṭha practice among Rāmānandī ascetics (the Jogapradīpikā)
the texts and practices behind modern postural yoga (recent)
HYP, GS and the kuṇḍalinī texts as the textual base of the school (recent)

distinctive_positions: Haṭha is taught solely for the sake of rājayoga (samādhi); rājayoga and haṭha each need the other (HYP 1.2, 2.76).
Mind and breath are bound together: stilling the breath stills the mind; when breath enters the central channel the mind dissolves (HYP 2.2, 4.21–25).
Death comes from the fall of bindu, life from its retention; the moon's nectar dripping from the palate is consumed by the sun at the navel (HYP 3.77, 3.88).
Kuṇḍalinī, the goddess asleep at the mouth of the central channel, must be awakened; then the knots are pierced and the mind becomes supportless (HYP 3.1–5).
Practice alone, not scriptural learning, sectarian garb or talk, is the cause of success; anyone may succeed — young, old, sick (HYP 1.64–66; DYŚ 37–42).
The four yogas — mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja — and the four stages — ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti (DYŚ 9–10; HYP 4.69).
Samādhi has many names that denote one state: rājayoga, unmanī, manonmanī, amaratva, laya, śūnyāśūnya, amanaska, sahaja, turyā (HYP 4.3–4).
Secrecy: the teaching is potent when kept secret and powerless when divulged; it must come from a guru (HYP 1.11, 3.129).
The body can be perfected and made to cheat time (kālavañcana) — a goal the Amanaska and some Vedāntins subordinate or reject.
summary: The textual tradition of haṭha ('force') yoga, from the Amṛtasiddhi (c. 11th c.) through the Haṭhapradīpikā (c. 1450) to the great 17th–18th-c. compilations. It teaches postures, breath-retention, seals and locks, cleansing acts and absorption in the inner sound as means to rājayoga, the mindless state of samādhi, and aims at liberation while living and the conquest of death. Its lineage is traced to Ādinātha (Śiva), Matsyendra and Gorakṣa; its texts circulated among Nāth, Daśanāmī, Rāmānandī and householder practitioners, and borrowed their metaphysics from Advaita, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and (at its origin) Buddhist tantric sources.
notes: U28 owns this lineage. Sectarian home: not a single sect — the texts are Śaiva (HYP, SS), Vaiṣṇava (DYŚ, GS), Vedic-orthodox (VS, YY), Śākta (ṢCN) and at the start Buddhist (Amṛtasiddhi). Family set to 'vedic' following the convention of the other Hindu tantric lineages; the Buddhist origin is recorded in transmissions_received.

name: Heze school
distinctive_positions: Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (as later summarised by Zongmi).
Knowing (zhi 知) — 'the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders' — as the substance of mind (Zongmi's report of Heze teaching).
No-thought (wunian) as the tenet; Huineng as the true Sixth Patriarch.
summary: The line of Heze Shenhui (684–758), who championed Huineng and sudden awakening; Zongmi counted himself its heir and systematised its teaching of numinous knowing.

name: Hongzhou school

scholarly.text: later 8th–9th c.; its heirs formed the Linji and Guiyang houses

distinctive_positions: 'This very mind is buddha' and 'neither mind nor buddha' (Mazu).
'The ordinary mind is the Way'; all activity is the function of buddha-nature.
Encounter dialogue: shouts, blows and everyday gestures as direct pointing.
summary: The school of Mazu Daoyi (709–788) in Jiangxi, which taught that the ordinary functioning mind is buddha and developed encounter dialogue; its heirs Baizhang, Huangbo, Linji, Guishan and Zhaozhou shaped classical Chan.

name: Hossō school (Japanese Faxiang)

scholarly.text: transmitted to Japan from 653 (Dōshō) onward; one of the six Nara schools; continues at Kōfukuji and Yakushiji

distinctive_positions: The Cheng weishi lun system of eight consciousnesses and five gotras, as transmitted from Xuanzang and Kuiji.
summary: The Japanese continuation of the Chinese Faxiang (Yogācāra) school, one of the six Nara schools, still maintained at Kōfukuji and Yakushiji.
notes: Scope overlaps U54 (Faxiang) and U55 (Japan); created here because no unit owns it.

name: Huanglong branch (of the Linji house)

scholarly.text: from Huanglong Huinan (1002–1069); faded in the 13th c.

transmissions_given.what: Eisai's transmission from Xu'an Huaichang (1191)

distinctive_positions: Huanglong's 'three barriers' (Buddha's hand, donkey's leg, one's birth-conditions).
Lettered Chan (wenzi Chan) of Juefan Huihong.
summary: The branch of the Linji house from Huanglong Huinan, prominent in the Northern Song and the source of Eisai's Rinzai transmission.

name: Jainism (Jaina dharma)
alt_names: Nirgrantha / Niggaṇṭha dharma (the 'knotless' ones; the name in Pali and early Prakrit sources)
regions: Magadha and Videha (Bihar) — the homeland of Mahāvīra

tradition.text: beginningless: the dharma is re-proclaimed by twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in every half of each time-cycle; in this descending half the first was Ṛṣabha and the last Mahāvīra (nirvāṇa traditionally 527 BCE)

scholarly.text: Pārśva (probably historical) c. 8th–7th c. BCE; Mahāvīra 6th–5th c. BCE (nirvāṇa dated by scholars between c. 527 and c. 425 BCE)

transmissions_received.what: the wider śramaṇa milieu of wandering renunciation, karma, rebirth and release shared with the Ājīvikas and Buddhists
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly account; the tradition itself regards its dharma as beginningless and not derived from any other

transmissions_given.what: Kundakunda's niścaya teaching, read by Banārsīdās and the Adhyātma circle
Tamil didactic verse forms and ethics (contested; see dsp:affiliation-of-tirukkural)

distinctive_positions: Innumerable individual souls (jīva), each by nature endowed with infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy, obscured by karma conceived as subtle matter that binds to the soul
No creator or controlling God; the universe (loka) is uncreated and eternal, running through endless ascending and descending time-cycles
Non-harm (ahiṃsā) toward all six classes of living beings, including earth-, water-, fire-, wind- and plant-bodied beings, as the pure and eternal law proclaimed by all Arhats
Liberation by right faith, right knowledge and right conduct (with austerity), by one's own effort; the liberated soul (siddha) rises to the summit of the universe and remains individual
Twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras ('ford-makers') in each half-cycle, who found the fourfold community (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen)
Many-sidedness (anekānta), standpoints (naya) and conditional predication (syādvāda) as the way of stating truth
Voluntary, peaceful death by gradual fasting (sallekhanā) as the culmination of a disciplined life — under strict conditions (restricted; summary only)
summary: The Jain tradition of the Jinas ('conquerors'), re-proclaimed in this era by Ṛṣabha and, last, by Vardhamāna Mahāvīra, a contemporary of the Buddha. It teaches the eternal reality of innumerable souls and of matter, karma as subtle matter binding the soul through passion and activity, and liberation through the three jewels, austerity and non-harm. It divided into the Śvetāmbara ('white-clad') and Digambara ('sky-clad') traditions, with the Yāpanīya between them, and within the Śvetāmbaras into image-worshipping and non-image-worshipping orders.

name: Jangter (the Northern Treasures)

tradition.text: treasures revealed by Rigdzin Gödem in 1366 at Zangzang Lhadrak

scholarly.text: 14th c.

distinctive_positions: Holds the Gongpa Zangthal ('Unobstructed Intention of Samantabhadra'), a Dzogchen treasure containing the Aspiration of Samantabhadra.
Seat: Dorje Drak monastery, one of the principal Nyingma monasteries.
summary: The tradition of the Northern Treasures revealed by Rigdzin Gödem (1337-1409), including the Dzogchen cycle Kuntuzangpo Gongpa Zangthal, later centred on Dorje Drak monastery.

name: Ji-shū (the Time school of Ippen)
regions: Japan (itinerant; head temple Shōjōkō-ji / Yugyō-ji, Fujisawa)

tradition.text: founded 1274 at Kumano, when Ippen received the oracle of the Kumano deity

scholarly.text: late 13th c.; organised as an order by Shinkyō after 1289

transmissions_received.what: Ippen's training under Shōtatsu, a disciple of Shōkū
transmissions_received.evidence: Ippen Hijiri-e

transmissions_received.what: Kūya's itinerant nenbutsu and 'casting off' as model
transmissions_received.evidence: Ippen Hijiri-e; Goroku

distinctive_positions: The birth of all beings was settled when Amida attained awakening ten kalpas ago; the name 'Namu Amida Butsu' itself is birth; the practitioner neither causes nor secures it.
Talismans (fusan) printed with the name are given to all, without choosing between those with and without faith, the pure and the impure (the Kumano oracle).
Casting off (sutete koso) everything — home, learning, even the thought of self and of faith — in the nenbutsu; a life of wandering (yugyō).
Dancing nenbutsu (odori nenbutsu) as joyful practice; recitation at the six times of day (whence 'Ji').
summary: The itinerant school of Ippen (1239–1289), who after the Kumano oracle of 1274 wandered through Japan distributing talismans inscribed 'Namu Amida Butsu — birth assured — six hundred thousand people' and leading dancing nenbutsu; he burned his writings at death. His successor Shinkyō organised the Ji-shū order, whose head bears the title Yugyō Shōnin.

name: Jingzhong school

scholarly.text: 8th c.

distinctive_positions: Musang's three phrases: no remembering (wuyi) = precepts, no thinking (wunian) = samādhi, no forgetting/no delusion (mowang) = wisdom (Lidai fabao ji).
Mass ordination-and-teaching assemblies opened with drawn-out recitation of the Buddha's name (Lidai fabao ji).
summary: The Sichuan lineage of Zhishen, Chuji and the Korean master Musang (Kim heshang, 684–762), known from the Lidai fabao ji.

name: Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja

tradition.text: Buddhajñānapāda received the teaching directly from Mañjuśrī after years of practice

scholarly.text: late 8th c.

transmissions_given.what: the Jñānapāda Guhyasamāja (Mañjuvajra) lineage

distinctive_positions: The Guhyasamāja is practised with Mañjuvajra (a form of Mañjuśrī) at the centre of a 19-deity maṇḍala.
The 'two stages' are presented in Buddhajñānapāda's 'Oral Instruction' (Dvikramatattvabhāvanā-mukhāgama), given, by the tradition's account, by Mañjuśrī himself.
summary: The second Indian exegetical tradition of the Guhyasamāja, founded by Buddhajñānapāda (late 8th c.), a teacher of Vikramaśīla's early masters, centred on Mañjuvajra and the 'Oral Instruction' on the two stages; continued by Dīpaṅkarabhadra's maṇḍala ritual (Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi).
notes: The 19-deity count and the Mukhāgama's reception from Mañjuśrī are recalled, not checked in a text.

name: Jōdo Shinshū (the True Pure Land school of Shinran)
regions: Japan (Kyoto: Nishi and Higashi Honganji; Kantō; Hokuriku; Mikawa)

tradition.text: founded in 1224 (Gennin 1), the year taken by Honganji as that of the Kyōgyōshinshō

scholarly.text: 13th c. (Shinran's communities in the Kantō); a school from Kakunyo's Honganji (14th c.), mass movement under Rennyo (15th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Hōnen's exclusive nenbutsu; permission to copy the Senchakushū (1205)
transmissions_received.evidence: Kyōgyōshinshō postscript

transmissions_received.what: the seven masters: Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, Tanluan, Daochuo, Shandao, Genshin, Hōnen
transmissions_received.evidence: Shōshinge; Kōsō wasan

distinctive_positions: Shinjin — the entrusting mind — is the true cause of birth; it is not produced by the practitioner but given (transferred) by Amida; the nenbutsu that follows is the expression of gratitude.
Both going to the Pure Land (ōsō) and returning to this world to save others (gensō) are Amida's transfer of merit.

At the moment shinjin is settled, one enters the rightly established state (shōjōju) in this life; birth in the true Pure Land at death is at once attaining great nirvāṇa; no deathbed welcome need be awaited.
The evil person is the true object of the vow: 'even a good person attains birth, how much more an evil person' (Tannishō 3).
Other practices and self-power nenbutsu lead only to the transformed land (19th and 20th vows); Shinran turned through the three vows to the eighteenth.
Jinen hōni: things become so of themselves by the working of the vow, free of the practitioner's calculation (hakarai).
Neither monk nor layman (hisō hizoku): married clergy, no precepts as condition of birth, no worship of other deities for worldly benefit, the name (myōgō) as object of reverence.
summary: The school descended from Shinran (1173–1263), Hōnen's disciple, who after exile (1207) lived as 'neither monk nor layman' among ordinary people in Echigo and the Kantō and in the Kyōgyōshinshō taught that teaching, practice, entrusting (shinjin) and realization are all Amida's transfer of merit to beings. Organised around Shinran's mausoleum (Honganji) by Kakunyo and spread by Rennyo's letters in the 15th c., it is today divided mainly into the Honganji (Nishi), Ōtani (Higashi) and Takada branches among the 'ten schools of Shinshū'.

name: Jōdo-shū (the Pure Land school of Hōnen)
alt_names: the school of exclusive nenbutsu (senju nenbutsu)
regions: Japan (Kyoto: Chion-in, Kurodani Konkai Kōmyō-ji; Edo: Zōjō-ji; Kyushu)

tradition.text: founded in 1175 (Angen 1) when Hōnen, reading Shandao, turned to the exclusive nenbutsu

scholarly.text: late 12th c.; institutionalised under the Chinzei line from the 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: Shandao's teaching ('relying solely on Shandao')
transmissions_received.evidence: Senchakushū postscript

transmissions_received.what: Hōnen's training on Mt Hiei; Genshin's Ōjōyōshū; the bodhisattva precepts transmitted in Jōdo-shū
transmissions_received.evidence: biographies

transmissions_given.what: Hōnen's exclusive nenbutsu received by Shinran (1201)
Ippen trained in the Seizan line (Shōtatsu)

distinctive_positions: Of the two gates, set aside the holy path and enter the Pure Land gate; of the right and miscellaneous practices, set aside the miscellaneous and take the right; of the right, the calling of the name is the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's primal vow (Senchakushū).
The eighteenth vow 'selected' (senchaku) the nenbutsu as the one practice for birth, above all other practices, being both superior (the name holds all virtues) and easy (open to all).

The settled mind (anjin: the three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra), the practice undertaken (kigyō: the five right practices) and the manner of practice (sagyō: the four modes) — terms from Shandao.
Believe that birth is attained by even one calling, yet keep calling all one's life (Hōnen's letters).
At death Amitābha comes to welcome the practitioner (raigō); right mindfulness at death is sought.
Monastic and lay alike; the bodhisattva precepts (Tendai line) kept alongside the nenbutsu; the fivefold transmission (gojū sōden) as the school's rite of entrusting the teaching.
summary: The Jōdo school founded by Hōnen (1133–1212), who after decades of Tendai study found in Shandao's commentary that calling Amitābha's name wholeheartedly at all times is 'the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's vow', and taught exclusive nenbutsu to all, monastic and lay, good and evil. Its classic is the Senchakushū; its creed the One-Sheet Document. After persecution (1207, 1227) Hōnen's disciples formed lines — Chinzei (Benchō), Seizan (Shōkū), and the extinct lines of Kōsai, Ryūkan and Chōsai — of which Chinzei became the main body of modern Jōdo-shū.

name: Jōdo-shū Chinzei line
regions: Japan (Kyushu, then Kamakura and Kyoto; Chion-in, Zōjō-ji)

scholarly.text: 13th c. onward

distinctive_positions: Nenbutsu is the practice of the primal vow; other practices can also lead to birth (shogyō ōjō) but are not the vow's own practice (as usually stated for Benchō's line).
Many-calling: continue the nenbutsu throughout life.
summary: The line of Hōnen's disciple Benchō (Shōkō-bō, 1162–1238), active in Kyushu (Chinzei), continued by Ryōchū (Nen'a); it became the mainstream of Jōdo-shū, with Chion-in and Zōjō-ji, and systematised the fivefold transmission (gojū sōden) under Shōgei.
notes: Chinzei doctrinal positions stated in general terms only; exact formulations to be checked.

name: Jōdo-shū Seizan line
regions: Japan (Nishiyama near Kyoto: Kōmyō-ji, Zenrin-ji/Eikandō, Seigan-ji)

scholarly.text: 13th c. onward

distinctive_positions: All practices are taken up into (and have their meaning in) the nenbutsu; the Buddha's attainment ten kalpas ago and the beings' birth are one (as usually summarised for Shōkū's line).
summary: The line of Hōnen's disciple Shōkū (Zenne-bō, 1177–1247), who had Tendai esoteric training and taught at Nishiyama (Seizan) near Kyoto; Ippen's teacher Shōtatsu belonged to it. Today three Seizan schools (Jōdo-shū Seizan, Seizan Zenrinji-ha, Seizan Fukakusa-ha).
notes: Seizan doctrinal summary given only in general terms (low confidence on exact formulations).

name: Jogye order

tradition.text: the name recalls Caoxi (Jogye), Huineng's mountain; Jinul's Suseonsa community (Songgwangsa) is taken as its heartland; the modern order counts Doui as founder and Taego as reviver

scholarly.text: a Goryeo Jogye school existed from the 12th c.; the modern Jogye Order was constituted in 1962

distinctive_positions: Ganhwa Seon combined with doctrinal study (the four-text curriculum, sajip).
summary: The Korean Seon order named after Huineng's Caoxi, which regards Jinul and Taego as its great masters; today the largest order of Korean Buddhism.

name: Jushe school (Abhidharmakośa school)
regions: Japan (one of the six Nara schools)

scholarly.text: 6th–8th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Study of the Abhidharmakośa in Paramārtha's (563–567) and Xuanzang's (651–654) translations as a preparatory discipline, later absorbed into Faxiang/Hossō study.
summary: The East Asian scholastic tradition of the Abhidharmakośa; in Japan the Kusha-shū, attached to the Hossō school.

name: Jyotiṣa (the science of the lights)
regions: Ujjayinī (the prime meridian of the siddhāntas)

tradition.text: revealed science of the seers: taught by Brahmā, Sūrya and the eighteen promulgators; the same science told anew in every age (SS 1.8–9)

scholarly.text: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa in the later first millennium BCE; horoscopy from the early centuries CE; siddhānta astronomy from the 5th c. CE (Āryabhaṭa 499); continuous to the present

transmissions_received.what: the lunar mansions, the five-year yuga and time-reckoning for the sacrifice
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; the nakṣatra lists of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas

transmissions_received.what: horoscopy with signs, houses and planetary rulers (scholarly account: of Hellenistic origin)
transmissions_received.evidence: Yavanajātaka; Greek-derived technical words in the Bṛhajjātaka (1.8, 1.17–18, 2.2–3); BS 2.14

transmissions_received.what: annual horoscopy, Arabic lots and aspect-yogas (scholarly account: from Perso-Arabic astrology)
transmissions_received.evidence: Tājika texts from the 13th c.; Nīlakaṇṭha 1587

transmissions_given.what: muhūrta rules, tithi decisions and the planetary sacrifice in the smṛtis and digests
site, house and temple rules and auspicious times (BS 52–57; MC vāstu-prakaraṇa)
calendrical astronomy taken up in the Kālacakra system (scholarly account)
later Jain horoscopy and Tājika authors (Hemaprabha)

distinctive_positions: Jyotiṣa is the eye of the Veda and stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas, because rites depend on times (VJ; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 41–42).
The science has three branches (skandha): gaṇita/siddhānta (computation), saṃhitā (omens and mundane matters) and horā (nativities) (BS 1.9; BPHS 1.2).
The birth chart reveals the ripening of good and bad karma earned in a former birth, as a lamp shows objects in darkness (BJ 1.3; LJ 1.3).
The planets are forms of Janārdana that give beings the fruits of their karma (BPHS 2.3); their wrath can be pacified by worship, gifts, mantra and fire-offering (YājñSm 1.295–308; BPHS 84).
Fate (daiva) is karma made in another birth; success needs fate and human effort together, like farming (Yogayātrā 1.3–4).
Time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and measurable time (SS 1.10).
Eclipses occur by the shadow of the earth and the body of the moon; Rāhu is present at the eclipse by Brahmā's boon and receives its offerings (BS 5.8–15).
A king or householder should act at a time when the planets are well placed (BS 103.59–60; Muhūrta Cintāmaṇi).
summary: Jyotiṣa, the Vedāṅga of the heavenly lights, began as the reckoning of times for the Vedic sacrifice (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa) and grew into three branches: mathematical astronomy (siddhānta), mundane astrology and omens (saṃhitā), and horoscopy (horā/jātaka), later also interrogation (praśna), electional timing (muhūrta) and the Indo-Persian Tājika. It teaches that the planets, signs and lunar mansions reveal — and as divine powers dispense — the fruits of past karma, and prescribes timing and pacificatory rites. It is a limb of the Veda rather than a path to liberation, though it names signs of renunciation and liberation in the chart.

name: Kabīr Chaurā Maṭh (Mūl Gādī), Varanasi

tradition.text: founded by Surat Gopāl, Kabīr's disciple (panth account)

distinctive_positions: Celibate succession of mahants at the site of Kabīr's teaching in Varanasi.
The Bījak is the scripture; the Dharamdāsī cosmogony is less central here.
summary: The monastic seat of the Kabīr Panth in Varanasi, at the place where Kabīr is said to have lived and taught; its line traces itself to Surat Gopāl.

name: Kabīr Panth

tradition.text: founded by Kabīr's disciples after his departure at Maghar (1518 in the panth's reckoning)

scholarly.text: organized as a panth with monastic seats by the 17th c.; the Dharamdāsī line's written corpus (Kabīr Sāgar, Anurāg Sāgar) is dated by scholars to the 18th–19th c.

transmissions_received.what: Kabīr's songs and sayings
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

distinctive_positions: Kabīr is the incarnation of the Sat Puruṣ (the True Being) who descends in every age to free souls (haṃs) from Kāl (in the Dharamdāsī literature: as Sat Sukṛt, Munīndra, Karuṇāmay and Kabīr in the four ages).
A cosmogony (Anurāg Sāgar) in which Kāl Nirañjan, a fallen son of the Sat Puruṣ, creates and rules the three worlds and binds souls; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are his sons.
Initiation (dīkṣā) with a kaṇṭhī necklace; in the Dharamdāsī line also the pān-parvānā and the caukā rite.
Two main branches: the celibate Kabīr Chaurā line in Varanasi, whose scripture is the Bījak, and the Dharamdāsī line of 42 generations of householder ācāryas in Chhattisgarh.
Vegetarianism, abstention from intoxicants, and rejection of caste distinctions within the panth are enjoined.
summary: The Kabīr Panth is the organized following of Kabīr, with monastic and householder members, sādhus and mahants, initiation and ritual. It venerates Kabīr as the incarnate True Being, which stands in some tension with Kabīr's own rejection of ritual and of worshipping persons; its Dharamdāsī branch developed an elaborate cosmogony of Kāl Nirañjan and the Sat Puruṣ.
notes: Scholarly studies (e.g. D. N. Lorenzen, F. E. Keay) are used only for dating labels.

name: Kāla saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Founded by Gopāla Ātā of Bhavānīpur (seat at Kālajhār).
Strongly guru-centred and egalitarian, drawing many low-caste and tribal followers; the Māyāmarā (Moāmoriyā) sattra of Aniruddhadeva belonged to it.
summary: The saṃhati founded by Gopāla Ātā, a disciple of Mādhavadeva, marked by intense devotion to the guru and wide recruitment among low castes and tribes.

scholarly.text: formed after Mādhavadeva's death (1596), 17th c.

name: Kālacakra tradition in India

tradition.text: taught by the Buddha at Dhānyakaṭaka to King Sucandra of Śambhala; abridged by Mañjuśrīyaśas and commented on by Puṇḍarīka (the Vimalaprabhā); brought to India from Śambhala

scholarly.text: Laghukālacakra and Vimalaprabhā composed c. 1025–1040; epoch year 1027 (start of the sixty-year cycle)

transmissions_given.what: the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar

distinctive_positions: The outer (cosmos and time), inner (body, channels, winds) and other/alternative (the deity and maṇḍala) Kālacakras correspond; liberation reverses the flow of time within the body.
The six-branch yoga (pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, samādhi) leads through ten signs to empty form (śūnyatābimba) joined with immutable bliss (akṣarasukha) (Sekoddeśa 24–27, 146).
The Ādibuddha, the primordial buddha, is the non-dual gnosis of immutable bliss.
Śambhala's kings will in the future defeat the barbarian (mleccha) religion and restore the dharma (a prophecy in the first chapter).
Its own astronomy and calendar, and a prophecy of the kalkin rulers of Śambhala.
summary: The last major Indian tantric system (11th c.), the 'Wheel of Time', which correlates cosmos, body and deity, teaches the six-branch yoga culminating in empty form and immutable bliss, gives its own astronomy and calendar (epoch 1027) and the Śambhala narrative; taught by Kālacakrapāda, Nāropa and Abhayākaragupta and transmitted to Tibet (Jonang, Gelug, Sakya).

name: Kālāmukha
regions: Karnataka (Balligāve/Belagāmi in Shimoga district and many other sites)

scholarly.text: c. 9th–14th c.; most inscriptions 11th–13th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Lākula doctrine and observance
transmissions_received.evidence: inscriptions describe Kālāmukha ācāryas as masters of the Lakula-siddhānta; scholarly identification

transmissions_given.what: temples and monasteries, possibly also members (disputed; see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva)

distinctive_positions: A temple- and monastery-based Śaiva order: its ācāryas served as temple heads and royal preceptors (rājaguru), and their maṭhas were centres of learning and charity (inscriptions).
Organised in 'assemblies' (pariṣad): the Śakti-pariṣad, whose chief seat was the Kōḍiya-maṭha of the Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāve, and the Siṃha-pariṣad.
Inscriptions praise its ācāryas as learned in the Lakula-siddhānta, Pātañjala yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Sāṃkhya, Buddhist doctrine, grammar and poetry.
Opponents (Yāmuna; Rāmānuja) report that they eat from a skull, bathe in and eat the ash of corpses, carry a club, and set up a pot of liquor and worship the deity placed in it.
summary: The Kālāmukhas are the Śaiva ascetics of numerous Karnataka inscriptions of the 11th–13th centuries, where they appear as learned heads of temples and monasteries, above all at Balligāve. Scholarship identifies them with the Lākula division of the Atimārga. Vaiṣṇava opponents describe skull and corpse-ash practices under their name. They disappear from the record by the 14th–15th century; how far their institutions passed to the Vīraśaivas is disputed.

name: Kālīkula (the Kālī lineages)
alt_names: Uttarāmnāya (the Northern transmission, in the āmnāya scheme)

tradition.text: Revealed by Śiva as Mahākāla/Bhairava to the Goddess; the tantras present themselves as eternal and as the scripture proper to the Kali age

scholarly.text: Kālī as a goddess in the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.); the Kashmirian Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala) c. 9th–10th c.; the eastern Kālī tantras mostly c. 14th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Yāmala cults of fierce goddesses and the cremation-ground observances
transmissions_received.evidence: Jayadrathayāmala as a Vidyāpīṭha Yāmala (U08, U19)

transmissions_received.what: kaulācāra, the five tattvas, the bhāvas and the āmnāya scheme
transmissions_received.evidence: Kulārṇava and Kaulāvalīnirṇaya are cited throughout the eastern Kālī digests

transmissions_received.what: Kālī as the power of time and cognition (the twelve Kālīs)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared Kālīkula scripture (Jayadrathayāmala, Kālīkulapañcaśataka)

transmissions_given.what: the Dakṣiṇakālī cult, the Mahāvidyā system and Kālī-pūjā
Kālī worship at Dakshineswar as practised by Ramakrishna (recent)
Kālī as a village and temple goddess (documented only in part)

distinctive_positions: Kālī devours (kalana) time itself: Mahākāla is so called because he devours all beings, and she is the primordial Kālikā because she devours Mahākāla (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32).
Without Śakti Śiva is a corpse (śava): this is why Kālī stands upon Sadāśiva lying as a corpse (Toḍala 1.20-25).
In herself the Goddess is formless; her terrible cremation-ground form is imagined according to her qualities and acts for the benefit of worshippers (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-140; 13.5-13).
The ten Mahāvidyās are her forms, shown by Satī to Śiva (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa, Mahābhāgavata Purāṇa) and matched with Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (Toḍala 10.9-11).
Worship is graded by disposition (bhāva): paśu, vīra, divya; the Kālī tantras disagree whether vīra and divya worship is allowed in the Kali age (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3 against Mahānirvāṇa 5-8).
In Bengal the fierce Mother is approached with intimate devotion (Śyāmā-saṅgīt): the devotee may plead with, reproach and claim her as her child.
summary: The lineages that worship Kālī (and the goddesses of her 'family') as the supreme power. In Kashmir the Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala) fed the Krama; in Nepal the Uttarāmnāya worships Guhyakālī; in eastern India (Bengal, Assam, Mithilā) a large body of later tantras (Kālī, Toḍala, Nirvāṇa, Mahānirvāṇa, Kālīvilāsa, Niruttara, Kulacūḍāmaṇi, Śaktisaṅgama) and digests (Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra) teach the worship of Dakṣiṇakālī and the ten Mahāvidyās, by dakṣiṇa and vāma (Kaula) modes, which culminates in the Bengali Śākta devotional poetry of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta.

name: Kāmaśāstra (the science of love and pleasure)
distinctive_positions: The three aims are to be pursued so that each supports and does not harm the others, distributed over a life of a hundred years; of dharma, artha and kāma each earlier one is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).
Kāma needs a śāstra because its right means must be learned; the text records and answers the Mīmāṃsaka and Lokāyatika objections (Kāmasūtra 1.2).
summary: The śāstra of the third aim of life (kāma), represented by Vātsyāyana Mallanāga's Kāmasūtra; recorded here only for its teaching on the three aims (trivarga) and its reported debate with Lokāyatikas.
notes: New lineage id (not in the registry) created by U02 for the puruṣārtha scope; the orchestrator may reassign.

checks.note: Kāmasūtra 1.2.1ff was found: 'śatāyur vai puruṣo vibhajya kālam anyonyānubaddhaṃ parasparasyānupaghātakaṃ trivargaṃ seveta'. The order of weight (each earlier aim weightier) is at 1.2.14. The Mīmāṃsaka objection (kāma needs no śāstra) and the Lokāyatika objection (the pigeon today) are both reported and answered in KS 1.2. The id is a new, non-registry lineage created by the unit.

name: Kāpālika (Somasiddhānta)

scholarly.text: possible earliest mention in Hāla's Sattasaī (anthology of uncertain date, early centuries CE onward); literary portraits c. 7th–11th c.; later references to c. 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the model of the skull-bearing penance for killing a brahmin
transmissions_received.evidence: Dharmaśāstra penance for brahmahatyā; Bhairava's penance in Kūrma P. 2.31 (scholarly hypothesis for the link)

transmissions_given.what: skull-bowl, skull-staff, bone ornaments and cremation-ground setting (disputed; see brw:kapalika-to-vajrayana)

distinctive_positions: The great vow (mahāvrata) of the skull, modelled on Bhairava's (Śiva's) penance for cutting off Brahmā's head (Kūrma P. 2.31): the ascetic lives as a Kapālin with a skull-bowl and skull-topped staff.

As reported by Yāmuna (Āgamaprāmāṇya) and Rāmānuja: liberation comes from knowing and wearing the six insignia (necklace/ear-ornament, rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash, sacred thread) with skull and khaṭvāṅga as sub-insignia, and from a meditation on the self seated in the yoni (opponents' report).
As reported: by mere entry into initiation one becomes a brahmin at once, and by taking the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic (Yāmuna, opponent's report).
Their doctrine is called Somasiddhānta; its content is not preserved.
Opponents' dramas portray Kāpālikas worshipping Bhairava and Cāmuṇḍā with liquor and alleged human offerings (Mālatīmādhava act 5; Prabodhacandrodaya act 3).
summary: The Kāpālikas, 'skull-men', were Śaiva ascetics who kept the great vow of the skull in imitation of Bhairava's penance. Their own scriptures are not identified; they are known through Purāṇic myth, Vaiṣṇava and Advaita polemic (Yāmuna, Rāmānuja, the Śaṅkaradigvijaya), Jain and Buddhist reports, and satirical or hostile portraits in Sanskrit drama (Mattavilāsa, Mālatīmādhava, Prabodhacandrodaya). Some sources group them with the Atimārga; others connect them with the Bhairava cults of the Mantramārga.
notes: Almost every statement about Kāpālika doctrine comes from opponents or satirists and is tagged reported_by_opponent. Continuity with later Aghorīs is a hypothesis, not a documented lineage.

name: Kartābhajā
alt_names: the worshippers of the Kartā (the Master)

tradition.text: Āulcānd appeared as a youth in a betel garden in Nadia and was recognized as Caitanya returned; he departed in the later 18th c.

scholarly.text: late 18th c. origin; Rāmśaraṇ Pāl (d. c. 1783) and Satī Mā organized the community; Rāmdulāl (Dulālcānd, c. 1775–1832) composed the Bhāber Gīt; much growth in 19th-c. Calcutta

transmissions_received.what: Caitanya as the source (Āulcānd as Caitanya returned), Vaiṣṇava vocabulary and kīrtana
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: sahaja mānuṣa, secrecy, the living human as the site of the divine
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary

distinctive_positions: God is the Kartā, the Master, present as the living guru (Mahāśay); 'worship the human' (mānuṣ bhajan).
Open to all castes and to Muslims; caste distinctions are void within the fellowship.
A double life: 'in the world, worldly custom; with the true guru, oneness' — outward conformity, inner Kartābhajā practice.
The Bhāber Gīt (Songs of Bhāva) as scripture, rich in the mercantile imagery of Calcutta (bazaar, company, trade).
The Dol Pūrṇimā festival at Ghoshpara, with healing at the Himsāgar tank and the pomegranate tree of Satī Mā.
Hereditary Kartā of the Pāl family; disciples (barātī) pay dues through the Mahāśays.
summary: The Kartābhajā is a Bengali sect founded in the late 18th c. around Āulcānd, held to be Caitanya returned, and organized by Rāmśaraṇ Pāl and his wife Satī Mā at Ghoshpara; it worships the Kartā (Master) in the living guru, admits all castes and Muslims, keeps its teaching secret behind outward conformity, and sings the Bhāber Gīt.
notes: Much of its organized history is post-1800 (flagged recent). Scholarly study: H. B. Urban (used only for dating labels).

name: Kashmir Śaivism (non-dual Śaiva tantra of Kashmir)
alt_names: Trika (in the broad sense used by Abhinavagupta and modern writers)
Īśvarādvayavāda (Utpaladeva's name for the non-duality of the Lord, Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti ch. 2)
regions: Jālandhara (seat of Abhinavagupta's Kaula teacher Śambhunātha)
South India / Cola country (Maheśvarānanda's Krama, c. 1300)

tradition.text: The Śaiva scriptures issue from Śiva's five faces; after they were lost at the start of the Kali age, Śiva as Śrīkaṇṭha commissioned Durvāsas to restore them (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-111); the Śiva Sūtras were revealed to Vasugupta on Mahādeva mountain.

scholarly.text: c. 850 CE (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa) - 11th c. classical period (Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, Kṣemarāja); commentarial and devotional continuation to the 18th-19th c.; revived in the 20th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhairava tantras (Svacchanda, Netra, Mālinīvijayottara, Siddhayogeśvarīmata) as scriptural base; the 36 tattvas, the three malas, śaktipāta and dīkṣā
transmissions_received.evidence: Kṣemarāja's Svacchandoddyota and Netroddyota; Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka built on the Mālinīvijayottara (TĀ 1.18)

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual and the kula/akula doctrine, via Śambhunātha of Jālandhara
transmissions_received.evidence: Tantrāloka 29; TĀ 5.52 (the seven ānandas as taught by Śambhu[nātha])

transmissions_received.what: Bhartṛhari's doctrine of speech (vāc) and pratibhā, reworked as vimarśa = supreme speech
transmissions_received.evidence: ĪPK 1.5.13; Śivadṛṣṭi ch. 2 critique
