transmissions_received.what: the epistemological framework and vocabulary of Dharmakīrti's school, engaged polemically
transmissions_received.evidence: ĪPK 1.2 (Buddhist pūrvapakṣa), 1.6, 2.3

transmissions_given.what: prakāśa-vimarśa metaphysics and Spanda/Pratyabhijñā exegesis used by Śrīvidyā commentators (e.g. Jayaratha's Vāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa; Maheśvarānanda)
Abhinavagupta's aesthetics (rasa as relished consciousness; śānta rasa)
the oral and textual lineage continued in the 20th c. by Swami Lakshmanjoo

distinctive_positions: Reality is one consciousness (saṃvit, citi), Paramaśiva, whose nature is light (prakāśa) inseparably joined with reflexive awareness (vimarśa); an awareness without vimarśa would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).

The world is a real manifestation (ābhāsa) of that consciousness by its own freedom (svātantrya), displayed on its own screen (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 2) - not an illusory appearance (Advaita's vivarta) and not a separate matter.

Bondage is the contraction of consciousness through the three impurities; the root impurity is ignorance, not a substance (TĀ 1.22-23 citing the Mālinīvijayottara); liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Śiva.
Knowledge (jñāna) is the sole cause of liberation; ritual and yoga are means graded to the recipient's grace.
The thirty-six tattvas (Śiva to earth), extending Sāṃkhya's twenty-five with the pure principles and the five kañcukas.
Four means (upāya): anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava - graded by the intensity of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) with full activity in the world; the liberated sees the world as his own play.
Śiva performs five acts (emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace); the bound individual also performs them (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 10-11).
Spanda: the ultimate is dynamic vibration, the opening and closing of Śaṅkara's eyes (Spandakārikā 1.1).
Kaula ritual, including its antinomian elements, is interpreted by Abhinavagupta as an expression and means of non-dual consciousness (TĀ 29) - summary only.
summary: The non-dual Śaiva exegetical tradition of Kashmir (9th-11th c. classical period) that interpreted the Bhairava and Kaula tantras (Mālinīvijayottara, Svacchanda, Netra, Vijñāna Bhairava, Parātrīśikā) through four interlocking systems - Spanda (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa), Pratyabhijñā (Somānanda, Utpaladeva), Trika (culminating in Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka) and Krama (the Kālī-centred Mahānaya) - with the Kula and the little-known Mata alongside. It teaches that the self is Śiva, the world his free self-manifestation, bondage a contraction and liberation its recognition, attained by four graded means. Continued by Kṣemarāja, Jayaratha, the Kashmiri devotional poets (Lal Ded, Rūpa Bhavānī, Sāhib Kaul) and, recently, Swami Lakshmanjoo.
notes: 'Kashmir Śaivism' is a modern umbrella name; the tradition itself speaks of Trika, Ṣaḍardha, Pratyabhijñā, Spanda, Krama, Kula. Parent set to the Mantramārga because its scriptures are Bhairava tantras of the Mantramārga; its Kaula side derives from the Kulamārga (lin:kaula).

name: Kāṣṭhā Saṅgha

tradition.text: founded (per Devasena's Darśanasāra) by Kumārasena; dated there in the Vikrama era (low confidence)

scholarly.text: attested c. 10th–17th c. CE

distinctive_positions: uses a whisk of yak-tail hair (gopuccha) instead of peacock feathers; accused in the Darśanasāra of permitting women's initiation and other deviations (low confidence)
summary: A Digambara lineage of north and west India (named after the town Kāṣṭhā) condemned as 'false' by Devasena but later accepted as a Digambara branch with its own bhaṭṭārakas.

name: Kāśyapīya
distinctive_positions: Past karma whose fruit has not yet ripened exists; past karma that has given its fruit, and the rest of the past, do not (Vasumitra; the Vibhajyavādin position of AKBh 5.25; Kathāvatthu 1.8 'some exist').
A Prātimokṣa survives in Chinese (T1460).
summary: A Sthavira branch (from the Sarvāstivāda in Vasumitra's list, from the Sabbatthivāda in the Pali list) holding that only unripened past karma exists; the Chinese Bieyi Saṃyuktāgama (T100) has been attributed to it.

name: Kaukkuṭika
distinctive_positions: Only the Abhidharma teaching is essential; the sūtra and vinaya are expedient (Vasumitra, per Xuanzang's version; low confidence).
summary: An early branch of the Mahāsāṃghika (Gokulika in the Pali lists).

name: Kaula (the Kula tradition)

tradition.text: The Kaula teaching was brought down (avatārita) at Candradvīpa by Matsyendra (Macchaghna), and was taught earlier in each age by Siddhas (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.8-9; 22.10-12)

scholarly.text: Kaula scriptures from c. 9th–10th c. (Kaulajñānanirṇaya; the Kula stratum of the Trika); the Kulārṇava is usually placed c. 11th–14th c. (Muktabodha catalogue: 'post-1100')

transmissions_received.what: the yoginī cults and cremation-ground rites of the Yāmala tantras
transmissions_received.evidence: shared rites and the yoginī-kaula (U08, U19)

transmissions_received.what: Kāpālika observances, reinterpreted as inner and domestic worship
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_given.what: Kula ritual and doctrine integrated by Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 29)
kaulācāra and the five tattvas in Kālī worship
the Kaula mode of Śrīvidyā worship
Matsyendra's Kaula teaching as the root of the Nāth lineage (tradition's account)

distinctive_positions: Kula is Śakti and Akula is Śiva; the Kaulas are skilled in joining kula and akula (Kulārṇava 17.27).
Kaula is the highest of the seven modes of conduct: Veda < Vaiṣṇava < Śaiva < Dakṣiṇa < Vāma < Siddhānta < Kaula (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).
In the Kula dharma enjoyment itself becomes yoga, sin becomes merit and saṃsāra becomes liberation (Kulārṇava 2.23-24).
The Kula truth is beyond both duality and non-duality (Kulārṇava 1.110).
The body is the temple and the jīva is Sadāśiva; bound it is jīva, freed it is Śiva (Kulārṇava 9.41-43).
The teaching passes only from ear to ear from a tested guru to a tested disciple, never to the deceitful (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 6.9-14; Kulārṇava 14.19, 14.25).

Worship with the kula substances (summary only) is held to reveal the bliss of Brahman latent in the body, and is condemned when done for pleasure or without initiation (Kulārṇava 2.117; 5.79-80; 5.99; 5.104).
In the circle of worship (bhairavīcakra) all castes are twice-born; outside it they are separate (Kulārṇava 8.96-97).
summary: The Kaula or Kula tradition teaches the worship of the Goddess and her 'family' (kula) of powers — the yoginīs and mothers — together with Bhairava, as a path of both enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). Its early scripture is the Kaulajñānanirṇaya ascribed to Matsyendra; its classic later exposition is the Kulārṇava Tantra (17 ullāsas) on the guru, initiation, the āmnāyas, the seven ullāsas and the Kula worship with the five tattvas; it branches into the four or five āmnāyas (Kubjikā's Paścimāmnāya, the Kālī Uttarāmnāya, Śrīvidyā's Dakṣiṇāmnāya, the Pūrva and Ūrdhva), shaped the Trika of Abhinavagupta and the eastern Kālī and Tārā cults, and insists on secrecy, the guru's authority and graded eligibility.

name: Kaula Śrīvidyā (the Vāmakeśvara–Yoginīhṛdaya exegetical line)

tradition.text: The teaching descends from Śiva (Parameśvara) through the divine, perfected and human streams of gurus.

scholarly.text: Puṇyānanda and Amṛtānanda c. 13th-14th c. (uncertain); Bhāskararāya and Umānandanātha 18th c.

transmissions_received.what: Kaula conduct and ritual frame
transmissions_received.evidence: Yoginīhṛdaya Dīpikā on 2.81 (kaulācāra); Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra 1.12, 1.24

distinctive_positions: Outer worship of the cakra is performed even by the omniscient Śiva because it leads to the knowledge of non-difference (Yoginīhṛdaya 3.3 with the Dīpikā); inner and outer worship together.

Bliss is the form of Brahman, present in the body; the five 'M's manifest it and are used in secret; exposure leads to hell; when they are unavailable the daily worship continues without them (PKS 1.12, 1.24).
The Goddess is at once Kaula and Samaya (Bhāskararāya on Lalitā Sahasranāma 36-37).
Initiation in stages (Bālā first, then the higher vidyās) with initiatory names ending in '-ānandanātha' (PKS 1.39-41).
The Vedic standing of Śrīvidyā is defended by Mīmāṃsā reasoning (Bhāskararāya).
summary: The line of Śrīvidyā that follows the Vāmakeśvara tantra and Yoginīhṛdaya within a Kaula frame: Puṇyānanda's Kāmakalāvilāsa, Amṛtānanda's Dīpikā, the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra with Umānandanātha's Nityotsava, and Bhāskararāya's commentaries. It combines outer Śrīcakra worship, Kaula conduct kept secret, and non-dual knowledge.
notes: 'Kaula Śrīvidyā' is a descriptive grouping used here for the Kaula-affiliated exegetical line; the texts call their conduct kaulācāra. Many living lines practise its rites with substitutes (dakṣiṇa mode).

name: The Aṣṭavaidya physician families of Kerala
distinctive_positions: Hereditary transmission of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya as the root text, learnt by heart.
Family lineages each master of the eight branches ('aṣṭa-vaidya').
summary: Hereditary Nampūtiri Brahmin physician families of Kerala who transmit Āyurveda through Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, with their own Malayalam and Sanskrit commentaries and treatment specialities.
notes: Names and number of the families, and their commentaries, not recorded here (uncertain); see REPORT gaps.

name: The Kerala tradition of jyotiṣa

scholarly.text: Parahita system 683 CE; the Saṅgamagrāma school c. 1350–1650; Praśna Mārga 1649

distinctive_positions: Follows the Āryabhaṭa school (āryapakṣa) in astronomy, corrected by observation (Parahita, Dṛggaṇita).
Cultivates horā through Malayalam-country commentaries on the Bṛhajjātaka (Rudra's Vivaraṇa, Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri's Daśādhyāyī).
Developed an elaborate interrogation ritual (aṣṭamaṅgala-praśna; devaprāśna for temples) codified in the Praśna Mārga.
summary: The Kerala stream of jyotiṣa: astronomers of the Āryabhaṭa school (Haridatta's Parahita, Parameśvara's Dṛggaṇita, the Saṅgamagrāma lineage of Mādhava, Parameśvara, Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī and Jyeṣṭhadeva) and a strong horā and praśna tradition carried in Nambūtiri and Piṣāraṭi families, with the Praśna Mārga as its manual of interrogation and remedies.

name: Kerala tantra (temple-tantra tradition of Kerala)

scholarly.text: the Tantrasamuccaya is a 15th-c. work; the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is older (c. 11th–12th c.); the Prapañcasāra and Śāradātilaka are earlier pan-Indian mantra manuals used in Kerala

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva Siddhānta ritual via the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Viṣṇu ritual
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: mantra procedures of the Prapañcasāra and the Śāradātilaka
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

distinctive_positions: Temple worship is conducted according to tantra texts, above all the Tantrasamuccaya, by hereditary Nampūtiri brahmin tantri families who alone perform installations (pratiṣṭhā), festivals (utsava) and the major purifications.
The Tantrasamuccaya treats the installation and worship of seven deities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa, Durgā, Subrahmaṇya, Gaṇapati and Śāstā.
Daily worship is performed by resident priests (śānti) under the tantri's authority; the day is structured by a series of pūjās and processional offerings (śīveli).
Kerala tantra combines Vedic (smārta) Nampūtiri practice with Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta tantric procedures.
summary: Kerala's temple-tantra tradition is the body of ritual texts and hereditary tantri lineages that govern temple building, installation, daily worship, festivals and purification in Kerala's Hindu temples. Its central text is Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan's Tantrasamuccaya, supported by the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, the Prapañcasāra, the Śāradātilaka and Malayalam manuals.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority. Tantri families named in REPORT.md (Cēnnās, Taraṇanallūr, Tāḻaman) are given with moderate/low confidence and not as separate lineages.

name: Kharatara Gaccha

tradition.text: the epithet 'kharatara' ('sharper, keener') given to Jineśvarasūri after his victory over the temple-dwelling monks at Aṇahilapāṭaka in 1024 CE

scholarly.text: 11th–12th c. CE

distinctive_positions: born of the reform against temple-dwelling (caityavāsa) monks, insisting that monks live in lodgings (vasati) given by laypeople
veneration of the four 'Dādāgurus' (Jinadatta, Maṇidhārī Jinacandra, Jinakuśala, Jinacandra) at shrines called dādābāḍīs
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha tracing itself to Jineśvarasūri's 1024 debate against the temple-dwelling monks at the Caulukya court; known for its Dādāguru cult and strong presence in Rajasthan.

name: Krama (the 'Sequence'; Mahānaya, Mahārtha)
regions: Oḍḍiyāna (in the tradition's account of Jñānanetra's revelation)

tradition.text: Revealed by the goddess to Jñānanetra (Śivānanda) - the tradition's account.

scholarly.text: Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala etc.) before c. 900; Kashmirian Krama c. 850-1000; Maheśvarānanda c. 1300; Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa later.

transmissions_received.what: the Kālīkula scriptures and the cult of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī
transmissions_received.evidence: Jayadrathayāmala; Kālīkulapañcaśataka

transmissions_given.what: the twelve Kālīs integrated as a form of śāktopāya (TĀ 4.148-172)
Krama ideas in Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī, which also draws on Śrīvidyā

distinctive_positions: Worship and contemplation of Kālī as the power that 'counts', emits and devours (kalana) all things; the five senses of the root kal: projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).

The twelve Kālīs as the phases of every act of cognition - emission, persistence, withdrawal and the nameless (anākhya) - across object, means of knowledge and knowing subject (TĀ 4.148-172; Abhinavagupta's Kramastotra).
The five flows (pañcavāha) of goddesses: Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī, Bhūcarī (low confidence).
Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, 'she who draws in time', is supreme.
The sequence (krama) of cognition leads into the sequenceless (akrama).
summary: The Kālī-centred Kaula tradition of the northern transmission as practised in Kashmir (Mahānaya, Mahārtha), rooted in the Jayadrathayāmala and related Kālīkula scriptures and said to have been revealed to Jñānanetra. Abhinavagupta absorbed its doctrine of the twelve Kālīs into the Trika (TĀ 4; Kramastotra); Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī and Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa are later statements. Much of its scripture survives only in manuscript or citation.
notes: Parent set to the Kashmirian grouping; historically a Kālīkula (lin:kalikula) Kaula system.

name: Kubjikā tradition (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission')
regions: the western Himalaya (Oḍḍiyāna, in the tradition's account)
Candradvīpa and Śrīśaila (the tradition's geography; locations debated)

tradition.text: The Goddess received the transmission at Candradvīpa and spread it from the western Himalaya (the 'western' of all paths) to Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and Oḍḍiyāna (Kubjikāmata 2.20-40)

scholarly.text: Kubjikāmata perhaps c. 10th c. or earlier; the Kubjikā cult survives in Nepal among Newar tantric priests

transmissions_received.what: the Kaula yoginī and siddha framework
transmissions_received.evidence: the Kubjikāmata calls itself the Kulālikāmnāya

transmissions_received.what: the Mālinī letter-order and Trika goddess mantras
transmissions_received.evidence: KMT ch. 4-5 (Mālinī), Goudriaan–Schoterman edition

transmissions_given.what: shared ritual culture of Newar tantric priests (Kubjikā worship in Bhaktapur and Kathmandu)
cakra vocabulary and Siddha lists shared with the Nāth tradition (scholarly hypothesis)

distinctive_positions: The Goddess Kubjikā ('the Bent One') emerged from the liṅga, dark and hunch-backed, and became bent out of shame (lajjā) when Bhairava asked for the transmission (Kubjikāmata 2.3-5, 2.14).
Śiva and the Goddess are mutually dependent: 'nothing is without me, nothing without you'; Bhairava calls her his guru (Kubjikāmata 2.17-18).
The four seats are four levels of the supreme yoni: Kāmākhya (beyond form), Pūrṇagiri (form), Jālandhara (word), Oḍra/Oḍḍiyāna (body) (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).
The six centres (ṣaṭprakāra, with their goddesses) are the body of the Goddess; Kubjikā is the coiled power (Kubjikāmata 2.2 hymn; chs. 11-15).
The disciple who breaks the samayas and slanders the guru becomes 'dead while living' (Kubjikāmata 12.3-9).
summary: Kubjikā ('the Bent One', Kujā), consort of Navātman/Kujeśa Bhairava, is the goddess of the Paścimāmnāya, the western of the Kaula transmissions. Its root scripture, the Kubjikāmata (25 paṭalas, c. 3,500 verses in the Kulālikāmnāya recension), with the Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā and the vast Manthānabhairava, teaches the Goddess's descent through the sacred seats, a mantra-maṇḍala system of six centres and their yoginīs, and strict samaya discipline. Absorbed into the Kālī and Śrīvidyā cults elsewhere, it survives as a living cult in Nepal.

name: Lākula
regions: known through Kashmirian and Nepalese scriptural sources

scholarly.text: attested in Śaiva scriptures from c. 6th–7th c. (Niśvāsa corpus) and, as Kālāmukhas, in inscriptions c. 9th–14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Pāśupata base of observance and doctrine
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly reconstruction from the Niśvāsamukha and later Śaiva sources

transmissions_given.what: the Lākula doctrine (inscriptions praise Kālāmukha ācāryas as learned in the 'Lakula-siddhānta')

distinctive_positions: Its observance is the great vow (mahāvrata), also called the skull observance (kapālavrata) or observance 'beyond the world' (lokātīta): the ascetic carries a human skull as his bowl and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and smears himself with ash (as described in Śaiva scriptures; details reconstructed).
The Svacchanda Tantra names the skull-observers (kapālavratin) beside the Pāśupatas as those who stand 'in the Īśvara and in the Dhruva' and are not re-created (11.184).
It is described by scholarship as a system intermediate between Pāñcārthika Pāśupatism and the Mantramārga, with its own hierarchy of worlds; its scriptures are lost.
summary: The Lākulas form the second division of the Atimārga. They are known almost only through the Mantramārga scriptures that describe them (the Niśvāsamukha, the Svacchanda Tantra) and through the Kālāmukhas of Karnataka inscriptions, whom scholarship identifies with them. Their observance was the great vow of the skull, 'beyond the world'. No Lākula scripture survives complete.
notes: Low confidence throughout; reconstruction depends on A. Sanderson's work on the Niśvāsamukha and the Lākulas (scholarly metadata only).

name: Ledi Sayadaw tradition

tradition.text: Ledi Sayadaw began teaching insight to monks and laypeople at the Ledi forest monastery near Monywa from the 1880s

scholarly.text: late 19th – early 20th c. onward

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidhamma and commentarial tradition as studied in Burma
transmissions_received.evidence: Ledi's Pali and Burmese manuals on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha

transmissions_given.what: the lay insight practice passed through Saya Thetgyi to U Ba Khin

distinctive_positions: Laypeople as well as monks should study the Abhidhamma and practise insight now, because the time of the Buddha's dispensation in which liberation is possible is limited.
Mindfulness of breathing (or other calm) as a base, then insight into the four elements, feeling and the aggregates, may be enough for liberation without full absorption (the 'dry-insight' vehicle).
Critical re-examination of the Abhidhamma sub-commentaries (the Paramatthadīpanī's critique of the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī).
The thirty-seven requisites of awakening must be developed; merely wishing for a future birth with a Buddha is unwise.
summary: Lineage stemming from the Burmese scholar-monk Ledi Sayadaw (1846–1923), who wrote a series of Pali and Burmese manuals (dīpanī) and made the Abhidhamma and insight meditation accessible to laypeople; the root of the U Ba Khin – Goenka tradition.

name: Linji house

tradition.text: founded by Linji Yixuan (d. 866/867)

scholarly.text: 9th-c. origin; dominant Chan house from the Song onward; living in Chinese Chan

transmissions_given.what: Huanglong and Yangqi lines
Ming Linji line
Yangqi line via Shiwu Qinggong / Pingshan Chulin to Taego and Naong

distinctive_positions: The true person of no rank (wuwei zhenren) and the 'person of the Way who depends on nothing' (wuyi daoren) listening to the Dharma here and now.
Shouts (he 喝) and blows as means; the four classifications (siliaojian), four guest-host relations, four illumination-function relations, three mysteries and three essentials.
'Be master wherever you are; wherever you stand is true'; nothing to do (wushi 無事).
In the Song, kōan commentary (Yuanwu) and the critical phrase (Dahui's kanhua Chan).
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, stemming from Linji Yixuan (d. 866) in the line of Mazu and Huangbo, known for its shouts and devices; through its Yangqi branch it became the main Chinese Chan lineage and the source of Japanese Rinzai and Ōbaku.

name: Lokottaravāda
alt_names: Shuo chushi bu 說出世部 (Chinese)
regions: Middle Country (madhyadeśa, per the Mahāvastu colophon)

tradition.text: Branched from the Mahāsāṃghika in the second century after the parinirvāṇa (Vasumitra)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE – 7th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: Vinaya and buddhology
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāvastu colophon: 'according to the recitation of the Lokottaravādin Mahāsāṃghikas of the Middle Country, the beginning of the Mahāvastu of the Vinaya Piṭaka' (Mvu i.2)

distinctive_positions: The Buddha's conduct, roots of merit, walking, standing, sitting and lying, his body, robes and food are all supramundane (Mvu i.167–168).
The Buddhas conform to the world (lokānuvartanā): they wash, eat, drink, take medicine and show old age though they have no dirt, hunger, thirst, illness or ageing (Mvu i.168–169).
The bodhisattva career runs through four conducts (caryā) and ten grounds (bhūmi) named durārohā … abhiṣeka (Mvu i.1, i.76).
The Mahāvastu belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka (its colophon), framing the Buddha's biography as the introduction to the monastic code.
summary: The Lokottaravāda, a branch of the Mahāsāṃghika, is named for its teaching that the Buddhas are 'beyond the world' (lokottara) and only appear to conform to worldly life. Its Sanskrit Vinaya texts survive: the Mahāvastu (a vast biography of the Buddha with jātakas and the ten bodhisattva grounds), the Prātimokṣa, the Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya and the Abhisamācārikā.

name: Longchen Nyingthig (the Heart-essence of the Great Expanse)

tradition.text: revealed as a mind treasure to Jigme Lingpa in visions of Longchenpa (from 1757)

scholarly.text: late 18th c.

distinctive_positions: The most widely practised Nyingma cycle: ngöndro, guru sādhana (Rigdzin Düpa), ḍākinī practice (Yumka) and Dzogchen instruction (Yeshe Lama) in one mind-treasure.
Received by Jigme Lingpa from Longchenpa in three visions; it condenses the Nyingthig Yabzhi.
summary: The mind-treasure cycle of Jigme Lingpa, received in visions of Longchenpa, which became the main Nyingma framework for preliminaries, guru yoga and Dzogchen, spread by Jigme Lingpa's disciples and Patrul Rinpoche.

name: Loṅkā Gaccha

scholarly.text: from c. 1470s CE

distinctive_positions: rejection of image worship and of monastic laxity on the basis of the Āgamas as copied and read by Loṅkā Śāh
summary: The aniconic Śvetāmbara movement that arose from the teaching of Loṅkā Śāh of Ahmedabad; its later lax 'yatis' were in turn reformed by the founders of the Sthānakavāsī orders.

name: Lü school (Vinaya school, Nanshan lineage)
alt_names: Nanshan lü zong 南山律宗

scholarly.text: 7th c. CE (Daoxuan, 596–667) –

transmissions_received.what: the Four-Part Vinaya
transmissions_received.evidence: Daoxuan's commentaries (T1804 and others)

transmissions_given.what: the Nanshan Vinaya lineage taken to Japan by Jianzhen

distinctive_positions: The Four-Part (Dharmaguptaka) Vinaya is the standard code for all Chinese monastics.
Daoxuan interpreted the Vinaya in Mahāyāna terms (precepts grounded in the 'seed' of the mind; low confidence on details).
summary: The Chinese Vinaya school founded by Daoxuan on Zhongnan mountain, which made the Dharmaguptaka Four-Part Vinaya the monastic code of East Asia.

name: Madhyamaka
alt_names: Śūnyavāda / Śūnyatāvāda (name mostly used by others)
regions: South India (Andhra: Śrīparvata / Nāgārjunakoṇḍa in the tradition's accounts)
Valabhī / western India (Bhāviveka in some accounts)

tradition.text: founded by Nāgārjuna, prophesied (Laṅkāvatāra) to appear four hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa; Tibetan histories give him a life of six hundred years

scholarly.text: Nāgārjuna c. 150–250 CE; Indian Madhyamaka active until the 12th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras' teaching that all dharmas are empty, unborn and like illusions
transmissions_received.evidence: MMK and its commentaries cite the Prajñāpāramitā, Akṣayamatinirdeśa, Anavataptanāgarājaparipṛcchā and Kāśyapaparivarta

transmissions_received.what: dependent origination as the middle between 'is' and 'is not'; the unanswered questions; no-self
transmissions_received.evidence: MMK 15.7 names the Kātyāyanāvavāda (= Kaccānagotta Sutta); MMK 11.1 and 27 rework āgama teachings

transmissions_given.what: the Middle Treatise, Twelve Gate Treatise and Hundred Treatise translated by Kumārajīva (Three-Treatise school)
MMK 24.18 read as the basis of the three truths (emptiness, provisional, middle)
Candrakīrti's Madhyamaka through Atiśa and the Kadam lineage
Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka as the final view in Tsongkhapa's system
Madhyamaka as the view of the sūtra path
Nāgārjuna named as the fourteenth Indian patriarch in Chan transmission lists (the tradition's account)
the 'easy path' chapter of the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā attributed to Nāgārjuna; Nāgārjuna as the first of Shinran's seven patriarchs

distinctive_positions: Every dharma is empty (śūnya) of own-nature (svabhāva) because it arises in dependence; emptiness = dependent origination = dependent designation = the middle way (MMK 24.18).
Things do not arise from themselves, from another, from both, or without cause (MMK 1.1).

The Buddhas teach by relying on two truths, the worldly-conventional and the ultimate; without relying on the conventional the ultimate cannot be taught, and without reaching the ultimate nirvāṇa is not attained (MMK 24.8–10).
Emptiness is not a view: it is the relinquishing of all views, and those who make emptiness a view are called incurable (MMK 13.8).
The Mādhyamika has no thesis of his own to defend (VV 29) and refutes the opponent's positions on their own terms.
There is not the slightest difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa (MMK 25.19–20); nirvāṇa is neither existent nor nonexistent (25.4–10).
Emptiness is not nihilism: for one for whom emptiness is possible, everything — the four truths, karma, the path — is possible (MMK 24.14; VV 70).
The self is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates; it is a designation dependent on them (MMK 18.1; 27; MA 6).
The bodhisattva path unites wisdom (emptiness) and method (compassion, bodhicitta, the perfections) (RĀ; BCA; BhK).
summary: The Middle Way school founded by Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd c. CE) on the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras. It teaches that all things, including the Buddha, nirvāṇa and emptiness itself, lack own-nature because they arise dependently, and that this emptiness, rightly understood through the two truths, is the middle way between eternalism and annihilationism. Its Indian lines — the commentators on Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva (Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka, Candrakīrti), the bodhisattva manuals (Śāntideva) and the synthesis with Yogācāra and Buddhist logic (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla) — were classified by later Tibetan doxographers as Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika; the school's view became the philosophical centre of Tibetan Buddhism and, as Sanlun, of East Asian Madhyamaka.

name: Mahānubhāva panth
regions: maṭhs in Punjab and the north-west (reported; verify)

tradition.text: Parameśvara has incarnated in every age; the five Kṛṣṇas culminate in Cakradhar

scholarly.text: founded by Cakradhar in the 1260s; Cakradhar left Maharashtra c. 1274

transmissions_received.what: Dattātreya counted among the five incarnations of Parameśvara
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account; direction and extent disputed

transmissions_received.what: Kṛṣṇa of the Gītā and Bhāgavata as an incarnation of Parameśvara
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; the classic poems retell Bhāgavata episodes

distinctive_positions: Four eternal, distinct realities: souls (jīva), deities (devatā), the world (prapañca) and the one Supreme (Parameśvara).
Parameśvara alone gives liberation; he has incarnated as the five Kṛṣṇas (pañca-kṛṣṇa): Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu (Guṇḍam Rāüḷ) and Cakradhar.
The devatās — the gods of the Vedas and Purāṇas — are powerful beings who can grant only worldly fruit; worshipping them binds, so it is forbidden.
Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) with wandering, begging and strict non-violence is the ideal, open to women and to all castes; caste distinctions and Vedic ritual are rejected.
Devotion is through remembrance of the incarnations' līlās and through places and relics they touched (sthāna, sambandha).
Marathi is the sacred language; the scriptures were long kept secret in special scripts.
summary: The Mahānubhāva panth, founded in 13th-c. Maharashtra by Cakradhar Svāmī, worships one Supreme (Parameśvara) incarnated as the five Kṛṣṇas and rejects the worship of all other gods, caste and Vedic ritual. Its Marathi prose scriptures — the Līḷācaritra and Sūtrapāṭh — are among the oldest Marathi literature; its monks and nuns live by renunciation, wandering and non-violence.

name: Mahāsāṃghika

tradition.text: Formed at the first schism, a century or more after the parinirvāṇa — according to the Sthavira accounts over the ten points of Vaiśālī or the five points of Mahādeva; according to its own account over the Sthaviras' enlargement of the Vinaya

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE (first schism) – c. 7th c. CE and later

transmissions_received.what: the sūtras and the Vinaya
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya T1425; Śāriputraparipṛcchā

transmissions_given.what: the supramundane buddhology, the original purity of mind and the ten-stage bodhisattva career (much discussed as a source of Mahāyāna ideas; scholarly hypothesis)
the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya translated by Buddhabhadra and Faxian (used in early Chinese monasteries alongside other Vinayas)

distinctive_positions: The Buddhas are supramundane (lokottara); their bodies, powers and lifespans are without limit; the Buddha is always in concentration, never sleeps, and teaches all dharmas with a single sound (Vasumitra).
The mind is by nature luminous; it is defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Past and future do not exist as entities (Vasumitra).
There is no intermediate existence between death and rebirth (Vasumitra; Kathāvatthu 8.2 attributes the contrary view to others).
Stream-enterers can fall back; arhats cannot (Vasumitra).
Nine unconditioned dharmas (Vasumitra: the two cessations, space, the four formless spheres, the nature of dependent origination and of the noble path) — per Vasumitra, low confidence on the list.
The five points of Mahādeva on the imperfections of the arhat were accepted by the Mahāsāṃghika side according to the Sarvāstivāda accounts.
summary: The Mahāsāṃghika ('those of the great community') formed one side of the first schism of the Buddhist order, the other being the Sthaviras. It divided into several branches (Ekavyavahārika, Lokottaravāda, Kaukkuṭika/Gokulika, Bahuśrutīya, Prajñaptivāda, Caitika and the Andhra Śaila schools). Its Vinaya survives in Chinese and its Lokottaravāda branch's Mahāvastu in Sanskrit; its doctrines are known largely through Vasumitra's doxography.

name: Mahāsi Sayadaw tradition (the 'new Burmese method')

tradition.text: Mahāsi Sayadaw taught at Mahāsi monastery (Seikkhun) from 1938 and at the Sāsana Yeiktha in Rangoon from 1949

scholarly.text: 1938/1949 onward

transmissions_received.what: the satipaṭṭhāna practice as taught by Mingun Jetavana Sayadaw
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāsi's own acknowledgement of his teacher

distinctive_positions: Bare, moment-to-moment noting of whatever arises — beginning with the rising and falling of the abdomen and extending to all sensations, thoughts and actions — develops momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi) sufficient for insight without prior absorption (the vipassanā-yānika or dry-insight vehicle).
Intensive retreat with alternating sitting and walking, continuous noting in daily activities and regular interviews with the teacher.
The meditator passes through the insight knowledges in the order described in the Visuddhimagga and Paṭisambhidāmagga, which Mahāsi described from practice in The Progress of Insight.
summary: The intensive insight method of Mahāsi Sayadaw (1904–1982), based on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta and the Visuddhimagga's insight knowledges, taught at the Sāsana Yeiktha from 1949 and spread across Theravāda Asia and to the West.

name: The Mahāsiddhas (the eighty-four great adepts)

tradition.text: Saraha, 'the great brahmin', counted first of the human teachers of mahāmudrā; the siddhas lived long lives, some for centuries (Nāgārjuna), and some are said not to have died

scholarly.text: c. 8th–12th c. CE; Abhayadatta's collection of lives c. 11th–12th c.

transmissions_received.what: the tantras (esp. Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Guhyasamāja) and their empowerments
transmissions_received.evidence: the lives name the tantra and instruction each siddha received

transmissions_given.what: Saraha's and Tilopa's mahāmudrā, Nāropa's six yogas, the dohā-song idiom (mgur)
Virūpa's Path and Result (lam 'bras) based on the Hevajra
Niguma's and Sukhasiddhi's instructions
Ghaṇṭāpa's, Lūipa's and Kāṇha's Cakrasaṃvara and Nāropa's Vajrayoginī
shared siddha names and songs (disputed direction; see brw:natha-mahasiddha)
sahaja as the goal, body-cosmology (disputed; see brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya)

distinctive_positions: The innate (sahaja), the nature of one's own mind, is the ultimate; it is found not by learning, ritual or contrived meditation but through the true guru's instruction (People Dohā v19, v38–39).
Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist monastic observances and even tantric ritual are criticized when taken as ends in themselves (People Dohā v2–15; Queen Dohā v32).
Realization is lived in ordinary life — householder, courtesan, weaver, cobbler, fisherman, king — and each siddha's own trade becomes the image of the path (Caturaśītisiddhabodhihṛdaya).
The songs (dohā, caryā) use intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā): outer images for inner yoga.
Unconventional conduct (vratacaryā, unmattacaryā) is undertaken only after realization and with discernment (Caturaśītisiddhabodhihṛdaya: Nāgārjuna's song; Mekopa's song).
summary: The Indian tantric adepts (siddhas) of c. 8th–12th c. — the eighty-four of Abhayadatta's lives and others — whose songs (dohās, caryāgīti) and instructions teach the innate (sahaja) and mahāmudrā beyond ritual and conceptual meditation, and whose lineages passed into the Tibetan Kagyu, Sakya and other schools and overlap with the Nāth siddhas.

name: Mahāvihāra fraternity (Mahāvihāra-vāsins)

tradition.text: founded with the Great Monastery given to Mahinda by King Devānampiya Tissa (3rd c. BCE); sole recognized fraternity after Parakkamabāhu I's unification

scholarly.text: 3rd c. BCE – 1165 CE as a separate fraternity; its commentarial orthodoxy continues in all modern Theravāda

transmissions_given.what: the Pali commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) and the Visuddhimagga as the orthodox exegesis of the canon; Sri Lankan ordination lineages sent to Burma and Thailand

distinctive_positions: The Pali Tipiṭaka including the seven Abhidhamma books is the Buddha's word; the Sinhala commentaries (rendered into Pali by Buddhaghosa and others) are the authoritative explanation.
Rejection of the Vetulya (Vaitulya) texts accepted at the Abhayagiri as not the Buddha's word.
The path as the seven purifications and the forty meditation subjects as systematized in the Visuddhimagga.
summary: The fraternity of the Great Monastery at Anurādhapura, whose commentarial tradition Buddhaghosa rendered into Pali in the 5th century and which, after the 12th-century unification of the Sri Lankan saṅgha, became the normative Theravāda.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U37 for the commentarial orthodoxy; parent lin:theravada (owned by U36). The rival fraternities were the Abhayagiri and (later) the Jetavana.

name: Mahāyāna
regions: historically Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia

tradition.text: Taught by the Buddha Śākyamuni himself; some sūtras were withheld (e.g. kept by the nāgas) and brought forth later when there were beings able to receive them

scholarly.text: Mahāyāna sūtras appear from c. 1st c. BCE / 1st c. CE (first Chinese translations by Lokakṣema, c. 179 CE; Gāndhārī Prajñāpāramitā fragment c. 1st-2nd c. CE); composition continued to c. 5th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Buddha's teaching, the Vinaya ordination lineages (Dharmaguptaka in East Asia, Mūlasarvāstivāda in Tibet) in which Mahāyāna monks and nuns were ordained
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account; Vinaya lineages

transmissions_given.what: the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras as scriptural basis of emptiness
the Saṃdhinirmocana and Laṅkāvatāra as basis of the ālaya and three-nature doctrines
the three Pure Land sūtras
the Laṅkāvatāra, Vajracchedikā and Vimalakīrti as early Chan scriptures
the Lotus as the final and complete teaching
the Avataṃsaka as the Buddha's first, unconcealed teaching
the bodhisattva path, bodhicitta and emptiness as the ground of the Mantrayāna ('the perfection vehicle' as its cause)

distinctive_positions: The goal is the full awakening of a buddha (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi) for the sake of all beings, not the personal nirvāṇa of the arhat; the practitioner is a bodhisattva who vows to liberate all beings
All dharmas are empty (śūnya) of own-being (svabhāva), unborn and like an illusion — including the aggregates, the path and nirvāṇa itself (Prajñāpāramitā)
The six (or ten) perfections, grounded in the perfection of wisdom and in skillful means, are the path
The three vehicles are the Buddha's skillful means; there is ultimately one buddha-vehicle (Lotus, Śrīmālā) — or, per other sūtras, beings have fixed lineages (gotra) (Laṅkāvatāra, Saṃdhinirmocana)

The Buddha is not only the historical teacher: his dharmakāya is suchness; his lifespan is immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa a skillful display (Lotus 16, Mahāparinirvāṇa); countless buddhas teach in buddha-fields in the ten directions
All beings possess the tathāgatagarbha / buddha-nature (Tathāgatagarbha sūtras, Mahāparinirvāṇa)
The sūtras themselves are objects of worship: where a sūtra is kept or taught is a shrine (caitya); copying, reciting and teaching them is supreme merit
Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, defilement and purity, are not two (Vimalakīrti); the bodhisattva does not abandon saṃsāra (non-abiding nirvāṇa)
summary: The 'Great Vehicle': the body of sūtras and the movement, within the Buddhist monastic and lay communities of India from around the turn of the common era, that takes the bodhisattva's path to full buddhahood for all beings as the highest aim, teaches the emptiness of all dharmas, skillful means, innumerable buddhas and buddha-fields, and (in some sūtras) the buddha-nature in all beings. It became the Buddhism of East Asia and Tibet. This umbrella entry covers the sūtra layer; the scholastic schools (Madhyamaka, Yogācāra), Pure Land, Chan/Zen, the Chinese schools and Vajrayāna have their own entries.
notes: parent set to lin:early-buddhism for lineage-root purposes (the Mahāyāna did not arise as a separate ordination lineage: its monastics were ordained in the Nikāya Vinayas). The tradition itself regards the Mahāyāna sūtras as the word of the Buddha; the scholarly account treats them as later compositions.

name: Mahīśāsaka
regions: Sri Lanka (Faxian obtained its Vinaya there)

tradition.text: Split from the Sarvāstivāda (Vasumitra) or from the Theravāda (Dīpavaṃsa)

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE – c. 5th c. CE

transmissions_given.what: descent of the Dharmaguptaka (Vasumitra, Dīpavaṃsa)

distinctive_positions: Past and future do not exist; the present and the unconditioned exist (Vasumitra).
There is no intermediate existence (Vasumitra).
Since the Buddha is included in the Saṅgha, a gift to the Saṅgha yields great fruit, not a separate gift to the Buddha (Vasumitra).
Stream-enterers can fall back; arhats cannot (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Nine unconditioned dharmas including the 'suchness' of good, bad and neutral dharmas, of the path and of dependent origination (Vasumitra; low confidence on the list).
The Five-Part Vinaya (Wufen lü) with 251 rules for bhikṣus (low confidence on the count).
summary: The Mahīśāsaka was a Sthavira-derived school whose Five-Part Vinaya was brought from Sri Lanka by Faxian and translated into Chinese in 423–424. Vasumitra records a first group holding that only the present exists and a later group closer to Sarvāstivāda.

name: Mantramārga (the Path of Mantras)
alt_names: mantra-tantra (Kāmika's name for the fifth stream)
regions: Cambodia (Khmer inscriptions record Śaiva tantric texts)

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva/Sadāśiva through his five faces at the beginning of creation and handed down through chains of divine and semi-divine transmitters (tantrāvatāra; Kāmika pūrva 1; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)

scholarly.text: earliest surviving scripture (core of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā) c. 450–550 CE; most major scriptures c. 6th–10th c.; systematic exegesis 7th–12th c.

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva ascetic observances, the five brahma-mantras and the Pāśupata heritage
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis (the Niśvāsa and later texts present the Atimārga as the prior, lower Śaiva path; historians such as A. Sanderson treat the Mantramārga as having developed after it)

transmissions_given.what: the yoginī cults of the Vidyāpīṭha, reformulated in the Kaula traditions
Śaiva ritual procedures via paddhatis such as the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati
Vīraśaiva recensions of Siddhānta scriptures (e.g. Candrajñāna, Makuṭa, Vīra)

distinctive_positions: Scripture is revealed by Sadāśiva through five faces as five streams: Siddhānta (upper face), Gāruḍa (east), Vāma (north), Bhūta (west) and Bhairava (south) (Kāmika pūrva 1.20–27).

Knowledge is twofold by eligibility: Śiva's knowledge (śivajñāna), revealing the Lord, is the higher; the Veda and the rest, revealing the bound soul and its bonds, are the lower (Kāmika pūrva 1.14–17).
Religion is graded as worldly (laukika), Vedic (vaidika), spiritual (ādhyātmika: Sāṃkhya-Yoga), the Atimārga and the Mantramārga, the last being highest (Niśvāsamukha; Kāmika pūrva 1.17–19).
Initiation (dīkṣā) is a rite on the soul, not on caste or body; liberation comes through it (Kiraṇa 6.3–9).
The Mantramārga offers both supernatural powers/enjoyments (bhukti) and liberation (mukti), to householders as well as ascetics; initiates are graded samayin, putraka, sādhaka and ācārya.

The Siddhānta's 28 scriptures (10 Śivabheda, 18 Rudrabheda) and the 64 Bhairava tantras (eight groups of eight) are all Śiva's teaching; the Kashmirian exegetes rank them as teaching difference, difference-in-identity and non-difference respectively (Tantrāloka 1.18 with Jayaratha).
Worship is performed with mantras through which the deity is present; the officiant first purifies himself, the place, the substances, the mantras and the liṅga (Kāmika pūrva 4.37–38).
summary: The Mantramārga is the initiatory, mantra-based division of Śaivism, distinguished in its own scriptures (Niśvāsa, Kāmika) from the ascetic Atimārga. It comprises the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta with its 28 scriptures and their upāgamas, and the non-Saiddhāntika tantras: the Bhairava tantras (Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha), the Vāma tantras of Tumburu, and the Gāruḍa and Bhūta tantras. It teaches initiation, daily and temple worship, mantra-practice for powers, and yoga, as means to both enjoyment and liberation.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority. Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine is owned by U18, Kashmir traditions by U19, Śākta by U23/U24; this entry covers the division and its scriptural catalogue.

name: Mantrapīṭha (the Seat of Mantras)

scholarly.text: the Svacchandatantra predates the 10th c. (commented on by Kṣemarāja, 11th c.; known to Abhinavagupta)

distinctive_positions: The Bhairava tantras of the southern stream divide into the Mantrapīṭha and the Vidyāpīṭha; in the Mantrapīṭha the central deity is a male Bhairava, above all Svacchandabhairava with his consort Aghoreśvarī.
The first group of the 64 Bhairava tantras in the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list (the Bhairavāṣṭaka) opens with the Svacchanda and was 'spoken by Bahurūpa' (Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18).
summary: Division of the Bhairava tantras centred on a male Bhairava (chiefly Svacchandabhairava). Its main surviving scripture, the Svacchandatantra with Kṣemarāja's Uddyota, shaped Kashmirian Śaiva ritual.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08 for the Mantramārga's internal division (not in the registry). The Netratantra (Amṛteśvara/Mṛtyuñjaya cult) is listed here provisionally; its classification is not settled here. family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Mantraśāstra (the science of mantras: the smārta-tantric mantra manuals)
regions: Kashmir (as source of the Śaiva background)

tradition.text: mantras are eternal and revealed by Śiva, the Goddess or Viṣṇu; the manuals only collect them

scholarly.text: Prapañcasāra c. 10th–11th c. (uncertain); Śāradātilaka c. 11th–12th c.; Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary 1493/94; Mantramahodadhi 1589

transmissions_received.what: the Śaiva cosmogony of sound (Śiva–Śakti–nāda–bindu), mantra-initiation and nyāsa
Vaiṣṇava mantras and rites (Nārāyaṇa, Gopāla, Nṛsiṃha)
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT and Mantramahodadhi chapters on Vaiṣṇava mantras

transmissions_received.what: Goddess mantras and the letters as the Goddess's body
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT chapters on Tripurā, Tvaritā and others

transmissions_received.what: the name śabda-brahman and the levels of speech (the Padārthādarśa quotes grammarians)
transmissions_received.evidence: tea:saradatilaka:1.12-13

transmissions_received.what: Oṃ, the vyāhṛtis and the Gāyatrī
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT chapter on the Gāyatrī (reference from memory)

transmissions_given.what: the Śāradātilaka and Prapañcasāra as authorities for temple and domestic tantra
the cosmogony of nāda and the verse 'caitanyaṃ sarvabhūtānām' (ŚR 1.3.1)

distinctive_positions: From the supreme Lord, being-consciousness-bliss, arose Śakti; from her nāda; from nāda bindu (ŚT 1.7); the supreme bindu divides into bindu, nāda and bīja — Śiva, Śakti and their union (ŚT 1.8–9).
From the dividing bindu arose unmanifest sound, called śabda-brahman; śabda-brahman is not the word or its meaning (both insentient) but the consciousness of all beings (ŚT 1.11–13).
Śabda-brahman dwells in the body of beings as kuṇḍalinī and manifests as the letters, in prose and verse (ŚT 1.14).
The fifty letters (mātṛkā) are the body of the Goddess and of every mantra; mantras are placed on the body (nyāsa).
Every mantra has a seer, metre and deity, a seed (bīja), power (śakti) and pin (kīlaka); mantras are male, female or neuter by their endings.
A mantra may be defective in some fifty ways (ŚT 2.64–70) and is purified by ten rites (ŚT 2.112–122); secrecy (gopana) is itself one of the ten.
Only a qualified guru may give a mantra, to a qualified disciple tested for one to four years (ŚT 2.141–153); a mantra is 'mastered' by puraścaraṇa before it is used.
Japa is spoken, whispered or mental, each far superior to the previous.
summary: The tradition of learned manuals that collect the mantras of many deities with their seers, metres, seeds, rules of initiation, purification, placement and repetition — above all the Śāradātilaka (with Rāghavabhaṭṭa's Padārthādarśa), the Prapañcasāra and the Mantramahodadhi. Their theory: the supreme becomes sound (nāda, bindu), sound becomes the fifty letters, the letters become mantras, and the mantra, given by a guru and repeated with its purifications, gives enjoyment and liberation.

name: Mata (the 'Doctrine'; the Mata scriptures)
regions: Kashmir (as known to Abhinavagupta and Jayaratha)

scholarly.text: Known only through references by Abhinavagupta (c. 1000) and Jayaratha (13th c.); origin and dates unknown.

distinctive_positions: Its scriptures (mataśāstra) reject the samaya observances and similar rules as based on difference, teaching instead that one's own awareness, unbounded and complete, is to be realized (TĀ 4.262-263 with Jayaratha, who quotes the Mata line 'nirmaryādaṃ svasambodhaṃ sampūrṇaṃ budhyatām').
They forbid restricting eating and the worship of the cakra to members of one's own lineage (santāna), because such division fragments the undivided reality (TĀ 4.268-270).

In the Kashmirian scriptural hierarchy the Mata stands between the Dakṣiṇa (right-hand Bhairava) scriptures and the Kula (TĀ 13.300-301 and the verse quoted there by Jayaratha); a variant verse quoted in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa places it after the Kula and just below the Trika.
summary: A Śaiva/Kaula scriptural tradition, now lost, that the Kashmirian exegetes count as one of the systems alongside Kula, Krama and Trika. What is known comes almost entirely from the Tantrāloka and Jayaratha's Viveka: its rejection of the samaya rules and of lineage-based exclusions, and its rank in the scriptural hierarchy. Its own texts, deities and teachers are not securely identified in this skeleton.
notes: Low confidence throughout. Jayaratha on TĀ 4.262 calls the Mata scriptures 'samaviṣamalakṣaṇa' - sense unclear. Modern scholarship (Sanderson) associates the Mata with a Kālīkula/northern-transmission cult; that identification is not asserted here and is listed as a gap.

name: Māthura Saṅgha
distinctive_positions: 'niḥpicchika' — its monks carried no whisk at all (per the Darśanasāra; low confidence)
summary: A Digambara lineage named in Devasena's Darśanasāra as founded by Rāmasena; known mainly from Digambara polemic and a few inscriptions.

name: Mīmāṃsā (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā)
regions: across the subcontinent; later centres of study at Vārāṇasī, Mithilā, and in South India (Tamil country, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra)

tradition.text: Jaimini, pupil of Vyāsa (Bādarāyaṇa), taught at the close of the Dvāpara age (the tradition's account)

scholarly.text: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra c. 3rd c. BCE – 1st c. CE (estimates vary widely); Śabara c. 3rd–5th c. CE; unbroken commentarial tradition to the present

transmissions_received.what: the śrauta ritual corpus and the Brāhmaṇa exegesis of injunction (vidhi) and explanatory praise (arthavāda) that Mīmāṃsā systematizes
transmissions_received.evidence: every adhikaraṇa of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra takes its topic (viṣaya) from Vedic ritual texts

transmissions_received.what: procedural knowledge of the kalpa (śrauta) sūtras and grammatical analysis of Vedic words
transmissions_received.evidence: Śabara and Kumārila cite kalpa-sūtras and discuss the authority of grammar (MS 1.3.24–29; Tantravārttika vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa)

transmissions_given.what: the adhikaraṇa method, rules of textual interpretation (the basis of the six marks of purport), and — for Advaita — the Bhāṭṭa account of the means of knowledge in empirical matters
interpretive maxims (nyāya) used by Dharmaśāstra commentators and digest writers
the teaching (via the Vṛttikāra cited by Rāmānuja) that Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā form one continuous śāstra; Vedānta Deśika's theistic reading of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra

distinctive_positions: Dharma is a beneficial object known only through Vedic injunction (codanā); perception and reasoning based on it cannot know dharma (MS 1.1.2, 1.1.4).
The relation of word and meaning is original (autpattika), not made by any person; hence the Veda's injunctions are a self-sufficient means of knowledge (MS 1.1.5).
Words (letters) are eternal; utterance only manifests them (MS 1.1.6–23).
The Veda is authorless (apauruṣeya) and beginningless; names attached to its recensions derive from their expounders (MS 1.1.27–32).
Every cognition is valid of itself; invalidity is established only by a defect in its cause or a later contradicting cognition (svataḥ-prāmāṇya).
The Veda consists of injunction, mantra, name, prohibition and explanatory praise; all of it is meaningful through connection with injunctions (MS 1.2.7).
A ritual act, though perishable, produces an unseen potency (apūrva) that yields the promised result later (MS 2.1.5 with Śabara).
The sacrificial act, not the deity, is principal; the deity is that to which the offering is directed as named in the injunction or mantra (MS 9.1.9).
No creator god and no total creation or dissolution of the world are established by any means of knowledge (Kumārila; Śālikanātha).
No person — human, yogin or god — perceives dharma directly; claims of omniscience in matters of dharma are rejected (Kumārila).
Heaven (svarga) is the original declared goal of Vedic rites; later teachers add liberation (mokṣa) as the ending of embodiment through the exhaustion of karma.
summary: The school of Vedic exegesis founded on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: it inquires into dharma as known from Vedic injunctions and develops a system of rules for interpreting the Veda (the adhikaraṇa method), a realist epistemology built around the intrinsic validity of cognition and the authorless, eternal Veda, and a theory of ritual action and its unseen result (apūrva). After Śabara's commentary it divided into the schools of Kumārila (Bhāṭṭa) and Prabhākara (Prābhākara), with Murāri Miśra's short-lived 'third path'.
notes: 'Vākyaśāstra' (science of the sentence) is the traditional name that pairs Mīmāṃsā with grammar (padaśāstra) and logic (pramāṇaśāstra); moderate confidence. Status 'living': Mīmāṃsā is still taught in traditional institutions.

name: Mīrābāī's devotion (the Mīrā song-tradition)

tradition.text: Mīrā's life c. 1498–1547

scholarly.text: 16th c. onward

transmissions_received.what: Raidās as Mīrā's guru
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account in songs attributed to her; chronologically doubted

transmissions_received.what: a meeting with Jīva Gosvāmī in Vṛndāvana
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Priyādās and later legend)

distinctive_positions: Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl / Giridhar Nāgar is her only husband; she refuses the conduct expected of a royal widow and the family's honour (lok-lāj, kul-kī-maryādā).
Love-in-separation (viraha) and madness of love (prem-dīvānī) are the texture of devotion.
The company of sādhus regardless of caste; the name as the jewel-treasure.
No formal sampradāya: the tradition lives in song, in shrines (Meṛtā, Chittor, Vṛndāvana) and in the hagiographies; several traditions claim her.
notes: Created by U26 because the coverage map lists Mīrābāī among 'other lineages' (A9); it is not a formal sampradāya. See REPORT.md.
summary: The devotion of Mīrābāī, a 16th-c. Rajput princess of Meṛtā married into Mewar, who took Kṛṣṇa as her husband and defied her in-laws. Her songs (mostly attributed) of love, separation and defiance are sung everywhere; the Bhaktamāl praises her for casting off family honour to worship Giridhar.

name: Mitākṣarā school of Dharmaśāstra
regions: most of India outside Bengal (with regional sub-traditions)
distinctive_positions: Ownership of ancestral property arises by birth (janmasvatva): sons have a share in the family property from birth.
Sapiṇḍa relationship is defined by sharing particles of the same body (avayavānvaya).
summary: The interpretive tradition following Vijñāneśvara's Mitākṣarā (late 11th–early 12th c.) on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, the most widely followed authority in Dharmaśāstra, especially for inheritance and family law.
notes: The later statutory codification of Hindu law is outside the scope of this ontology.

checks.note: Both distinctive positions are in the GRETIL Mitākṣarā. Ownership by birth is stated in the partition section on YS 2.114ff: 'tasmāt paitṛke paitāmahe ca dravye janmanaiva svatvam'. The sapiṇḍa definition is on YS 1.52 (asapiṇḍām): 'sapiṇḍatā ca ekaśarīrāvayavānvayena bhavati'. The dating of Vijñāneśvara (late 11th–early 12th c.) matches the tch:vijnanesvara and src:mitaksara checks.

name: Mogok Sayadaw tradition

scholarly.text: mid-20th c. onward

distinctive_positions: Understanding dependent origination (taught with a chart) is the foundation for insight.
Contemplation of mind and feeling: seeing each arising consciousness and feeling vanish (seeing arising and passing away) as the direct road to the path.
summary: Burmese insight lineage of Mogok Sayadaw (U Vimala, 1899–1962), stressing an intellectual grasp of dependent origination followed by contemplation of the arising and passing of mind and feeling.
notes: Low confidence on details; no digitized texts of this tradition located.

name: Mūla Saṅgha (Digambara)
alt_names: with the Nandi, Sena, Deva and Siṃha gaṇas
distinctive_positions: the 'root' Digambara lineage, claiming descent through Kundakunda (Kundakundānvaya); its bhaṭṭāraka seats and monks use the peacock-feather whisk
summary: The principal historical Digambara monastic lineage, subdivided into gaṇas and gacchas, whose inscriptions name Kundakunda as ancestor; most present Digambara monks and bhaṭṭārakas belong to it.

name: Mūlasarvāstivāda
alt_names: Genben shuo yiqie you bu 根本說一切有部 (Chinese)
gzhi thams cad yod par smra ba (Tibetan)
regions: Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan, the Himalaya (through its Vinaya)

tradition.text: The 'root' (mūla) Sarvāstivāda, whose Vinaya was recited in the Buddha's time (Tibetan tradition)

scholarly.text: Vinaya compiled c. 1st–4th c. CE; named as a school from the 7th c. (Yijing); living through its Vinaya

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidharma of the seven books and the Kośa
transmissions_received.evidence: shared Abhidharma; Yijing reports the Mūlasarvāstivāda as one of four nikāyas

transmissions_given.what: the monastic ordination lineage brought by Śāntarakṣita (the 'lower Vinaya' line)
the Vinaya lines of the later spread
Vinaya study through Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra, one of the five great texts of the monastic curriculum

distinctive_positions: A very large Vinaya in seventeen sections (vastu) with a Vibhaṅga, Kṣudrakavastu and Uttaragrantha, rich in narratives (avadāna).
The only Indian Vinaya transmitted in Tibetan; the basis of all Tibetan monastic ordination.
Doctrinally at one with the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma (the Kośa is the Abhidharma of the Tibetan curriculum).
The bhikṣuṇī ordination of this Vinaya was never established in Tibet; whether it can be supplied from another Vinaya lineage is debated (recent).
Prātimokṣa: 258 rules in the Sanskrit text (the Tibetan tradition speaks of 253 vows of a gelong) — low confidence on both counts.
summary: The Mūlasarvāstivāda is known chiefly through its enormous Vinaya, preserved in Tibetan, partly in Chinese (Yijing) and in Sanskrit from the Gilgit manuscripts. Its relation to the Sarvāstivāda (identical, a later reorganisation, or a separate Mathurā-based group) is disputed. Its Vinaya is the living monastic code of Tibetan Buddhism.
notes: Parent set to Sarvāstivāda for convergence purposes; the tradition regards it as the root of which the others are branches. Scholarly views differ (identity, a later compilation, or a separate group).

name: Murāri Miśra's school (the 'third path' of Mīmāṃsā)

scholarly.text: c. 12th–13th c. CE (before Gaṅgeśa, who cites his view)

distinctive_positions: Validity of a cognition is intrinsic but is grasped by the reflective after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) that apprehends the first cognition — a third account beside the Bhāṭṭa (inference from knownness) and the Prābhākara (self-luminosity) ones, as reported by Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi.
summary: A minor third school of Mīmāṃsā associated with Murāri Miśra, proverbially 'Murāri's third path' (murāres tṛtīyaḥ panthāḥ). Only fragments of his works survive; his account of how validity is known is discussed by Navya-Nyāya.
notes: Created as a sub-lineage because the tradition names it a third path; almost nothing of its wider doctrine survives. Low confidence on region and dating; the numbering of homonymous Murāris (II/III) in modern literature is inconsistent.

name: Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka
alt_names: Caityavāsī (historically, a different sense: temple-dwelling monks)
distinctive_positions: Accepts a canon of forty-five Āgamas (11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 10 Prakīrṇakas, 6 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras, 2 Cūlikāsūtras) together with the niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi and ṭīkā layers
Worship of consecrated images of the Jinas (Jina-pūjā) in temples as a support for the inner state; material worship (dravya-pūjā) is for householders, inner worship (bhāva-pūjā) for all
Pilgrimage to the tīrthas (Śatruñjaya, Girnār, Ābu, Sammeda Śikhara) and consecration rites re-enacting the five kalyāṇakas
Organized in gacchas (Tapā, Kharatara, Añcala and others) that differ in ritual details and calendars
summary: The image-worshipping majority of the Śvetāmbaras, who accept forty-five Āgamas with their commentaries, worship Jina images in temples and are organized in monastic lineages called gacchas; the Tapā Gaccha is today the largest.

name: Nāḍī jyotiṣa (palm-leaf readings ascribed to the seers)

tradition.text: the seers (Agastya, Bhṛgu, Kauśika, Vasiṣṭha and others) wrote the leaves in ancient times, foreseeing each seeker

scholarly.text: surviving manuscripts and documented reading practice are late (mostly 19th–20th c.)

distinctive_positions: The tradition's claim: the seers foresaw every individual who would come to consult them and wrote their lives on palm leaves.
Leaves are located by thumb-impression classes and read aloud in Tamil verse, in chapters (kāṇḍa) including past-birth karma and remedies (śānti-parihāra).
summary: The nāḍī tradition claims palm-leaf manuscripts written by ancient seers that record the life, past births and remedies of the individual who comes to consult them. Recorded here as the tradition's claim; the documented practice and manuscripts are recent.

name: Nairukta school (the Vedic etymologists)

scholarly.text: flourished before and with Yāska (mid-1st millennium BCE); continued in the Nirukta commentaries

distinctive_positions: All nouns are derived from verbs (nāmāny ākhyātajāni) — the doctrine of Śākaṭāyana and 'the convention of the Nairuktas' (Nirukta 1.12).
There are only three deities — Agni on earth, Vāyu or Indra in the atmosphere, Sūrya in the sky — the many names being their functions (Nirukta 7.5).
Vedic figures are read as natural powers: Vṛtra is the cloud, against the Aitihāsikas' 'an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ' (Nirukta 2.16; cf. 12.1 on the Aśvins).
summary: The school of Vedic word-explanation (nirvacana) to which Yāska belongs and whose opinions he reports; it explained words from verbal roots and interpreted deities and myths through natural phenomena.

checks.note: Nirukta 1.12 was found: 'tatra nāmāny ākhyātajānīti śākaṭāyano nairuktasamayaś ca'. Nirukta 7.5 was found: 'tisra eva devatā iti nairuktāḥ | agniḥ pṛthivīsthāno vāyur vendro vāntarikṣasthānaḥ sūryo dyusthānaḥ'. Nirukta 2.16 was found: 'tat ko vṛtraḥ | megha iti nairuktāḥ | tvāṣṭro 'sura ity aitihāsikāḥ'. Nirukta 12.1 has the Aśvins read as heaven and earth, day and night, or sun and moon. The low-confidence date range of 700–400 BCE is consistent with Yāska's usual dating.

name: Nāth tradition (Nātha Siddhas; Nāth / Kānphaṭa Yogīs)

tradition.text: Ādinātha (Śiva) is the first Nāth; Matsyendra received the teaching from him; Gorakṣa is held to be immortal and to have appeared in each of the four ages

scholarly.text: Matsyendra c. 9th–10th c. (honoured by Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka 1.7); Gorakṣa c. 11th–13th c.; the order with its twelve panths is consolidated later (c. 15th–18th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Matsyendra's Kaula teaching: the body as the locus of the divine, the Kula/Akula, the centres of the body, the nectar of the moon, the conquest of death and the yoginīs
transmissions_received.evidence: Kaulajñānanirṇaya colophons name Macchaghnapāda/Matsyendra as its bringer; Nāth lists begin with Ādinātha and Matsyendra (HYP 1.5).

transmissions_received.what: the ascetic style of the skull-bearing and ash-smeared Śaiva ascetics (earrings, ash, cremation-ground associations)
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis only (the tradition does not claim Kāpālika descent).

transmissions_received.what: shared siddha figures and songs (Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Virūpa, Carpaṭi)
transmissions_received.evidence: overlap of the Nāth and Buddhist eighty-four siddha lists (Varṇaratnākara; Abhayadatta); see brw:natha-mahasiddha.

transmissions_given.what: the haṭha corpus attributed to Gorakṣa and the lineage of Nāth siddhas at the head of the Haṭhapradīpikā (1.4–9)
Nāth initiation passed through Gahinīnāth to Nivṛttināth and Jñāneśvar (Jñāneśvarī 6.291; closing lineage ovīs of ch. 18)
the vocabulary of sahaja, śūnya, the unstruck sound, the tenth door and reversed speech (ulaṭbāṃsī) used by Kabīr and other Sants
Korakkar (Gorakṣa) and Macchamuni (Matsyendra) counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars
the cult of Matsyendranātha as Karuṇāmaya / Buṅga-dyaḥ in the Kathmandu valley (mutual; see dsp:identity-of-matsyendra)
regional Nāth saints and householder Jogī communities

distinctive_positions: The body (piṇḍa) contains the whole cosmos (brahmāṇḍa); liberation is realised in and through the body.
The goal is sahaja-samādhi / samarasa: the mind seeing the mind, the stilling of breath and mind in the void (śūnya) beyond the pairs (AmŚ 54; GŚ 94).
Perfection of the body (kāya-siddhi): an adamantine, deathless siddha body; conquest of death and time (kāla-vañcana) through retaining bindu and the moon's nectar.
Reversal (ulṭā sādhana): turning the downward flows of breath, bindu and mind upward to the head.
The guru is indispensable; the teaching passes ear to ear and is kept secret from the untested.
Rejection of caste, image-worship, pilgrimage, fasting and Vedic ritual as means to liberation for the knower (Akulavīra A.43–46; Gorakh Bānī).
Moderation and restraint (saṃyam), the 'middle way' of the yogī (Gorakh Bānī).
Distinctive order: split-ear initiation (kān-phaṛāī), earrings (darśan / mudrā), the nād horn on the selī thread, the dhūnī fire, the greeting 'ādeś', burial (samādhi) of yogīs rather than cremation.
Siddhis are signs, not the goal; the knower does not grasp them (Akulavīra B.83–84).
summary: The Nāth tradition traces itself to Ādinātha (Śiva), Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha and to the nine Nāths and eighty-four Siddhas. It joins the Kaula teaching of Matsyendra's Yoginīkaula with the body-centred yoga later called haṭha, aiming at sahaja, the samarasa of Śiva and Śakti, liberation while living and the perfected, deathless body. Its ascetics (Kānphaṭa yogīs) are organised in twelve panths with monasteries from Gorakhpur and Tilla Jogian to Kadri and Nepal; its vernacular sayings (Gorakh Bānī) and sagas (Gopīcand, Bharthari, Mayanāmatī, the rescue of Matsyendra) shaped Sant, Vārkarī and folk religion across India.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the tradition's own rejection of Vedic ritual authority (see dsp:natha-varna-and-ritual) nor its overlap with the Buddhist Mahāsiddhas (C; brw:natha-mahasiddha).

name: Navya-Nyāya

scholarly.text: from Gaṅgeśa (first half of the 14th c.) to the present

transmissions_received.what: the whole problem-set of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika
transmissions_received.evidence: Gaṅgeśa's four khaṇḍas follow the four pramāṇas of NS 1.1.3; Udayana ('the Ācārya') is its constant authority.

transmissions_given.what: technical language and method of definition and refutation (e.g. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi)
technical language, used in the critique of Nyāya itself (Vyāsatīrtha's Tarkatāṇḍava)
the analysis of verbal cognition, debated with the grammarians

distinctive_positions: Organizes philosophy around the four means of knowledge (the four khaṇḍas of the Tattvacintāmaṇi).

Analyses every cognition into qualificand (viśeṣya), qualifier (prakāra) and relation (saṃsarga), and specifies properties by their delimitors (avacchedaka), counterpositives (pratiyogin) and relations, yielding a precise technical language.
Gives exact definitions of pervasion (vyāpti) — testing and rejecting five provisional ones before its own — and of consideration (parāmarśa), subjecthood (pakṣatā) and the adjunct (upādhi).
Recognizes extraordinary sense-contacts (via the universal, via a prior cognition, and yogic) to explain the grasp of pervasion, some errors, and yogic perception.
Validity of cognition is extrinsic (Gaṅgeśa's Prāmāṇyavāda).
Liberation is the absolute cessation of pain, defined technically as a destruction of pain not co-temporal with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).
The denotative power (śakti) of a word is the Lord's convention that 'this meaning is to be understood from this word'; verbal cognition requires expectancy, compatibility, proximity and intention.
Raghunātha Śiromaṇi re-examines the traditional list of categories (Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa).
summary: Navya-Nyāya ('New Nyāya') begins with Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's Tattvacintāmaṇi in Mithilā (14th c.) and flourished there and, from Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (c. 1500), in Navadvīpa in Bengal. It restates Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika doctrine in a precise technical language for analysing cognitions and their contents; this language became the common idiom of later Sanskrit learned discourse (Vedānta, Mīmāṃsā, grammar, law and poetics).
notes: The tradition's accounts of the rivalry between Mithilā and Navadvīpa (e.g. Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma carrying the Tattvacintāmaṇi to Navadvīpa from memory; Raghunātha's debate with Pakṣadhara) are recorded in the teacher entries at low confidence.

name: The Nāyaṉmārs and the Tirumuṟai (Tamil Śaiva bhakti)
regions: Sri Lanka (Tiruk kōṇamalai and Tiruk kētīccaram are sung in the Tēvāram)

tradition.text: saints of all ages; Māṇikkavācakar placed before the Tēvāram poets by much of the tradition

scholarly.text: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār c. 6th c.; Appar and Campantar 7th c.; Cuntarar 8th–9th c.; Māṇikkavācakar c. 9th c.; canon compiled c. 10th–12th c.

transmissions_given.what: the Tirumuṟai canon and the model of the four samayācāryas and their four paths

distinctive_positions: Love (aṉpu) for Śiva, expressed as service (toṇṭu) to him and to his devotees, outweighs birth, caste, learning and rite.
Śiva is present in named temples of the Tamil land; pilgrimage and song at each shrine are worship.
The four samayācāryas exemplify four relationships: servant (Appar), son (Campantar), friend (Cuntarar), and the true path of knowledge (Māṇikkavācakar).
Śiva's grace saves from all danger; the five syllables (namaccivāya) are the devotee's support.
Polemic against the Jains and Buddhists of the Tamil country (the tenth verse of Campantar's hymns).
summary: The Tamil Śaiva devotional movement of the sixty-three saints (Nāyaṉmārs) and nine groups of devotees celebrated in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai and Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam, whose hymns — the Tēvāram of Appar, Campantar and Cuntarar, Māṇikkavācakar's Tiruvācakam, Tirumūlar's Tirumantiram and others — form the twelve Tirumuṟai, the Tamil Śaiva canon still sung in temples by ōtuvārs.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U18. The living tradition counts the Nāyaṉmārs within Śaiva Siddhānta; scholars note that the hymnists predate the Tamil systematization and were absorbed into it retrospectively (the Tēvāram's theology is devotional, not scholastic).

name: Nikā saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Emphasis on ritual cleanliness and strict conduct (nikā = clean).
Traced to disciples of Mādhavadeva such as Mathurādāsa Ātā and Badulā Padma Ātā (names to verify).
summary: The saṃhati emphasising purity and discipline of conduct, traced to disciples of Mādhavadeva.

scholarly.text: formed after Mādhavadeva's death (1596), 17th c.

name: Nirañjanī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 16th–17th c. (Haridās Nirañjanī's dates uncertain)

distinctive_positions: Worship of Nirañjan, the stainless formless one, joining Nāth yogic language with Sant devotion.
Praised by Rajasthani anthologists alongside the Dādūpanthīs.
summary: A Rajasthani Sant sampradāya founded by Haridās Nirañjanī that names the ultimate Nirañjan and stands between the Nāth yogīs and the Sants.

name: Oxhead school

tradition.text: founded by Farong (594–657), said to have been instructed by the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin

scholarly.text: the lineage is attested from the 8th c.; the link to Daoxin is regarded by scholars as a later construction

distinctive_positions: The Way is fundamentally empty; 'forgetting feelings' (wangqing) rather than guarding mind (Zongmi's report).
Insentient things possess the Way (Jueguan lun, as generally described).
summary: A Tang Chan lineage of the Jiangnan region traced to Niutou Farong, which stressed emptiness and non-attachment and was classed by Zongmi as the school that 'eliminates traces'.

name: Northern school of Chan

scholarly.text: c. 700–c. 800 (imperial favour 701–730s; declined after Shenhui's attacks and the An Lushan rebellion)

distinctive_positions: Contemplating the mind (guanxin) and 'viewing purity' (kanjing).
The five expedient means (wu fangbian) of the Dasheng wusheng fangbian men.
The mind is originally pure but obscured by adventitious dust; practice removes it (the view the Platform Sūtra ascribes to Shenxiu's verse).
summary: The metropolitan Chan of Shenxiu (d. 706) and his heirs Puji and Yifu, favoured by the Tang court; Shenhui attacked it in 730–732 as collateral and gradual, a characterization later Chan histories adopted.

name: Nyāya

tradition.text: from the sage Gautama Akṣapāda (no fixed date in the tradition)

scholarly.text: Nyāya Sūtra redacted c. 2nd–3rd c. CE; commentarial line from the 5th c.; merged with Vaiśeṣika from c. the 10th–11th c.; continued as Navya-Nyāya from the 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the ontology of categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence), atomism, and the account of the self's qualities
transmissions_received.evidence: Vātsyāyana acknowledges the six Vaiśeṣika categories as further objects of knowledge (NBh 1.1.9) and cites the Vaiśeṣika account of the yogin's perception of the self (NBh 1.1.3, cf. VS 9.13); later manuals are explicitly 'for the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Nyāya' (Tarkasaṅgraha).

transmissions_received.what: religious affiliation of several authors (Śaiva / Pāśupata)
transmissions_received.evidence: Uddyotakara is called a Pāśupata teacher in the Nyāyavārttika colophon; Vācaspati's Tātparyaṭīkā opens by invoking Pinākin (Śiva); Bhāsarvajña's Nyāyasāra ends with a Śaiva account of the path (moderate/low confidence).

transmissions_given.what: its categories, method and problems, recast by Gaṅgeśa
the theory of debate and inference that Buddhist logicians criticized and reshaped (Dignāga against Vātsyāyana)
the vocabulary of pramāṇa and the rules of debate used by all later Vedānta schools

distinctive_positions: The highest good (niḥśreyasa) is attained from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), above all of the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self (NS 1.1.9).
Bondage runs from false knowledge through faults, activity and birth to pain; removing false knowledge by knowledge of truth removes the rest and yields liberation (NS 1.1.2).
Four means of knowledge — perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3); tradition, presumption, inclusion and absence are reduced to these (NS 2.2.1–2).
The self is an eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition; desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition are its marks (NS 1.1.10); selves are many.
The mind (manas) is one per body and atomic, which is why cognitions do not arise simultaneously (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56, 3.2.59).

Liberation (apavarga) is absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), in which — on the mainstream view — the self has neither pleasure nor cognition (NBh 1.1.22); Bhāsarvajña dissents, holding that eternal bliss is experienced.
Validity of cognition is extrinsic (parataḥ); error is misplaced apprehension (anyathākhyāti).

Īśvara is a distinct self, free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, who assists human effort and makes action fruitful (NS 4.1.19–21; NBh); later he is proved by inference as maker of the world (Udayana, NK 5.1) and as author of the Veda, whose validity is like that of mantra and medicine because its speaker is reliable (NS 2.1.69).
Effects are new beginnings not pre-existing in their causes (ārambha / asatkārya); the whole is a new substance distinct from its parts (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).

Realism: external objects, universals, relations and enduring things are real; momentariness, idealism and the thesis that everything lacks own-nature are refuted (NS 3.2.10–17, 4.1.25–40, 4.2.26–37).

A developed theory of debate: honest discussion (vāda), wrangling (jalpa) and cavilling (vitaṇḍā), with pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat; jalpa and vitaṇḍā are permitted to protect truth like a thorn-fence around a sprout (NS 4.2.50).
Sound is a non-eternal quality of ākāśa; the relation of word and meaning is conventional (NS 2.1.56–57, 2.2.13ff.).
summary: Nyāya ('method', 'reasoning') is the Vedic darśana of the means of valid knowledge and of reasoned debate, founded on Gautama Akṣapāda's Nyāya Sūtra and developed by Vātsyāyana, Uddyotakara, Vācaspati Miśra, Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, Bhāsarvajña and Udayana. It teaches that liberation — absolute release from pain — follows from knowledge of the truth about the self and the other objects of knowledge, won by the means of knowledge, reasoning, study, discussion and yoga. From about the 10th–11th c. it merged with Vaiśeṣika into a single realist system, and from Gaṅgeśa (14th c.) continued as Navya-Nyāya.

name: Nyingma (the Ancient / Old Translation school)

tradition.text: founded in the 8th century under King Trisong Detsen, when Padmasambhava, Śāntarakṣita and Vimalamitra taught in Tibet and Samye was built

scholarly.text: the 8th-9th c. imperial translations; the name 'Nyingma' (the old ones) came into use from the 11th c. in contrast to the new (gsar ma) translations

transmissions_received.what: the Indian tantras (Mahāyoga, Anuyoga) and their empowerments, through Padmasambhava, Vimalamitra, Buddhaguhya and the 8th-9th c. translators
