transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Dudjom Rinpoche's history; Nyangral's Chöjung)

transmissions_received.what: Śāntarakṣita's Madhyamaka and the monastic foundation at Samye
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: the Mūlasarvāstivāda ordination given to the first Tibetan monks (the 'seven men who were tested')
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

transmissions_given.what: Dzogchen and the Nyingthig combined with Mahāmudrā (the Third Karmapa; Karma Chagme's union of Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen)
the treasure (terma) cycles and Dzogchen that stand at the centre of the non-sectarian movement
shared Dzogchen, treasure and nine-vehicle frameworks (direction disputed; see dsp:bon-and-buddhism)

distinctive_positions: The teaching is ordered as nine vehicles (theg pa rim pa dgu), culminating in the three inner tantras Mahāyoga, Anuyoga and Atiyoga (Dzogchen).
Three streams of transmission: the long lineage of the spoken word (bka' ma), the short lineage of treasures (gter ma) and profound pure visions (dag snang).
The primordial buddha Samantabhadra (Kuntuzangpo) is the dharmakāya teacher; Garab Dorje the first human teacher of Dzogchen; Padmasambhava the 'second Buddha' for Tibet.
The Guhyagarbha is the root Mahāyoga tantra: all phenomena are primordially the maṇḍala of deities — 'great purity and equality' (dag mnyam chen po).

Atiyoga distinguishes awareness (rig pa) from ordinary mind (sems) and teaches the ground as primordial purity and spontaneous presence, realized by cutting through (khregs chod) and direct crossing (thod rgal).
Its tantras (the rnying rgyud) were translated in the first diffusion; their Indian authenticity was disputed by later critics and defended by the school (see dsp:authenticity-of-nyingma-tantras).
A double sangha: celibate monastics and lay tantric householders (sngags pa, the 'white-robed, long-haired' community).
summary: The oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism, tracing itself to the 8th-century imperial translations and to Padmasambhava, Śāntarakṣita, Vimalamitra and the translator Vairocana. It arranges the whole Dharma as nine vehicles, keeps its own canon of Old Tantras (the Nyingma Gyubum), transmits teachings both by unbroken spoken lineage (kama) and by revealed treasures (terma), and holds the Great Perfection (Dzogchen, Atiyoga) as the summit of the path, systematized by Longchenpa and Jigme Lingpa.

name: Ōbaku Zen

tradition.text: from Ingen Ryūki's arrival in Nagasaki (1654) and the founding of Ōbakusan Manpukuji (1661)

scholarly.text: 17th c. Ming-dynasty Linji transmission; living

transmissions_received.what: Ming Linji lineage of Miyun Yuanwu and Feiyin Tongrong at Wanfusi, Mount Huangbo (Fujian)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition records

distinctive_positions: Ming-style monastic observance: Chinese-pronounced sūtra chanting, Ming precepts platform and rules (Ōbaku shingi).
Combination of kōan meditation with recitation of Amitābha's name (nenbutsu Zen), which Hakuin's Rinzai line criticised.
Printing of the complete canon (Tetsugen edition) as Dharma work.
summary: The third Japanese Zen denomination, founded by the Chinese Linji master Yinyuan Longqi (Ingen, 1592–1673), which preserves Ming Chinese monastic forms and combines Zen with Pure Land recitation.

name: Pa-Auk tradition (Pa-Auk Tawya)
regions: branches in Asia and the West

tradition.text: Pa-Auk Sayadaw (Āciṇṇa, b. 1934) became abbot of Pa-Auk Tawya in 1981

scholarly.text: late 20th c. onward

distinctive_positions: Close adherence to the Visuddhimagga and Abhidhamma as a practical manual.

Samatha-first route: mindfulness of breathing to the fourth jhāna with a bright counterpart sign, then the kasiṇas, the formless attainments and the immeasurables; or, for the pure-insight vehicle, four-elements meditation to access concentration.

Insight requires seeing ultimate realities directly: the tiny material groups (rūpa-kalāpa) and their elements, the mind-moments of cognitive processes with their mental factors, and dependent origination across past and future lives, before contemplating the three characteristics.
summary: The Burmese forest tradition of Pa-Auk Sayadaw (b. 1934), which teaches the Visuddhimagga's full sequence of calm and insight, including direct discernment of Abhidhamma ultimate realities.

name: Pañcācārya (Pañcapīṭha) tradition

tradition.text: the five ācāryas appear in every yuga from liṅgas; in the Kali age as Revaṇa (Reṇuka), Maruḷa, Ēkōrāma, Paṇḍitārādhya and Viśvārādhya

scholarly.text: the five-pīṭha organization and its Sanskrit literature are attested from the late medieval period; dates debated

distinctive_positions: Vīraśaiva dharma is beginningless (anādi), taught by Śiva in the later portion of the Śaiva Āgamas (SSM 5.14) and consistent with the Veda (SSM 5.5–13).
Basava is honoured as a great devotee and reviver within this older stream, not as its founder.
The Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's 101 sthalas are the full map of the path; doctrine is Śivādvaita (SSM 3.86) — in Śrīpati's formulation, Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita.
Five pīṭhas (seats), each founded by one ācārya, transmit initiation through the guru lineage.
summary: The strand of Vīraśaivism organized around five ācāryas — Revaṇa (Reṇuka), Maruḷa, Ēkōrāma, Paṇḍitārādhya and Viśvārādhya — who, in the tradition's account, emerged from liṅgas at five sacred sites and founded the five pīṭhas. Its scripture is the Śaiva Āgamas read in their Vīraśaiva portion, the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi and Śrīpati's Śrīkarabhāṣya.
notes: The commentary on the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi (Tattvapradīpikā) already speaks of the 'world-famous Pañcācārya lineage' (e-text M00207, ch. 6 commentary). Seat names (siṃhāsana) are recorded on the teacher entries at low confidence.

name: Pāñcarātra
regions: Kashmir (early saṃhitās known there by the 10th c.)

tradition.text: spoken by Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva himself and received by sages such as Nārada and Śāṇḍilya; one account derives the name from Nārāyaṇa's five-night (pañcarātra) sacrifice (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.6.1)

scholarly.text: the Pāñcarātra is named in the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya; the surviving saṃhitās date from roughly the 8th/9th c. onward (the Jayākhya is quoted in 10th-c. Kashmir), with many South Indian saṃhitās later

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata/Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva and the vyūha doctrine
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account and the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya

transmissions_given.what: temple ritual, the five forms of God, and scriptural support for surrender (prapatti)
Viṣṇu ritual (e.g. the Viṣṇu Saṃhitā; Viṣṇu chapters of the Tantrasamuccaya)
ritual procedures later adapted in Gauḍīya manuals

distinctive_positions: The Pāñcarātra (Bhagavacchāstra) was spoken by Bhagavān himself and is therefore authoritative (Āgamaprāmāṇya).
The supreme Brahman is the ṣāḍguṇya: knowledge, power (śakti), lordship, strength, virility and splendour; knowledge is its very form, the other five are its aspects (Ahirbudhnya 2.53–62).
God exists as para, vyūha (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha), vibhava (39 descents in the Ahirbudhnya), antaryāmin and arcā (the consecrated image).
Saṅkarṣaṇa manifests knowledge and strength, Pradyumna lordship and virility, Aniruddha power and splendour; each vyūha still possesses all six (Ahirbudhnya 5.16–19).
Śrī/Lakṣmī is Nārāyaṇa's eternal Śakti, performing the five acts: concealment, creation, maintenance, dissolution and grace (Lakṣmī Tantra 12.12–14).
Creation is pure (śuddha: the vyūhas and their realm) and other-than-pure (śuddhetara, from prakṛti); the Jayākhya distinguishes Brahmā's, primordial-matter's and the pure creation (JS 2–4).
Grace (anugraha), called śaktipāta, brings the soul's karmas into equilibrium (karmasāmya) and lifts it from saṃsāra (Ahirbudhnya 14.28–34).
Surrender (śaraṇāgati/nyāsa) with six limbs attains what other means cannot (Ahirbudhnya 37.25–29; Lakṣmī Tantra 17.56–62).
The Pāñcarātrin's day has five periods (pañcakāla): approach (abhigamana), gathering (upādāna), worship (ijyā), study (svādhyāya) and meditation (yoga).
The Pāñcarātra is fourfold by siddhānta: Mantra-, Āgama-, Tantra- and Tantrāntara-siddhānta (Pādma jñānapāda 1.76–82).
summary: The Pāñcarātra is the Vaiṣṇava tantric tradition of revealed saṃhitās (traditionally 108) teaching the theology of Bhagavān with six qualities and his five modes, Lakṣmī as his Śakti, the pure and impure creations, initiation, temple building, image installation, daily worship in five periods, mantra, yoga and surrender. It governs worship in major South Indian Viṣṇu temples (e.g. Śrīraṅgam, Melkote, Kāñcī) and was defended as scripture by Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Pārśvacandra Gaccha

scholarly.text: 16th c. CE

distinctive_positions: an early-16th-century offshoot of the Tapā Gaccha; small
summary: A small Mūrtipūjaka gaccha named after Pārśvacandrasūri (16th c.), a Gujarati author of vernacular commentaries (ṭabos) on the Āgamas.

name: Pāśupata (Pāñcārthika Pāśupata)

tradition.text: the Lord's descent in a brahmin body at Kāyāvataraṇa and his teaching to Kuśika (Kauṇḍinya); Śiva's 28th incarnation, contemporary with Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva and Vyāsa Dvaipāyana (Liṅga P. 1.24.125-131)

scholarly.text: Lakulīśa c. 2nd c. CE (by counting back from the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE); Kauṇḍinya c. 4th–6th c.; the order is attested epigraphically into the 13th–14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the five brahma-mantras (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna) that close the five adhyāyas of the Pāśupata Sūtra
transmissions_received.evidence: the same mantras stand in Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10 (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad)

transmissions_received.what: the ash vow called pāśupata and a verbal parallel to PS 5.35-38
transmissions_received.evidence: Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad 5 (direction of borrowing not settled)

transmissions_given.what: the Pāśupata observance as the base on which the Lākula (lokātīta) observance and cosmology were built (scholarly reconstruction)
pati-paśu-pāśa vocabulary, five-mantra liturgy, ash observances
a Pāśupata affiliation of Naiyāyikas (Uddyotakara called 'Pāśupatācārya'; Bhāsarvajña author of the Ratnaṭīkā); Jain doxographers call the Naiyāyikas Śaivas and the Vaiśeṣikas Pāśupatas

distinctive_positions: Five categories (pañcārtha) sum up the teaching: effect (kārya), cause (kāraṇa), union (yoga), rule (vidhi) and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta) (PABh on PS 1.1; reported by Śaṅkara at BSBh 2.2.37).

The Lord (pati) is the cause who produces the whole effect - knowledge-qualities (vidyā), the insentient 'parts' (kalā) and the souls (paśu) - at will, all at once or in sequence, depending neither on karma nor on the soul (PABh on PS 2.5-6).
All sentient beings except the Lord are paśus, including the gods from Brahmā down and those liberated through Sāṃkhya-Yoga (PABh on PS 1.1).
The end of suffering is reached by the Lord's grace (īśaprasāda, PS 5.40), not by knowledge, dispassion, merit, powers or renunciation alone (PABh on PS 1.1).
The end of suffering is twofold: the absolute cessation of all suffering, and the attainment of the Lord's powers of knowing and acting (Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha ch. 6).
Yoga is the union of the self with the Lord through the mind (PABh on PS 1.1, 1.20).
The observance is 'beyond the āśramas' (atyāśrama) and open only to brahmin men (PABh on PS 1.1, 4.20).
Seeking dishonour is the highest austerity: the reviled ascetic's demerit passes to those who revile him and their merit passes to him (PS 3.6-9, 3.19, 4.9).
By this rule a brahmin who reaches Rudra's proximity does not return (PS 4.19-20).
summary: The Pāśupatas are the earliest Śaiva ascetic order known from texts. They trace their teaching to Lakulīśa, Śiva's incarnation at Kāyāvarohaṇa in Gujarat, and to his four disciples Kuśika, Garga, Mitra and Kauruṣya. Their root text, the Pāśupata Sūtra, survives with Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya, which organises it by five categories and five stages of practice. Initiated brahmin ascetics bathe and lie in ash, worship with laughter, song, dance, a bull-like sound, prostration and mantra, then leave the temple to court dishonour by feigned madness, and finally seek the end of suffering in caves and cremation grounds through constant remembrance of Rudra and his grace. The Gaṇakārikā and its Ratnaṭīkā systematise the path as eight pentads and one triad.
notes: A 20th-century revival of Lakulīśa worship at Kāyāvarohaṇa (Karvan) is associated with Swami Kripalvananda (recent; low confidence; it is not a continuation of the medieval order). Jain doxographers (Guṇaratna, Rājaśekhara) list eighteen Pāśupata tīrthakaras from Nakulīśa to Vidyāguru.

name: Pātañjala Yoga (the Yoga darśana)
alt_names: Rājayoga (later name for the samādhi-centred yoga of Patañjali)
Aṣṭāṅga-yoga (later name for its eight-limbed method)

tradition.text: Yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha at the beginning of creation; re-taught (anuśāsana, YS 1.1) by Patañjali, whom the tradition regards as an incarnation of Śeṣa (not dated by the tradition)

scholarly.text: Yoga Sūtra with its bhāṣya c. 325–425 CE as one work (Maas); other proposals range from the 2nd c. BCE to the 5th c. CE; commentaries continue to the 18th–20th c.

transmissions_received.what: the analysis of puruṣa and prakṛti, the guṇas and the principles (tattvas); the bhāṣya's colophons call the work 'sāṃkhya-pravacana' and it quotes Sāṃkhya authorities
transmissions_received.evidence: colophons 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre'; Vārṣagaṇya named in YBh 3.53; unnamed quotations in YBh 1.25, 1.36, 2.5, 2.6, 2.17, 2.18, 2.20, 2.22 that the commentators assign to Pañcaśikha; 'śāstrānuśāsana' quoted at YBh 4.13

transmissions_received.what: yoga as the firm holding of the senses (Kaṭha), the Śvetāśvatara's yoga chapter, the Maitrī's six-limbed yoga; YBh 3.34 uses the Chāndogya's 'small lotus-house in the city of Brahman' and 3.35 quotes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka
transmissions_received.evidence: textual parallels; explicit quotation in YBh 3.35 ('vijñātāram are kena vijānīyāt')

transmissions_received.what: the yoga of the Mokṣadharma and the Gītā; the Mahābhārata names Hiraṇyagarbha as the knower of yoga
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition account; textual parallels

transmissions_received.what: shared meditative vocabulary (the four attitudes, kleśa and anuśaya, samāpatti, the five faculties of YS 1.20, the four inversions of YS 2.5) — direction debated
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis; see the brw: entries of this unit

transmissions_given.what: the eight limbs and 'rājayoga' (samādhi) as the goal to which haṭha leads
Pātañjala definitions and methods used by Advaita authors (the Vivaraṇa ascribed to Śaṅkara; later Advaita manuals quoting the Yoga Sūtra)
Jain yoga works (Haribhadra, Hemacandra) engage and adapt Patañjali's yoga
Purāṇic yoga chapters teach an eight-limbed yoga in Pātañjala terms
Vivekananda's Rāja Yoga (1896) presents the Yoga Sūtras (recent)
modern teaching of the Yoga Sūtras alongside āsana practice (recent)

distinctive_positions: Yoga is the stilling (nirodha) of the activities (vṛtti) of the mind (YS 1.2); then the seer abides in its own form (1.3). Vyāsa: 'yoga is samādhi', a property of the mind at all its levels (YBh 1.1).

Accepts the Sāṃkhya analysis of the seer (puruṣa, pure consciousness, many) and the seen (prakṛti, the three guṇas), and adds Īśvara, a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), the teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by Oṃ (1.27).
Means: practice and dispassion (1.12); devotion to Īśvara (1.23); for the unconcentrated, kriyā-yoga (2.1); the eight limbs (2.29).

The five afflictions (kleśa), rooted in ignorance (avidyā), produce the store of karma that ripens as birth, life-span and experience (2.3–14); the conjunction of seer and seen, caused by ignorance, is the cause of the suffering to be avoided (2.17, 2.24).
The śāstra has four parts like medicine: what is to be avoided, its cause, avoidance, and the means of avoidance (YBh 2.15).
Samādhi is with full awareness (samprajñāta: with reasoning, reflection, bliss, I-am-ness) or beyond it (asamprajñāta); with seed (sabīja) or seedless (nirbīja) (1.17–18, 1.46, 1.51).
Three means of valid knowledge: perception, inference, testimony (1.7).
Things transform in property, time-mark and state (3.13); past and future exist in their own form (4.12).
The mind is not self-luminous; it is seen by the unchanging puruṣa, who always knows its activities (4.18–19); objects do not depend on a single mind (4.15–16).

Powers (vibhūti, siddhi) arise from saṃyama but are obstacles in samādhi (3.37); dispassion even toward the highest of them leads to kaivalya (3.50); the yogin should not be attached or proud when the celestials invite him (3.51).

Liberation is kaivalya, the aloneness of the seer, when the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, return to their source (4.34); Vyāsa: when afflictions and karma cease, the wise one is liberated while living (YBh 4.30).
Practitioners are graded by the intensity of their means and ardor (1.21–22).
summary: The Yoga darśana of Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra (four pādas, 195 sūtras) and its commentaries — Vyāsa's bhāṣya, Vācaspati Miśra's Tattvavaiśāradī, the Vivaraṇa ascribed to Śaṅkara, Bhoja's Rājamārtaṇḍa, Vijñānabhikṣu's Yogavārttika and later vṛttis. It teaches the stilling of the mind through practice, dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and the eight limbs, leading through the samādhis to discriminative discernment between sattva and puruṣa and to kaivalya. The tradition names Hiraṇyagarbha as the first teacher of yoga.
notes: Status 'living': the classical commentarial school continued into the 18th–20th c. (Nāgeśa, Nārāyaṇatīrtha, Sadāśiva Brahmendra; Hariharānanda Āraṇya's Kāpil Maṭh, recent) and the Yoga Sūtra is widely taught in modern lineages.

name: Peling (the treasure tradition of Pema Lingpa)

tradition.text: treasures revealed by Pema Lingpa from 1476 (the Burning Lake, Mebar Tsho)

scholarly.text: late 15th - early 16th c.

distinctive_positions: Bhutan's own Nyingma treasure tradition, with the Kunzang Gongdü cycle and sacred dances; carried by Pema Lingpa's three reincarnation lines (moderate confidence).
summary: The lineage of the Bhutanese treasure revealer Pema Lingpa (1450-1521), central to Nyingma practice and ritual culture in Bhutan.

name: Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā
regions: South India, especially Kerala (tradition); also Mithilā (Bhavanātha)

tradition.text: Prabhākara is presented in Bhāṭṭa legend as Kumārila's pupil, who earned the title 'Guru'

scholarly.text: Prabhākara c. 7th c. CE (relation to Kumārila disputed); independent Prābhākara works continue to c. 16th c. (Rāmānujācārya's Tantrarahasya)

distinctive_positions: Five means of knowledge: perception, inference, verbal testimony (śāstra), comparison and postulation; non-apprehension is not a separate means (Prakaraṇapañcikā, Pramāṇapārāyaṇa).
Words convey their meanings only as already connected with other meanings, ultimately with what is to be done (anvitābhidhāna / kāryānvitābhidhāna).

Error is non-apprehension (akhyāti): 'this is silver' is two cognitions — a perception ('this') and a memory ('silver') — whose difference is not grasped (Prakaraṇapañcikā, Nayavīthī and Pramāṇapārāyaṇa).
Every cognition is self-luminous and manifests knower, known and knowing together (tripuṭī-pratyakṣa); the self appears only as the subject of cognition.
The meaning of an injunction is the command or 'what is to be done' (niyoga / kārya), identified with the apūrva known only from the Veda.
The Veda does not convey accomplished (siddha) things for their own sake; hence descriptions of a blissful liberation have no independent authority (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
Eight categories, adding power (śakti), similarity (sādṛśya), number (saṅkhyā) and dependence (paratantratā) to substance, quality, action and universal.
Liberation is the absolute ending of embodiment caused by the complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma; the liberated self remains in mere being, without cognition (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
No Īśvara directs dharma and adharma or creates the world; things arise and perish gradually, and the usage of elders from which word-meaning is learned is beginningless (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).
summary: The school of Prabhākara Miśra ('the Guru'), based on his Bṛhatī and Laghvī on Śabara's commentary and systematized by Śālikanātha's Prakaraṇapañcikā, then by Bhavanātha and later Prābhākara authors. It holds five means of knowledge, the self-luminosity of cognition, the akhyāti account of error, and the doctrine that words mean in connection with what is to be done (kārya).
notes: Status set to 'unknown': few independent Prābhākara works are known after c. the 16th century, though its doctrines are still studied in traditional curricula.

name: Prajñaptivāda
distinctive_positions: Suffering is not an aggregate; the twelve sense-bases are not real (designations); conditioned things are designated in mutual dependence (Vasumitra; low confidence).
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch distinguishing what is real from what is designation (prajñapti).

name: Buddhist epistemology and logic (pramāṇa school)
alt_names: the school of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti
Buddhist logicians (bauddha naiyāyika in opponents' texts)
regions: South India and Kāñcī (tradition's account of Dignāga)

scholarly.text: Dignāga c. 480–540; Dharmakīrti c. 6th–7th c.; the school active in India until the late 12th c. and continued in Tibet

transmissions_received.what: mind-only, self-awareness and the ultimate non-duality of cognition
transmissions_received.evidence: Ālambanaparīkṣā; PV ch. 3 (Tibetan order)

transmissions_received.what: momentariness, causal efficacy, representational cognition
transmissions_received.evidence: textual parallels

transmissions_received.what: the vocabulary and genre of debate, the members of proof, points of defeat — critically revised
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit-citation (PS criticizes Nyāya definitions)

transmissions_given.what: the challenge that reshaped Nyāya (Uddyotakara, Vācaspati, Udayana answer Dignāga and Dharmakīrti)
the apoha and omniscience debates (Kumārila)
the categories and arguments Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta engage and invert
a logic culture engaged by Akalaṅka, Haribhadra, Prabhācandra
the tshad ma curriculum and the Collected Topics (bsdus grwa)
Sakya Paṇḍita's Treasury of Reasoning

distinctive_positions: There are exactly two means of valid cognition — perception and inference — because there are exactly two kinds of object, the unique particular and the universal (PS 1.2; NB 1.2–3, 1.12–17).
Perception is free of conceptual construction and non-erroneous (NB 1.4); it has four kinds: sensory, mental, reflexive self-awareness and yogic (NB 1.7–11).

A valid reason has three characteristics (trairūpya): present in the subject, present only in similar cases, absent from all dissimilar cases (NB 2.5); there are three kinds of valid reason — effect, own-nature and non-perception (NB 2.11).
Words and concepts do not reach real universals; they operate by exclusion of the other (anyāpoha).
Whatever exists is momentary, since to exist is to be causally efficacious (Ratnakīrti: yat sat tat kṣaṇikam).
Every cognition is reflexively aware of itself (svasaṃvedana); the result of a means of knowledge is this self-awareness.

The Buddha is a 'person of valid cognition' (pramāṇabhūta) because he knows what is to be abandoned and adopted with its means, a knowledge born of compassion cultivated over many lives (PV Pramāṇasiddhi chapter).
No creator god, no authorless scripture, no permanent self: each is refuted by reasoning.
summary: The Buddhist tradition of logic and epistemology founded by Dignāga and recast by Dharmakīrti, which recognized only perception and inference, grounded all reasoning in causal efficacy and momentary particulars, explained language by exclusion, and used this apparatus both to defend the Buddha's authority and liberation and to refute self, God and the authority of the Veda. Its Indian line ended with the monasteries of Bengal and Bihar; it lives on in the Tibetan monastic curriculum.

name: Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka

scholarly.text: Buddhapālita c. 470–540 CE; Candrakīrti c. 600–650 CE; the label 'Prāsaṅgika' (thal 'gyur ba) is a Tibetan doxographical category of the 11th–12th c., not a name Candrakīrti used

transmissions_received.what: Nāgārjuna's and Āryadeva's texts and method of refuting by consequences

transmissions_given.what: Candrakīrti's view through Atiśa
Prāsaṅgika as the highest view, as systematized by Tsongkhapa

distinctive_positions: The Mādhyamika need only draw out the unwanted consequences (prasaṅga) of the opponent's own theses; he does not use autonomous inferences (svatantra-anumāna) whose subject and reasons would have to be established for both parties by their own nature (Candrakīrti, Prasannapadā ch.1).
Nothing has own-nature even conventionally; the conventional is accepted only as the world accepts it (lokaprasiddhi).
Each thing bears two natures, the one found by correct seeing (the ultimate) and the one found by false seeing (the conventional) (MA 6.23).
Reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana) and a storehouse consciousness are rejected even conventionally (MA 6; BCA 9.17–25).
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also realize the selflessness of phenomena (Candrakīrti, MA bhāṣya on 1.8).
The ultimate is not within the domain of the intellect; the intellect is conventional (BCA 9.2).
summary: The line of Madhyamaka exegesis that follows Buddhapālita's commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā as defended by Candrakīrti against Bhāviveka's criticism: emptiness is shown by reducing the opponent's positions to absurd consequences, without autonomous proofs, and no own-nature is admitted at any level. Śāntideva, Prajñākaramati, Jayānanda and Atiśa are counted in it by Tibetan doxographers, for whom (from Patsab Nyima Drak onward) it became the highest Buddhist view.

name: Pratyabhijñā (the philosophy of recognition)

scholarly.text: Somānanda c. 900-950; Utpaladeva c. 925-975; Abhinavagupta's Vimarśinī dated Laukika 90 (c. 1014/15 CE); Kṣemarāja c. 1000-1050.

transmissions_received.what: the logical-epistemological idiom of Dharmakīrti's school, answered polemically
the idea that awareness is intrinsically verbal (vāc); critique of paśyantī as ultimate
transmissions_received.evidence: Śivadṛṣṭi ch. 2; ĪPK 1.5.13

distinctive_positions: Liberation is the recognition that one's own self is the Lord (Īśvara), endowed with the powers of knowing and acting; the Lord cannot be proved or denied since he is the ever-established knower (ĪPK 1.1.2-3).
Consciousness is essentially reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), 'supreme speech arising of itself', and this is the Lord's freedom and sovereignty (ĪPK 1.5.13-14).

Memory, cognition and exclusion (jñāna, smṛti, apohana) are possible only if a single conscious subject contains the diverse within itself (ĪPK 1.3.7, 1.4.3) - against the Buddhist denial of an enduring self.
Objects are manifestations (ābhāsa) of consciousness shown as if external by the power of māyā.
The ultimate is not the grammarians' paśyantī (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1ff.).
Devotion (bhakti) is the enjoyment of the identity with Śiva already recognized (Utpaladeva's Śivastotrāvalī).
summary: The philosophical school founded by Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi) and systematized by Utpaladeva (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his two commentaries), commented on by Abhinavagupta and summarized by Kṣemarāja (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya). It argues, in dialogue with Buddhist logicians, grammarians, Naiyāyikas and Vedāntins, that the individual can recognize himself as Maheśvara, and that this recognition itself is liberation.

name: Pudgalavāda
regions: Bengal and eastern India (Saṃmitīya per Xuanzang and Yijing)

tradition.text: The Vātsīputrīya split from the Sarvāstivāda (Vasumitra) or from the Theravāda's Vajjiputtakas (Dīpavaṃsa) in the third century after the parinirvāṇa

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE – c. 12th c. CE; the Saṃmitīya was one of the largest orders in 7th-c. India (Xuanzang)

distinctive_positions: There is a person (pudgala) that is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates; it is designated in dependence on the present, appropriated aggregates, as fire is designated in dependence on fuel (AKBh 9, Pradhan p. 461; Vasumitra).
The person is 'inexpressible' (avaktavya) — a fifth kind of knowable besides the past, the future, the present and the unconditioned (AKBh 9, p. 462–463).
Dharmas do not pass from one life to the next apart from the person; the person is the bearer of the burden of the aggregates (Bhārahāra-sūtra, as they read it).
Three designations of the person — by support, by transmigration and by cessation (Saṃmitīyanikāya-śāstra; low confidence on the terms).
Some conditioned things are momentary, others (e.g. the body) endure for a time (Vasumitra; low confidence).
An arhat can fall back (Kathāvatthu 1.2, per the commentary); an intermediate existence exists (Kathāvatthu 8.2, per the commentary: Sammitiyas).
summary: The Pudgalavāda ('those who affirm the person') comprised the Vātsīputrīya and its offshoots, above all the Saṃmitīya, which Xuanzang and Yijing describe as one of the four great orders of 7th-century India. They taught an inexpressible person, neither identical with nor different from the aggregates, and were refuted by the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu 1.1), the Sarvāstivāda (Vijñānakāya, Mahāvibhāṣā) and Vasubandhu (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya ch. 9). Few of their own texts survive, in Chinese.

name: The Purāṇic tradition (paurāṇika)
regions: all of South Asia; recited at Naimiṣa (the tradition's frame), in temples, tīrthas and homes

tradition.text: The Purāṇa is remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas (Matsya 53.3); in every Dvāpara age Vyāsa condenses it to four lakh verses in eighteen Purāṇas (Matsya 53.8-11); the present Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, taught it to Romaharṣaṇa at the junction of Dvāpara and Kali (Kali reckoned from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: Purāṇa is named as a class of lore from the Atharvaveda and Brāhmaṇas on; the extant Purāṇas were composed and continually redacted from about the 3rd-4th c. CE to the second millennium CE

transmissions_received.what: itihāsa-purāṇa recitation as part of Vedic ritual (the pāriplava cycle of the Aśvamedha) and the name 'fifth Veda'
transmissions_received.evidence: ChU 7.1.2; ŚB 13.4.3.13 (U01/U03 own the refs); BhP 1.4.20

transmissions_received.what: narrative material, genealogies and teaching dialogues shared with the Mahābhārata and Harivaṃśa
transmissions_received.evidence: textual parallels (see brw:mahabharata-to-puranic)

transmissions_received.what: the order of creation from pradhāna through mahat, ahaṃkāra, tanmātras, elements and senses
transmissions_received.evidence: VP 1.2; BhP 2.10.3, 3.26 (see brw:samkhya-to-puranic)

transmissions_received.what: the eight limbs, the definition of yoga as restraint of the activities of citta, the list of obstacles
transmissions_received.evidence: LiP 1.8.7-9, 1.9.1-16; VP 6.7.36-45; ŚiP 7.2.37-38 (see brw:patanjala-yoga-to-puranic)

transmissions_received.what: Pāśupata yoga and the Pāśupata vow in the Śaiva Purāṇas
the Sātvata/Pāñcarātra doctrine of Vāsudeva and the vyūhas
transmissions_received.evidence: BhP 1.3.8 (Nārada 'expounded the Sātvata tantra')

transmissions_given.what: the Bhāgavata as the root scripture of rasa theology and of the practice of the name
the Bhāgavata (Vallabha's Subodhinī) as scripture of the path of grace
the Lalitopākhyāna's narrative of Lalitā; the Lalitā Sahasranāma's self-attribution to the Brahmāṇḍa
the Devī Māhātmya as the root Śākta scripture; the Devī Bhāgavata
Dattātreya as avadhūta teacher of yoga (Mārkaṇḍeya 16-44; BhP 1.3.11, 11.7-9)
the Bhāgavata's devotion to the name
the Bhāgavata as the scripture retold by Śaṅkaradeva

distinctive_positions: The Purāṇa (with itihāsa) is the 'fifth Veda' and expands the meaning of the Veda (BhP 1.4.20; Matsya 53.3); it was taught out of compassion for those without access to the Veda (BhP 1.4.25).
A Purāṇa has five marks - sarga, pratisarga, vaṃśa, manvantara, vaṃśānucarita (VP 3.6.24; KūP 1.1.12; Matsya 53.65); the Bhāgavata gives two lists of ten marks (BhP 2.10.1; 12.7.9-10).
Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and further Upapurāṇas, with lists that differ in detail (VP 3.6.21-23; BhP 12.7.23-24; KūP 1.1.13-20; Matsya 53).
Cyclical cosmology: yugas, mahāyugas, manvantaras, kalpas and the lifetime of Brahmā; four kinds of dissolution (nitya, naimittika, prākṛtika, ātyantika).
A layered cosmos of fourteen worlds, Bhū-maṇḍala of seven island-continents and seven oceans around Meru, and hells beneath the earth.
Death is followed by Yama's messengers, a year-long road, judgment, and a preta state that the rites of the sons (piṇḍa, śrāddha, sapiṇḍīkaraṇa) end (Garuḍa Pretakalpa).

Devotion (bhakti) to the chosen supreme deity - Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, Śiva or the Goddess - is the highest dharma and the easy means in the Kali age; the divine name purifies (BhP 1.2.6; 6.2.9-10; 12.3.51-52; VP 6.2.17).
Yoga is taught in the eightfold form, directed to the deity's form as its support (VP 6.7; BhP 3.28; LiP 1.8-9; ŚiP 7.2.37-39); powers are obstacles (BhP 11.15.33).
Sectarian variety about the ultimate: each Purāṇa exalts its deity, while many passages identify Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva as functions of one reality (VP 1.2.66).
summary: The tradition of the Purāṇas ('ancient lore'): Sanskrit compendia recited by sūtas and paurāṇikas, attributed to Vyāsa, teaching cosmology and time, genealogies of gods, sages and kings, the dharma of vows, pilgrimage and gifts, the rites of death and the ancestors, yoga, and above all devotion to Viṣṇu, Śiva or the Goddess. It carries the Vedic family's teaching to all classes and both sexes and supplies the scriptural base for most later devotional lineages.

name: Pure Land (Jingtu / Jōdo): birth in Amitābha's land
alt_names: Jōdokyō 浄土教 (Pure Land teaching, Japan)
regions: China (Lushan, Bingzhou/Xuanzhong si, Chang'an, Wutai, Hangzhou)

tradition.text: Amitābha attained buddhahood ten kalpas ago (Smaller & Larger Sūtras); in China the Lotus school counts from Huiyuan's vow on Lushan in 402 CE

scholarly.text: Sukhāvatī sūtras c. 1st–2nd c. CE; Chinese Pure Land as a self-conscious tradition from Tanluan, Daochuo and Shandao (6th–7th c.); lineage of 'patriarchs' constructed in the Song (Zongxiao 1200, Zhipan 1269)

transmissions_received.what: the Sukhāvatī sūtras, the Pratyutpanna-samādhi, the Contemplation Sūtra, the practice of recollecting buddhas (buddhānusmṛti)
Nāgārjuna's distinction of the difficult and easy paths; Tanluan's training in the Four Treatises (Sanlun) shapes 'the birth that is no birth'
transmissions_received.evidence: T1521 ch. 9; Tanluan's Commentary

transmissions_received.what: Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise with its śamatha–vipaśyanā gates; the Mahāyānasaṃgraha's 'intention for another time' (occasion of debate)
transmissions_received.evidence: T1524; Anle ji, Huaigan

transmissions_received.what: the constantly-walking samādhi; Tiantai Pure Land commentaries and societies (Zunshi, Zhili, Chuandeng, Ouyi)
transmissions_received.evidence: Jingtu shiyi lun (attrib. Zhiyi); T1968, T1975

transmissions_given.what: Shandao's exclusive calling of the name, received by Hōnen in 1175
the seven masters' teaching of the primal vow and other-power, through Hōnen to Shinran
constantly-walking nenbutsu samādhi (brought by Ennin), Genshin's Ōjōyōshū
recitation of the name within Chan practice; dual cultivation; the 'who is reciting' huatou
the Ming Chan–Pure Land synthesis carried to Japan (1654)

distinctive_positions: Amitābha (Immeasurable Light, Immeasurable Life), who as the monk Dharmākara made vows, presides now over Sukhāvatī in the west; beings born there never fall back and attain awakening.
Birth (wangsheng / ōjō) in the Pure Land is the condition for completing the path: awakening is finished there, not here.
Practice centres on recollecting (nian) Amitābha — contemplating his body and land, and above all calling his name (chengming) — with faith and the aspiration to be born.
Nāgārjuna's easy path versus difficult path; Daochuo's two gates (the holy path and the Pure Land) matched to the last age of the Dharma.
Other-power (tali/tariki): birth is accomplished by the power of Amitābha's vow, not by one's own power (Tanluan), with differing degrees of emphasis in the later schools.

Even an evil-doer who calls the name ten times at death is born in the lowest grade (Contemplation Sūtra); the eighteenth vow excludes the five grave offenders and slanderers of the Dharma — reconciled by Shandao as restraint rather than rejection.
Later Chinese Pure Land joins recitation with Chan (dual cultivation) and reads the Pure Land also as mind-only while insisting on real birth in the West (Yanshou, Zhuhong, Ouyi).
summary: The Pure Land tradition teaches reliance on the buddha Amitābha and aspiration to be born in his land Sukhāvatī, where awakening is assured. Grounded in the Larger and Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha and the Contemplation Sūtra, in Nāgārjuna's 'easy practice' and Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise, it became a self-conscious tradition in China through Tanluan (other-power), Daochuo (the last age; the two gates) and Shandao (the calling of the name as the rightly determined act), was later counted as a lineage of patriarchs beginning with Huiyuan of Lushan, merged with Chan and Tiantai practice in the Song–Ming, and in Japan passed through Genshin and the hijiri to the independent schools of Hōnen (Jōdo-shū), Shinran (Jōdo Shinshū), Ippen (Ji-shū) and Ryōnin (Yūzū Nenbutsu).

name: Puruṣa saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Led by Śaṅkaradeva's grandsons Puruṣottama and Caturbhuja Ṭhākur.
Emphasis on the name and on Śaṅkaradeva's own line.
summary: The saṃhati of the sattras led by Śaṅkaradeva's descendants, above all his grandsons Puruṣottama and Caturbhuja Ṭhākur.

scholarly.text: formed after Mādhavadeva's death (1596), 17th c.

name: Pūrvaśaila
alt_names: Dongshan zhu bu 東山住部
distinctive_positions: Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes to the Pubbaseliyas (with the Aparaseliyas) that others can impute impurity to an arhat, that an arhat has ignorance and doubt, and is instructed by others (Kv 2.1–2.4) — the five points.
The Lokānuvartana-sūtra on the Buddha's conformity to the world is attributed to the Pūrvaśailas (low confidence).
summary: An Andhra branch of the Mahāsāṃghika (Amarāvatī, Nāgārjunakoṇḍa inscriptions), one of the Andhakas of the Pali commentary.

name: Puṣṭimārga (Vallabha Sampradāya; Śuddhādvaita Brahmavāda)

tradition.text: Vallabha 1479–1531 CE; the Lord's command at Gokul on Śrāvaṇa śukla ekādaśī, VS 1549 (1492/93 CE)

scholarly.text: founded c. 1490s–1530s CE; organised by Viṭṭhalanātha (1516–1586)

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as the fourth and decisive scripture
transmissions_received.evidence: Tattvārthadīpanibandha 1.7; Subodhinī

distinctive_positions: Pure non-dualism (śuddhādvaita): Brahman, untouched by māyā, is the sole reality; the world is Brahman's own real form.
Unmodified transformation (avikṛta-pariṇāma-vāda): Brahman becomes the world without undergoing change.
The world (jagat) is real; only the soul's 'I and mine' construction (saṃsāra) is unreal and to be ended.
Brahman manifests or conceals (āvirbhāva/tirobhāva) its being, consciousness and bliss: matter shows only sat, souls sat and cit, the Lord all three.
Three forms of the ultimate: Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa (highest), Akṣara Brahman (his abode, the goal of knowers) and Antaryāmin.
Brahman is the locus of contradictory attributes (viruddha-dharmāśraya).
Four authoritative scriptures: Veda, the Gītā, the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhāgavata (the samādhi-bhāṣā of Vyāsa).
Grace (puṣṭi = poṣaṇa, BhP 2.10.4) is the sole cause of the highest devotion, independent of means; the maryādā path follows scriptural discipline.
Three kinds of souls: puṣṭi, maryādā and pravāha.
Initiation by brahmasambandha removes the five kinds of faults; everything is used only after being offered (samarpaṇa).
Loving service (sevā) of the Lord's form in the home is the path and the fruit; mental sevā is highest; the goal is absorption (nirodha) and love in separation (viraha), not liberation.
summary: The householder path of grace founded by Vallabhācārya: a non-dualism in which the world is Brahman's real, unchanged self-manifestation and the soul, a spark of Brahman with its bliss concealed, is restored by Kṛṣṇa's grace to loving service (sevā) of his child and youthful forms, above all Śrīnāthjī. Organised by his son Viṭṭhalanātha into the eight daily periods of temple (havelī) service and the music of the aṣṭachāp poets, it is led by Vallabha's descendants (the Gosvāmī 'houses').

name: Radha Soami Satsang Beas

scholarly.text: from 1891 (Jaimal Singh settled at Beas); successors Sawan Singh 1903–1948, Jagat Singh 1948–1951, Charan Singh 1951–1990, Gurinder Singh Dhillon from 1990

distinctive_positions: The five names given at initiation (held confidential) and the five sounds of the inner regions.
Strict separation from ritual; the teaching presented as the universal core of all religions.
Seva (voluntary service) and the Dera as a working community.
summary: The largest Sant Mat organization, founded at Beas in the Punjab by Baba Jaimal Singh (a disciple of Soamiji), which spread the teaching worldwide under Sawan Singh and Charan Singh.
notes: A successor-designate (Jasdeep Singh Gill) was announced in 2024 (moderate confidence).

name: Radhasoami Satsang, Agra lines (Soamibagh, Peepal Mandi / Huzuri Bhawan, Dayalbagh)

scholarly.text: from 1878 (Soamiji's death); Dayalbagh colony founded 1915

distinctive_positions: 'Radhasoami' is the true name of the supreme being, revealed by Soamiji.
Soamiji and his successors as the incarnation of the Supreme (Sant Satguru).
Dayalbagh: a planned community joining spiritual practice with work, industry and education.
summary: The Agra branches of Radhasoami after Soamiji: Soamibagh (Soamiji's family and followers), Peepal Mandi / Huzuri Bhawan (Rai Salig Ram's line) and Dayalbagh (from 1915 under Anand Swarup).

name: Rādhāvallabha sampradāya

tradition.text: founded when Hita Harivaṃśa settled in Vṛndāvana and installed Rādhāvallabha (1535 CE)

scholarly.text: 16th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Kṛṣṇa of Braj and the gopīs' love
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; the tradition itself traces its mantra to Rādhā, not to a human lineage

distinctive_positions: Rādhā is supreme: Kṛṣṇa is 'Rādhā's beloved' (Rādhāvallabha) and her devotee; the Rādhāvallabha temple has no image of Rādhā, her presence being marked by a seat (gaddī) beside Kṛṣṇa.
Hita — love — is the ultimate principle; the divine pair are its two forms.
The eternal love-play (nitya-vihāra) in the groves has no separation, no birth-story and no departure to Mathurā or Dvārakā; separation is felt only within union.
The devotee serves as a sakhī (companion), finding joy in the pair's joy (tatsukha), never seeking union for herself.
Rules of injunction and prohibition (vidhi-niṣedha) are secondary to love; liberation is not sought.
Hita Harivaṃśa received his mantra from Rādhā herself, so the sampradāya counts itself outside the four classical Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas.
summary: The Rādhāvallabha tradition of Vṛndāvana, founded by Hita Harivaṃśa in the 16th c., worships Rādhā as supreme and Kṛṣṇa as her beloved, contemplating their eternal, unbroken love-play in the groves. Its scripture is Harivaṃśa's Braj Hita Caurāsī (and, by its account, the Sanskrit Rādhā-sudhānidhi); love (hita) is its first principle and sakhī-like service its practice.

name: Rāghavendra Maṭha (Mantrālaya)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha whose pontiffs included Surendra Tīrtha, Vijayīndra Tīrtha (Kumbhakonam), Sudhīndra Tīrtha and Rāghavendra Tīrtha; since Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya on the Tuṅgabhadrā (1671) the seat and pilgrimage centre have been there.
notes: Its descent from Madhva via the Kavīndra Tīrtha line and a later division (Vibudhendra Tīrtha) is recorded at low confidence.

name: Rāmānandī sampradāya

tradition.text: Rāmānanda lived 1299–1410 (Rāmānandī reckoning); the lineage descends from Rāma through Sītā, Hanumān and a succession of ṛṣis (independent account) or from Rāmānuja through Rāghavānanda (older account)

scholarly.text: Rāmānanda probably 14th–15th c. and poorly documented; the order's institutions (Galtā, the akhāṛās) consolidated 16th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: descent through Rāghavānanda and qualified non-dualist doctrine
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account in older Rāmānandī guruparamparās; rejected by the 20th-c. independent faction (see dsp:ramanandi-descent-from-ramanuja)

transmissions_received.what: the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa's non-dual Rāma theology and Śabarī's nine devotions
transmissions_received.evidence: textual-parallel in the Rāmcaritmānas

transmissions_given.what: Kabīr, Raidās, Pīpā, Sena and Dhanna are counted Rāmānanda's disciples in the Bhaktamāl (tradition-account; disputed)
the Vaiṣṇava ascetic akhāṛās, largely Rāmānandī

distinctive_positions: Rāma with Sītā is the supreme Brahman; Hanumān is the model devotee-servant.
The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) and the name 'Rāma' — the tāraka ('ferrying') mantra Śiva whispers to the dying at Kāśī — are the heart of practice.

Refuge in Rāma is open to all castes and to women; the tradition remembers Rāmānanda as initiating a weaver, a cobbler, a barber, a Jāṭ farmer, a Rajput king and women; the saying 'jāti pāṃti pūchai nahiṃ koī, hari ko bhajai so hari ko hoī' is ascribed to him in oral tradition.
Teaching in the vernacular: Tulsīdās's Awadhi Rāmcaritmānas became the scripture of north Indian Rāma-bhakti.
Rāma is both formless and with form; the name is greater than either (Tulsī).
Two styles of devotion: the ascetic (tyāgī, tapasvī) and the rasik, who contemplates the eternal love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
Whether the order descends from Rāmānuja or is independent is debated within the tradition.
summary: The Rāmānandī sampradāya, the largest Vaiṣṇava ascetic order of north India, looks to Rāmānanda of Vārāṇasī and worships Rāma with Sītā through the Rāma mantra and name. Its hagiography (Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl) assigns Rāmānanda disciples of every caste, including Kabīr and Raidās; its greatest poet, Tulsīdās, made the Awadhi Rāmcaritmānas the devotional scripture of the Hindi-speaking world. It comprises ascetic (tyāgī) akhāṛās, householders, and a rasik branch.

name: Rāmdāsī sampradāya (Samartha sampradāya)
regions: Maharashtra (Sajjangaḍ, Cāphaḷ, Jāmb, Śivthar, the eleven Māruti temples)

scholarly.text: mid-17th c.

distinctive_positions: Worship of Rāma and of Māruti (Hanumān) as the embodiment of strength and service; the thirteen-syllable mantra 'śrī rām jay rām jay jay rām'.
Devotion joined to discriminating knowledge of the self (Advaita in the Dāsbodh) and to vigilant, effortful action in the world (prayatna).
The seeker passes through the conditions of the bound, the seeker, the practitioner and the accomplished.
The ideal leader (mahant) organises, teaches and protects dharma; physical strength is cultivated.
The mind is instructed directly (Manāce Śloka).
summary: The Samartha sampradāya founded by Samartha Rāmdās (1608–1681/82) of Maharashtra: devotion to Rāma and Hanumān, discrimination of the self, disciplined effort and service to society, taught in the Dāsbodh and the Manāce Śloka and organised through maṭhs and Māruti temples.

name: Rāmsnehī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Rāmcaraṇ (1720–1798) at Shāhpurā

distinctive_positions: Remembrance of the nirguṇa Rām as the sole practice; no images.
Several independent seats (Shāhpurā, Rain, Sinhthal, Kheṛāpā), each with its own founder.
Renunciant sādhus in distinctive (pink/ochre) dress and householder followers.
summary: An eighteenth-century Rajasthani Sant sampradāya of 'lovers of Rām', with seats at Shāhpurā (Rāmcaraṇ), Rain (Dariyāv Sāhib), Sinhthal and Kheṛāpā.

name: Rasa Śāstra (the science of mercury) and the Raseśvara-darśana
alt_names: Raseśvara-darśana (the philosophy of the Lord of rasa)

tradition.text: revealed by Bhairava (Śiva) to the Goddess (Rasārṇava); mercury is Śiva's own seed

scholarly.text: alchemical tantras c. 10th–13th c. CE; medical rasa compendia 13th–17th c.; still used in Āyurvedic pharmacy

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva tantric frame: initiation, mantra, liṅga worship, Bhairava and the Goddess as speakers
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: rasāyana and the pharmacological categories
transmissions_received.evidence: shared-vocabulary

transmissions_given.what: mercurial and metallic medicines (bhasmas) absorbed into later Āyurvedic compendia (Śārṅgadhara, Bhāvaprakāśa)
mercurial and mineral alchemy (see brw:rasa-sastra-tamil-siddha)
the parallel of mercury and breath/mind (Rasārṇava 1.18-19; HYP 4.26-27)

distinctive_positions: Liberation in life (jīvanmukti) requires a stable, undecaying body; liberation promised only after the body falls cannot be seen and is 'meaningless' (Rasārṇava 1.8-13; SDS Raseśvara 4-5).
Mercury (pārada, 'that which carries across to the far shore of saṃsāra') is Śiva's seed; mica (abhraka) the Goddess's; their union yields the divine body (SDS Raseśvara 1-10).
The discipline of action (karmayoga) that stabilizes the body is twofold: mercury and breath (Rasārṇava 1.18-19).
Knowledge liberates; knowledge comes from practice; practice needs a stable body (Rasahṛdaya 1.10).
The goal of mercury is the body (dehavedha) and through it liberation, not the making of gold (SDS Raseśvara 23-25).
Mercury with its impurities is poison; only purified mercury is nectar (Rasaratnākara, Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.30).
summary: A Śaiva tantric science, presented as revealed by Bhairava to the Goddess, that seeks a stable, undecaying 'divine body' through mercury processed with sulphur, mica and other minerals and joined with breath-control, mantra and worship. Its goal is liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in that body; the metal-transmuting work (lohavedha) serves as a test before the body is treated (dehavedha). Its medical side supplied the mercurial and metallic medicines of later Āyurveda. RESTRICTED: recorded here as summary and the texts' own warnings only.
notes: family 'shared': predominantly Śaiva (the Raseśvara is counted among the Māheśvara systems in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha), but alchemical works are ascribed to the Buddhist Nāgārjuna and a Jain (Merutuṅga) commented on the Rasādhyāya. No processes, quantities or recipes are recorded anywhere in this unit.

name: Rasik Rāma-bhakti (Rasik sampradāya of the Rāmānandīs)

scholarly.text: from the late 16th c. (Agradās); flourishing in Ayodhyā from the 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: Contemplates the eternal, private love-play of Sītā and Rāma in the inner Ayodhyā (Sāketa) rather than the heroic epic deeds.
The practitioner takes an inner identity as a female companion (sakhī) of Sītā, serving the divine couple.
Sītā's grace is the gate to Rāma.
summary: A branch of the Rāmānandīs, traced to Agradās of Raivāsā, that practises the sweet (mādhurya) contemplation of Sītā and Rāma's eternal love in the manner of the Kṛṣṇa rasik traditions, the devotee taking the role of a sakhī.

name: Ravidāsī (Ravidassia) tradition
alt_names: Ravidassia Dharam (2010 designation of Dera Sachkhand Ballan)
regions: Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh

tradition.text: Guru Ravidās is dated by his followers from 1377 (birth celebrated on Māgh Pūrṇimā); tradition gives him a very long life

scholarly.text: Ravidās flourished in the 15th–early 16th c.; the organized Ravidāsī community and its deras are 19th–20th c.; Ād Dharm 1925; Ravidassia Dharam declared 2010

distinctive_positions: Ravidās, a leatherworker (Camār) of Banaras, is the guru; his hymns are the scripture.
Begampura, the 'city without sorrow', where there is no tax, no fear, no second or third class, is the goal and the ideal.
Rejection of caste and untouchability; dignity of the Camār community.
The relation of self and God is like gold and bracelet, water and wave: 'between you and me, me and you, what difference?'
Since 2010 the Dera Sachkhand Ballan line has a separate scripture (Amritbāṇī) and symbol (Har), distinct from the Sikh Ādi Granth.
summary: The community and religious tradition of the followers of Guru Ravidās (Raidās), predominantly of the Camār (leatherworker) caste. It venerates Ravidās's hymns (forty preserved in the Ādi Granth, more in Rajasthani manuscripts), his vision of Begampura and his rejection of caste; in the 20th c. it organized around deras in Punjab and declared a separate Ravidassia Dharam in 2010.
notes: The modern organized forms (deras, Ād Dharm 1925, Ravidassia Dharam 2010) are post-1800 and flagged recent; Ravidās himself is pre-modern.

name: Unaffiliated regional bhakti poets (classificatory grouping)
distinctive_positions: Not a sampradāya: a grouping made by this ontology for vernacular devotional poets who founded no order and are claimed by several traditions.
Common ground: the name, the saints' company, love and longing for a personal God (Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Veṅkaṭeśvara), often joined to a non-dual vision ('you alone appear in all forms').
notes: Created by U26 so that teachers without a sampradāya of their own can be recorded; convergence counts should not treat it as an independent lineage root. See REPORT.md.
summary: A classificatory grouping (not a tradition) for regional devotional poets in U26's scope — Narsinh Mehta (Gujarati), Annamācārya, Tyāgarāja and Bhadrācala Rāmadās (Telugu), Caṇḍīdās (Bengali) and Vidyāpati (Maithili) — each also linked to the traditions that claim them.

name: Rinzai Zen

tradition.text: from Eisai's Huanglong-line transmission (1191)

scholarly.text: Kamakura and Muromachi Five Mountains (gozan) and the rinka lines; all present-day Rinzai lines descend through Hakuin (18th c.) from the Ōtōkan line (Nanpo–Daitō–Kanzan)

transmissions_received.what: Linji house lineages (Huanglong via Eisai; Yangqi via Enni, Lanxi, Wuxue, Nanpo's master Xutang)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition records

distinctive_positions: Kōan introspection under a teacher in private interview (sanzen/dokusan) as the path to kenshō.
Great doubt (daigi), great faith and great determination as the three essentials of practice.
Post-kenshō training (gogo no shugyō) through a graded kōan curriculum systematised in Hakuin's line.
Hakuin's teaching that seeing the nature must issue in the 'four wisdoms' and compassionate activity.
summary: The Japanese form of the Linji house: introduced by Eisai and Chinese émigré masters in the Kamakura period, patronised through the Five Mountains, revived in the 18th century by Hakuin, whose kōan system all living Rinzai lines follow.

name: Ritsu-shū (Japanese Vinaya school)

scholarly.text: 753/754 CE (Jianzhen's arrival) –

distinctive_positions: Formal ordination on an ordination platform (kaidan) by the Four-Part Vinaya, introduced by Jianzhen; one of the six Nara schools.
summary: The Japanese Vinaya school established by Jianzhen (Ganjin), with its head temple Tōshōdaiji.

name: Ruhani Satsang and its successor missions
alt_names: Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission / Science of Spirituality

scholarly.text: founded 1951 by Kirpal Singh after Sawan Singh's death; successor missions from 1974

distinctive_positions: The same surat-śabd yoga, with emphasis on the first-hand inner experience given at initiation and on self-introspection (the daily diary).
Unity of man; the teaching presented as the science of the soul.
summary: The line of Kirpal Singh (1894–1974), a disciple of Sawan Singh, who founded Ruhani Satsang in Delhi in 1951; after him the line divided among Darshan Singh (then Rajinder Singh), Thakar Singh, Ajaib Singh and others.

name: Sāhebdhanī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: Worship of Dīnadayāl ('merciful to the poor') as the supreme; a mixed Hindu–Muslim membership of low castes.
Songs (notably Kubir Gõsāi's) in the Bāul-Sahajiyā idiom.
summary: A small Bengali sect of low-caste Hindus and Muslims in Nadia, known for its songs (Kubir Gõsāi) in the Sahajiyā-Bāul idiom.
notes: Known mainly from 20th-c. ethnographic reports; low confidence on founder and dates.

name: Śaiva Siddhānta

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva (Sadāśiva) at the beginning of creation through the 28 Āgamas; transmitted by divine and human teachers

scholarly.text: scriptures from c. 5th–7th c. CE (Niśvāsa earliest); exegetes from c. 675 CE (Sadyojyoti); Tamil systematization 12th–14th c.; living today

transmissions_received.what: the Siddhānta scriptures (the ten Śiva and eighteen Rudra Āgamas) and their ritual
transmissions_received.evidence: the Āgamas themselves (tradition's account: revelation)

transmissions_received.what: the lower 25 principles (prakṛti to earth, puruṣa), re-set within the 36 tattvas
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; the Siddhānta presents Sāṃkhya's tattvas as a lower revelation

transmissions_given.what: the Āgamic doctrine of pati–paśu–pāśa, the malas, dīkṣā and the four pādas, systematized in Tamil by Meykaṇṭār and his successors
the ritual base and categories (36 tattvas, dīkṣā, six adhvans) that the non-dual exegetes re-read
the Siddhānta Āgamas, which Vīraśaivas also accept as scripture (moderate confidence)

distinctive_positions: Three eternal, uncreated realities: the Lord (pati = Śiva), bound souls (paśu), and the bonds (pāśa: āṇava mala, karma, māyā).
Souls are countless, eternal and distinct from Śiva; each has innate powers of knowing and acting that are covered, not created, by mala.
Āṇava mala is a real, beginningless substance (dravya); knowledge alone cannot remove it — Śiva removes it by his power through initiation (dīkṣā).
Śiva is the efficient cause only; māyā (and bindu, pure māyā) is the material cause; his single power (śakti) is the instrument.
Śiva performs five acts — emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace — all for the souls' release.
Liberation (Sanskrit exegetes): the soul becomes equal to Śiva (śivasamatva), its omniscience and omnipotence manifested, yet it remains numerically distinct and does not perform the cosmic acts.
The path is fourfold: caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna, whose fruits are sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya.
The world is real, not an appearance; the Siddhānta rejects Advaita's unreality of the world and the non-dualists' identity of soul and Śiva.
summary: The dualist (or 'realist') ritual Śaivism of the Mantramārga, grounded in the 28 Siddhānta Āgamas. Its Sanskrit exegesis runs from Sadyojyoti (c. 700) through the Kashmirian commentators Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and Rāmakaṇṭha to the South Indian ritual authors Somaśambhu and Aghoraśiva; in the Tamil country it merged with the devotional corpus of the Nāyaṉmārs (the twelve Tirumuṟai) and was systematized in Tamil by Meykaṇṭār and the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras. It remains the theology of most Śiva temples of South India and Sri Lanka.
notes: U18 created two sub-lineages so that the Sanskrit exegetes' and the Tamil school's positions can be recorded side by side: lin:tamil-saiva-siddhanta (the Meykaṇṭa school) and lin:nayanmar (the Tirumuṟai bhakti stream). Definitions under lin:saiva-siddhanta give the Sanskrit exegetes' view unless stated.

name: Āśvalāyana (Ṛgveda school)
regions: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra and elsewhere
distinctive_positions: Recites the Śākala Saṃhitā and follows the Āśvalāyana Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras (Aitareya tradition).
Tradition makes Āśvalāyana a pupil of Śaunaka.
summary: The most widespread living Ṛgveda ritual school, reciting the Śākala Saṃhitā with the Āśvalāyana sūtras; listed among the Ṛgveda śākhās by the Caraṇavyūha.

checks.note: Confirmed: listed in Śaunaka's Caraṇavyūha; recites the Śākala Saṃhitā with the Āśvalāyana sūtras (the most widespread living Ṛgveda school). Āśvalāyana as Śaunaka's pupil is the tradition's report (not separately checked).

name: Bāṣkala śākhā (Ṛgveda)
distinctive_positions: Named by the tradition (e.g. the Caraṇavyūha) as the second Ṛgveda recension.
Later reports say it differed from the Śākala chiefly in the number and order of a few hymns (e.g. including some supplementary material); no complete Bāṣkala Saṃhitā survives.
summary: A Ṛgveda recension known by name and by reports of its differences from the Śākala; not transmitted as a separate complete text.

queries: Baskala shakha Rigveda recension differences from Sakala
checks.note: Confirmed as a named Ṛgveda recension (Caraṇavyūha). The reported difference is specific: the Bāṣkala counts 8 of the Vālakhilya hymns among its regular hymns (1,025 hymns) and has its own khila appendix. Status: sources call its survival 'reported but uncertain' — the entry's 'extinct' is a defensible conservative choice.

notes: Details of the Bāṣkala hymn-count are reconstructed from memory of later reports; to be checked (see REPORT.md).

name: Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) śākhā (Sāmaveda)
distinctive_positions: Has its own Saṃhitā and song-books, the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, which contains the Kena Upaniṣad.
Its melodies and style of singing differ from the Kauthuma tradition.
summary: The third surviving Sāmaveda recension, named after Jaimini, preserved chiefly in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

queries: Jaiminiya Talavakara Samaveda Kerala Tamil Nadu
checks.note: Confirmed: two streams, Nambūtiri (central Kerala) and Tamil (districts near Kerala, Srirangam).

name: Kāṇva śākhā (White Yajurveda)
distinctive_positions: Its Saṃhitā and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa differ in arrangement and wording from the Mādhyandina; the Kāṇva Bṛhadāraṇyaka is the text Śaṅkara comments on.
summary: The second White Yajurveda recension, living chiefly in the Deccan and Odisha.

queries: Kanva shakha Maharashtra Karnataka Odisha Andhra
checks.note: Confirmed: followed in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra, Odisha (also Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, MP).

name: Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha śākhā (Black Yajurveda)
distinctive_positions: A branch of the Kaṭhas whose Saṃhitā survives only in part.
summary: An extinct Black Yajurveda branch known from a fragmentary Saṃhitā.

checks.note: Confirmed as a branch known from a fragmentary Saṃhitā (digitized locally).

name: Kaṭha śākhā (Black Yajurveda)
distinctive_positions: Its Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā survives; its Brāhmaṇa survives only in portions; the Kaṭha Upaniṣad is associated with it by name.
Its domestic ritual (Laugākṣi/Kāṭhaka Gṛhya Sūtra) long remained in use among Kashmiri Brahmins while recitation of the Saṃhitā lapsed.
summary: A Black Yajurveda tradition of the north-west whose Saṃhitā survives in manuscript; living recitation is largely lost.

queries: catalog: kathaka samhita; kathaka grhya; laugaksi
checks.note: Confirmed: Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā extant in manuscript (DCS); Kāṭhaka/Laugākṣi Gṛhya Sūtra extant; Kashmiri connection standard. Status 'absorbed' is a classification choice.

name: Kauthuma śākhā (Sāmaveda)
regions: Gujarat, North India, Tamil Nadu and elsewhere
distinctive_positions: Its Saṃhitā (Pūrvārcika and Uttarārcika) and four song-books (grāmageya, āraṇyageya, ūha, ūhya) are the standard Sāmaveda.
The Pañcaviṃśa (Tāṇḍya) and Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇas and the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa and Upaniṣad belong to its tradition.
summary: The principal living Sāmaveda recension, preserving the verse-books and the melodies (gānas) sung by the udgātṛ priests.

checks.note: Confirmed: principal living Sāmaveda recension with the gāna books.

name: Mādhyandina śākhā (White Yajurveda)
distinctive_positions: Keeps mantra (Saṃhitā) and explanation (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) apart — the mark of the 'White' (clear) Yajurveda.
Tradition: Yājñavalkya received these Yajus fresh from the Sun in the form of a horse (vājin), hence 'Vājasaneyi' (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.26–29).
Its Saṃhitā ends with the Īśa Upaniṣad (VS 40).
summary: The dominant White Yajurveda recension of North India, with the Kātyāyana and Pāraskara sūtras.

checks.note: Confirmed: dominant White Yajurveda recension of North India with Kātyāyana and Pāraskara sūtras; VS 40 = Īśa Upaniṣad (located); Sun-as-horse legend in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5 (located; the cited range 3.5.26–29 matches the local verses 3.5.27–29).

name: Maitrāyaṇīya śākhā (Black Yajurveda)
distinctive_positions: Its Saṃhitā in four books mixes mantra and brāhmaṇa prose; the Mānava and Vārāha sūtras belong to it.
The Maitrī (Maitrāyaṇīya) Upaniṣad belongs to its tradition.
summary: A Black Yajurveda tradition surviving in a small community of reciters.

queries: Maitrayaniya Brahmins Nashik Maharashtra living tradition
checks.note: Confirmed: Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā recited by a few Brahmins of Nashik (reports of near-extinction of the traditional style). Gujarat not confirmed in the sources found (entry: 'as reported').

name: Māṇḍūkāyana (Ṛgveda śākhā)
distinctive_positions: Named in the traditional list of five Ṛgveda śākhās (Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana) in the Caraṇavyūha.
summary: A Ṛgveda śākhā known only by name from the traditional lists.

queries: Caranavyuha Saunaka five Rigveda sakhas Mandukayana
checks.note: Confirmed as a name in Śaunaka's list of five Ṛgveda śākhās, with no surviving text — as the entry says. (AVPariś 49 lists 'māṇḍūkāḥ' among seven.)

notes: Name only; nothing of its text is known to survive.

name: Paippalāda śākhā (Atharvaveda)
distinctive_positions: Its Saṃhitā, also in twenty books, overlaps the Śaunaka only in part and was long known only from a single Kashmiri birch-bark manuscript before Odisha manuscripts and reciters were found.
The Praśna Upaniṣad's teacher Pippalāda is its eponym.
summary: The second Atharvaveda recension, surviving in Odisha and in a Kashmiri manuscript.

checks.note: Confirmed: living in Odisha (palm-leaf manuscripts and reciters), formerly known from the Kashmiri manuscript.

name: Rāṇāyanīya śākhā (Sāmaveda)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Kauthuma Saṃhitā with minor differences of reading and pronunciation; follows the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta and Khādira Gṛhya Sūtras (as reported).
summary: A Sāmaveda recension close to the Kauthuma, living in a smaller community of reciters.

checks.note: Confirmed (entry low confidence): Rāṇāyanīya reported in Karnataka (Havyaka community), Maharashtra and also Odisha; close to the Kauthuma.

notes: Sūtra affiliations and regions from memory; to be checked.

name: Śākala śākhā (Ṛgveda)
regions: all India; the standard Ṛgveda of every living Ṛgvedin
distinctive_positions: Its Saṃhitā is the only fully preserved Ṛgveda: 10 maṇḍalas, 1,028 hymns counting the 11 Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59).
Its word-by-word text (Padapāṭha) is ascribed to Śākalya and guards the continuous text.
The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka belong to the Ṛgveda tradition that recites this Saṃhitā.
summary: The Ṛgveda recension named after Śākalya, the only complete Ṛgveda Saṃhitā transmitted; the sūtra schools of Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana recite it.

checks.note: Confirmed: the only fully preserved Ṛgveda recension, 1,028 hymns with the 11 Vālakhilya (local count); Padapāṭha ascribed to Śākalya.

name: Śāṅkhāyana / Kauṣītaki (Ṛgveda school)
distinctive_positions: Uses the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka and the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras.
The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad belongs to its Āraṇyaka.
summary: A Ṛgveda ritual school with its own Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka and Sūtras, surviving notably among Kerala's Nambūtiri reciters.

queries: surviving Vedic shakhas regions Kaushitaki Shankhayana Kerala Nambudiri
checks.note: Confirmed (entry low confidence): Kauṣītaki learnt by Nambūtiris of Kerala; Śāṅkhāyana reported in Gujarat (and Rajasthan, where a revived/last-surviving line is reported).

notes: Regions from memory; to be checked.

name: Śaunaka śākhā (Atharvaveda)
regions: Gujarat, Maharashtra (small and partly revived tradition, as reported)
distinctive_positions: Its twenty-book Saṃhitā is the standard Atharvaveda; the Kauśika and Vaitāna Sūtras give the uses of its hymns.
The Muṇḍaka and Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣads are affiliated with the Atharvaveda.
summary: The Atharvaveda recension named after Śaunaka, the text usually meant by 'the Atharvaveda'.

queries: Shaunaka Atharvaveda Gujarat Maharashtra reciters revival
checks.note: Confirmed: studied mostly in Gujarat, Maharashtra (and Uttar Pradesh); declining and partly revived tradition — as the entry says.

notes: Status of living recitation from memory; to be checked.

name: Taittirīya śākhā (Black Yajurveda)
alt_names: Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, Hiraṇyakeśin, Bhāradvāja, Vādhūla, Vaikhānasa (its sūtra schools)
regions: South India above all (Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Karnataka, Kerala), Maharashtra
distinctive_positions: Mixes mantra and explanatory prose (brāhmaṇa) in one Saṃhitā — the mark of the 'Black' Yajurveda.
Its Saṃhitā contains the Śatarudrīya (TS 4.5) and Camaka (TS 4.7); its Āraṇyaka contains the Taittirīya and Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣads.
Tradition derives its name from Vaiśampāyana's pupils who, as partridges (tittiri), picked up the Yajus disgorged by Yājñavalkya (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.13).
summary: The most widespread Black Yajurveda tradition, with a complete Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka and several living sūtra schools.

checks.note: Confirmed: most widespread Black Yajurveda tradition, strongest in South India; complete Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka; name-legend Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.13 (located).

name: Śākta traditions

tradition.text: The Goddess is praised from the Veda onward (the hymn of Speech, RV 10.125; the Śrī Sūkta; Umā Haimavatī in the Kena Upaniṣad); her supremacy is revealed in the Purāṇas and tantras.

scholarly.text: Śākta theology is first fully formulated in the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th-6th c. CE); Śākta tantras from c. 7th-9th c. onward; the Devī Bhāgavata and the Śākta Upaniṣads are later (c. 11th-16th c.).

transmissions_received.what: hymns to Vāk, Śrī, Rātrī and Aditi read as praise of the Goddess
transmissions_received.evidence: RV 10.125 (Vāk Sūkta) and the Śrī Sūkta are recited in Śākta worship

transmissions_received.what: Brahman-language and the great sayings applied to the Goddess
transmissions_received.evidence: Bahvṛca and Devī Upaniṣads; Kena 3-4 (Umā Haimavatī)

transmissions_received.what: the Devī Māhātmya and Devī Bhāgavata as root scriptures of Goddess devotion
transmissions_received.evidence: Saptaśatī recitation is the most widespread Śākta rite

transmissions_received.what: the tantric frame of initiation, mantra, maṇḍala and the 36 principles
transmissions_received.evidence: Śākta tantras are revealed as dialogues of Bhairava and the Goddess

transmissions_given.what: kuṇḍalinī understood as the Goddess in the body (shared, direction disputed)
the Goddess as one of the five deities of pañcāyatana worship
Śrīcakra worship in the maṭhas (the tradition's account)

distinctive_positions: The supreme reality is the Goddess (Devī, Mahādevī, Parā Śakti), the Mother of all; the Śākta Upaniṣads and the Devī Gītā make her declare herself Brahman.
Śakti is the power of the absolute; without her even Śiva cannot stir (Saundaryalaharī 1).
The world is her form and her play; māyā is her power, by which she both binds and liberates (Devī Māhātmya 1).
She has gentle and fierce forms — Lalitā, Umā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī; Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā — all one Goddess (Devī Māhātmya 11: all knowledges and all women are her forms).
Worship through name, mantra, yantra and image; recitation of her deeds (Saptaśatī) and names (Sahasranāma).
Enjoyment and liberation (bhukti and mukti) are both granted by the Goddess.
Kuṇḍalinī is the Goddess herself asleep in the body; her rise to Śiva in the crown is union.
Esoteric branches require initiation (dīkṣā) from a qualified guru and keep their rites secret.
summary: The umbrella of Goddess-centred traditions: Purāṇic devotion to the Devī of the Devī Māhātmya and Devī Bhāgavata, the tantric cults of the Śrīkula (Śrīvidyā) and Kālīkula, Kaula and Kubjikā lines, and regional goddess worship. They share the doctrine that the ultimate is Śakti, the Mother, identical with Brahman.

name: Samaya school of Śrīvidyā (Samayācāra)
alt_names: the Vedic way of the five Śubhāgamas

tradition.text: Taught by the five sages Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra in the five auspicious āgamas; followed by Śaṅkara (Bhagavatpāda), whose view Lakṣmīdhara claims to follow.

scholarly.text: Known chiefly from Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on the Saundaryalaharī (c. 16th c.); the five Śubhāgama saṃhitās are known only through his citations.

distinctive_positions: Worship of the Śrīcakra only in the inner space (dahara-ākāśa, heart / the thousand-petalled lotus); external worship on a plate or cloth is 'Kaula worship' (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8).
The Śrīcakra is the moon-disc in the crown lotus (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).
Samayā (the Goddess) and Samaya (Śiva) share a fivefold equality: of seat, of state, of action, of form and of name (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).

Rejects external worship of a young woman's triangle and the Kaula rites; rejects the sixty-four tantras as aimed at worldly powers and outside the Vedic path; the eight Candrakalā tantras are 'mixed' (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 31).
Follows the Vedic way of the five auspicious āgamas; eligibility tied to the three higher classes (Lakṣmīdhara).
Śiva is not subordinate to Śakti nor Śakti to Śiva: they are equal in primacy (sama-prādhānya).
summary: The branch of Śrīvidyā that restricts worship to internal contemplation of the Śrīcakra and the Goddess in the body's cakras, holds Śiva and Śakti to be of equal primacy, and rejects Kaula and left-hand practices as non-Vedic. Its classical statement is Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on the Saundaryalaharī.
notes: Name used by the tradition itself (samaya-mata, samayinaḥ). Whether a continuous Samaya teaching lineage existed before Lakṣmīdhara is not established here.

name: Sāṃkhya
alt_names: Ṣaṣṭitantra (as a name of the system)

tradition.text: taught by Kapila, the first knower, at the beginning of creation (the tradition's account)

scholarly.text: proto-Sāṃkhya ideas in the Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata (c. last centuries BCE – early centuries CE); classical Kārikā c. 350–450 CE; commentaries to c. 10th c.; revival 15th–16th c. (Sāṃkhya Sūtra, Aniruddha, Vijñānabhikṣu)

transmissions_received.what: the hierarchy of principles (senses, objects, mind, buddhi, the great self, the unmanifest, puruṣa: Kaṭha Up. 3.10–11) and the word 'sāṃkhya' (Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.13)
transmissions_received.evidence: textual parallels; the Sāṃkhya readings of these passages are contested by the Brahma Sūtra (1.4.1–13)

transmissions_received.what: early enumerations of principles and the teachers Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha (Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharma)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition account; textual parallels

transmissions_given.what: ontology of puruṣa and prakṛti, the guṇas and principles, discrimination and kaivalya
the principles (tattvas) and the guṇas in the account of the person
the order of emergence from pradhāna, taken up under a Lord
the principles and a theistic Ṣaṣṭitantra
the lower twenty-five of the thirty-six principles
the lower twenty-five of the thirty-six principles
the guṇas, subtle elements and inner instrument used in accounts of māyā's products

distinctive_positions: Two irreducible kinds of reality: many conscious puruṣas and one unconscious prakṛti (SK 3, 11, 18).
Twenty-five principles (tattvas) emerging from prakṛti in a fixed order (SK 3, 22).
The effect pre-exists in its cause (satkārya); causation is real transformation (pariṇāma) (SK 9, 16).
Prakṛti is constituted by the three guṇas — sattva, rajas, tamas (SK 12–13).
Puruṣa is witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent; agency belongs to the guṇas (SK 19–20).
Bondage and release belong to prakṛti, not to puruṣa (SK 62).
Three means of valid knowledge: perception, inference and reliable testimony (SK 4).
Vedic ritual means are impure, perishable and graded; only discriminating knowledge liberates (SK 2).
Liberation (kaivalya) comes from the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64), completed at the body's end (SK 68).
No Īśvara is established as creator (SS 1.92, 5.2–12); classical Sāṃkhya is non-theistic, though theistic forms exist.
Liberation while living: the knower remains embodied by the momentum of impressions, like a potter's wheel (SK 67; SS 3.78–84).
summary: Sāṃkhya ('enumeration', 'discrimination') is the darśana that analyses reality into twenty-five principles in order to discriminate the conscious puruṣa from unconscious prakṛti and its evolutes. Its tradition traces it to the sage Kapila, who taught Āsuri, who taught Pañcaśikha; the lost Ṣaṣṭitantra was condensed in Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya Kārikā (c. 4th–5th c.), commented on by Gauḍapāda, Māṭhara, the Yuktidīpikā, the Jayamaṅgalā and Vācaspati Miśra. A late Sāṃkhya Sūtra ascribed to Kapila was commented on by Aniruddha and Vijñānabhikṣu. As an independent school it was largely absorbed into Yoga, Vedānta, the Purāṇas, Āyurveda and the tantras, while remaining a studied darśana; in modern times a Sāṃkhya-Yoga monastic line (Kāpil Maṭh, Madhupur) was founded by Hariharānanda Āraṇya.
notes: Status 'absorbed' refers to the classical independent school; the Kāpil Maṭh (recent) is recorded through its teachers rather than as a separate lineage entity.

name: Saṃmitīya
distinctive_positions: The person is real, designated on the basis of the aggregates, neither the same as nor different from them (Saṃmitīyanikāya-śāstra).
Counted by Yijing among the four great nikāyas of India; by Xuanzang as present in very many monasteries (low confidence on figures).
Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes to the Sammitiyas the person (Kv 1.1) and the intermediate existence (Kv 8.2).
summary: The largest Pudgalavāda school, prominent in western and eastern India in the 7th century; one of the four nikāyas of Yijing and of the Tibetan four-group classification.

name: Saṅgītaśāstra (the science of music: song, instrument and dance)
regions: all India; the northern (Hindustānī) and southern (Karṇāṭaka) traditions diverge after c. 13th–16th c.

tradition.text: music (gāndharva) descends from Brahmā and Śiva, taught by Nārada, Tumburu and Bharata; its mārga form was 'sought out' by Brahmā and others (ŚR 1.1.22)

scholarly.text: Nāradīya Śikṣā and Dattila c. early centuries CE (uncertain); Bṛhaddeśī c. 6th–9th c.; Saṅgītaratnākara c. 1210–1247; Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā c. 1620

transmissions_received.what: the seven notes of Sāman chant mapped to the flute's notes (Nāradīya Śikṣā 1.5.1–2)
transmissions_received.evidence: tea:naradiya-siksa:1.5.1-2

transmissions_received.what: rasa as the goal of performance; the Nāṭyaśāstra's music chapters (28–33)
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚR chapter 7 on nartana and rasa

transmissions_received.what: the body's channels and centres as the seat of nāda (ŚR 1.2.120–144)
transmissions_received.evidence: tea:sangita-ratnakara:1.2.120-139
