transmissions_received.what: the verse 'caitanyaṃ sarvabhūtānām' and the nāda–bindu cosmogony (textual parallel with ŚT 1.13)
transmissions_received.evidence: tea:sangita-ratnakara:1.3.1; tea:saradatilaka:1.12-13

transmissions_given.what: the saṅgīta grammar of Karṇāṭaka music used for devotional song (Purandara Dāsa)
rāga-based padāvalī-kīrtana
nāda-upāsanā as devotion (Tyāgarāja)

distinctive_positions: Song, instrumental music and dance together are called saṅgīta; it is twofold, mārga (divine, fixed, giving merit when performed before Śiva) and deśī (regional, pleasing the heart) (ŚR 1.1.21–23).
Song is made of nāda, instrument manifests nāda, dance follows both: everything depends on nāda; from nāda come letters, words, sentences, all dealings (ŚR 1.2.1–2; Bṛhaddeśī 16–17).
Nāda is twofold, struck (āhata) and unstruck (anāhata), and manifests in the body (piṇḍa) (ŚR 1.2.3).
Nāda-brahman is the consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world; by worshipping nāda one worships Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara (ŚR 1.3.1–2).
Sages worship the unstruck nāda by the guru's path, but because it lacks charm (rakti) the struck nāda is taught, which delights people and breaks worldly existence (ŚR 1.2.163–167).
Nāda is named from na (breath) and da (fire): it arises from their union (ŚR 1.3.6; Bṛhaddeśī 22).
Twenty-two śrutis arise from twenty-two channels attached to the upward channel at the heart; seven svaras arise from the śrutis (ŚR 1.3.8–25).
One who knows the vīṇā, the śrutis and tāla goes the way of liberation without effort (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.115).
summary: The classical science of music as recorded from the Nāradīya Śikṣā, Dattila and Mataṅga to Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgītaratnākara and the later rāga treatises. Beyond its technical content (śrutis, svaras, grāmas, mūrchanās, jātis, rāgas, tālas, instruments and dance), it teaches that the whole world depends on nāda, that nāda is Brahman, and that music is a path to both enjoyment and liberation — a view carried into practice by the singer-saints.

name: Ṣaṇṇagarika
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya; no separate doctrines recorded.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in the lists of the eighteen schools.

name: Saṃnyāsa — the renunciate ideal of the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads
regions: pan-Indian; the later Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads largely South Indian

tradition.text: Eternal; taught by Prajāpati, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa and Yājñavalkya in the Upaniṣads themselves

scholarly.text: Renunciation as a recognized āśrama appears in the Dharmasūtras (last centuries BCE); the older Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads around the turn of the era, the later ones c. 12th–15th c. (Olivelle 1992)

transmissions_received.what: the knower who, abandoning desire for sons, wealth and worlds, lives as a mendicant (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.5.1, 4.4.22); the Self as the goal of renunciation
transmissions_received.evidence: Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads quote and expand these passages (e.g. the three desires in the rite)

transmissions_received.what: the āśrama frame, eligibility and the renouncer's daily rules
transmissions_received.evidence: shared rules on alms, rains-retreat and marks

transmissions_given.what: the rite, the kinds of renouncer, the one-staff (ekadaṇḍa) paramahaṃsa ideal; the Maṭhāmnāya's four seats
the triple-staff (tridaṇḍa) renunciation of the Vaiṣṇava ascetic (Śāṭyāyanīya; Yādavaprakāśa's Yatidharmasamuccaya)
the doctrine of the knower's (vidvat) and the seeker's (vividiṣā) renunciation and liberation while living (Jīvanmuktiviveka)
the avadhūta ideal (Avadhūta, Jābāla 6)

distinctive_positions: One may renounce 'on the very day one becomes dispassionate', from any stage of life (Jābāla 4).
True renunciation is the union of the individual and supreme Self, not merely abandoning rites or uttering the formula (Maitreya 2.17).
The outer topknot and sacred thread are replaced by inner ones: knowledge is the topknot, the Self or praṇava the thread (Jābāla 5; Brahma; Paramahaṃsa; Parabrahma).

Renunciation is spoken of as fourfold (from dispassion, knowledge, both, ritual) and renouncers are of four or six kinds — kuṭīcaka, bahūdaka, haṃsa, paramahaṃsa, turīyātīta, avadhūta — with rising freedom from marks.
The staff of knowledge, not the wooden staff, makes the ekadaṇḍin (Paramahaṃsa); a Vaiṣṇava strand instead requires the triple staff, topknot and thread for life (Śāṭyāyanīya).
Renunciation is a ritual death: the renouncer performs his own śrāddha, places the fires in himself, gives fearlessness to all beings and leaves the ritual world.
The paramahaṃsa and avadhūta live with unmanifest marks and conduct, beyond castes and stages, 'not mad but acting mad' (Jābāla 6; Avadhūta 2).
The renouncer takes no disciples for gain, keeps no books, gives no lectures and avoids householders (Nāradaparivrājaka 5; Sannyāsa 2.79–85) — though the Avadhūta allows action for the world's good.
Alms are taken in the bee's way (mādhukarī) from many houses; food from a single house is forbidden.
Last thought and kind of renunciation determine the world attained; the turīyātīta and avadhūta attain kaivalya.
summary: The ideal of the wandering renouncer (saṃnyāsin, parivrājaka, yati) as set out in the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads: who may renounce and when, the rite that makes the renouncer ritually dead to the world, the kinds of renouncer and their marks, rules of alms, dwelling and conduct, and the claim that true renunciation is knowledge of the Self. Living orders (Daśanāmī, Vaiṣṇava tridaṇḍins and others) are treated under their own lineages; this entry is the textual ideal.
notes: Owned by U04. The Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads are not a single school: most later ones are Advaitin, the Śāṭyāyanīya Vaiṣṇava.

name: Sant tradition (nirguṇa bhakti of North India)
alt_names: Sant Mat (older generic sense: 'the doctrine of the Sants')

tradition.text: Kabīr is placed by his panth in 1398–1518 (a life of 120 years); the Sants count Nāmdev and the other bhagats before Kabīr as their forerunners

scholarly.text: Sant poetry from the 15th c. (Kabīr c. 1440–1518 on many accounts; Ch. Vaudeville argued 1398–1448), with the Maharashtrian Nāmdev (c. 1270–1350) as forerunner; panths organized 16th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: yogic vocabulary: sahaj, śūnya, the unstruck sound (anāhad), the tenth door, the sky-circle (gagan-maṇḍal), the address 'avadhū', upside-down speech (ulaṭbāṃsī)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; Kabīr's songs address the avadhū (Nāth yogī); see brw:natha-to-sant

transmissions_received.what: the name of Rām; the tradition that Rāmānanda initiated Kabīr, Ravidās, Pīpā, Sen and Dhannā
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Anantadās's Paracaīs; Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl); disputed by the Kabīr Panth and doubted by scholars on chronological grounds; see dsp:kabir-guru-ramananda

transmissions_received.what: Nāmdev's Hindi padas; Nāmdev venerated as a Sant forerunner (named by Ravidās)
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit mention: Ravidās's pad 'aisī lāl tujh binu kaunu karai' names Nāmdev, Kabīr, Trilocan, Sadhnā and Sain

transmissions_given.what: the Sant poets as authorities; Kabīr, Paltū, Tulsī Sāhib and others cited as masters of the inner sound current

distinctive_positions: The ultimate is nirguṇa (beyond attributes) and yet is loved: it is called Rām, Hari, Sāhib, Alakh, Nirañjan, Satnām — Rām not as the son of Daśaratha but as the one who pervades all.
The Name (nām) and the Word (śabd), revealed by the true guru (satguru), are the means; outward repetition on beads without the mind is rejected.
The true guru is praised as highly as God, sometimes higher ('guru and Govind both stand before me — whose feet shall I touch?').
The divine is within the body (ghaṭ); temple and mosque, idols, pilgrimage, ritual bathing, fasting, sectarian garb, the Veda and the Qur'ān, Hindu and Turk forms are all rejected as outward.
Caste has no standing before God; many Sants were of low or 'untouchable' birth (weaver, leatherworker, barber, cotton-carder) and spoke of it openly.
Liberation is sought now, in this body: 'dying while living' (jīvan-mṛtak), the natural state (sahaj), in the company of sants (satsang), mostly as householders at honest work.
Teaching is sung in the vernacular: sākhī couplets, pad/śabd songs and ramainī verses, gathered in anthologies arranged by topic (aṅg).
summary: The Sants are the poet-saints of North India, from Kabīr, Ravidās and Dādū onward, who taught love of a formless God (nirguṇa bhakti) through the Name and the true guru, located the divine within the body, and rejected caste, idols, pilgrimage, scripture-learning and the rival formalisms of Hindus and Muslims. Their songs were gathered into anthologies and their followers formed panths (Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth, Ravidāsī, Nirañjanī, Rāmsnehī, Caraṇdāsī, Satnāmī, Garībdāsī); the nineteenth-century Sant Mat (Radhasoami) is their recent heir.
notes: Family 'vedic' is used here for the Hindu side of the ontology, as for other bhakti lineages; the Sants themselves reject the authority of both Veda and Kitāb (Qur'ān). The Sikh Gurus are counted among the Sants by many scholars and the Ādi Granth (1604) preserves Kabīr, Ravidās, Nāmdev and other bhagats; Sikh scripture is outside this ontology's scope and is noted as context only. Exchanges with Sufis are recorded as context only (Sufism is outside scope). The Maharashtrian Vārkarī saints are the 'southern Sants' (owned by U26).

name: Sant Mat (Radhasoami and its successor lines)
alt_names: Sant Mat ('the teaching of the Sants', modern specific sense)

tradition.text: public satsang opened by Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj) at Agra on Basant Pañcamī 1861

scholarly.text: founded 1861 at Agra; branches from 1878 onward (Agra lines, Beas 1891, Dayalbagh 1915, Ruhani Satsang 1951)

transmissions_received.what: the older Sants (Kabīr, Nānak as context, Tulsī Sāhib, Paltū, Dariyā) read as teachers of the inner sound current
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation in Sār Bachan and in the Beas and Ruhani Satsang literature

distinctive_positions: Surat-śabd yoga: the soul (surat) is withdrawn to the eye centre and rises by attaching itself to the audible life stream (śabd, dhun) through inner regions to its source.
The necessity of a living Sant Satguru, who initiates (nām-dān) and guides the soul inwardly.
Creation in grand divisions — piṇḍ (physical), aṇḍ, brahmāṇḍ (ruled by Kāl, the negative power), above which are the purely spiritual regions of Dayāl up to Anāmī / Radhasoami Dhām.
Practice as simran (repetition of the names given at initiation), dhyān (contemplation of the Master's form) and bhajan (listening to the sound).
Vows at initiation: lacto-vegetarian diet, no alcohol or drugs, a moral life, daily meditation (two and a half hours in the Beas line).
summary: The modern Sant Mat, begun in 1861 at Agra by Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj) as Radhasoami, teaches the ascent of the soul on the inner sound current under a living master. It divided into the Agra lines (Soamibagh, Peepal Mandi, Dayalbagh), Radha Soami Satsang Beas, Kirpal Singh's Ruhani Satsang and its successors, Maharshi Mehi's Santmat of Bihar and others.
notes: Post-1800: flagged recent. Western derivatives (e.g. Eckankar, MSIA) are outside scope and not recorded.

name: Santmat Satsang of Maharshi Mehi (Bihar)

scholarly.text: 20th c.; Maharshi Mehi 1885–1986

distinctive_positions: Santmat as the common teaching of the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and the Sants, compiled in the Satsang Yog.
Graded practice: mental repetition (mānas jap), mental contemplation of form (mānas dhyān), point-focus (dṛṣṭi yoga) and then the inner sound (nādānusandhān).
summary: A Bihar Santmat lineage founded by Maharshi Mehi Paramhans, independent of the Radhasoami organizations, teaching the inner light and sound in a Vedāntic-Sant synthesis.

name: Śaraṇa–vacana tradition

tradition.text: founded by Basava and the śaraṇas of Kalyāṇa in the 12th c.

scholarly.text: 12th-c. movement; its literature compiled 15th–16th c.; revived through the printing of the vacanas from the 1920s

distinctive_positions: The vacanas of the śaraṇas, spoken from experience (anubhava), are the tradition's scripture.
Basava (with Allama Prabhu presiding over the Anubhava Maṇṭapa) inaugurated the tradition in Kalyāṇa.
Caste, the five pollutions, Vedic sacrifice and temple worship are rejected; all initiates, women included, are equal.
Work as worship (kāyaka) and sharing its fruit (dāsōha) are the social form of devotion.
Renunciant (virakta) maṭhas carry the teaching; many of its writers regard the Pañcācārya account of origins as later.
summary: The strand of the tradition that looks to Basava and the twelfth-century śaraṇas of Kalyāṇa — Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi, Cennabasava, Siddharāma and some two hundred vacanakāras of every occupation — and holds their vacanas as scripture. It is carried by the Virakta maṭhas and by the modern vacana revival.

name: Sarvāstivāda
alt_names: Shuo yiqie you bu 說一切有部 (Chinese)

tradition.text: Arose in the third century after the parinirvāṇa by division from the Sthaviras (Vasumitra); the Abhidharma was fixed at the council of King Kaniṣka in Kashmir (Xuanzang)

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE (as a named school) – c. 10th c. CE in India; attested by inscriptions from the 1st c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the sūtras (Āgamas), the Vinaya and the mātṛkā lists
transmissions_received.evidence: Madhyamāgama (T26) and Saṃyuktāgama (T99) in Chinese; Sanskrit Āgama fragments from Turfan and Gilgit

transmissions_received.what: the Sthavira identity; the split into Sarvāstivāda and Haimavata
transmissions_received.evidence: Samayabhedoparacanacakra

transmissions_given.what: Abhidharma categories (dharma lists, the path of seeing and cultivation, the nirvedhabhāgīyas) reworked in the Yogācārabhūmi and Abhidharmasamuccaya
the Abhidharmakośa and Vaibhāṣika scholasticism in China and Japan
shared Abhidharma (the seven books, the Kośa)
the framework of the path later expanded into the five paths; the bodhisattva career of three incalculable aeons

distinctive_positions: Everything exists (sarvam asti): dharmas of the past, present and future all exist as real entities (dravya); only the activity (kāritra) of a dharma distinguishes the times (AK 5.25–26).
Seventy-five dharmas in five groups (in the later scholastic count): matter, mind, mental factors, conditioned factors dissociated from mind, and three unconditioned dharmas.
Real dissociated factors: possession (prāpti) and non-possession, the four characteristics of the conditioned (birth, duration, decay, impermanence), the life faculty, homogeneity (AK 2.35–48).
Unmanifest matter (avijñapti-rūpa) carries vows and non-vows through time (AK 1.11, 4.13).
Six causes, four conditions and five results (AK 2.49–64).
Realization of the truths is gradual: sixteen moments, fifteen of which make up the path of seeing (AK 6.25–28).
An arhat can fall back from arhatship (six kinds of arhat, AK 6.56–60); a stream-enterer cannot.
An intermediate existence (antarābhava) links death and rebirth (AK 3.10–14).
The Abhidharma is the word of the Buddha, arranged by his disciples (Vaibhāṣika view reported by Yaśomitra).
The Buddha's physical body is impure (sāsrava); his dharmakāya is the pure qualities of the aśaikṣa.
summary: The Sarvāstivāda ('those who say everything exists') was the most influential Abhidharma school of northern India, centred in Mathurā, Kashmir and Gandhāra. Its canonical Abhidharma of seven books (the Jñānaprasthāna and six 'feet') was systematized in the Mahāvibhāṣā and summarized — and partly criticized — in Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośa, defended by Saṅghabhadra. Its categories and path structure became the base of later Indian, Tibetan and East Asian scholasticism.
notes: Parent set to lin:early-buddhism (umbrella) so that the school counts as its own root in convergence; its Sthavira ancestry is recorded under lin:sthavira. Relationship to the Mūlasarvāstivāda is disputed (see lin:mulasarvastivada).

name: Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh (Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's Aghora organisation)
alt_names: Avadhūt Bhagavān Rām Kuṣṭh Sevāśram (its service institution)

scholarly.text: founded 1961 (as generally reported)

transmissions_received.what: the Kīnārāmī Aghora lineage
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhagavān Rām's initiation in the Aghora line (tradition's account)

distinctive_positions: Aghora expressed as service (especially of leprosy patients) and as rejection of caste and social evils, open to householders; the cremation-ground practices are not required of lay members.
summary: A recent Aghora organisation founded by Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām at Varanasi, known for its leprosy service and for presenting Aghora as naturalness and service rather than as spectacular ascetic practice.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U21. Founding year and institutional names as commonly reported; to be sourced.

name: Satnāmī movements

scholarly.text: three movements sharing the name: Narnaul (17th c.; rising of 1672), Jagjīvandās (1670s–1761), Ghāsīdās (early 19th c.)

distinctive_positions: The 'true name' (sat nām) of the formless God as the centre of practice.
Rejection of images and (in Chhattisgarh) of caste hierarchy; the Chhattisgarh Satnāmīs are largely of Camār origin.
Vegetarianism and abstention from intoxicants (Ghāsīdās's rules).
summary: Several distinct Sant movements named after the 'true name': the Satnāmīs of Narnaul (Bīrbhān, 17th c.), the Satnāmī sampradāya of Jagjīvandās in Awadh (18th c.), and the Satnāmī panth of Ghāsīdās in Chhattisgarh (19th c., flagged recent).
notes: One id covers three historically separate movements that share the name; they may need splitting after sourcing.

name: Satyākāravāda (True-Aspect Yogācāra)
distinctive_positions: The images (ākāra) that appear in cognition are real as cognition itself; the manifold image is one non-dual variegated cognition (citrādvaita).
Only the duality of grasped and grasper, not the images themselves, is false.
summary: A late Indian Yogācāra position (and Tibetan doxographic class) holding that cognition's appearing aspects are real; associated especially with Jñānaśrīmitra and Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla.
notes: The division into 'true' and 'false' aspect is partly a later doxographic construction (Tibetan grub mtha'); Indian authors use sākāra/nirākāra with shifting meanings. Membership lists are the doxographers'.

name: Sautrāntika
alt_names: Sautrāntika ('those who take the sūtras as the end/authority')

tradition.text: Split from the Sarvāstivāda in the fourth century after the parinirvāṇa, claiming Ānanda as its teacher (Vasumitra)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–5th c. CE as a recognisable current

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidharma categories it criticized; membership of the Sarvāstivāda ordination lineage
transmissions_received.evidence: Vasumitra; the Abhidharmakośa

transmissions_received.what: the Dārṣṭāntika positions (e.g. mental karma as volition itself, rejection of avijñapti)
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāvibhāṣā; AKBh 4

transmissions_given.what: the theory of seeds (bīja) and the specific transformation of the series, reworked as the storehouse consciousness
momentariness, the causeless destruction argument and the representationalist theory of perception used by Dignāga and Dharmakīrti (Sautrāntika tenets in Tibetan doxography)

distinctive_positions: Only the sūtras are authoritative; the Abhidharma treatises are works of disciples, not the word of the Buddha (Yaśomitra: 'ye sūtraprāmāṇikā na śāstraprāmāṇikāḥ te sautrāntikāḥ').
Only the present exists; past and future dharmas do not exist as entities: a conditioned thing 'arises having not been, and having been, ceases' (AKBh 5.27).
Everything conditioned is momentary; destruction has no cause (AKBh 4.2–3).

Karmic efficacy and latent defilements are carried as seeds (bīja) — capacities in the psycho-physical series that ripen through its specific transformation (santati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa) (AKBh 2.36, 5.2, ch. 9).
Possession (prāpti), the characteristics of the conditioned, avijñapti-rūpa and the unconditioned dharmas are designations, not real entities (AKBh 2.36, 2.46, 2.55, 4.3).
Cognition bears the form (ākāra) of its object; external objects are inferred, not directly grasped (later doxographic summary).
An arhat does not fall back from arhatship (AKBh 6.58).
summary: The Sautrāntikas were a critical current within the northern Sarvāstivāda ordination tradition that accepted only the sūtras as authoritative and reduced many of the Vaibhāṣika's real entities to designations. Their positions are known mainly through Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Yaśomitra's commentary and Saṅghabhadra's refutations; they shaped Yogācāra (seeds) and the Buddhist logicians (momentariness, representationalism).
notes: The relation between the earlier 'Dārṣṭāntikas' of the Mahāvibhāṣā and the later 'Sautrāntikas' is not settled; Tibetan doxography (grub mtha') systematizes Sautrāntika tenets differently from the Indian sources. Parent set to Sarvāstivāda (tradition: split from it).

name: Seon (Korean Chan)

tradition.text: Beomnang is said to have received Chan from the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin (7th c.); Doui returned from Tang China in 821 with Hongzhou transmission

scholarly.text: from the 9th c. (Nine Mountain schools); Goryeo synthesis (Jinul, 12th–13th c.); Joseon suppression and survival; modern Jogye Order (1962)

transmissions_received.what: Mazu's Hongzhou lineage via Xitang Zhizang and others (Doui, Hongcheok, Hyecheol)
transmissions_received.evidence: Seon lineage records; tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: Yangqi-Linji transmission to Taego Bou and Naong Hyegeun (14th c.)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: Huayan (Hwaeom) doctrine integrated by Jinul through Li Tongxuan and Zongmi
transmissions_received.evidence: Jinul's own works

distinctive_positions: Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (dono jeomsu 頓悟漸修) as the normative path (Jinul).
The mind as 'empty and calm, numinous awareness' (gongjeok yeongji 空寂靈知) to be recognised by tracing back the radiance (Jinul, after Zongmi).
Harmony of Seon and the doctrinal teachings (seon-gyo ilchi), yet the hwadu 'shortcut' is the highest gate (Jinul, Hyujeong).
Ganhwa Seon (observing the critical phrase) as the mainstream practice of the Jogye order.
In the 20th c. Seongcheol argued for sudden awakening/sudden cultivation (dono donsu) against Jinul (see dsp:seon-sudden-cultivation-debate).
summary: Korean Chan: introduced from Tang China from the 9th century as the Nine Mountain schools, unified in doctrine and practice by Jinul (1158–1210) around sudden awakening/gradual cultivation and hwadu practice, and carried on by Taego, Hyujeong and the modern Jogye Order.

name: Shelun school (Chinese 'Mahāyānasaṃgraha' school)

scholarly.text: founded on Paramārtha's translation of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha (563); absorbed into Faxiang in the 7th c.

transmissions_given.what: a body of Yogācāra exegesis superseded by Xuanzang's translations

distinctive_positions: Studied Asaṅga's Mahāyānasaṃgraha in Paramārtha's version.
Taught (following Paramārtha) a ninth, 'stainless consciousness' (amalavijñāna) beyond the ālaya, identified with suchness.
summary: The Chinese tradition of studying Paramārtha's translation of Asaṅga's Mahāyānasaṃgraha, notable for the doctrine of a ninth, pure consciousness; superseded by Xuanzang's Faxiang.

name: Jōdo Shinshū Honganji-ha

scholarly.text: 1602 (split of the Honganji)

distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: The western branch of the Honganji after the split of 1602, when Kyōnyo was given land for a separate Honganji; head temple Nishi Honganji. The largest Shinshū body; led historically by Shinran's descendants.

name: Shinshū Ōtani-ha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: The eastern branch of the Honganji, from Kyōnyo (1558–1614), who received land from Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1602; head temple Higashi Honganji; home of the Meiji reform movement of Kiyozawa Manshi.

name: Shinshū Takada-ha

scholarly.text: 13th c. community; separate school

distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: Branch descending from Shinran's Kantō disciple Shinbutsu of Takada (Shimotsuke); head temple Senju-ji, moved to Isshinden (Ise) in the 15th c.; preserves early manuscripts of Shinran.

name: Siddha medicine (cittā maruttuvam)

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva to Pārvatī, passed through Nandi to the Siddhars, above all Agastya

scholarly.text: the attributed Tamil medical verse-treatises are mostly placed in the 15th–19th c.; the humoral vocabulary is attested in the Tirukkuṟaḷ (ch. 95)

transmissions_received.what: the Siddhars' anatomy (96 tattvas), kāya kaṟpam and alchemy
transmissions_received.evidence: the medical works are ascribed to Siddhars

transmissions_received.what: shared humoral theory (vātam, pittam, kapam) and pharmacy terms; direction disputed
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary

transmissions_given.what: varmam (vital points) as a branch of Siddha medicine

distinctive_positions: Health is the balance of the three vital humours (uyir tātu) — vaḷi (vātam), aḻal (pittam), aiyam (kapam) — whose excess or deficiency causes disease (Tirukkuṟaḷ 941).
The body is built of the five elements and the 96 principles; the same anatomy serves medicine and yoga.
Diagnosis by eight examinations (eṇvakait tērvu), above all the pulse (nāṭi) and the urine (nīrkkuṟi, neykkuṟi).

Medicines are drawn from plants (mūlikai), minerals and metals (tātu) and animal products (jīvam); mineral and metal preparations (parpam, centūram) are held to be most potent and most dangerous if wrongly made.
The tradition counts 4,448 diseases.
Rejuvenation (kāya kaṟpam) aims at long life as a support for yoga and liberation.
summary: The Tamil medical system ascribed to the Siddhars, above all Agastya, with Bogar, Tēraiyar, Yūkimuṉi, Tirumūlar and others as authorities. It explains health and disease by the three humours on a base of the five elements and ninety-six principles, diagnoses by pulse and eight examinations, and uses herbal, mineral-metal and animal medicines, including calcined metal and mineral preparations. Recorded here in summary only; no preparations, doses or procedures.
notes: Family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the Siddhars' own rejection of Vedic ritual and caste (see dsp:siddhar-veda-and-scripture). Summary only by design (coverage map A7/A11). Recent institutional forms (government colleges, the 20th-c. textbooks) are flagged recent where they appear.

name: Śiva-viśiṣṭādvaita (Śaiva Vedānta of Śrīkaṇṭha)

tradition.text: Vīraśaiva tradition places Śrīkaṇṭha early, even before Śaṅkara

scholarly.text: Śrīkaṇṭha c. 11th–13th c. CE (after Rāmānuja, whose commentary his closely parallels); revived by Appayya Dīkṣita (1520–1593)

transmissions_given.what: Śrīkaṇṭha's commentary is claimed by Vīraśaiva authors as their own Vedānta (e.g. Nīlakaṇṭha's Kriyāsāra)

distinctive_positions: Brahman is Śiva (Parameśvara), inseparably endowed with his power (cit-śakti, identified with Umā); souls (paśu) and the world are his body and qualification.
Śiva is both material cause (through his śakti, in which the world lies subtly) and efficient cause of the world, which is a real transformation of that power.
The supreme ether (paramākāśa, dahara) of the Upaniṣads is Śiva's cit-śakti; meditation on the small space in the heart (dahara-vidyā) is central.
The Veda and the Śaiva Āgamas are not different in authority; both come from Śiva.
Liberation is freedom from bonds (pāśa) and equality with Śiva (śiva-sāmya) in bliss, without the power of cosmic governance (BS 4.4.17).
Appayya Dīkṣita reads Śrīkaṇṭha's qualified non-dualism as a stage pointing to Advaita (Śivādvaitanirṇaya) — a reading contested by Vīraśaiva authors.
summary: A Śaiva reading of the Brahma Sūtras by Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya, structurally close to Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita but with Śiva and his Śakti in place of Nārāyaṇa and Śrī. It survived chiefly through Appayya Dīkṣita's commentary Śivārkamaṇidīpikā and through Vīraśaiva authors who adopted it; Śrīpati's Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (lin:virasaiva) is its Vīraśaiva counterpart.

name: Sōtō Zen

tradition.text: from Dōgen's transmission from Tiantong Rujing (1225) and return (1227)

scholarly.text: founded 13th c.; spread widely among provincial laity from Keizan onward; Tokugawa sectarian reforms (Manzan, Menzan); living

transmissions_received.what: Caodong lineage (Furong Daokai → … → Tiantong Rujing → Dōgen)
transmissions_received.evidence: Dōgen's Shisho; Hōkyōki

transmissions_received.what: former Daruma-shū monks (Ejō, Gikai, Giin, Gien) joined Dōgen's community
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition records

distinctive_positions: Just sitting (shikantaza) as the whole of practice, not a means to a later awakening.
Oneness of practice and realization (shushō ittō): sitting is itself the enactment of buddhahood.
Dropping off body and mind (shinjin datsuraku) as Dōgen's account of his awakening under Rujing.
Being-time (uji), impermanence as buddha-nature (mujō busshō), and the whole world as the 'kōan realized' (genjōkōan).
Deep faith in cause and effect (jinshin inga) against readings that deny karma after awakening.
summary: The Japanese Caodong lineage founded by Dōgen (1200–1253) after training with Tiantong Rujing, centred on just sitting as the enactment of original awakening, expanded by Keizan (1268–1325) into Japan's largest Zen denomination.

name: Spanda (the doctrine of vibration)

tradition.text: The Śiva Sūtras were revealed to Vasugupta on Mahādeva mountain - in a dream by Paramaśiva who showed him a rock that turned over at his touch (Kṣemarāja, Śivasūtravimarśinī intro.), or 'by a siddha's command' (Bhāskara, Śivasūtravārttika 1.3).

scholarly.text: c. 850-900 CE (Vasugupta and Kallaṭa; Kallaṭa is placed under King Avantivarman, 855-883, by the Rājataraṅgiṇī); commentaries to Kṣemarāja (c. 1000-1050) and later.

transmissions_given.what: the Spanda texts were read together with Pratyabhijñā by Kṣemarāja
Spanda doctrine is a pillar of Abhinavagupta's and Kṣemarāja's Trika

distinctive_positions: The ultimate is Śaṅkara, from whose opening (unmeṣa) and closing (nimeṣa) of the eyes the world arises and dissolves; this dynamic pulsation is spanda (Spandakārikā 1.1).
The knowing and acting subject never ceases through waking, dream and deep sleep; what is lost in sleep is only the effort turned to objects, not the inner agent (SK 1.3, 1.14-16).
Spanda can be grasped in intense states - great anger, joy, perplexity, running - and at the gap where one thought ends and another arises (SK 1.22, 3.9).
Bondage comes from the powers arising from the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) when they are not recognized; recognized, the same power grants perfection (SK 3.13-16).
'Consciousness is the self; knowledge [limited] is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.1-2); 'effort is Bhairava' (1.5).
The Śiva Sūtras are read (by Kṣemarāja) as teaching the three means in three sections: śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava.
summary: The earliest systematic current of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism, founded on the Śiva Sūtras revealed to Vasugupta and the Spandakārikā (ascribed to Vasugupta by Kṣemarāja, to Kallaṭa by Rāmakaṇṭha, Bhagavadutpala and Bhāskara). It presents the ultimate as vibrant, self-aware power (spanda), identical with one's own agency, discoverable in every moment of intense experience, and absorbed later into the Trika synthesis.

name: The śramaṇa movement

scholarly.text: Named śramaṇa teachers are attested in the early Pali and Jain canons for the time of the Buddha and Mahāvīra (scholarly: c. 5th c. BCE); the word śramaṇa occurs already in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka; Aśoka's edicts (3rd c. BCE) pair 'brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas'.

transmissions_given.what: Sāriputta, Moggallāna and some 250 wanderers who left Sañjaya (Vinaya Mahāvagga 1.23–24); the shared ascetic vocabulary of going forth, alms, homelessness and vows
Jain canon lists the rival 'pravādins' and adopts the frame of kriyāvāda vs akriyāvāda
the natthika / uccheda doctrine reported of Ajita Kesakambalī is the earliest statement of the view later called Lokāyata (the texts do not link them by lineage)

distinctive_positions: Leaving the household (pabbajjā) for a homeless, mendicant life outside the Vedic sacrificial order.
Teachers lead their own orders (saṅghī gaṇī gaṇācariyo) and are called 'ford-makers' (titthakara) in the Pali texts.
The recurring question debated between orders: is there fruit of good and bad deeds, another world, spontaneously born beings, and does the perfected one exist after death?

The Buddhist and Jain canons sort the rival teachers into doctrines of non-action (akiriya), no-cause (ahetu), annihilation (uccheda), eternal bodies, fixed destiny (niyati) and suspension of judgment (amarāvikkhepa / ajñāna).
Public debate in the 'halls of curiosity' (kutūhalasālā) and wanderers' parks is a common practice.
summary: The śramaṇas (Pali/Prakrit samaṇa) were the renunciant wanderers and ascetics of the Ganges plain who stood outside the brāhmaṇa sacrificial order. Besides the Buddha and Mahāvīra, the Pali canon names six rival leaders — Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalī, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (Mahāvīra) and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta — whose doctrines are known only through Buddhist and Jain reports. This lineage entry groups the movement as a whole and the lost teachers who do not belong to a surviving order.
notes: Jainism (U34) and Buddhism (U36) are śramaṇa traditions but are NOT listed as sub-lineages here, so that the merge does not count them as one root. The Greek report of Megasthenes (Brachmanes and Sarmanes, via Strabo 15.1.59–60) is scholarly metadata only.

name: Śramaṇa Saṅgha (Vardhamāna Sthānakavāsī Jain Śramaṇa Saṅgha)

scholarly.text: formed 1952 at the Sādaḍī convention by uniting many Sthānakavāsī sampradāyas

distinctive_positions: a single federated order of formerly separate Sthānakavāsī groups under one ācārya (first: Ātmārām)
summary: The union of most Sthānakavāsī lineages formed in 1952 (recent); several groups remained outside it.

name: Śrīvidyā

tradition.text: Revealed by Śiva; worshipped by twelve great devotees (Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Śiva, Krodhabhaṭṭāraka/Durvāsas); taught by Hayagrīva to Agastya and by Dattātreya to Paraśurāma.

scholarly.text: The root tantra (Vāmakeśvarīmata / Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava) is usually placed c. 10th-11th c.; Kashmiri exegesis (Jayaratha) 12th-13th c.; South Indian systematization from c. 13th-14th c.; Bhāskararāya in the 18th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Kaula ritual frame, yoginī classes, pīṭhas, the eight bonds, secret conduct
transmissions_received.evidence: the Yoginīhṛdaya and its Dīpikā speak of kaulācāra; Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra 1.12

transmissions_received.what: the 36 principles, prakāśa-vimarśa, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā vocabulary
transmissions_received.evidence: Jayaratha's Vivaraṇa; Kāmakalāvilāsa; Amṛtānanda's Dīpikā quotes the Vijñānabhairava

transmissions_received.what: the Lalitopākhyāna narrative and the Sahasranāma's Purāṇic frame
transmissions_received.evidence: Hayagrīva-Agastya dialogue of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa

transmissions_received.what: rules of interpretation applied to tantric injunctions
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhāskararāya's Setubandha and Saubhāgyabhāskara

transmissions_given.what: Śrīcakra worship in the Śaṅkara maṭhas (the tradition's account)
the Navāvaraṇa kṛtis of Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar

distinctive_positions: The supreme is Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī, the union (sāmarasya) of Śiva as light (prakāśa) and Śakti as self-awareness (vimarśa); she sits on Kāmeśvara's lap and is 'the form of the oneness of Śiva and Śakti' (Lalitā Sahasranāma 183).

Worship centres on the Śrīcakra, the 'king of cakras', with nine enclosures (āvaraṇa) from the outer square to the central point (bindu), and on the fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra (with its sixteen-syllable form) in three sections (kūṭa) that are the Goddess's subtle body.
The vidyā has twelve forms after its twelve great devotees; the Kādi and Hādi forms are the living ones.
Knowledge of the unity of cakra, mantra, deity, guru and one's own self is liberation (Yoginīhṛdaya; Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra 1.11); self-awareness (svavimarśa) is the goal of life (PKS 1.6).
Worship is threefold: outer worship of the cakra (aparā), meditative worship (parāparā) and abiding in non-duality (parā) (Yoginīhṛdaya 3.2-3).
The body itself is the Śrīcakra; contemplating the non-difference of knower, knowing and known is the worship of the Śrīcakra and makes one liberated while living (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
Two modes: the internal Samaya way and the Kaula way; the Goddess is called both 'intent on Samaya conduct' and 'Kaulinī' (Lalitā Sahasranāma 36-37).
Strict initiation (three dīkṣās), guru-lineage (the three streams of gurus), initiatory names ending in '-ānandanātha', and secrecy.
A Vedic self-understanding: the Gāyatrī is read as Śrīvidyā; the Tripurā, Tripurātāpinī, Bhāvanā and Bahvṛca Upaniṣads are its śruti.
summary: The Śākta tradition of the Goddess Lalitā Tripurasundarī worshipped through the Śrīcakra and the Śrīvidyā mantra. Rooted in the Vāmakeśvara tantra (Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava and Yoginīhṛdaya), the Tantrarāja and the Lalitā Sahasranāma, it was systematized in Kashmir and South India, and has Samaya (internal) and Kaula branches. Its metaphysics is the non-dual union of Śiva-light and Śakti-awareness; its aim is liberation while living together with worldly well-being (saubhāgya).

name: Sthānakavāsī

tradition.text: Loṅkā Śāh's reform in the 15th c. (c. 1451/1476 CE); the Sthānakavāsī orders formed by Lavjī, Dharmasiṃha and Dharmadāsa in the 17th c.

scholarly.text: 15th–17th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Rejects the worship of images: the thirty-two Āgamas it accepts contain no injunction to image worship, and worship with water, flowers and fire harms living beings
Accepts thirty-two Āgamas: 11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 4 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras and the Āvaśyaka; rejects the Prakīrṇakas and later commentarial layers as authorities
Monks and nuns wear the mouth-cloth (mukhavastrikā) at all times to protect beings of the air
Religious life centres on the 'sthānaka' (hall for monks and for lay sāmāyika), not the temple
summary: The non-image-worshipping Śvetāmbara order descending from the 15th-century critic Loṅkā Śāh and the 17th-century reformers Lavjī, Dharmasiṃha and Dharmadāsa. It accepts thirty-two Āgamas, rejects temple worship, and its mendicants always wear the mouth-cloth; many groups united in the Śramaṇa Saṅgha in 1952.

name: Sthavira (the Elders' group of the first schism)
alt_names: Theravāda in the wide sense of the Pali chronicles

tradition.text: The side of the elders at the first schism, a century or more after the parinirvāṇa

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE

distinctive_positions: At the first schism the elders rejected the relaxations of Vinaya (Pali account) or the five points on the arhat (Vasumitra); the Mahāsāṃghika account says the elders enlarged the Vinaya.
All later Sthavira branches (Sarvāstivāda, Vibhajyavāda/Theravāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, Vātsīputrīya) trace themselves to this side of the split.
summary: A classificatory grouping: the 'Elders' who formed one side of the first schism of the Saṅgha against the Mahāsāṃghikas, and from whom the Sarvāstivāda, the Vibhajyavāda and Theravāda, the Mahīśāsaka, the Dharmaguptaka, the Kāśyapīya and the Pudgalavāda derived.
notes: A classificatory group: the member schools keep lin:early-buddhism as parent so that each counts as its own root in convergence. Recommend adding lin:sthavira to the merge's UMBRELLAS set.

name: Suan Mokkh (Buddhadāsa's tradition)

tradition.text: Buddhadāsa founded Suan Mokkh in 1932

scholarly.text: 1932 onward

distinctive_positions: Return to the Buddha's words (the suttas) over later commentarial layers; the essential teaching is the emptying of 'I' and 'mine' (tua-ku khong-ku).
Dependent origination describes the arising of suffering and of the 'self' within a single sequence of sense-contact in present experience, not only across three lives.
'Birth' in its Dhamma-language sense is the birth of the ego-sense; nibbāna is the coolness of the extinction of defilements here and now.
Everyday language and Dhamma language (phasa khon, phasa tham) must be distinguished.
Mindfulness with breathing in its sixteen steps as a complete path; work done with a mind void of self (chit wang).
summary: The reformist Thai tradition of Buddhadāsa Bhikkhu (1906–1993) and his forest monastery Suan Mokkh, teaching emptiness of self, present-moment dependent origination and the sixteen-step mindfulness with breathing.

name: Sunlun Sayadaw tradition
regions: Burma (Sunlun monastery, Myingyan; Sunlun Gu Kyaung, Yangon)

tradition.text: founded by the formerly unlettered farmer-monk Sunlun Sayadaw (U Kawi) after his own attainment in the 1920s

scholarly.text: early 20th c. onward

distinctive_positions: Vigorous, strong breathing at the start of a sitting to build concentration quickly, followed by unmoving attention to the sensation of touch (at the nostrils and then throughout the body).
Painful feeling is not avoided: the meditator sits without moving and watches pain with great energy until it breaks up — effort (viriya) is emphasized.
Practice without reliance on scriptural learning; mindfulness of touch as the direct way.
summary: A Burmese insight lineage from Sunlun Sayadaw (U Kawi, 1878–1952), known for its strong-breathing opening and its unflinching mindfulness of touch and painful sensation.
notes: Method summary only; no breath counts or durations recorded. Dates of founding approximate.

name: Svātantrika-Madhyamaka
regions: India (Nālandā; Bhāviveka's seat given in some accounts as in the south)

scholarly.text: Bhāviveka c. 500–570 CE; Jñānagarbha 8th c.; the name 'Svātantrika' (rang rgyud pa) is a Tibetan doxographical category

transmissions_received.what: Dignāga's formal inference (the three-mode reason) applied to proving emptiness

transmissions_given.what: early Tibetan Madhyamaka (Ngok Loden Sherab's line) read Madhyamaka through Svātantrika authors

distinctive_positions: A Mādhyamika must be able to state an autonomous inference (svatantra-anumāna) with thesis, reason and example; Buddhapālita's bare consequences are faulty (Bhāviveka, Prajñāpradīpa ch.1).
Negations of arising and the like are qualified 'ultimately' (paramārthataḥ); conventionally things arise as they appear.
Conventional truth is divided into the correct conventional (tathya-saṃvṛti), capable of efficacy as it appears, and the incorrect (mithyā-saṃvṛti) (Jñānagarbha).
The ultimate is divided into the nominal or concordant ultimate (paryāya-paramārtha), the object of reasoning, and the non-nominal ultimate beyond elaboration (Bhāviveka).
Bhāviveka accepts external objects conventionally (hence 'Sautrāntika-Svātantrika' in Tibetan doxography) and criticizes Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā in the Madhyamakahṛdaya.
summary: The line of Madhyamaka that, following Bhāviveka's criticism of Buddhapālita, holds that emptiness must be established by autonomous formal inferences in Dignāga's manner, qualifying its negations as 'ultimate', and that admits conventional arising as it appears. Tibetan doxographers divided it into the Sautrāntika-Svātantrika (Bhāviveka, Jñānagarbha, Śrīgupta) and the Yogācāra-Svātantrika (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla, Haribhadra). Its Indian authors did not use the name.

name: Śvetāmbara

tradition.text: the continuous line of Sudharman; the canon redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa)

scholarly.text: a distinct Śvetāmbara identity is visible from roughly the early centuries CE (Mathurā inscriptions name gaṇas and kulas matching the Kalpa Sūtra's list); the canon was fixed in writing in the 5th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Monks and nuns wear white garments and carry bowls; holding clothes and bowls without attachment is not 'possession' (parigraha is defined as attachment, mūrcchā)
The naked, solitary Jinakalpa mode was followed by the Jinas and early monks but lapsed after Jambū; the Sthavirakalpa (living in groups with minimal equipment) is the valid mode now
Women can attain liberation in a female body; the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara Mallī was a woman
The omniscient (kevalin) continues to take food while his body lasts
The canon of Āgamas survives in large part (the twelfth Aṅga, the Dṛṣṭivāda with the fourteen Pūrvas, is lost)
In Mahāvīra's life: the transfer of the embryo from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to the kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā; fourteen dreams of the mother; Mahāvīra's marriage to Yaśodā
summary: The 'white-clad' branch of the Jain tradition, which preserves the Ardhamāgadhī canon of Āgamas redacted at Valabhī and holds that women can reach liberation and that the omniscient eats. It comprises the image-worshipping Mūrtipūjakas (organized in gacchas) and the two non-image-worshipping orders, the Sthānakavāsīs and the Terāpanthīs.

name: Tājika (Indo-Persian annual and interrogational astrology)

scholarly.text: c. 13th c. CE onward; systematized by Nīlakaṇṭha 1587

distinctive_positions: The annual chart (varṣaphala) cast for the sun's return to its birth position.
Sixteen aspect-combinations with Perso-Arabic names (itthaśāla, īsarāpha, etc.).
Sensitive points called sahama and the progressed point muntha.
summary: Tājika is the branch of jyotiṣa that took over Perso-Arabic methods — annual revolutions, the sixteen Tājika yogas, sahamas and muntha — written in Sanskrit from the 13th century by Brahmin and Jain authors and standardized in Nīlakaṇṭha's Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī (1587). The name itself (tājika, 'Persian/Arab') marks the tradition's awareness of its foreign source.
notes: Family set to 'shared' because Jain authors (Hemaprabha) wrote Tājika texts. No separate lineage id exists for Perso-Arabic astrology (outside scope).

name: Tamil Jain tradition
regions: Tamil Nadu (Maturai hills, Kāñcīpuram and Tiruparuttikkuṉṟam, Ciṅkavaram, Mēlcittāmūr, Tirumalai)

tradition.text: Tamil Jains trace their teachers to Bhadrabāhu's migration and to Kundakunda (Elācārya); inscriptions in Tamil-Brāhmī in hill caves are claimed as the earliest Jain presence

scholarly.text: Tamil-Brāhmī cave inscriptions c. 2nd c. BCE onward; the Jain literary flowering c. 5th–13th c. CE; decline after the Śaiva revival (7th c. onward)

distinctive_positions: Digambara in doctrine and practice; the monastic seats (maṭhas) at Mēlcittāmūr and Arahantagiri (Tirumalai) with their bhaṭṭārakas
a major literary contribution to Tamil: the Nālaṭiyār and other didactic works, the epics Cīvakacintāmaṇi and Nīlakēci, grammar (Naṉṉūl) and prosody (Yāpparuṅkalam)
summary: The Digambara Jain community of the Tamil country, whose monks and poets produced much of classical Tamil didactic and narrative literature and whose memory of conflict with the Śaiva Nāyaṉmārs is recorded on both sides.

name: Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta (the Meykaṇṭa school)

tradition.text: teaching descended from Śrīkaṇṭha Rudra through Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin and Parañcōti to Meykaṇṭār

scholarly.text: 12th c. forerunners (Tiruvuntiyār 1147/48); Meykaṇṭār early 13th c.; Umāpati 1306–1313; monastic (ātīṉam) tradition continuing

transmissions_received.what: Āgamic doctrine (pati–paśu–pāśa, malas, dīkṣā, pādas, 36 tattvas)
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition holds the Civañāṉa Pōtam renders twelve Sanskrit verses of the Raurava Āgama

transmissions_received.what: the Tirumuṟai as scripture and the Nāyaṉmārs as exemplars
transmissions_received.evidence: Meykaṇṭa authors cite the Tēvāram and Tiruvācakam

distinctive_positions: Advaita understood as inseparability (ananya): God is one with souls, other than them, and together with them (oṉṟāy, vēṟāy, uṭaṉāy) — as the vowel 'a' pervades every letter.
The malas are eternal; in liberation their power is quelled, not their existence destroyed.
Grace (aruḷ) comes when the two deeds are balanced (iruviṉaiyoppu) and āṇava has ripened (malaparipākam); Śiva himself comes as the guru.
The liberated soul abides at Śiva's feet in bliss, knowing through his grace; it is not a doer of the five acts.
The freed soul should live among devotees and revere the devotees' garb and the temple as Śiva (Civañāṉa Pōtam 12).
Vedas and Āgamas are both Śiva's word — the Veda general, the Āgama special.
summary: The Tamil systematization of Śaiva Siddhānta in the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras, above all Meykaṇṭār's twelve-sūtra Civañāṉa Pōtam, Aruṇanti's Civañāṉa Cittiyār and Umāpati Civācāriyār's eight works. It reads the Āgamic dualism as a 'pure non-dualism' of inseparability and is carried by the non-brahmin monastic houses (ātīṉams) of Tiruvāvaṭuturai, Dharmapuram and others, with Civañāṉa Muṉivar's Māpāṭiyam (18th c.) as its classical commentary.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U18 (not in the registry) to keep the Tamil school's positions distinct from the Sanskrit exegetes'.

name: The Tamil Siddhars (cittar)
regions: Tamil Nadu (Potikai/Potiyil hills, Palani, Kolli hills, Caturakiri, Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, Chidambaram)

tradition.text: the Siddhars are held to be ancient and, in their jīva-samādhis and hill retreats, still living

scholarly.text: named authors and texts c. 10th–18th c.; most of the song corpus is usually placed after c. 1400, the medical-alchemical corpus later still

transmissions_received.what: The Tirumantiram's yoga, kāya-siddhi and 'love is Śiva' teaching; Tirumūlar is counted first among the Siddhars
transmissions_received.evidence: TM 3rd tantra (kāyasitti upāyam, 724–725); TM 67–70 lineage verses; the Siddhars' songs echo the Tirumantiram

transmissions_received.what: Macchamuni and Kōrakkar are identified by the tradition with Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha; shared goal of the perfected, deathless body
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account; shared vocabulary (nātar, kāya-siddhi); see brw:natha-tamil-siddha

transmissions_received.what: mercurial and mineral alchemy (vātam, racam, pāṣāṇam); direction disputed
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; scholarly hypothesis; see brw:rasa-sastra-tamil-siddha

transmissions_given.what: Siddha medicine is taught as the Siddhars' science of the body (kāya kaṟpam, humours, metals)
Ramalinga Swamigal (Vallalar) inherits the Siddhar critique of caste and ritual, the 'deathless body' and the harmony (camaracam) of Vedānta and Siddhānta
the vital-point (varmam) lore is ascribed to Agastya and the Siddhars

distinctive_positions: The body is the temple and the instrument of liberation: it is to be preserved and perfected (kāya-siddhi, kāya kaṟpam), not despised — 'when the body perishes the life perishes and true knowledge is not reached' (TM 724).

God (Civam) is within; love itself is Śiva (TM 270); the stone image, temple, pilgrimage, Vedic recitation and ritual without inner knowledge are mocked (Sivavākkiyar; Kaṭuveḷi 15; Pattirakiriyār 16; Kuṭampai).
Caste is rejected: 'one family, one God' (TM 2104); the castes said to be unequal are one (Kaṭuveḷi 32).

Breath (vāci), the root centre (mūlam), the six supports (ātāram), the goddess Vālai/Maṉōṉmaṇi and the open space above the crown (veṭṭa veḷi) frame an inner yoga that culminates in 'dying without dying' (cākāmal cātal).
Teaching in veiled, coded language (paripāṣai, maṟaipporuḷ), with secrecy around alchemy and medicine.
Mastery of the powers (citti) is claimed, yet stillness of mind is held harder and higher (Tāyumāṉavar; Kuṭampai 2).
The 96 principles (toṇṇūṟṟāṟu tattuvam) map body, mind and bondage; medicine and liberation share one anatomy.
summary: A loose, non-institutional stream of Tamil perfected ones (cittar) — yogins, poets, physicians and alchemists — counted conventionally as eighteen, with lists that vary. They trace their knowledge to Śiva through Nandi, Agastya and Tirumūlar, teach an inner Śaiva-Śākta yoga of breath, the root centre and the goddess Vālai aimed at a perfected, deathless body and union with Civam, and in their songs attack caste, idols, temples, pilgrimage and Brahmanical ritual. Their songs (Sivavākkiyar, Pāmbāṭṭi, Iṭaikkāṭar, Kuṭampai, Aḻukaṇṇi, Kaṭuveḷi, Pattinattār, Pattirakiriyār) are anthologized as the Siddhar songs (Cittar pāṭalkaḷ); Tāyumāṉavar (18th c.) joins Siddha, Vedānta and Siddhānta. Siddha medicine is their medical branch.
notes: Family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the Siddhars' own rejection of Vedic ritual and caste (see dsp:siddhar-veda-and-scripture). Parent left null: the tradition has Śaiva (Tirumantiram), Nāth and alchemical roots but no single institutional parent.

name: Tapā Gaccha

tradition.text: the name 'Tapā' given in 1228 CE to Jagaccandrasūri for his austerities (tapas) by the ruler of Mewar

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE

distinctive_positions: the largest Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka gaccha; celebrates Saṃvatsarī on the fourth of Bhādrapada (bright half)
reformist in origin, stressing austerity and strict monastic discipline
summary: The largest Mūrtipūjaka monastic lineage, named after Jagaccandrasūri's austerities; its monks include the Mughal-era Hīravijayasūri and the philosopher Yaśovijaya.

name: Tāraṇapantha (Samaiyā)

tradition.text: Tāraṇa Svāmī (1448–1515 CE)

scholarly.text: 15th–16th c. CE, Bundelkhand and Malwa

distinctive_positions: no image worship: its shrines (caityālayas) house scriptures, which are venerated
open to members of all castes; emphasis on the soul's inner nature in Tāraṇa Svāmī's fourteen works
summary: An aniconic Digambara-derived community of central India founded by Tāraṇa Svāmī, whose shrines keep books instead of images.

name: Tathāgatagarbha (Buddha-nature) tradition
alt_names: de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po / bde gshegs snying po (Tibetan)

tradition.text: Taught by the Buddha in the 'third turning' (Tibetan) / in his last teaching before parinirvāṇa (Mahāparinirvāṇa); the Ratnagotravibhāga taught by Maitreya to Asaṅga (Tibetan account)

scholarly.text: Tathāgatagarbha sūtras c. 3rd c. CE (Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, Śrīmālā, Mahāparinirvāṇa core); Ratnagotravibhāga c. 4th-5th c.; Chinese translation 511

transmissions_received.what: the Mahāyāna path and the Prajñāpāramitā teaching of emptiness, which the Tathāgatagarbha texts re-read ('empty of adventitious stains, not empty of the buddha-qualities')
transmissions_received.evidence: RGV 1.154-155; Śrīmālā ch. 9

transmissions_received.what: the luminous mind (pabhassara citta) obscured by adventitious defilements (AN 1.51-52)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared-vocabulary

transmissions_given.what: buddha-nature, the one mind, 'seeing the nature'
the tathāgatagarbha as the one mind (Awakening of Faith)
buddha-nature of all beings, including insentient (Zhanran)
shentong: the dharmakāya empty of other
buddha-nature as ground of Mahāmudrā (Gampopa, Rangjung Dorje)
buddha-nature as the ground (gzhi) in Dzogchen
buddha-nature read as the emptiness of the mind (a naturally abiding lineage), the RGV read through Madhyamaka

distinctive_positions: All sentient beings have (or are) the tathāgatagarbha: the embryo/womb of the Tathāgata, the buddha-element (dhātu) or buddha-nature, covered by adventitious defilements (Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra; RGV 1.27-28)
The dharmakāya is permanent, blissful, self and pure — the four perfections of qualities (Śrīmālā; Mahāparinirvāṇa; RGV 1.35)
The garbha is empty of the separable defilements and not empty of the inseparable buddha-qualities (Śrīmālā ch. 9; RGV 1.154-155)
The realm of beings neither increases nor decreases; the sattvadhātu, the tathāgatagarbha and the dharmakāya are one (Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa)
Buddha-nature was taught to remove five faults: discouragement, contempt for others, grasping the unreal, denying the real, and excessive self-love (RGV 1.156-157)
The one vehicle is final (Śrīmālā); even icchantikas have buddha-nature (later Mahāparinirvāṇa)
summary: The strand of Mahāyāna sūtras and treatises teaching that every sentient being contains the tathāgatagarbha — the buddha-nature, the pure dharmakāya obscured by adventitious defilements — which, once cleansed, is revealed as a buddha endowed with permanent, blissful, self-like and pure qualities. In India it was never a separate school; its sūtras and the Ratnagotravibhāga were read into Yogācāra and Madhyamaka, and it became central to East Asian Buddhism (Awakening of Faith, Chan, Huayan, Tiantai) and to Tibetan debates on buddha-nature (rangtong/shentong).
notes: Status 'absorbed': not an independent institutional lineage; the teaching lives on in the Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Tibetan schools listed in transmissions_given.

name: Teṅkalai (southern school of Śrīvaiṣṇavism)
regions: Śrīraṅgam and the southern Tamil country

tradition.text: from Piḷḷai Lokācārya (1205–1311 in commonly given traditional dates) and Maṇavāḷa Māmuni (1370–1443)

scholarly.text: doctrinal differences take shape 13th–14th c.; separate institutions and marks by c. 17th–18th c.

distinctive_positions: The Lord alone is the means (siddhopāya); prapatti is not a means but the soul's acceptance of, and awakening to, its dependence; to treat it as a means is a fault.
Grace is without cause (nirhetuka-kṛpā); 'mārjāra-kiśora-nyāya': the mother cat carries the kitten, which does nothing.

Śrī is the mediator (puruṣakāra) who turns the soul to the Lord and the Lord to the soul; she is not herself the means; she is commonly reported as atomic (aṇu) and of the rank of souls (jīva-koṭi), though ever inseparable from him.
The Lord relishes the faults of his devotees as a cow licks its newborn calf (doṣa-bhogya).
The surrendered keep scriptural duties as service (kainkarya) and for the sake of the world, not as a means or under threat.
The teacher's gracious regard (ācārya-abhimāna) is itself sufficient for those who can do nothing else; the Tamil Prabandham has primacy of place.
Kaivalya is an eternal state from which there is no return.
summary: The Śrīvaiṣṇava school following Piḷḷai Lokācārya and Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, centred on Śrīraṅgam and on the Maṇipravāḷa commentaries on the Tamil Prabandham; it holds that the Lord's grace alone saves, with Śrī as mediator. It wears the Y-shaped mark with the line extending down the nose.

name: Terāpantha (Digambara)

scholarly.text: 17th c. CE (Agra, Sanganer and Jaipur region), growing out of Banārsīdās's Adhyātma circle

distinctive_positions: rejects the authority of the bhaṭṭārakas
offers only dry and non-living substances (e.g. rice, dry fruits) in image worship, no fresh flowers or lamps, and standing worship
rejects the worship of attendant deities (śāsanadevatās) as wrong faith
summary: A lay-led Digambara reform movement of the 17th–18th c. (not connected with the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth) that rejected the bhaṭṭārakas and reduced image worship to non-harming offerings; Paṇḍit Ṭoḍarmal's Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka is its classic.

name: Śvetāmbara Terāpanth
alt_names: Terāpantha ('the path of thirteen' / 'your path, Lord')

tradition.text: founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu on leaving the Sthānakavāsī ācārya Raghunāth in 1760 CE (Vikrama 1817)

distinctive_positions: One ācārya governs the whole order; all monks and nuns are initiated by and answerable to him, under a written code (maryādā)
Accepts thirty-two Āgamas and rejects image worship

Distinguishes worldly (laukika) duty from spiritual (lokottara) dharma: only acts that stop karmic inflow and foster self-restraint are dharma; saving or feeding the unrestrained is not in itself spiritual merit (a disputed position)
In the 20th c. (recent): the Aṇuvrata movement (Tulsī), the samaṇ/samaṇī intermediate order and prekṣā-dhyāna (Mahāprajña)
summary: A strictly centralized Śvetāmbara order founded in 1760 by Ācārya Bhikṣu, who broke with the Sthānakavāsīs over laxity and over what counts as dharma. It is aniconic, has a single ācārya, and is known in recent times for Ācārya Tulsī's Aṇuvrata movement and Ācārya Mahāprajña's prekṣā meditation.

name: Thai Forest tradition (Kammaṭṭhāna forest tradition)
regions: the West (Wat Pah Nanachat, Amaravati, Metta Forest Monastery, etc.)

tradition.text: Ajahn Sao and Ajahn Mun took up the ascetic wandering life (dhutaṅga) in the forests of Isan from the late 19th/early 20th century; the tradition regards it as a return to the practice of the Buddha's time

scholarly.text: c. 1900 onward, within the Dhammayut order and later also the Mahānikāya

transmissions_received.what: the reformed Vinaya discipline and ordination of the Dhammayut order
transmissions_received.evidence: Ajahn Sao and Ajahn Mun were Dhammayut monks

distinctive_positions: Strict observance of the Vinaya and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga): forest dwelling, alms-round, one meal a day, wandering (tudong) in wilderness and charnel places.

Meditation with the parikamma word 'buddho' and on the breath, and contemplation of the body (its thirty-two parts, foulness, elements) until the mind converges in calm and sees the body's true nature.
Calm and insight developed together; direct experience in the heart (citta) is valued over textual learning, though the teachers used the Pali terms.
The mind in itself is radiant; defilements are visitors (āgantuka) — with the later teaching (Ajahn Maha Boowa) that even the radiant citta must be seen through, since ignorance can dwell in it.
The tradition's biographies record visions, signs and the teachers' attainments (the tradition's account).
summary: The Thai forest meditation lineage descending from Ajahn Sao Kantasīlo (1861–1941) and Ajahn Mun Bhūridatta (1870–1949), emphasizing Vinaya, dhutaṅga austerities, 'buddho' and body contemplation, and realization in the heart; spread internationally through Ajahn Chah's and Ajahn Lee's lines.

name: Theravāda

tradition.text: The doctrine of the elders fixed at the First Council (Rājagaha, the first rains after the parinibbāna), upheld at the Second (Vesālī, a century later) and Third (Pāṭaliputta, under Asoka, 218 years after the parinibbāna) Councils, and brought to Laṅkā by Mahinda

scholarly.text: the Sthavira (Vibhajjavāda) branch established in Sri Lanka c. 250 BCE; the canon written down at the Āloka-vihāra c. 1st c. BCE; the Mahāvihāra orthodoxy fixed by the commentaries of the 5th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Dhamma-Vinaya in Pali (the Tipiṭaka)
transmissions_received.evidence: Cullavagga 11–12 (the first two councils); Dīpavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa (the chronicles) for the mission of Mahinda

transmissions_given.what: the Abhidhamma and satipaṭṭhāna revival in Burma
satipaṭṭhāna insight practice
the dhutaṅga forest practice and the Vinaya

distinctive_positions: The Pali Tipiṭaka is the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) as recited at the First Council; its commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) transmit the old Sinhalese exegesis.
Vibhajjavāda — 'the doctrine of analysis' — as the orthodoxy vindicated at the Third Council (Kathāvatthu).
The arahant ideal for disciples; the bodhisatta path fulfilling the ten perfections (pāramī) for one who aspires to Buddhahood (Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, Jātaka nidāna).
Lineage of valid higher ordination (upasampadā) and of the Pātimokkha as the life of the Sāsana; the Sāsana is held to decline and to be renewed by the future Buddha Metteyya (DN 26).
The bhikkhunī order died out in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia; its revival is disputed within the tradition (recent).
Commentarial two truths (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca) and the analysis of ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma: citta, cetasika, rūpa, nibbāna) — see U37.
summary: The school of the elders, the one early Indian school that survives, carrying the Pali Tipiṭaka, its commentaries and a continuous monastic ordination lineage from Sri Lanka to Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. It holds its canon to be the word of the Buddha as recited at the First Council and reads it through Buddhaghosa's commentaries and the Abhidhamma; its practice is the Vinaya, the precepts and uposatha of the laity, merit-making, paritta chanting, and meditation (samatha and vipassanā).
notes: Abhidhamma, commentaries and the modern meditation lineages are U37's; this unit supplies the canonical base. Councils are recorded in teachings from Cullavagga 11–12 and in teacher entries.

name: Trika ('the Triad')

tradition.text: Revealed by Bhairava; the Mālinīvijayottara presents itself as taught by Kārttikeya to the sages (MVT 1.1-7).

scholarly.text: Trika scriptures of the Vidyāpīṭha (Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Mālinīvijayottara) c. 6th-9th c.; exegetical Trika of Abhinavagupta c. 990-1020; Jayaratha 13th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Vidyāpīṭha Trika tantras
transmissions_received.evidence: TĀ 1.18: the essence of the Lord's scripture is Trika, its essence the Mālinīvijaya

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual and doctrine (the Kaula form of Trika)
transmissions_received.evidence: TĀ 29

transmissions_received.what: Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī and the twelve Kālīs

distinctive_positions: The triad of goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā with Bhairava; in Abhinavagupta's Trika Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī stands above them as the fourth.
The triads Śiva-Śakti-Nara (aṇu), icchā-jñāna-kriyā, and non-difference, difference-in-non-difference, difference.
The Trika is the essence of all Śaiva scripture and the Mālinīvijayottara is the essence of the Trika (TĀ 1.18).
Scriptural hierarchy: Veda < Śaiva (Siddhānta) < Vāma < Dakṣiṇa < Mata < Kula < Kaula < Trika (verse quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 13.301; TĀ 13.300-301 grades śaktipāta in the same order).
Four means of immersion (samāveśa): anupāya (TĀ 2), śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava (MVT 2.21-23, TĀ 1.168-170).
Phonematic emanation: the letters as mātṛkā (A to KṢA) and in the scrambled order mālinī (NA to PHA); the Heart (hṛdaya) as the seed of the universe (Parātrīśikā 24).
summary: The 'Triad' tradition: a Vidyāpīṭha cult of the goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā grounded in the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and Mālinīvijayottara, which Abhinavagupta made the frame of his synthesis of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism in the Tantrāloka and Tantrasāra, incorporating Kaula, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā. It ranks itself highest among Śaiva revelations.

name: Tristuti Gaccha

scholarly.text: revived in the 19th c. by Rājendrasūri (1827–1906)

distinctive_positions: recites only three praise-verses (stuti) in caityavandana, omitting the fourth addressed to the attendant deities (śruta- and śāsana-devatās)
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha revived by Rājendrasūri, compiler of the Prakrit encyclopaedia Abhidhāna Rājendra, which rejects worship of the guardian deities in the monastic rite.

name: U Ba Khin – S. N. Goenka tradition (Sayagyi U Ba Khin lineage)

tradition.text: the tradition's account: the technique was preserved in its purity in Burma by a chain of teachers from the Buddha's time (via the missionaries Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi) and revived by Ledi Sayadaw; U Ba Khin founded the IMC in 1952; Goenka began teaching in India in 1969

scholarly.text: IMC Yangon 1952; Goenka's courses from 1969; Dhamma Giri 1976

transmissions_received.what: the practice of observing sensations (vedanā) with awareness of impermanence, via Saya Thetgyi
transmissions_received.evidence: the lineage's own account

distinctive_positions: A ten-day residential course: five precepts (sīla), mindfulness of respiration at the nostrils (samādhi) for the first days, then insight by systematic observation of bodily sensations with equanimity (paññā), ending with loving-kindness (mettā).
Reacting to sensations with craving or aversion multiplies saṅkhāras; equanimous observation of sensations as impermanent eradicates them.
The teaching is presented as non-sectarian and universal; courses are given free, supported by donations of past students.
U Ba Khin: 'the clock of vipassanā has struck' — the revival of the practice 2,500 years after the Buddha (the tradition's account).
summary: The lay insight lineage of Saya Thetgyi, Sayagyi U Ba Khin (1899–1971) and S. N. Goenka (1924–2013), whose standardized ten-day courses of mindfulness of respiration and body-scanning insight spread from Burma and India worldwide.

name: The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi (aṣṭa-maṭha)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: Eight monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Madhva for eight of his ascetic disciples, who worship in turn the image of Kṛṣṇa that Madhva installed at Uḍupi: Palimaru (Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha), Adamaru (Narasiṃha Tīrtha), Krishnapura (Janārdana Tīrtha), Puttige (Upendra Tīrtha), Shirur (Vāmana Tīrtha), Sode (Viṣṇu Tīrtha, Madhva's brother), Kaniyooru (Rāma Tīrtha) and Pejavara (Adhokṣaja Tīrtha). The worship rotates among them (paryāya); the tradition credits Vādirāja Tīrtha of Sode with changing the turn from two months to two years (from 1522).
notes: The maṭhas are paired (Palimaru–Adamaru, Krishnapura–Puttige, Shirur–Sode, Kaniyooru–Pejavara) — recorded from memory, moderate confidence. The two-monthly original rotation and the 1522 date should be checked.

name: Upakeśa Gaccha
distinctive_positions: claims descent from Pārśva's disciple-line through Keśin, i.e. from before Mahāvīra (the tradition's account)
associated with Osiyā (Upakeśapura) in Marwar and the Osvāl caste
summary: A historical Śvetāmbara gaccha of Marwar that traced itself to Pārśva's lineage via Keśin and is linked to the conversion of the Osvāls at Osiyā; its present status is uncertain.

name: Upaniṣadic tradition (the teaching of the early Upaniṣads)
alt_names: Vedānta in its original sense ('end of the Veda')

tradition.text: Revealed scripture (śruti): in the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta view without human author and beginningless; the texts themselves trace their teaching through lineages of teachers back to Brahma/Prajāpati and brahman, the self-existent

scholarly.text: earliest prose Upaniṣads (BAU, ChU) c. 7th-6th c. BCE; the verse Upaniṣads (Katha, Isa, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka) in the last centuries BCE; Māṇḍūkya and Maitrī around the turn of the era (rough consensus estimates, disputed)

transmissions_received.what: the ritual thought of the Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas (correspondences, speculation on prāṇa, the udgītha, the fire altar), internalized and reinterpreted as knowledge of the self
transmissions_received.evidence: the Upaniṣads are embedded in or attached to Vedic texts of particular sakhas: BAU closes the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; AU is Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4-6; TU is Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7-9; KauU is Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka 3-6; Kena is Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa 4.18-21; Isa is Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 40

transmissions_given.what: the Upaniṣads are the first of the three foundations (prasthāna-traya) systematized by the Brahmā Sutra
the mahavakyas, neti neti, the three states and turiya, the five sheaths, śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana (BAU 2.4.5), the six virtues (BAU 4.4.23)
the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the world as the Lord's body, Śvetāśvatara's Lord; read as qualified non-difference
the two birds (MuU 3.1.1), the distinction of jīva and īśvara; tat tvam asi read as difference
vocabulary later systematized in Samkhya: avyakta, mahat, purusa (KU 1.3.10-11), pradhana, guna, ksetrajna, 'samkhya-yoga' and Kapila (SU)
yoga as firm holding of the senses (KU 2.3.11), the yoga chapter of the Śvetāśvatara, the six-limbed yoga of the Maitrī (6.18)
the ideal of rising above the three desires and living as a mendicant (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22; MuU 3.2.6)
verses and images reused in the Bhagavad Gītā (KU 1.2.18-19 ~ BhG 2.19-20; KU 2.3.1 ~ BhG 15.1; SU 3.16-17 ~ BhG 13.13-14)
the Śvetāśvatara's Rudra-Śiva, fetters (pāśa) and grace, cited as śruti by Śaiva authors

distinctive_positions: The self (ātman) is to be known; knowing it one knows all (ChU 6.1.3; BAU 2.4.5; MuU 1.1.3).
The self is brahman: ayam ātmā brahma, ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, prajñānaṃ brahma.
The ultimate is described through negation: neti neti (BAU 2.3.6), asthulam ananu (BAU 3.8.8), the fourth (MaU 7).
Consciousness is analysed through waking, dream, deep sleep and a fourth (BAU 4.3; ChU 8.7-12; MaU 3-7).
Action (karma) and desire determine rebirth; the desireless knower does not depart but, being brahman, goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.5-7).
Two paths after death: the path of the gods (no return) and the path of the fathers (return), with a third place for small creatures (ChU 5.10; BAU 6.2).
Knowledge of the self is higher than sacrifice; rites are 'unsafe boats' and yield finite worlds (MuU 1.2.7-10; BAU 3.8.10).
Breath (prāṇa) is the eldest and best of the vital powers (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1; PrU 2; KauU 2.14).
The teaching is secret (upanisad) and passed from teacher to qualified pupil who approaches with fuel in hand (MuU 1.2.12; SU 6.22).
In the later texts: a personal Lord (Rudra-Śiva, the deva) who is the māyā-wielder and gives grace; devotion to God and teacher (SU 4.10, 6.18, 6.23).
Yoga as a method: firm holding of the senses (KU 2.3.11), posture and breath (SU 2.8-10), six limbs (MaiU 6.18).
summary: The teaching of the early Upaniṣads, the concluding portions of the Vedic śākhās (hence 'Vedānta'). Through dialogues of named sages and kings (Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi, Śāṇḍilya, Sanatkumāra, Pippalāda, Yama) they teach that the self (ātman) is brahman, the ground of the world; that it is known by negation and by inquiry into waking, dream, sleep and the fourth; that action and desire bind to rebirth while knowledge frees; and, in the later texts, a personal Lord, grace, devotion and a method of yoga. The later Vedānta schools read these same texts in very different ways.
notes: 'The thirteen principal Upaniṣads' is a modern grouping (Hume 1921); the tradition's own groupings are the ten on which Śaṅkara commented (Isa, Kena, Katha, Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Taittirīya, Aitareya, Chāndogya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka) and the Muktikā canon of 108 (src:muktika-upanisad, owned by U04). The Muktikā (1.30) lists the ten first.
