Principal Upanishads chronology Olivelle Brihadaranyaka Chandogya pre-Buddhist Taittiriya Aitareya Kaushitaki Kena Katha Isha Shvetashvatara Mundaka Prashna Mandukya dates
checks.note: Confirmed as a recognized body of teaching: the thirteen principal Upaniṣads and their Vedic placements were all checked in this sweep. Those placements are BĀU closing the ŚB; AU = AĀ 2.4-6; TU = TĀ 7-9; KauU = KĀ 3-6; Kena = JUB 4.18-21 (DCS); Īśa = VS 40. Named key teachers are text-located (see the tch: checks). The distinctive positions cite refs that were all located (ChU 6.1.3, BĀU 2.4.5, MuU 1.1.3 …). The scholarly span -700/200 follows Olivelle's chronology as reported on the web. The transmissions to Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, Yoga and the Gītā match the borrowing checks below. Founders are rightly empty (śruti). All 38 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 3.3; BĀU 3.7; PrU 6.1; BĀU 2.4.5; BĀU 4.4.23; MuU 3.1.1; KU 1.3.10-11; KU 2.3.11; BĀU 3.5.1; BĀU 4.4.22; MuU 3.2.6; KU 1.2.18-19 …).

name: Uttarādi Maṭha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: One of the three principal Mādhva maṭhas (with the Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas). It traces its pontiffs from Madhva through Padmanābha Tīrtha, Narahari Tīrtha, Mādhava Tīrtha and Akṣobhya Tīrtha to Jayatīrtha and Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha; its later pontiffs include Raghūttama Tīrtha, Satyanātha Tīrtha and Satyadharma Tīrtha, most taking names beginning with 'Satya-'. It venerates Jayatīrtha's brindāvana at Malkheḍ.
notes: The division of the line after Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha (Kavīndra Tīrtha's line leading to this maṭha and, after a later split, to the Rāghavendra maṭha; Rājendra Tīrtha's line leading to the Vyāsarāja maṭha) is recorded here from memory at low confidence. The 'Mūla Rāma' images held by the tradition to have been brought from the Kaliṅga treasury by Narahari Tīrtha are claimed by this maṭha and the Rāghavendra maṭha — not verified.

name: Uttarāpathakas ('Northerners', as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold, among others, that a layman can be an arahant while remaining a householder and that space is unconditioned.
summary: An unidentified group of northern Indian Buddhists to whom the Kathāvatthu commentary attributes several refuted views.
notes: Identity unknown; reported by an opponent only. Created by U37.

name: Vaṭakalai (northern school of Śrīvaiṣṇavism)
regions: Kāñcīpuram and the northern Tamil country

tradition.text: from Vedānta Deśika (1268–1369) and the Kāñcī teachers before him

scholarly.text: doctrinal differences take shape 13th–14th c.; separate institutions and marks by c. 17th–18th c.

distinctive_positions: Prapatti (surrender) is a real means (upāya) to liberation, an alternative to bhakti-yoga for those unable to undertake it; it must be performed once, with its five limbs (aṅga) and self-offering as the principal (aṅgin).
The Lord's grace, though free, takes the soul's act of surrender as its occasion (vyāja); 'markaṭa-kiśora-nyāya': the baby monkey clings to its mother.
Śrī (Lakṣmī) is, with Viṣṇu, all-pervading (vibhu), of the rank of the Lord (Īśvara-koṭi), and together with him the means and the goal; the divine couple is the object of surrender.
The Lord overlooks (does not see) the faults of the surrendered; he does not relish them.
After prapatti the surrendered must keep the scriptural duties as the Lord's command (ājñā), and must expiate or renew surrender for deliberate offences.
Kaivalya (enjoyment of one's own self apart from the Lord) is not a permanent state.
summary: The Śrīvaiṣṇava school following Vedānta Deśika, stronger in Sanskrit scholastic writing and associated with Kāñcī; it holds that surrender is a means the soul performs and that Śrī shares the Lord's supremacy. It wears the U-shaped mark (tiruman) without the line on the nose.

name: Vaibhāṣika

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–7th c. CE

distinctive_positions: The Abhidharma, arranged by Kātyāyanīputra and others from the Buddha's scattered teaching, is the word of the Buddha (Yaśomitra's report).
The orthodoxy of the Mahāvibhāṣā: real existence of dharmas in three times, prāpti, avijñapti, the four characteristics as real forces.
Vasubandhu presented the Kośa as 'mostly the Abhidharma as established by the Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas' (AK 8.40).
summary: The Vaibhāṣikas ('followers of the Vibhāṣā') were the Kashmiri orthodoxy of the Sarvāstivāda, taking the Mahāvibhāṣā as authoritative. Saṅghabhadra's Nyāyānusāra defended their positions against the Sautrāntika criticisms of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

name: Vaikhānasa

tradition.text: the Vaikhānasa Sūtra was composed by Vikhanas — identified with Brahmā born of Nārāyaṇa, or with Nārāyaṇa himself — and is the first of all sūtras; his disciples Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci and Kāśyapa taught the rules of temple worship (Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa; Kriyādhikāra 1.1)

scholarly.text: the Vaikhānasa Sūtras belong to the late Taittirīya sūtra literature; the temple-worship saṃhitās are later; exact dates not established here

transmissions_received.what: Vedic (Taittirīya) ritual forms and mantras
transmissions_received.evidence: the Vaikhānasa Sūtras and Mantrapraśna

distinctive_positions: Vaikhānasa worship of Viṣṇu is Vedic (vaidika): performed with Vedic mantras by brahmins of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra.
Worship is twofold: formless (amūrta) through the fire and with form (samūrta) in an image; image worship (arcana) is praised as the best means.

Viṣṇu is partless (niṣkala) and with parts (sakala): the fixed image (dhruva-bera) stands for the niṣkala and receives only flowers; the movable image (kautuka-bera) stands for the sakala and receives full worship (Kriyādhikāra 11.148–152).
Viṣṇu is invoked in five forms: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha (Bhṛgu Saṃhitā 13.1).
Vaikhānasas are Vaiṣṇavas from the womb (garbha-vaiṣṇava) through the prenatal viṣṇubali rite and so do not take the Pāñcarātra branding initiation.
The Vaikhānasa Sūtra is the best of sūtras and its followers the highest, for ten reasons (Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa).
summary: The Vaikhānasas are a hereditary community of Vedic (Taittirīya) brahmins, followers of the Sūtra of Vikhanas, whose saṃhitās (ascribed to Marīci, Atri, Kāśyapa and Bhṛgu) govern image worship of Viṣṇu with Vedic mantras. They serve as priests in many South Indian Viṣṇu temples, above all Tirumala–Tirupati, and distinguish their Vedic worship from the tantric Pāñcarātra.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority. The term 'vaikhānasa' in Dharmaśāstra also names a class of forest hermits following the 'Vaikhānasa śāstra' (see src:vaikhanasa-dharmasutra).

name: Vaiśeṣika

tradition.text: from the sage Kaṇāda

scholarly.text: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra core perhaps c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE; Praśastapāda c. 6th c. CE; merged with Nyāya from c. the 10th–11th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Nyāya analysis of the means of knowledge and debate, in the syncretic manuals (Śivāditya, Keśava Miśra, Annambhaṭṭa)
transmissions_received.evidence: Saptapadārthī; Tarkabhāṣā; Tarkasaṅgraha ('for the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Nyāya').

transmissions_given.what: the ontology of categories and atoms
a categorial ontology, extended with capacity, similarity and number
the six categories named at the opening of the Caraka Saṃhitā (direction debated)

distinctive_positions: Dharma is that from which prosperity (abhyudaya) and the highest good (niḥśreyasa) result (VS 1.1.2); the authority of the Veda rests on its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).

Reality is analysed into categories (padārtha): substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity and inherence — six in Praśastapāda and the Upaskāra recension of the sūtras — with absence added as a seventh in later works (Udayana's Lakṣaṇāvalī, Śivāditya's Saptapadārthī).
Nine substances: earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self and mind (VS 1.1.4).
Twenty-four qualities (Praśastapāda), seventeen named in the sūtra (VS 1.1.5) and seven more included by its word 'ca'; five kinds of motion (VS 1.1.6).
Earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless, spherical atoms (paramāṇu) that combine into dyads and larger wholes; what exists without a cause is eternal (VS 4.1.1, 7.1.26).
Ultimate particularity (viśeṣa) distinguishes each eternal substance — traditionally connected with the school's name.
Only two means of knowledge: perception and inference; verbal knowledge is explained as inference (VS 9.18–19 in Candrānanda's recension; Praśastapāda).

Motions without visible cause — the needle's approach to a magnet, the ascent of sap, fire's upward flame, the first motion of atoms and minds, and the mind's departure at death and entry at birth — are caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa) (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.8, 5.2.14, 5.2.19).

Yoga is the state in which, the mind resting in the self, the embodied one has neither pleasure nor pain; liberation is the absence of contact with a body and the non-arising of a new one when adṛṣṭa is absent (VS 5.2.17, 5.2.20).
The world is periodically dissolved and recreated by the will of Maheśvara acting through the adṛṣṭa of selves (Praśastapāda).
Heat transforms qualities at the level of atoms (pīlupāka), against Nyāya's view that the whole is baked (piṭharapāka).
summary: Vaiśeṣika is the Vedic darśana of categorial analysis and atomism founded on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika Sūtra and systematized by Praśastapāda. It explains dharma as the source of prosperity and the highest good, and holds that knowledge of the truth of the categories — through their similarities and dissimilarities — produced by dharma leads to liberation. Its commentators (Vyomaśiva, Śrīdhara, Udayana) made it theistic and joined it to Nyāya; after the 11th c. it survives mainly within syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.
notes: Status 'absorbed': Vaiśeṣika ontology is still studied, but within Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika manuals.

name: Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā

tradition.text: the tradition claims Jayadeva, Vidyāpati, Caṇḍīdās, Caitanya, Rūpa, Sanātana and Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja as Sahajiyā masters

scholarly.text: Sahajiyā texts are post-Caitanya, mostly 17th–18th c.; continuity with the Buddhist Sahajiyā of the Caryāgīti is a scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory, the parakīyā ideal, Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body, the Caitanya-caritāmṛta's kāma/prema distinction
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation and re-reading (e.g. Vivartavilāsa on the Caitanya-caritāmṛta)

transmissions_received.what: sahaja as the innate goal, the body as microcosm, the union of the two principles, songs in coded language
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis (S. B. Dasgupta, Obscure Religious Cults) supported by shared vocabulary with the Caryāgīti

distinctive_positions: Every man and woman has two natures: the outward form (rūpa) and the divine nature (svarūpa) — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman.
By superimposition (āropa) of svarūpa on rūpa, human love (kāma) is transformed into divine love (prema), 'as gold is purified from ore'.
The parakīyā (love outside marriage) of the gopīs is taken as the model for human practice between partners — recorded in summary only (restricted).
The sahaja mānuṣa, the innate Man, dwells in the body; the goal is the sahaja state beyond the play of the two.
A graded path: pravarta (beginner, with name and mantra), sādhaka (practitioner, with bhāva), siddha (perfected, with prema).
Caitanya and the Gosvāmīs are read as secret Sahajiyās; orthodox Gauḍīyas reject this (dsp:sahajiya-and-gaudiya-orthodoxy).
summary: The Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā is a Bengali tradition that interiorizes the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa: the divine couple dwell as the innate natures of every woman and man, and through a guru-guided discipline culminating in the ritual union of partners (summary only) human love is refined into divine prema and the sahaja state. Its texts are 17th–18th-century Bengali manuals; its most famous voice is the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās.
notes: Family 'vedic' (as a Vaiṣṇava movement), with the Buddhist Sahajiyā continuity recorded only as a scholarly hypothesis (brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya). Sexual-yogic practice: summary and warnings only.

name: Vajrayāna (Mantranaya) in India
alt_names: Zhenyan / Mizong (Chinese, for the early stream)

tradition.text: taught by the Buddha in the form of Vajradhara (e.g. the Kālacakra at Dhānyakaṭaka, the Guhyasamāja to King Indrabhūti of Oḍḍiyāna); hidden and revealed to qualified disciples

scholarly.text: c. 6th–13th c. CE in India: kriyā/caryā texts from the 6th c. (dhāraṇī literature earlier); Mahāvairocana mid-7th c.; Tattvasaṃgraha late 7th c.; Guhyasamāja c. 8th c.; Yoginī tantras c. 9th–10th c.; Kālacakra early 11th c. (epoch 1027); decline after c. 1200

transmissions_received.what: the bodhisattva path, the six perfections and the goal of buddhahood for all beings
transmissions_received.evidence: the tantras present themselves as Mahāyāna (the mantra method within the Mahāyāna)

transmissions_received.what: emptiness as the view of the tantras (Ārya Guhyasamāja exegesis; Advayavajra)
transmissions_received.evidence: Pañcakrama and Advayavajrasaṃgraha frame the stages in Madhyamaka terms

transmissions_received.what: mind-only and the four gnoses (mirror-like etc.) mapped to the five buddha families
transmissions_received.evidence: the five gnoses (Yogācāra's four plus dharmadhātu gnosis)

transmissions_received.what: ritual technology (maṇḍala, homa, nyāsa), pīṭha lists and the cremation-ground idiom of the Yoginī tantras
transmissions_received.evidence: disputed; see brw:saiva-pithas-to-cakrasamvara, brw:kapalika-to-vajrayana, brw:saiva-vidyapitha-to-yogini-tantras

transmissions_given.what: the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Indian tantras, their empowerments, commentaries and siddha instructions (the later diffusion, 10th–13th c.; Nyingma: the earlier diffusion, 8th c.)
the Vajrācārya tradition of the Nepal valley, continuing Indian Vajrayāna ritual in Sanskrit
the Mahāvairocana and Tattvasaṃgraha (yoga-tantra) stream via Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra (8th c.)
the two-maṇḍala (womb and vajra) system via Huiguo to Kūkai

distinctive_positions: Buddhahood can be attained in this very life and body (Pañcakrama 3.12; the 'swift path'), by the Mahāyāna view joined with special methods (deity yoga, mantra, the subtle body).

The mantra method is superior to the perfection method in being unconfused, rich in means, not difficult and for those of sharp faculties (Tripiṭakamala's Nayatrayapradīpa, the classic Indian statement).
Entry requires consecration (abhiṣeka) from a qualified vajra master and keeping the pledges (samaya); the teacher is to be regarded as inseparable from Vajradhara (Gurupañcāśikā 22).

The path has two stages: generation (utpattikrama) — the practitioner arises as the deity in the maṇḍala — and completion (utpanna-/niṣpannakrama) — work with channels, winds and drops toward clear light and union.
The passions are not only abandoned but used as the path ('poison as medicine'); desire in particular is transformed into great bliss (mahāsukha) joined with emptiness.
The goal is the union (yuganaddha) of clear light and illusory body, or of immutable bliss and empty form (Kālacakra), the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Tantric statements are coded ('intentional language', sandhyābhāṣā) and must be read with the explanatory tantras and the guru's instruction (the six alternatives, ṣaṭkoṭi).
summary: The esoteric Mahāyāna of India that teaches the swift path to buddhahood by mantra, deity yoga in the maṇḍala, consecration by a vajra master and the yogas of the subtle body, codified in tantras revealed (by the tradition's account) by the Buddha as Vajradhara and, historically, composed c. 6th–11th c. and taught at Nālandā, Vikramaśīla and among the wandering siddhas; transmitted to Tibet, Nepal and East Asia.

name: Vāma stream (the left current of Tumburu)
distinctive_positions: Worship of Tumburu (a form of Śiva) with his four sister-goddesses (Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī/Ajitā, Aparājitā).
The Kāmika names the left (vāma) stream as issuing from the northern face, in 24 tantras beginning with the Nayasūtra (Kāmika pūrva 1.25–26).
A Khmer inscription (Sdok Kak Thom, 1052 CE) recounts that the brahmin Hiraṇyadāma taught King Jayavarman II the Vīṇāśikha, Nayottara, Sammoha and Śiraścheda (early 9th c.).
summary: The left current of Śaiva revelation, centred on Tumburu and four goddesses, known chiefly from the surviving Vīṇāśikhatantra and from Cambodian epigraphy.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08. Caution: 'Śiraścheda' in the Khmer list is probably a Vāma text; the Kashmirian Jayadrathayāmala also bears the name Śiraścheda (scholarly discussion; not resolved here). family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Vārkarī sampradāya
regions: Maharashtra (Paṇḍharpūr on the Bhīmā/Candrabhāgā; Āḷandī; Dehu; Paiṭhaṇ; Sāsvaḍ; Tryambakeśvar; Maṅgaḷveḍhe; Terḍhokī)

tradition.text: Viṭṭhala has stood on the brick for twenty-eight yugas since Puṇḍalīka's time; the saints appear as a succession within it

scholarly.text: Paṇḍharpūr cult attested from the 12th–13th c.; the saint-tradition from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev (late 13th c.); pālkhī processions organised from the late 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: initiation of Nivṛttināth by Gahinīnāth and through him of Jñāneśvar; the yoga of kuṇḍalinī described in Jñāneśvarī 6
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation: lineage verses at the close of Jñāneśvarī 18; tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as scripture (Eknāthī Bhāgavat) and the Viṭṭhala māhātmyas
transmissions_received.evidence: commentary and citation

transmissions_received.what: Eknāth's guru Janārdana Svāmī was a devotee of Dattātreya
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Eknāth's own verses on Janārdana; Mahīpati)

transmissions_given.what: Nāmdev's Hindi songs and example, revered by Kabīr and later northern Sants (Nāmdev's songs also stand in the Sikh scripture, context only)
a shared Marathi devotional idiom (Rāmdās's contemporaries and audience overlap)

distinctive_positions: God is worshipped as Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā, Pāṇḍuraṅga) of Paṇḍharpūr, standing on a brick with hands on hips — a form of Kṛṣṇa, identified also with Viṣṇu and, by some saints, with Śiva.
The name ('Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari', 'Viṭṭhala') and congregational singing (bhajan, kīrtan) are the main means; no renunciation is required — the householder's ordinary work becomes worship.

The twice-yearly vārī — walking pilgrimage to Paṇḍharpūr for the Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī ekādaśīs, in diṇḍīs following the pālkhīs of Jñāneśvar and Tukārām — is the defining observance; initiation is by wearing the tuḷsī-bead necklace (māḷ).
Knowledge and devotion are held together: Jñāneśvar's non-dual teaching is crowned by devotion that continues after realization.
Saints of every caste and gender — tailor, potter, gardener, barber, Mahār, maidservant, courtesan's daughter, Kuṇbī, brahmin woman — are equally revered; the saints' company is itself the tīrtha.
Scripture is in Marathi; the 'three foundations' (prasthānatrayī) of the Vārkarīs are the Jñāneśvarī, the Eknāthī Bhāgavat and the Tukārām Gāthā.
The sequence of saints is pictured as one temple: Jñāneśvar the foundation, Nāmdev the walls, Eknāth the pillar, Tukārām the pinnacle (Bahiṇābāī).
summary: The Vārkarī tradition of Maharashtra worships Viṭṭhala of Paṇḍharpūr through the name, bhajan, kīrtan and the walking pilgrimage (vārī). It looks to a chain of Marathi saints from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev (13th–14th c.) through Eknāth (16th c.) to Tukārām (17th c.), of every caste, whose songs and commentaries are its scripture. It joins non-dual knowledge (Jñāneśvar's Nāth-derived teaching) to devotion lived in the household.

name: Vātsīputrīya
distinctive_positions: The person is neither the aggregates nor other than them; it is designated in dependence on the aggregates (Vasumitra; AKBh 9).
Named in AKBh 9 as the holders of the pudgala doctrine ('vātsīputrīyāḥ pudgalaṃ santam icchanti', Pradhan p. 461).
summary: The root Pudgalavāda school, named after Vātsīputra; in Vasumitra's list it splits from the Sarvāstivāda and gives rise to the Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya and Ṣaṇṇagarika.

name: Vedāṅga (the six limbs of the Veda)
alt_names: the six auxiliary sciences of the Veda
regions: Gandhāra and the north-west (Pāṇini's Śalātura, by tradition)
South India (the Taittirīya schools of Āpastamba and Baudhāyana)

tradition.text: The limbs are as old as the Veda's transmission; the tradition says later seers, lacking the direct vision of the first seers, compiled the Veda and its limbs for ease of learning (Nirukta 1.20).

scholarly.text: Principal sūtra works c. 6th/5th c. BCE – 2nd c. BCE (Yāska, Pāṇini, Prātiśākhyas, Kalpasūtras, Kātyāyana, Patañjali), with commentaries continuing to the present

transmissions_received.what: the Saṃhitā texts, their recitation and the Brāhmaṇa ritual that the six limbs exist to preserve, interpret and time
transmissions_received.evidence: MuU 1.1.5 lists the six limbs after the four Vedas; PŚ 41–42; Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā

transmissions_given.what: Pāṇinian grammar grew into an independent school with its own philosophy of language (sphoṭa, śabda-brahman) — covered by U31
Vedic time-reckoning (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa) as the first text of the later astral science — covered by U32
the Dharmasūtras are the dharma part of the Kalpasūtras; the smṛti tradition grew out of them
Kalpa and Brāhmaṇa exegesis (injunction, explanatory passage, ritual application) is the material Mīmāṃsā systematizes

distinctive_positions: The Veda has six limbs — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual procedure (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and time-reckoning (jyotiṣa); the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (1.1.5) counts them with the four Vedas as 'lower knowledge' (aparā vidyā), and the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā (41–42) pictures them as the Veda's feet, hands, eye, ear, nose and mouth.

The exact sound, accent, quantity and sequence of the Vedic text must be preserved; a mantra defective in accent or sound turns into a verbal thunderbolt against the sacrificer, as Tvaṣṭṛ's mis-accented 'indraśatru' did (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52; ŚB 1.6.3.10).

The meaning of the mantras must be understood: the one who recites without understanding is 'a post, a mere bearer of loads' (Nirukta 1.18); Kautsa's thesis that mantras are meaningless is answered by Yāska (Nirukta 1.15–16).
All nouns derive from verbal roots, according to Śākaṭāyana and the Nairuktas; Gārgya and some grammarians deny that all do (Nirukta 1.12).

Grammar is the chief of the six limbs; it is studied to protect the Veda, adapt mantras, fulfil the scriptural command that a brāhmaṇa study the Veda with its six limbs as a duty without motive, save effort and remove doubt (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).
Time-reckoning exists for the sacrifices, which are enjoined for fixed times; it stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas like a peacock's crest (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, Ṛk recension 3, 35).
The first seers had direct vision of dharma (sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇaḥ) and 'saw' the hymns; later generations received the mantras by instruction (Nirukta 1.20; 2.11).
summary: The six auxiliary sciences through which the Vedic schools preserved, pronounced, analysed, interpreted, performed and timed the Veda: śikṣā (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā and the Prātiśākhyas), chandas (Piṅgala), vyākaraṇa (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, Patañjali), nirukta (the Nighaṇṭu and Yāska), kalpa (Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba sūtras) and jyotiṣa (Lagadha). They treat the Veda as sound to be kept intact and as meaning to be understood, and they stand to the Veda as limbs to a body.

checks.note: All the cited passages were found: Nirukta 1.20 has the later seers who lacked direct vision and compiled the Veda and its limbs ('sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇa ṛṣayo babhūvuḥ … avare … imaṃ granthaṃ samāmnāsiṣur vedaṃ ca vedāṅgāni ca'). MuU 1.1.5 lists the six limbs under the lower knowledge. Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 41–42 has the limbs as the Veda's body and PŚ 52 the verbal thunderbolt; ŚB 1.6.3.10 has 'indraśatru'. The scholarly span (c. 600–100 BCE for the sūtra works) matches the dates in the checked source entries (Yāska, Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, Patañjali). The dating confidence stays low, as the entry itself marks it.

name: Vedānta (Uttara Mīmāṃsā)

tradition.text: The Brahma Sūtras are ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa, identified with Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara age

scholarly.text: Sūtras compiled between c. 2nd c. BCE and c. 5th c. CE (final redaction often placed c. 400–450 CE); the named commentarial schools from c. 8th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Upaniṣads as the primary scripture (śruti-prasthāna) whose harmony (samanvaya) the sūtras establish
transmissions_received.evidence: BS 1.1.4 and the whole first adhyāya

transmissions_received.what: the exegetical method (adhikaraṇa structure, rules of interpretation, marks of purport)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared sūtra form; Jaimini cited by name in BS; BS called Uttara-mīmāṃsā

transmissions_given.what: the sūtra text and the prasthāna-traya canon
the sūtra text and the prasthāna-traya canon
the sūtra text and the prasthāna-traya canon
the sūtra text

distinctive_positions: The three foundations (prasthāna-traya): the Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtras; every Vedānta school establishes itself by commenting on all three.
Brahman is that from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the world proceed (BS 1.1.2).
Brahman is known only from scripture, not by independent inference (BS 1.1.3; 2.1.11).
All Upaniṣadic passages converge (samanvaya) on Brahman (BS 1.1.4).
The non-conscious pradhāna of Sāṃkhya is not the world-cause, because the cause 'thought' (īkṣati) (BS 1.1.5; 2.2.1).
Brahman is both the material and the efficient cause of the world (BS 1.4.23).
Liberation follows from knowledge of Brahman; the liberated do not return (BS 3.4.1; 4.4.22).
The nature of the relation between the individual self and Brahman is the defining question on which the Vedānta schools divide (already debated by Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna, BS 1.4.20–22).
summary: The school of the 'later inquiry' (uttara-mīmāṃsā) into the Upaniṣads, systematized in Bādarāyaṇa's Brahma Sūtras. Its four chapters establish that the Upaniṣads teach Brahman, defend this against rival systems, set out the means, and describe the result. Every later Vedānta school — Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, the Bhedābheda schools, Śuddhādvaita, Acintya-bhedābheda and Śaiva Vedānta — is constituted by a commentary on the sūtras.

name: Vedic Śrauta tradition (the Saṃhitā lineages)
alt_names: the Vedic recitation and sacrificial lineages
regions: the land of the seven rivers (sapta sindhavaḥ) named in the Ṛgveda (Greater Panjab)
Kuru-Pañcāla country (Yajurveda and Sāmaveda Saṃhitās, as located by scholars)
later all of India: Kerala (Nambūtiri reciters), Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Odisha, Varanasi, Kashmir (formerly)

tradition.text: beginningless (anādi) and authorless revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged into four Saṃhitās by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara age

scholarly.text: Ṛgveda c. 1500–1000 BCE; the other Saṃhitās c. 1200–800 BCE; living recitation to the present

transmissions_given.what: the Upaniṣads as the closing portion (Vedānta) of each śākhā; prāṇa, brahman, ātman, the two birds (RV 1.164.20), the two paths (RV 10.88.15), the Puruṣa hymn (RV 10.90), the yoking of mind (RV 5.81.1; VS 11.1–5)
the Saṃhitā texts that phonetics, metre, grammar, etymology, ritual and time-keeping exist to preserve and apply
the mantra and injunction corpus whose ritual purport Mīmāṃsā interprets
the Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī), the Puruṣa hymn's four varṇas, funeral and marriage mantras
the Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram) and the five-syllable formula it contains (TS 4.5.8)
the Vāk hymn (RV 10.125) recited as the Devī Sūkta; Śrī Sūkta (Ṛgveda Khila)
the Puruṣa Sūkta and Viṣṇu's highest step as central liturgy
verses on speech (RV 1.164.45, 4.58.3, 10.71) read as praise of grammar
the melodies (sāman) and their notes, the root of music in the tradition's own account
Atharvavedic healing (bhaiṣajya); Āyurveda counted as an upaveda / limb of the Atharvaveda

distinctive_positions: The Veda is heard revelation (śruti), 'seen' by the ṛṣis rather than composed; the named seers are its first seers and transmitters (Nirukta 1.20).
Ṛta, the true order, holds together the cosmos, the ritual and right conduct; satya (truth) is its spoken and lived form; its guardians are Varuṇa and Mitra.
The sacrifice (yajña) sustains gods and world; the first sacrifice was the gods' offering of the cosmic Person (Puruṣa), and 'these were the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16 = 1.164.50).
Truth is one; the inspired call it by many names — Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Yama, Mātariśvan (RV 1.164.46; cf. 10.114.5, 8.58.2, 3.55).
Speech (vāc) is a cosmic power: of her four quarters three are hidden, the fourth is human speech (RV 1.164.45); she chooses whom she makes a seer (RV 10.125.5).
Before creation there was neither being nor non-being; That One breathed windless by its own power; whether even the overseer in the highest heaven knows its origin is left open (RV 10.129).
Tapas (generative heat, austerity) is the source of ṛta and satya (RV 10.190.1) and the way the ancients reached heaven (RV 10.154.2).

The dead go by the ancient paths to Yama and the fathers in the highest heaven, rejoined with their merit of sacrifice and gift (iṣṭāpūrta) and a radiant body (RV 10.14.8); the ideal on earth is a full life of a hundred autumns.
The Veda is preserved by exact oral recitation in accent and letter within hereditary śākhās, guarded by the word-by-word and interwoven recitations (pada, krama, jaṭā, ghana).
The Atharvaveda adds healing, protection, concord and royal rites, and hymns on Skambha, Prāṇa, Kāla, the Brahmacārin and the Vrātya that name one supporting principle (jyeṣṭha brahman).
summary: The lineages that recite and ritually employ the four Vedic Saṃhitās — Ṛg (hymns), Sāma (chants), Yajus (sacrificial formulas; Black and White) and Atharva (hymns and spells) — each in hereditary branches (śākhās). Their teaching is carried in hymns to the gods (Agni, Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vāc …), in the liturgy of the śrauta sacrifice, and in a set of speculative hymns on the One, creation, speech, the self and death that the later Upaniṣads and all Vedic schools take up.

checks.note: Recognized as the Vedic śrauta/recitation tradition. Scholarly dating (RV c. 1500–1000, other Saṃhitās c. 1200–800 BCE) agrees with Witzel's ranges; the tradition's account (Vyāsa divides the Veda in the Dvāpara) located at Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4.6–7. Distinctive positions are backed by teachings verified in the local texts (RV 1.164.45–46, 10.90.16 = 1.164.50, 10.129, Nirukta 1.20).

name: Vetulyakas (as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary and Sri Lankan chronicles)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold that the Buddha did not really live in the human world and did not himself teach the Dhamma (a created form taught it), and that the Saṅgha does not really accept offerings.
summary: A group whose 'Vetulya' teachings were rejected by the Mahāvihāra; the chronicles report their suppression by Sri Lankan kings; the commentary calls them Mahāsuññatāvādins.
notes: Reported by opponents only; identification with any Mahāyāna school is a scholarly hypothesis and is not made here. Created by U37.

name: Vibhajyavāda
distinctive_positions: Some of the past and future exist and some do not — distinguishing rather than affirming that everything exists (AKBh 5.25).
The mind is by nature luminous (reported and refuted in the Mahāvibhāṣā; low confidence on the attribution).
The Theravāda calls itself Vibhajjavāda (the Buddha is a 'vibhajjavādī', Mahāvaṃsa; Kathāvatthu commentary).
summary: A designation used in two ways: by the Sarvāstivāda for opponents who 'distinguish' which past and future things exist; by the Theravāda for itself. Modern accounts group the Theravāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka and Kāśyapīya as Vibhajyavādins (scholarly hypothesis).
notes: Classificatory label rather than a single ordination lineage.

name: Vidyāpīṭha (the Seat of Vidyās)

scholarly.text: Brahmayāmala/Picumata perhaps 7th–8th c.; Nepalese manuscript dated 1052 CE; Jayadrathayāmala c. 9th–10th c. (Kashmir)

transmissions_given.what: yoginī cult and kula ritual reformulated in the Kaula traditions
the Śakti-tantras (Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Mālinīvijayottara) as scriptural base

distinctive_positions: The deity of the Vidyāpīṭha is Bhairava with, and increasingly subordinate to, goddesses and yoginīs; mantras are feminine (vidyā).
Its scriptures divide into Yāmala tantras (e.g. the Brahmayāmala/Picumata; the Jayadrathayāmala) and Śakti tantras (e.g. Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Tantrasadbhāva, Mālinīvijayottara).
Its sādhaka follows Kāpālika-style observances in cremation grounds (summary only; see prc:vidyapitha-observance).
summary: Division of the Bhairava tantras centred on goddesses, yoginīs and feminine mantras. Its Yāmala tantras and Śakti tantras are the roots of the Trika and of the Kālīkula/Krama, and of much Kaula practice.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08. Doctrine of the Trika and Kālīkula belongs to U19/U24. family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata
regions: Kāśī and Kedāra (seats of two of the five pīṭhas)

tradition.text: two accounts: (a) beginningless (anādi) dharma taught by Śiva in the Āgamas and renewed in every age by the five ācāryas; (b) begun by Basava and the śaraṇas in twelfth-century Kalyāṇa

scholarly.text: 12th-c. devotional movement in Karnataka with earlier Śaiva antecedents; Sanskrit systematization and anthologies 14th–16th c.; living community

transmissions_received.what: the Śaiva Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' as scripture, read as teaching Vīraśaiva dharma in their later portion
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation: Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi 1.25 and 5.14

transmissions_received.what: institutional continuity of Śaiva maṭhas and sites in Karnataka
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis only (see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva); not part of either tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: veneration of the Tamil Nāyaṉmārs as purātanas (ancient devotees)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account: Harihara's ragaḷes and the Basava Purāṇa narrate the purātanas

transmissions_received.what: the vocabulary of full I-ness (pūrṇāhantā) and this-ness (idantā)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary in Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi 14.38–39 (interpretive)

distinctive_positions: Śiva is worshipped as the liṅga, and every initiate wears a personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga) on the body for life, worshipping it on the palm rather than in temples.

The path runs through six stages (ṣaṭsthala: bhakta, māheśvara, prasādi, prāṇaliṅgi, śaraṇa, aikya) to the union of the soul (aṅga) with the liṅga (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya); the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi elaborates them as 101 sthalas.
Guru, liṅga and jaṅgama (the moving devotee-teacher) are one; the eight shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and five codes (pañcācāra) govern life.
Work is worship (kāyaka) and its fruit is to be shared (dāsōha).
Initiation is open to all irrespective of caste and sex; the vacanas reject caste, the five pollutions (pañcasūtaka), Vedic sacrifice and temple ritualism.

The vacanas — spontaneous utterances of experience (anubhava) — are scripture for the śaraṇa strand; the Āgamas, the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi and Śrīpati's Śrīkarabhāṣya are scripture for the Pañcācārya strand.
Death is union with the liṅga (liṅgaikya): the dead are buried, not cremated, and no ancestral rites are needed.
The two strands hold different accounts of the tradition's origin and different views on its relation to the Veda and to 'Hinduism' (recorded as internal debates, not settled here).
summary: The Vīraśaiva or Liṅgāyata tradition of Karnataka and neighbouring regions worships Śiva as the liṅga, worn by every initiate on the body. Its śaraṇa strand looks to Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi, Cennabasava and the twelfth-century vacana saints of Kalyāṇa; its Pañcācārya strand looks to five ācāryas who emerged from liṅgas in every age and to the Sanskrit Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi. Both teach the six stages to union with Śiva, the unity of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama, work as worship and the equality of devotees.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7); whether the tradition stands within or outside the Vedic/Hindu fold is itself a recorded internal debate (dsp:lingayata-hindu-identity).

name: Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta (Śrīvaiṣṇava sampradāya)
regions: Tamil country (Śrīraṅgam, Kāñcīpuram, Śrīperumbūdūr, Āḻvār Tirunagari, Kumbakonam)

tradition.text: traced by the tradition from Viṣṇu and Śrī through Viṣvaksena and Nammāḻvār to Nāthamuni (traditionally 9th–10th c.) and Rāmānuja (1017–1137)

scholarly.text: systematized 10th–12th c. CE (Yāmuna, Rāmānuja); school doctrine elaborated 13th–15th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (Nālāyira Divya Prabandham) as a second, Tamil Veda
transmissions_received.evidence: Nāthamuni's recovery of the Prabandham; the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries

transmissions_received.what: temple theology and ritual, the five forms of the Lord, six-limbed surrender
transmissions_received.evidence: Yāmuna's Āgamaprāmāṇya; Śrībhāṣya on BS 2.2.42–45

transmissions_received.what: the Brahma Sūtras and the earlier Vedāntins Bodhāyana, Ṭaṅka (Brahmanandin), Dramiḍa
transmissions_received.evidence: cited in the opening of the Śrībhāṣya and in the Vedārthasaṅgraha

transmissions_received.what: rules of scriptural interpretation; the unity of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā
transmissions_received.evidence: Śrībhāṣya 1.1.1; Vedānta Deśika's Seśvaramīmāṃsā

transmissions_given.what: lineage descent claimed by the Rāmānandīs (through Rāghavānanda); disputed
the whole doctrine, as read by Vedānta Deśika
the whole doctrine, as read by Piḷḷai Lokācārya and Maṇavāḷa Māmuni

distinctive_positions: Brahman is one, but qualified (viśiṣṭa): the one Brahman has sentient souls (cit) and insentient matter (acit) as its inseparable modes (prakāra).
The world and souls are the body (śarīra) of Brahman; Brahman is their self (śarīrin), inner controller and support; the relation is inseparable existence (apṛthak-siddhi).
Three realities (tattvatraya): cit, acit and Īśvara, all real and eternal; the world is real, not an appearance.
Brahman is Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Śrī, free of every defect and possessed of infinite auspicious qualities (ubhaya-liṅga); 'nirguṇa' texts deny only defective (prākṛta) qualities.
Co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya): identity statements such as 'tat tvam asi' refer to one Brahman under two modes, never to an attributeless identity.
Every cognition is of the real (satkhyāti); Advaita's avidyā is untenable in seven ways.
The self is an atomic, eternal knower, agent and enjoyer, essentially the servant (śeṣa) of the Lord; consciousness is its attribute (dharmabhūta-jñāna).
Liberation is attained by bhakti (loving meditation, dhruvānusmṛti) or by prapatti (surrender), through the Lord's grace; there is no liberation while living.
The liberated soul reaches Vaikuṇṭha by the path of light, keeps its individuality, shares the Lord's bliss and serves him eternally (kainkarya).
Ubhaya Vedānta: the Sanskrit Veda and the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs are of equal authority.
summary: The Vedānta of Nāthamuni, Yāmuna and Rāmānuja, carried by the Śrīvaiṣṇava community of South India. It teaches one Brahman, Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, who has souls and matter as his body, reached by devotion or surrender and served eternally in Vaikuṇṭha. From the 13th–14th c. its teachers divided into a northern (Vaṭakalai) and a southern (Teṅkalai) school over grace, surrender and Śrī's status.

name: Vivaraṇa school (Vivaraṇa-prasthāna)

scholarly.text: From Prakāśātman (c. 10th–11th c.) onward; the dominant line of later Advaita scholarship

transmissions_received.what: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā on Śaṅkara's BSBh 1.1.1–4
transmissions_received.evidence: Vivaraṇa is a sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikā

distinctive_positions: Ignorance (avidyā) has pure consciousness (Brahman) as both its locus (āśraya) and its object (viṣaya).
Avidyā is a positive entity (bhāva-rūpa), though indescribable, known through perception ('I am ignorant'), inference and presumption.

Reflection theory (pratibimba-vāda): the jīva is the reflection of Brahman in avidyā/the inner organ; the reflection is real and identical with its prototype; Īśvara is the prototype (bimba) consciousness.
Hearing (śravaṇa) of the Upaniṣads is the principal means (aṅgin), enjoined by a restrictive injunction (niyama-vidhi); reflection and contemplation are its auxiliaries.
The mahāvākya itself generates immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge of Brahman.
Vedic works, through purification, lead to knowledge itself (vedana), not merely to the desire to know.
summary: The line of post-Śaṅkara Advaita founded on Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā and Prakāśātman's Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa; it locates ignorance in Brahman, treats avidyā as a positive indescribable power, explains the jīva as a reflection, and makes hearing of the Upaniṣadic sentence the direct means of liberating knowledge. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi largely follows it.

name: Vyākaraṇa (the grammarian-philosophers; śabdādvaita)
alt_names: the school of the three sages (munitraya)

tradition.text: grammar is an eternal limb of the Veda; the phonemes were revealed by Śiva's drum to Pāṇini (Nandikeśvarakāśikā 1; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 56–57)

scholarly.text: Pāṇini c. 4th c. BCE; Patañjali c. 150 BCE; Bhartṛhari c. 5th c. CE; Nāgeśa d. c. 1755 CE

transmissions_received.what: speech (vāc) as a cosmic power with four quarters, three hidden (RV 1.164.45; RV 10.125; RV 4.58.3 read as praise of grammar)
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahābhāṣya Paspaśā reads RV 4.58.3 and 1.164.45 as praises of grammar (tea:mahabhasya:paspasa/4)

transmissions_received.what: Oṃ as the sound-form of Brahman and the two brahmans (śabda and para) (Maitrī 6.22)
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhartṛhari's Vṛtti cites Upaniṣadic passages on the word-brahman (reference from memory)

transmissions_received.what: the technical grammar of Pāṇini, Kātyāyana and Patañjali on which the philosophy is built
transmissions_received.evidence: VP 2 closing verses on the transmission of the Mahābhāṣya

transmissions_given.what: the levels of speech (vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī), pratibhā, and speech as reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), reworked with parā vāk above paśyantī
the name and model of dhvani (suggestion) — Ānandavardhana credits the grammarians' sphoṭa/dhvani doctrine; pratibhā
śabda-brahman, the levels of speech located in the body, and the theory of the letters (mātṛkā)
Maṇḍana Miśra's defence of sphoṭa and his sympathetic treatment of the word-brahman
Dignāga's engagement with Bhartṛhari on word-meaning and time (scholarly hypothesis)

distinctive_positions: Brahman, without beginning or end, is the principle of the Word (śabdatattva), the imperishable, which appears (vivartate) as things; from it the world proceeds (VP 1.1).
The one Brahman appears as many through its powers, of which time (kāla-śakti) is the chief (VP 1.2–3).
There is no cognition in the world not interpenetrated by the word; all knowledge shines as if pierced by the word (VP 1.123 Iyer).

The meaning-bearer is the sphoṭa, a partless, sequence-less word manifested by the sequential sounds (dhvani/nāda); the sentence (vākya-sphoṭa) is the real unit and word-meanings are abstractions from it (apoddhāra).
The meaning of a sentence is grasped as a flash of intuition (pratibhā), which even guides animals' instinctive action (VP 2.143–152).
Speech has three levels — vaikharī (articulated), madhyamā (mental, sequential), paśyantī (undivided, 'seeing'); the highest is the Veda's supreme station (VP 1.142 Iyer).
Grammar is the door to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech, the straight royal road to the highest (VP 1.14–16); the purified use of words is a yoga of the word (śabdapūrva-yoga).
Word, meaning and their relation are eternal (siddhe śabdārthasambandhe — Kātyāyana's first vārttika); grammar only restricts correct usage for the sake of merit (dharma-niyama).
Reasoning without scripture is unstable: what is inferred with effort by the skilled is explained otherwise by the more skilled (VP 1.34).
Every word ultimately denotes Being (sattā), the great universal, which is Brahman (VP 3.1, 3.2).
summary: The Pāṇinian grammarians as a school of philosophy of language. From Patañjali's question 'what is the word?' and Kātyāyana's doctrine of the eternal word, Bhartṛhari's Vākyapadīya built a monism of the Word: Brahman is the Word-principle that appears as the world, all cognition is word-permeated, meaning is borne by the indivisible sphoṭa and grasped as pratibhā, and grammar itself is a path to liberation. Maṇḍana Miśra defended sphoṭa; Helārāja, Puṇyarāja and Kaiyaṭa commented; Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa and Nāgeśa systematized the 'new' grammatical philosophy. Opposed by Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Buddhists, Jains and (on paśyantī) the Kashmir Śaivas.

name: Vyāsarāja Maṭha (Sosale)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha of Vyāsatīrtha (Vyāsarāja), disciple of Brahmaṇya Tīrtha; seated at Sosale (Mysuru district). Vyāsatīrtha's brindāvana is at Nava Brindāvana near Ānegondi (Hampi).
notes: Its descent from Madhva through Rājendra Tīrtha, Jayadhvaja, Puruṣottama and Brahmaṇya Tīrtha is recorded from memory at low confidence.

name: Yangqi branch (of the Linji house)
regions: China; transmitted to Japan and Korea

scholarly.text: from Yangqi Fanghui (992–1049); the main Linji line from the 12th c.

transmissions_given.what: most Japanese Rinzai lines (via Wuzhun Shifan, Xutang Zhiyu, Lanxi Daolong, etc.)

distinctive_positions: Kōan commentary (Yuanwu) and the critical-phrase practice (Dahui).
summary: The branch of the Linji house descending from Yangqi Fanghui, which produced Wuzu Fayan, Yuanwu Keqin and Dahui Zonggao and became the principal source of later Chinese, Korean and Japanese Rinzai lineages.

name: Yāpanīya
alt_names: Gopya / Āpulīya Saṅgha (names in some sources; low confidence)

tradition.text: Devasena's Darśanasāra (Digambara) says the Yāpanīya saṅgha was founded by Śrīkalaśa at Kalyāṇa (date given in the Vikrama era; low confidence)

scholarly.text: attested in Karnataka inscriptions from about the 5th c. CE (Kadamba grants) to about the 14th–15th c. CE, after which it disappears

distinctive_positions: Monks went naked and carried the peacock-feather whisk like the Digambaras
Yet held, with the Śvetāmbaras, that women can attain liberation (strī-nirvāṇa) and that the omniscient takes food (kevali-bhukti)
Accepted a form of the old canon (Āvaśyaka, Chedasūtras, niryuktis and others, as cited in Aparājita's commentary) rather than declaring it lost
Allowed that those who wear clothes by exception (apavāda-liṅga) and householders can in principle be liberated (reported in later sources; moderate confidence)
summary: An extinct Jain order of the Deccan and Karnataka that combined Digambara-style monastic nudity with Śvetāmbara positions on women's liberation and the kevalin's eating. Its chief surviving works are Śākaṭāyana (Pālyakīrti)'s Strīnirvāṇa- and Kevalibhukti-prakaraṇas; Aparājita's commentary on the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā is usually assigned to it.

name: The Yavana school of horā

scholarly.text: Yavaneśvara's prose rendering 149/150 CE and Sphujidhvaja's verse version 269/270 CE (Pingree's reading; the dates are debated)

distinctive_positions: Horoscopy by signs, houses (kendra, paṇaphara, āpoklima), decans and planetary rulers.
Its views are quoted and sometimes rejected by Varāhamihira (BJ 7.1, 11.1, 12.1).
summary: The 'Yavanas' are the teachers of horā whom Varāhamihira cites and honours: 'the Yavanas are mlecchas, yet this science is well established among them, and they are honoured like seers' (BS 2.14). Their texts (the Yavanajātaka of Sphujidhvaja, Mīnarāja's Vṛddhayavanajātaka) were absorbed into mainstream horā.

name: Yogācāra
regions: Gandhāra and Ayodhyā (tradition's account of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu)

tradition.text: Taught by Maitreya to Asaṅga in the Tuṣita heaven; propagated by Asaṅga and his half-brother Vasubandhu

scholarly.text: Yogācārabhūmi material from c. 3rd–4th c. CE; Asaṅga and Vasubandhu c. 4th–5th c. CE; Indian Yogācāra active to the 12th c.

transmissions_received.what: the abhidharma framework of dharmas, mental factors and the path (the Abhidharmasamuccaya re-works it)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account; textual parallels

transmissions_received.what: seeds (bīja) and the series (santāna); momentariness; the image-bearing cognition
transmissions_received.evidence: Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya and Karmasiddhi

transmissions_received.what: the bodhisattva path, the perfections, emptiness of the Prajñāpāramitā read through the three natures
transmissions_received.evidence: Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7; Bodhisattvabhūmi tattvārtha chapter

transmissions_given.what: the Cheng weishi lun system via Xuanzang and Kuiji
mind-only as a stage on the way to emptiness (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla)
the ālaya / tathāgatagarbha relation (Laṅkāvatāra; Ratnagotravibhāga as a Maitreya text)
the Laṅkāvatāra and mind-only teaching (the 'Laṅkā masters')
the three natures read as other-emptiness (shentong)
the cognition-only critique of external objects, used and transformed by Utpaladeva

distinctive_positions: The three realms are cognition-only (vijñaptimātra): what appears as an external object is cognition appearing as an object (Viṃśatikā 1; Triṃśikā 17).
Eight kinds of consciousness: six operative consciousnesses, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas) and the store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) holding all seeds (Triṃśikā 2–16; Mahāyānasaṃgraha ch. 1).

Three natures (trisvabhāva): the imagined, the dependent and the perfected; and the three naturelessnesses by which the Prajñāpāramitā's 'all dharmas are without own-being' is to be understood (Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 6–7; Triṃśikā 20–25).
Unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) exists; the duality of grasped and grasper does not; emptiness exists in it (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.2).
Liberation is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the store-consciousness turning into mirror-like wisdom and the other consciousnesses into the other three wisdoms.
Beings belong to different spiritual lineages (gotra), some with no lineage for liberation (Bodhisattvabhūmi; Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ch. 3) — a thesis later Mahāyāna authors contested.
The yogin's path of calm and insight is mapped in detail: nine stages of settling the mind, seven attentions, four kinds of meditation object (Śrāvakabhūmi).
summary: The 'practice of yoga' school of Indian Mahāyāna, founded (in its own account) on the revelation of the bodhisattva Maitreya to Asaṅga and systematized by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. It teaches that the world as experienced is the unfolding of cognition from the seeds in the store-consciousness, analyses experience through the three natures, and maps the path from calm and insight to the transformation of the basis and buddhahood with its four wisdoms and three bodies.

name: Yogācāra-Madhyamaka
alt_names: Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka (Tibetan doxography: rnal 'byor spyod pa'i dbu ma rang rgyud pa)
regions: Tibet (Samye; the first ordinations under Śāntarakṣita)

tradition.text: Śāntarakṣita was invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen and founded Samye with Padmasambhava; Kamalaśīla defended the gradual path at Samye

scholarly.text: 8th c. CE (Śāntarakṣita c. 725–788; Kamalaśīla c. 740–795) to the 11th c.

transmissions_received.what: mind-only (cittamātra) as the account of conventional reality
Dharmakīrti's epistemology and reflexive awareness
transmissions_received.evidence: Tattvasaṅgraha; MAL 16–17

transmissions_given.what: Śāntarakṣita's and Kamalaśīla's teachings at Samye; later commented on by Mipham (Madhyamakālaṃkāra commentary)
the Bhāvanākrama's gradual path of calm and insight

distinctive_positions: Nothing that is held to be real by ourselves or others is truly one or truly many; therefore it lacks own-nature, like a reflection (MAL 1).

Conventionally all appearances are mind only; ultimately even mind is without own-nature — relying on mind-only one understands the absence of external things, relying on Madhyamaka one understands that even that mind lacks self (MAL 92–93).
Consciousness is by nature self-illuminating (svasaṃvedana) at the conventional level (MAL 16–17).
Riding the two chariots of Yogācāra and Madhyamaka and holding the reins of reasoning, one is a true Mahāyānist (MAL 93, the tradition's summary).
Meditation must be preceded by correct analysis (bhūtapratyavekṣā); mere non-thought is not non-conceptual wisdom (Bhāvanākrama III).
summary: The 8th-century synthesis in which Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla combined Madhyamaka's emptiness (shown chiefly by the 'neither one nor many' argument), Yogācāra's mind-only as the description of conventional reality, and Dharmakīrti's epistemology; their encyclopaedic Tattvasaṅgraha and Pañjikā examine and reject the positions of every Indian school. Kamalaśīla's Bhāvanākramas set out the gradual path of compassion, bodhicitta, calm and insight. Tibetan doxography classifies the line as Yogācāra-Svātantrika, sub-divided into true-aspectarian and false-aspectarian branches.
notes: Parent set to lin:svatantrika following the Tibetan doxographical classification that the registry names follow; the Indian authors did not call themselves Svātantrika.

name: Yoginī Kaula (Yoginīkaula) of Matsyendra
alt_names: Siddha Kaula (as a stage in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya's account)
Matsyodara (the Kali-age form of the Kaula)

tradition.text: the Kaula descended in each age: as Jñānanirṇiti, Mahat, Siddhāmṛta and, in the Kali age, as Matsyodara 'from the fish's belly' (KJN 16.47–48)

scholarly.text: the oldest Kaulajñānanirṇaya manuscript (Nepal) was assigned by its editor to c. the 11th c.; the teaching is usually placed c. 9th–11th c.

transmissions_given.what: Matsyendra's Kaula teaching and his place at the head of the Nāth lineage
one of the Kaula currents named in later Kaula lists

distinctive_positions: The true liṅga is the body-liṅga, worshipped with eight inner flowers (non-harming, sense-restraint, compassion, feeling, patience, conquest of anger, meditation, knowledge) (KJN 3.24–29).
One whose tendency (vāsanā) rests in the body belongs to the Kula; one whose tendency is outward is a bound 'animal' (paśu) (KJN 3.31).
Śiva is not without Śakti nor Śakti without Śiva (KJN 17.8); the self is guru, siddha, disciple and Śiva (KJN 11.26).
Nectar-meditations conquer death and old age; eleven centres of the body grant powers (KJN 5).
The teaching is given only to a tested, devoted disciple, ear to ear (KJN 5.35; 6.9; 17.10–11).
The Kaula path is of two kinds, made (kṛtaka) and innate (sahaja); the aroused kuṇḍalī is 'made', the innate abides in samarasa (Akulavīra B.43).
Kaula rites with meat, wine, fish, sexual union and bodily substances are taught (summary only; restricted) (KJN 8; 11; 18).
summary: The Yoginīkaula is the Kaula current that the Kaulajñānanirṇaya says Macchaghnapāda (Matsyendra) brought down from Candradvīpa and that was 'in every house of the yoginīs' in Kāmarūpa (KJN 22.10). Its texts, edited by P. C. Bagchi, teach the body-liṅga, the centres and nectar of the body, the conquest of death, the Akula beyond all distinctions and the secrecy of the Kaula; the Nāth tradition places Matsyendra at its head.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U21 (Matsyendra's own Kaula school); U24 owns lin:kaula.

name: Yunmen house

tradition.text: founded by Yunmen Wenyan (864–949)

scholarly.text: 10th c.; flourishing in the Northern Song; absorbed by the Linji house in the Southern Song

distinctive_positions: One-word barriers (yizi guan 一字關) and terse replies.
Yunmen's three phrases as systematised by Deshan Yuanmi: containing heaven and earth, cutting off the myriad streams, following the waves.
'Every day is a good day' (Biyan lu case 6).
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, from Yunmen Wenyan (864–949) in Xuefeng's line; famed for single-word responses, it produced Xuedou Chongxian, whose verses on a hundred cases became the Blue Cliff Record.

name: Yūzū Nenbutsu-shū (the interfusing nenbutsu of Ryōnin)

tradition.text: 1117, when Amida revealed the interfusing nenbutsu to Ryōnin in samādhi

scholarly.text: early 12th c.; revived by Hōmyō in the 14th c. and recognised as a school in the Edo period

transmissions_received.what: Ryōnin's Tendai training and shōmyō chant (Ōhara)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: interfusion of one and all (as understood by the school)
transmissions_received.evidence: the revelation verse

distinctive_positions: One person is all people, all people are one person; one practice is all practices, all practices are one practice: each person's nenbutsu interfuses with everyone's, so the merit of all is shared (the revelation verse, as transmitted).
Members inscribe their names in a register (myōchō) and pledge a daily number of recitations.
summary: The school of 'interfusing nenbutsu' traced to the Tendai chant master Ryōnin (1073–1132), to whom Amida is said to have revealed that one person's nenbutsu and all others' pervade one another; Ryōnin enrolled people of every class in a nenbutsu register. Revived in the 14th c. by Hōmyō; head temple Dainenbutsu-ji in Osaka.

name: Zen (Japanese Chan)
regions: Japan (Kamakura, Kyoto, Echizen, Noto, Suruga, Uji)

tradition.text: Rinzai from Eisai's return in 1191; Sōtō from Dōgen's return in 1227; Ōbaku from Ingen's arrival in 1654

scholarly.text: earlier contacts (Dōshō 7th c., Yixuan/Gikū 9th c., Kakua 12th c.); Kamakura foundations 12th–13th c.; Five Mountains system 14th c.; Tokugawa reforms 17th–18th c.; living

transmissions_received.what: Huanglong- and Yangqi-branch Linji lineages (Eisai; Enni; émigré Chinese masters)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition records

transmissions_received.what: Caodong lineage from Tiantong Rujing to Dōgen
transmissions_received.evidence: Dōgen's Shisho, Hōkyōki

distinctive_positions: Zazen as the heart of practice, understood by Sōtō as just sitting (shikantaza) in which practice and realization are one, and by Rinzai as the field of kōan introspection leading to kenshō.
Transmission certified face to face (menju) with documents of succession (shisho, inka).
Monastic rule adapted from the Chinese qinggui; work, ritual and daily conduct as practice.
summary: Japanese Chan: the Rinzai, Sōtō and Ōbaku lineages established from the late 12th to the 17th century, teaching seated meditation (zazen), kōan introspection or just sitting, and monastic life as the direct realization of buddha-nature.

name: Zhang Zhung Nyengyü (the Oral Transmission of Zhang Zhung)
alt_names: the Aural Transmission of Zhang Zhung

tradition.text: an unbroken oral lineage never hidden as treasure; Tapihritsa taught Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo in the 8th c.

scholarly.text: written down by the 11th-13th c.

distinctive_positions: Bön Dzogchen held to have been transmitted orally without interruption (not a treasure); twenty-four masters of the lineage are said to have attained the rainbow body.
notes: Optional (Bön).
summary: The principal Dzogchen lineage of Bön, whose teaching passed from the Nine Buddhas of the mind transmission to Tapihritsa and Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo and was set down in four cycles (outer, inner, secret, innermost) plus the experiential transmission.
